question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's media library in Cloud Storage contains millions of audio and video files. Access patterns vary widely: recently published episodes are streamed constantly, while older podcasts and documentaries are rarely retrieved but occasionally see unpredictable spikes when a topic becomes newsworthy. Altostrat wants to reduce storage cost without incurring surprise retrieval fees and without building custom tooling to track access patterns. What should you do?
options: Create an Object Lifecycle Management rule that moves every object older than 30 days to Coldline storage.
Keep all content in Standard storage and write a Cloud Run function that moves objects to Archive storage based on access logs analyzed in BigQuery.
Enable Autoclass on the bucket so objects transition automatically between storage classes based on their actual access patterns.
Create one bucket per storage class and have the content team move files manually when content is retired.
explanation: The deciding factor is unpredictable access combined with the case-study requirement to optimize storage cost while keeping content highly available. Autoclass automatically moves objects to colder classes when they are not accessed and moves them back to Standard on access, and Autoclass buckets do not charge early-deletion or retrieval fees, so newsworthy spikes on old content do not generate surprise bills. Option A is wrong because a fixed age-based rule ignores access patterns and Coldline retrieval and early-deletion fees would apply when old content spikes. Option B rebuilds what Autoclass already provides and adds operational overhead. Option D is manual, error-prone, and does not scale to millions of objects. This is a cost-optimization pillar decision that also preserves availability.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Storage Autoclass): The deciding factor is unpredictable access combined with the case-study requirement to optimize storage cost while keeping content highly available.

whyWrong.0: Option A is wrong because a fixed age-based rule ignores access patterns and Coldline retrieval and early-deletion fees would apply when old content spikes.
whyWrong.1: Option B rebuilds what Autoclass already provides and adds operational overhead.
whyWrong.3: Option D is manual, error-prone, and does not scale to millions of objects.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. After a documentary is published, its raw high-bitrate master files are kept only for legal and future remastering purposes. Masters are practically never accessed in the first several years but must be retained for at least 10 years, and the compliance team requires that nobody, including project owners, can delete or overwrite them during that period. The finished transcoded renditions must remain instantly available to the GKE delivery platform. You want to minimize cost. What should you do?
options: Store masters in a dedicated bucket whose default storage class is Archive, configure a 10-year bucket retention policy and lock it; keep renditions in a separate Standard storage bucket.
Enable Autoclass on a single bucket holding both masters and renditions, and rely on Autoclass to prevent early deletion of the master files.
Store masters in Coldline with a lifecycle rule that deletes them after 10 years, and store renditions in Nearline to reduce cost further.
Store masters in Standard storage with a locked retention policy and enable Object Versioning so overwrites keep the previous copy.
explanation: Archive is the lowest-cost class for data accessed less than once a year, and a locked bucket retention policy provides WORM-style immutability that even project owners cannot remove, satisfying the compliance requirement. Separating masters from renditions lets each set use the right class. Option B is wrong because Autoclass optimizes class transitions but provides no deletion protection. Option C has no immutability control, and Nearline renditions would incur retrieval fees and a 30-day minimum on frequently streamed content. Option D meets the immutability requirement but stores rarely accessed petabytes in the most expensive class, contradicting the cost-management priority in the executive statement.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Storage retention and lifecycle): Archive is the lowest-cost class for data accessed less than once a year, and a locked bucket retention policy provides WORM-style immutability that even project owners cannot remove, satisfying the compliance requirement.

whyWrong.1: Option B is wrong because Autoclass optimizes class transitions but provides no deletion protection.
whyWrong.2: Option C has no immutability control, and Nearline renditions would incur retrieval fees and a 30-day minimum on frequently streamed content.
whyWrong.3: Option D meets the immutability requirement but stores rarely accessed petabytes in the most expensive class, contradicting the cost-management priority in the executive statement.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's on-premises ingestion systems push about 40 TB of new raw footage per day into Cloud Storage and will continue to do so until the ingestion workflow is migrated. Transfers currently traverse the public internet with inconsistent throughput. Altostrat needs secure, high-performance hybrid connectivity backed by a 99.99% availability SLA, and traffic to Google APIs must not traverse the public internet. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Deploy one HA VPN gateway with two tunnels to a single Cloud Router and route all Google API traffic through the tunnels.
Provision a single 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect connection in one edge availability domain and enable Private Google Access on the VPC subnets.
Use Partner Interconnect with a single 1 Gbps VLAN attachment and configure Cloud NAT so on-premises hosts can reach Cloud Storage.

Provision Dedicated Interconnect with four VLAN attachments across two metropolitan areas and both edge availability domains, connected to Cloud Routers in two regions, and advertise the private.googleapis.com range over BGP so ingestion traffic reaches Cloud Storage privately.
explanation: 40 TB per day is roughly 3.7 Gbps sustained, and the case study demands secure, high-performance connectivity with a 99.99% SLA. Only the 99.99% Dedicated Interconnect topology (four connections in two metros, two edge availability domains, Cloud Routers in two regions) meets that SLA, and advertising the private.googleapis.com range lets on-premises hosts reach Cloud Storage without the public internet. Option A cannot sustain this throughput reliably because HA VPN tunnels are capped around 3 Gbps each and still ride the internet. Option B provides only a 99.9% topology and a single point of failure. Option C is undersized at 1 Gbps, and Cloud NAT does not provide on-premises access to Google APIs. This is a reliability and performance-optimization decision.
hint: Core Rule (Dedicated Interconnect): 40 TB per day is roughly 3.7 Gbps sustained, and the case study demands secure, high-performance connectivity with a 99.99% SLA.

whyWrong.0: Option A cannot sustain this throughput reliably because HA VPN tunnels are capped around 3 Gbps each and still ride the internet.
whyWrong.1: Option B provides only a 99.
whyWrong.2: Option C is undersized at 1 Gbps, and Cloud NAT does not provide on-premises access to Google APIs.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat must provide scalable Kubernetes environments both on-premises (for the ingestion and archival workflows that will remain in the data center for another 18 months) and in Google Cloud. The platform team wants a single view of all clusters, consistent policy enforcement, and the same GitOps deployment workflow in both locations with the least operational overhead. What should you do?
options: Install upstream Kubernetes on on-premises VMs with kubeadm and replicate the GKE cluster configuration manually with shell scripts.

Deploy Google Distributed Cloud (GKE Enterprise) on the on-premises hardware, register the on-premises and GKE clusters into one fleet, and use Config Sync and Policy Controller to apply configuration and guardrails from a Git repository.
Migrate all on-premises workloads immediately to GKE Autopilot in Google Cloud and decommission the data center ahead of schedule.
Run Rancher-managed Kubernetes on-premises and self-managed Kubernetes on Compute Engine VMs, connected over Cloud VPN.
explanation: The technical requirement is performant Kubernetes on-premises and in the cloud with simplified management. GKE Enterprise fleets give a single management plane across Google Distributed Cloud and GKE clusters, and Config Sync plus Policy Controller enforce the same GitOps configuration and policies everywhere, which directly supports 'accelerate and enhance the reliability of operational workflows across all environments'. Option A creates two different, hand-maintained platforms. Option C ignores that the ingestion and archival systems are only slated for future migration and cannot move immediately. Option D introduces two unmanaged control planes and loses the centralized management the case study requires. This is an operational-excellence decision.
hint: Core Rule (GKE Enterprise and fleets): The technical requirement is performant Kubernetes on-premises and in the cloud with simplified management.

whyWrong.0: Option A creates two different, hand-maintained platforms.
whyWrong.2: Option C ignores that the ingestion and archival systems are only slated for future migration and cannot move immediately.
whyWrong.3: Option D introduces two unmanaged control planes and loses the centralized management the case study requires.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat wants to modernize CI/CD for its containerized GKE workloads using a centralized, managed platform. On every commit the pipeline must build container images from source, store them in a managed registry that scans for vulnerabilities, and promote releases through development, staging, and production GKE clusters with approval gates and one-click rollbacks. The team wants to run as little self-managed infrastructure as possible. Which three Google Cloud services should you use? (Choose three.)
options: Cloud Build
Jenkins on a Compute Engine managed instance group
Artifact Registry
Container Registry
Cloud Deploy
Cloud Deployment Manager
explanation: Cloud Build provides serverless, trigger-based image builds; Artifact Registry is the recommended managed registry with built-in vulnerability scanning through Artifact Analysis; and Cloud Deploy provides managed delivery pipelines that promote releases across GKE targets with approvals and rollbacks. Together they meet the case study's 'centralized management platform' requirement without self-managed servers. Jenkins on Compute Engine is self-managed infrastructure. Container Registry is deprecated in favor of Artifact Registry. Cloud Deployment Manager is a deprecated infrastructure-provisioning tool, not a release-promotion tool. This aligns with the operational-excellence pillar's automation guidance.
hint: Core Rule (CI/CD tooling): Cloud Build provides serverless, trigger-based image builds; Artifact Registry is the recommended managed registry with built-in vulnerability scanning through Artifact Analysis; and Cloud Deploy provides managed delivery pipelines that promote releases across GKE targets with approvals and rollbacks.

whyWrong.1: Option B ("Jenkins on a Compute Engine managed instance group") is incorrect because it does not meet the scenario's core requirement; Option A (Cloud Build), Option C (Artifact Registry), Option E (Cloud Deploy) is the Google Cloud recommended pattern here.
whyWrong.3: Option D ("Container Registry") is incorrect because it does not meet the scenario's core requirement; Option A (Cloud Build), Option C (Artifact Registry), Option E (Cloud Deploy) is the Google Cloud recommended pattern here.
whyWrong.5: Option F ("Cloud Deployment Manager") is incorrect because it does not meet the scenario's core requirement; Option A (Cloud Build), Option C (Artifact Registry), Option E (Cloud Deploy) is the Google Cloud recommended pattern here.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat authenticates users through Google Identity and several third-party identity providers. Content editors at a recently acquired studio sign in through the studio's own Okta tenant. Altostrat wants these editors to use the Google Cloud console and access Cloud Storage buckets with their existing corporate credentials. Security policy prohibits creating duplicate user accounts in Cloud Identity, and access must be revoked automatically when the studio deactivates an employee. What should you do?
options: Provision a Cloud Identity account for each editor with Google Cloud Directory Sync and enable SAML single sign-on to Okta.
Create a Workforce Identity Federation pool with the studio's Okta tenant as the provider and grant IAM roles to principal sets from that pool.
Create a service account per editor, distribute JSON keys, and rotate the keys every 90 days.
Configure Workload Identity Federation with Okta as an OIDC provider and have editors impersonate a shared service account.
explanation: Workforce Identity Federation lets human users from an external IdP access Google Cloud (console and APIs) without provisioning accounts in Cloud Identity; when Okta disables the user, they can no longer obtain federated credentials, so revocation is automatic. Option A synchronizes duplicate accounts, which the policy prohibits. Option C uses long-lived service-account keys, an anti-pattern that provides no per-user auditability or automatic revocation. Option D is wrong because Workload Identity Federation is designed for non-human workloads, not for interactive console access by employees. This is a security pillar decision favoring federated, keyless identity.
hint: Core Rule: Workforce Identity Federation lets human users from an external IdP access Google Cloud (console and APIs) without provisioning accounts in Cloud Identity; when Okta disables the user, they can no longer obtain federated credentials, so revocation is automatic.

whyWrong.0: Option A synchronizes duplicate accounts, which the policy prohibits.
whyWrong.2: Option C uses long-lived service-account keys, an anti-pattern that provides no per-user auditability or automatic revocation.
whyWrong.3: Option D is wrong because Workload Identity Federation is designed for non-human workloads, not for interactive console access by employees.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's new conversational self-service portal must let millions of consumers sign in with email and password, Google, Apple, and Facebook accounts. The team wants multi-factor authentication, brute-force protection, and drop-in client SDKs for web and mobile, and it does not want to operate its own identity server. What should you do?
options: Create a Cloud Identity account for each consumer and use Google Workspace single sign-on.
Configure Workforce Identity Federation with Facebook and Apple as workforce identity providers.
Build a custom authentication service on GKE that stores salted password hashes in Cloud SQL.
Use Identity Platform with the required identity providers enabled and integrate its client SDKs into the portal.
explanation: Identity Platform is Google Cloud's customer identity and access management (CIAM) service: it supports email/password and social providers, MFA, abuse protection, and client SDKs, scaling to millions of end users with no servers to manage. Option A is wrong because Cloud Identity is for workforce accounts and is not designed or priced for consumer sign-in. Option B is wrong because Workforce Identity Federation targets employees and partners accessing Google Cloud resources, not application end users. Option C adds significant security risk and operational overhead compared with a managed service, conflicting with the case study's simplification goal.
hint: Core Rule: Identity Platform is Google Cloud's customer identity and access management (CIAM) service: it supports email/password and social providers, MFA, abuse protection, and client SDKs, scaling to millions of end users with no servers to manage.

whyWrong.0: Option A is wrong because Cloud Identity is for workforce accounts and is not designed or priced for consumer sign-in.
whyWrong.1: Option B is wrong because Workforce Identity Federation targets employees and partners accessing Google Cloud resources, not application end users.
whyWrong.2: Option C adds significant security risk and operational overhead compared with a managed service, conflicting with the case study's simplification goal.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's SRE team runs self-managed Prometheus servers inside each GKE cluster. Retention is limited to 15 days, the servers run out of memory during traffic spikes, and metrics from different clusters cannot be queried together. The team wants to keep its existing PromQL dashboards and alerting rules while eliminating this operational burden. What should you do?
options: Enable Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus with managed collection on the GKE clusters, and query all clusters with PromQL through Cloud Monitoring.
Increase the memory limits of the Prometheus pods and deploy Thanos with a Cloud Storage bucket for long-term retention.
Replace Prometheus with the Ops Agent and rewrite every dashboard and alert using Monitoring Query Language.
Export Prometheus metrics to BigQuery every minute and rebuild the dashboards in Looker Studio.
explanation: Managed Service for Prometheus is a fully managed, PromQL-compatible backend with 24 months of retention and a global query view across clusters, so existing dashboards and rules keep working while the memory and retention problems disappear. Option B keeps the team operating Prometheus and Thanos, which is the burden they want to remove. Option C forces a rewrite of all PromQL assets and the Ops Agent is not the tool for GKE pod metrics. Option D turns a monitoring system into a batch analytics pipeline that cannot drive real-time alerting. This reflects the operational-excellence pillar's guidance to prefer managed observability.
hint: Core Rule: Managed Service for Prometheus is a fully managed, PromQL-compatible backend with 24 months of retention and a global query view across clusters, so existing dashboards and rules keep working while the memory and retention problems disappear.

whyWrong.1: Option B keeps the team operating Prometheus and Thanos, which is the burden they want to remove.
whyWrong.2: Option C forces a rewrite of all PromQL assets and the Ops Agent is not the tool for GKE pod metrics.
whyWrong.3: Option D turns a monitoring system into a batch analytics pipeline that cannot drive real-time alerting.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat currently delivers all alerts by email. During a weekend outage of the recommendation service, the alert email went unread for four hours and the availability objective was breached. Altostrat wants critical alerts to reach the on-call engineer immediately with escalation if unacknowledged, while low-severity alerts continue to go to the team mailbox. It does not want to build a custom notification service. What should you do?
options: Send every alerting policy to a Pub/Sub topic and write a Cloud Run function that emails the on-call engineer directly.
Lower the alert thresholds so that more emails are generated during incidents.

Assign severity levels to alerting policies and configure notification channels so critical policies route to an on-call tool such as PagerDuty (or SMS/Google Chat with escalation) while informational policies keep using the email channel.
Replace Cloud Monitoring alerting with Prometheus Alertmanager and send all alerts to a Slack channel.
explanation: Cloud Monitoring supports multiple notification channel types and severity labels on alerting policies, so critical alerts can page an on-call engineer through an integrated incident-management tool with escalation, while informational alerts remain on email. This directly addresses the case study's weakness of email-only alerting and improves reliability. Option A is the custom notification service the team wants to avoid and still ends in email. Option B increases noise rather than reaching the right person. Option D swaps one channel for another without escalation and discards the existing Cloud Monitoring integration. This is an operational-excellence decision about alerting strategy.
hint: Core Rule (Alerting strategy): Cloud Monitoring supports multiple notification channel types and severity labels on alerting policies, so critical alerts can page an on-call engineer through an integrated incident-management tool with escalation, while informational alerts remain on email.

whyWrong.0: Option A is the custom notification service the team wants to avoid and still ends in email.
whyWrong.1: Option B increases noise rather than reaching the right person.
whyWrong.3: Option D swaps one channel for another without escalation and discards the existing Cloud Monitoring integration.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat wants to offer 24/7 natural-language support inside its apps. The assistant must answer questions using Altostrat's help-center articles and subscription policies, look up a signed-in user's subscription status through an existing REST API, and hand off to a human agent when it cannot help. The team has no machine learning engineers and wants a managed solution. What should you do?
options: Fine-tune an open model from Model Garden on historical support transcripts and serve it on a GKE cluster with GPUs.
Build the assistant with Conversational Agents in Vertex AI Agent Builder, ground it in a data store created from the help-center content, and add an OpenAPI tool that calls the subscription API.
Use the Natural Language API to classify each question and return canned responses from a Firestore lookup table.
Call the Gemini API directly from the mobile app, pasting the full help-center text into every prompt.
explanation: Vertex AI Agent Builder's Conversational Agents provide a managed, generative assistant that can be grounded in enterprise content through data stores, call external systems through tools, and escalate to live agents, which matches the case-study requirements for advanced chatbots with personalized assistance and no ML staff. Option A requires ML expertise and GPU cluster operations, contradicting the constraint. Option C only classifies intent and cannot generate grounded answers or call APIs conversationally. Option D exposes API credentials in the client, sends huge prompts on every request (cost), and provides no grounding, tooling, or handoff mechanism.
hint: Core Rule: Vertex AI Agent Builder's Conversational Agents provide a managed, generative assistant that can be grounded in enterprise content through data stores, call external systems through tools, and escalate to live agents, which matches the case-study requirements for advanced chatbots with personalized assistance and no ML staff.

whyWrong.0: Option A requires ML expertise and GPU cluster operations, contradicting the constraint.
whyWrong.2: Option C only classifies intent and cannot generate grounded answers or call APIs conversationally.
whyWrong.3: Option D exposes API credentials in the client, sends huge prompts on every request (cost), and provides no grounding, tooling, or handoff mechanism.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat wants to automatically generate a concise text summary every time a new podcast episode or video is uploaded to its Cloud Storage media bucket. Summaries must reflect both the spoken and the visual content of videos. The team wants an event-driven design with minimal custom code and no self-hosted models. What should you do?
options: Train a custom sequence-to-sequence model on Vertex AI using past editorial summaries and run batch predictions every night.
Use Video Intelligence API label detection and concatenate the top labels into a summary paragraph.
Deploy an open-source summarization model on GKE with GPUs and poll the bucket every minute for new files.

Use an Eventarc trigger on object finalization to invoke a Cloud Run function that calls a Gemini multimodal model on Vertex AI with the file's Cloud Storage URI and stores the returned summary in BigQuery.
explanation: Gemini models on Vertex AI natively accept audio and video input referenced by Cloud Storage URI and can produce summaries in a single call, and Eventarc plus Cloud Run functions is the event-driven pattern Altostrat already uses for metadata extraction. Option A requires training data, ML expertise, and delays results to a nightly batch. Option B produces a list of labels, not a coherent summary of spoken content. Option C requires operating GPU infrastructure and polling, which the constraints exclude. This meets the 'automated summarization for diverse media' requirement with the least operational overhead.
hint: Core Rule (Gemini multimodal summarization): Gemini models on Vertex AI natively accept audio and video input referenced by Cloud Storage URI and can produce summaries in a single call, and Eventarc plus Cloud Run functions is the event-driven pattern Altostrat already uses for metadata extraction.

whyWrong.0: Option A requires training data, ML expertise, and delays results to a nightly batch.
whyWrong.1: Option B produces a list of labels, not a coherent summary of spoken content.
whyWrong.2: Option C requires operating GPU infrastructure and polling, which the constraints exclude.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's metadata extraction pipeline must identify objects, scenes, shot changes, and on-screen text in videos, and must produce time-stamped transcripts of speech in more than 50 languages. The team wants to use pre-trained APIs and avoid training or hosting any models. Which two services should you use? (Choose two.)
options: Vision API
Video Intelligence API
Natural Language API
Speech-to-Text with the Chirp model
A custom AutoML Video Classification model
Document AI
explanation: The Video Intelligence API is the pre-trained service for video: label detection, shot change detection, object tracking, and text (OCR) detection with timestamps. Speech-to-Text with the Chirp model provides accurate, time-stamped transcription in over 100 languages. Together they satisfy the 'extract rich metadata using NLP and computer vision' requirement without any model training. Vision API works on still images, so you would have to extract frames yourself and lose temporal information. Natural Language API analyzes text but does not process audio or video. AutoML Video requires training a custom model, which the constraint excludes. Document AI is for scanned documents and forms.
hint: Core Rule (Pre-trained AI APIs): The Video Intelligence API is the pre-trained service for video: label detection, shot change detection, object tracking, and text (OCR) detection with timestamps.

whyWrong.0: Option A ("Vision API") is incorrect because it does not meet the scenario's core requirement; Option B (Video Intelligence API), Option D (Speech-to-Text with the Chirp model) is the Google Cloud recommended pattern here.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's new viewer chatbot accepts free-text questions and comments, and its responses are generated by Gemini on Vertex AI. The Trust & Safety team requires that prompts attempting jailbreaks or prompt injection are blocked, that personal data typed by users is detected and de-identified before it reaches the model or logs, and that hateful or sexually explicit model responses are filtered before display. Policies must be defined centrally and apply to every application that calls the model. What should you do?
options: Create Model Armor templates that enable prompt-injection and jailbreak detection, Sensitive Data Protection inspection, and responsible-AI filters, and enforce them on all prompts and responses through the Vertex AI integration (or by calling Model Armor from the application).
Add a system prompt instructing Gemini to refuse harmful requests and never to repeat personal data it receives.
Configure Cloud Armor WAF rules on the external Application Load Balancer to block malicious text patterns in chatbot request bodies.
Run Natural Language API sentiment analysis on every prompt and reject prompts whose sentiment score is negative.
explanation: Model Armor is the managed service that screens LLM prompts and responses for prompt injection, jailbreaks, sensitive data (via Sensitive Data Protection), malicious URLs, and responsible-AI categories, using centrally managed templates that can be enforced across applications, which maps directly to 'design AI-powered detection of harmful content' and the securing-AI exam objective. Option B relies on the model following instructions, which is exactly what jailbreaks defeat, and it provides no PII redaction or central policy. Option C is a web-application firewall for HTTP attacks, not semantic prompt analysis. Option D measures sentiment, not safety, and would reject legitimate negative feedback while missing polite prompt-injection attempts.
hint: Core Rule: Model Armor is the managed service that screens LLM prompts and responses for prompt injection, jailbreaks, sensitive data (via Sensitive Data Protection), malicious URLs, and responsible-AI categories, using centrally managed templates that can be enforced across applications, which maps directly to 'design AI-powered detection of harmful content' and the securing-AI exam objective.

whyWrong.1: Option B relies on the model following instructions, which is exactly what jailbreaks defeat, and it provides no PII redaction or central policy.
whyWrong.2: Option C is a web-application firewall for HTTP attacks, not semantic prompt analysis.
whyWrong.3: Option D measures sentiment, not safety, and would reject legitimate negative feedback while missing polite prompt-injection attempts.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's internal audit team must be able to explain why the company's custom TensorFlow recommendation model promoted a specific piece of content to a specific user, prove which model version was serving at that moment, detect when live traffic drifts from the training distribution, and show who deployed or changed the model. What should you do?
options: Log every prediction request and response to Cloud Logging and keep each TensorFlow SavedModel in a Cloud Storage bucket with versioned object names.
Replace the custom model with Gemini and rely on its built-in safety filters to provide explanations.

Register every model version in Vertex AI Model Registry, deploy to a Vertex AI endpoint with Vertex Explainable AI feature attributions enabled, turn on Vertex AI Model Monitoring for skew and drift, and retain Cloud Audit Logs (Admin Activity and Data Access) for the project.
Store the model weights in Artifact Registry and enable Binary Authorization on the serving cluster.
explanation: The case study explicitly requires that AI systems be auditable and their decisions explainable. Vertex AI Model Registry provides versioned lineage, Vertex Explainable AI returns per-prediction feature attributions that explain individual recommendations, Model Monitoring detects training-serving skew and drift, and Cloud Audit Logs record who deployed or modified models. Option A records inputs and outputs but cannot explain a decision or detect drift. Option B changes the product and does not provide feature attributions for a recommendation ranking. Option D protects the software supply chain but says nothing about model explanations, versions in serving, or drift. This applies the security and operational-excellence pillars to responsible AI.
hint: Core Rule (Explainable and auditable AI): The case study explicitly requires that AI systems be auditable and their decisions explainable.

whyWrong.0: Option A records inputs and outputs but cannot explain a decision or detect drift.
whyWrong.1: Option B changes the product and does not provide feature attributions for a recommendation ranking.
whyWrong.3: Option D protects the software supply chain but says nothing about model explanations, versions in serving, or drift.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's content strategy analysts are proficient in SQL but not Python. They want to forecast weekly listening hours per podcast category for the next quarter and flag anomalous consumption patterns, using the playback events already stored in BigQuery. They want results with the least engineering effort. What should you do?
options: Export the events to Cloud Storage and train a custom forecasting model with TensorFlow in Vertex AI Workbench.
Create a BigQuery ML ARIMA_PLUS time-series model with CREATE MODEL, then use ML.FORECAST for the forecast and ML.DETECT_ANOMALIES for anomaly detection.
Stream the events into Bigtable and compute moving averages in a Dataflow pipeline.
Load the data into Vertex AI Feature Store and train an AutoML tabular classification model.
explanation: BigQuery ML lets SQL-proficient analysts train and use forecasting models where the data already lives; ARIMA_PLUS handles multiple time series (one per category) in a single model and exposes ML.FORECAST and ML.DETECT_ANOMALIES functions. This satisfies 'analyze media content to identify trends' with minimal effort. Option A requires Python and ML skills the analysts lack and moves data unnecessarily. Option C builds a streaming system for a batch analytics problem and does not produce forecasts. Option D uses classification rather than time-series forecasting and adds services without benefit. This is a cost-optimization and skills-fit decision.
hint: Core Rule (BigQuery ML forecasting): BigQuery ML lets SQL-proficient analysts train and use forecasting models where the data already lives; ARIMA_PLUS handles multiple time series (one per category) in a single model and exposes ML.FORECAST and ML.DETECT_ANOMALIES functions.

whyWrong.0: Option A requires Python and ML skills the analysts lack and moves data unnecessarily.
whyWrong.2: Option C builds a streaming system for a batch analytics problem and does not produce forecasts.
whyWrong.3: Option D uses classification rather than time-series forecasting and adds services without benefit.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat wants viewers to discover content by describing it in natural language, for example 'the interview where a climate scientist discussed glacier melt in the Andes', across transcripts, documents, and metadata for millions of assets stored in Cloud Storage and BigQuery. The solution must understand intent and synonyms rather than exact keywords, return generative answers with citations, and require minimal ML expertise. What should you do?
options: Build a full-text keyword index over the transcripts in Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL.
Run Elasticsearch on GKE with BM25 ranking over the transcript text.
Generate embeddings with a custom pipeline and store them in Memorystore for Redis for vector similarity lookups.
Create a Vertex AI Search app in Agent Builder with data stores connected to the Cloud Storage and BigQuery content, and enable search summaries with citations.
explanation: Vertex AI Search is a managed semantic and generative search engine that ingests unstructured content from Cloud Storage and structured data from BigQuery, understands natural-language intent, and returns grounded summaries with citations, meeting the 'LLMs and conversational AI for personalized experiences and content discovery' goal with almost no ML work. Option A and Option B are keyword systems that miss synonyms and intent and cannot generate answers. Option C requires building and operating an embedding pipeline and vector store and still lacks generative answers with citations, which violates the minimal-expertise constraint.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's video transcoding runs in Cloud Run functions triggered by uploads. Feature-length documentaries exceed the function timeout, causing failed and duplicated jobs, and the team maintains custom FFmpeg containers and encoding presets. Reliability and cost are Altostrat's top priorities, and the team wants to minimize custom code. What should you do?
options: Replace the custom transcoding logic with the Transcoder API: the upload-triggered Cloud Run function submits a transcoding job with the required output profiles, and results are written back to Cloud Storage.
Raise the Cloud Run function timeout and memory to the maximum and add retries with exponential backoff.
Move transcoding to a GKE Standard GPU node pool with a custom job queue built on Memorystore.
Run FFmpeg on a large Compute Engine instance with a cron job that scans the bucket every hour.
explanation: The Transcoder API is a fully managed service purpose-built for converting media files into streaming formats; it handles long inputs asynchronously, removes the custom FFmpeg containers, and bills per minute of output, which satisfies reliability, cost, and minimal-code constraints at the same time. Option B still leaves long files at risk of hitting limits and keeps the custom encoder. Option C solves the timeout but adds a GPU cluster and a hand-built queue to operate. Option D is a single point of failure, introduces up to an hour of latency, and wastes an always-on VM. This is a build-versus-buy disposition decision favoring the managed service.
hint: Core Rule: The Transcoder API is a fully managed service purpose-built for converting media files into streaming formats; it handles long inputs asynchronously, removes the custom FFmpeg containers, and bills per minute of output, which satisfies reliability, cost, and minimal-code constraints at the same time.

whyWrong.1: Option B still leaves long files at risk of hitting limits and keeps the custom encoder.
whyWrong.2: Option C solves the timeout but adds a GPU cluster and a hand-built queue to operate.
whyWrong.3: Option D is a single point of failure, introduces up to an hour of latency, and wastes an always-on VM.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's on-premises archival system holds 3 PB of historical broadcast footage that must be migrated to a Cloud Storage bucket within six weeks, when the data-center lease expires. The site has one 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect that also carries the daily production ingestion traffic of roughly 4 Gbps on average. Data must be encrypted in transit and at rest. What should you do?
options: Use Storage Transfer Service for on-premises data over the Interconnect and cap its bandwidth at 6 Gbps so production ingestion is not affected.
Run gsutil -m rsync in parallel from several on-premises servers over the Interconnect until the copy finishes.

Order multiple Transfer Appliances, load the archive locally, ship them to Google for ingestion into the bucket, and use the Interconnect only for the small delta produced while the appliances are in transit.
Compress the footage with an on-premises Dataflow pipeline and upload it over the public internet with Storage Transfer Service.
explanation: At the roughly 6 Gbps left over after production traffic, 3 PB would take about 46 days at perfect utilization, exceeding the six-week deadline with no margin. Transfer Appliance is the recommended option when data exceeds what the network can move in time; the appliances are encrypted, so the in-transit and at-rest requirements are met, and the Interconnect remains free for production ingestion and the final delta. Option A is the right tool for online transfer but the math shows it cannot make the deadline. Option B is slower and less robust than Storage Transfer Service and has the same bandwidth problem. Option D compresses already-compressed video for little gain, uses the slower public internet, and Dataflow does not run on-premises.
hint: Core Rule (Data transfer planning): At the roughly 6 Gbps left over after production traffic, 3 PB would take about 46 days at perfect utilization, exceeding the six-week deadline with no margin.

whyWrong.0: Option A is the right tool for online transfer but the math shows it cannot make the deadline.
whyWrong.1: Option B is slower and less robust than Storage Transfer Service and has the same bandwidth problem.
whyWrong.3: Option D compresses already-compressed video for little gain, uses the slower public internet, and Dataflow does not run on-premises.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's GKE bill has doubled in a year. Analysis shows a steady baseline of user-facing content-delivery services plus a large, spiky batch workload that generates thumbnails and previews and can tolerate interruption and retries. The reliability of the user-facing services must not decrease. Which two actions should you take to reduce cost? (Choose two.)
options: Move all node pools, including the content-delivery services, to Spot VMs.
Run the thumbnail batch workload on a Spot VM node pool (or Autopilot Spot Pods) with tolerations, checkpointing, and automatic retries.
Disable the cluster autoscaler and fix node counts at peak capacity to avoid scaling delays.
Move the user-facing services into a single zone to eliminate inter-zone traffic charges.
Purchase committed use discounts that cover the predictable baseline compute of the content-delivery services.
Increase every pod's CPU request to guarantee extra headroom.
explanation: The cost-optimization pillar recommends matching purchasing models to workload characteristics: fault-tolerant, interruptible batch jobs belong on Spot capacity (60–91% cheaper), and steady, predictable baseline usage should be covered by committed use discounts. Option A would expose latency-sensitive user-facing services to preemption, reducing reliability. Option C removes elasticity and pays for peak capacity all the time. Option D lowers availability, contradicting the reliability priority in the executive statement. Option F increases requested resources and therefore cost, the opposite of right-sizing.
hint: Core Rule (GKE cost optimization): The cost-optimization pillar recommends matching purchasing models to workload characteristics: fault-tolerant, interruptible batch jobs belong on Spot capacity (60–91% cheaper), and steady, predictable baseline usage should be covered by committed use discounts.

whyWrong.0: Option A would expose latency-sensitive user-facing services to preemption, reducing reliability.
whyWrong.2: Option C removes elasticity and pays for peak capacity all the time.
whyWrong.3: Option D lowers availability, contradicting the reliability priority in the executive statement.
whyWrong.5: Option F increases requested resources and therefore cost, the opposite of right-sizing.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's on-premises ingestion servers upload footage to Cloud Storage over the Dedicated Interconnect. The security team requires that these uploads never traverse the public internet, and the servers have no public IP addresses and no NAT path to the internet. The Google Cloud VPC uses a private-only design. How should you configure access to the Cloud Storage API?
options: Enable Private Google Access on the VPC subnets; on-premises hosts automatically inherit it through the VLAN attachment.

Configure on-premises DNS to resolve *.googleapis.com to the private.googleapis.com virtual IP range, advertise that range as a custom route from Cloud Router over the Interconnect, and add on-premises routes for it toward the VLAN attachments.
Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway in the VPC and route on-premises traffic through it to reach storage.googleapis.com.
Create a proxy VM with an external IP address in the VPC and configure the ingestion servers to use it as an HTTP forward proxy.
explanation: Private Google Access for on-premises hosts requires three things: DNS records that map Google API names to the private.googleapis.com (or restricted.googleapis.com) VIP, a custom route advertisement of that range from Cloud Router over the Interconnect, and matching routes on-premises. Traffic then reaches Cloud Storage entirely over the Interconnect. Option A is wrong because subnet-level Private Google Access applies only to VM instances in the VPC, not to on-premises hosts. Option C is wrong because Cloud NAT only serves VMs in the VPC and would send traffic to the public internet anyway. Option D introduces a public IP and a single-VM bottleneck, violating the security requirement. A Private Service Connect endpoint for Google APIs would be an equally valid alternative design.
hint: Core Rule: Private Google Access for on-premises hosts requires three things: DNS records that map Google API names to the private.googleapis.com (or restricted.googleapis.com) VIP, a custom route advertisement of that range from Cloud Router over the Interconnect, and matching routes on-premises.

whyWrong.0: Option A is wrong because subnet-level Private Google Access applies only to VM instances in the VPC, not to on-premises hosts.
whyWrong.2: Option C is wrong because Cloud NAT only serves VMs in the VPC and would send traffic to the public internet anyway.
whyWrong.3: Option D introduces a public IP and a single-VM bottleneck, violating the security requirement.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat streams audio and video from its Cloud Storage media library through the GKE platform to a global audience. Network egress from Cloud Storage now dominates the monthly bill, and viewers in Asia and South America report buffering during premieres. Reliability and cost management are the executive team's top priorities. What should you do?
options: Add more GKE nodes in the existing region and increase the pod count of the streaming service before every premiere.
Create a regional external Application Load Balancer in each continent with its own copy of the media bucket.
Serve the media library through Media CDN with the Cloud Storage bucket as origin so segments are cached at Google's edge close to viewers.
Replicate the media library into a multi-region bucket and have clients download directly from storage.googleapis.com.
explanation: Media CDN is Google's planet-scale CDN built for streaming; caching at the edge reduces both origin egress cost and latency for distant viewers, addressing both of Altostrat's top priorities. Option A scales compute, not the network path, and does nothing about egress cost or distance to viewers. Option B duplicates storage and still serves from a regional origin without an edge cache. Option D improves storage availability but every request still leaves Google's network from the bucket, so egress cost and buffering are not solved. This is a performance and cost-optimization decision.
hint: Core Rule: Media CDN is Google's planet-scale CDN built for streaming; caching at the edge reduces both origin egress cost and latency for distant viewers, addressing both of Altostrat's top priorities.

whyWrong.0: Option A scales compute, not the network path, and does nothing about egress cost or distance to viewers.
whyWrong.1: Option B duplicates storage and still serves from a regional origin without an edge cache.
whyWrong.3: Option D improves storage availability but every request still leaves Google's network from the bucket, so egress cost and buffering are not solved.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat is preparing to migrate its legacy on-premises content ingestion and archival systems to Google Cloud. Several dozen VMs, databases, and file servers are involved, dependencies between them are undocumented, and finance wants a cost estimate before committing to a migration wave plan. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do first?
options: Use Migration Center to discover the on-premises inventory, capture utilization and dependency data, and generate a total cost of ownership estimate for target Google Cloud services.
Lift-and-shift every VM to Compute Engine with Migrate to Virtual Machines and analyze dependencies afterwards.
Rewrite the ingestion pipeline as Cloud Run functions immediately and decommission the on-premises servers.
Order a Transfer Appliance and copy all archival data to Cloud Storage before assessing the applications.
explanation: Google's migration methodology starts with the assess phase; Migration Center provides agentless discovery, performance data, dependency mapping, and TCO reports that are needed to design migration waves and give finance the cost estimate. Option B migrates before understanding dependencies, risking outages and cost surprises. Option C skips assessment and commits to a rearchitecture without knowing whether it fits the workload. Option D moves data without knowing which applications depend on it or how they will access it in the cloud. The assess-plan-deploy-optimize sequence is the recommended practice.
hint: Core Rule (Migration planning): Google's migration methodology starts with the assess phase; Migration Center provides agentless discovery, performance data, dependency mapping, and TCO reports that are needed to design migration waves and give finance the cost estimate.

whyWrong.1: Option B migrates before understanding dependencies, risking outages and cost surprises.
whyWrong.2: Option C skips assessment and commits to a rearchitecture without knowing whether it fits the workload.
whyWrong.3: Option D moves data without knowing which applications depend on it or how they will access it in the cloud.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's GKE platform runs in a single region and includes a stateful metadata service that stores its data on persistent volumes. The media library lives in a single-region Cloud Storage bucket. Following a regional incident, management set a recovery objective for a regional outage of RTO 1 hour and RPO 15 minutes for both the metadata service and newly uploaded media. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Enable Backup for GKE with a scheduled backup plan for the metadata namespace and volumes, and prepare a restore plan into a standby cluster in a second region.
Take manual persistent disk snapshots once a week and store the snapshot names in a spreadsheet.
Convert the media library to a dual-region bucket with turbo replication enabled.
Add an Object Lifecycle Management rule that moves media to Nearline after 30 days.
Run a nightly gsutil cp job from a Compute Engine VM to copy new media to a bucket in another region.
Enable Object Versioning on the existing single-region bucket.
explanation: Backup for GKE captures both Kubernetes configuration and persistent volume data on a schedule and can restore into a cluster in another region, meeting the RTO/RPO for the stateful service. Dual-region buckets with turbo replication replicate newly written objects across regions with a 15-minute RPO SLA, exactly matching the media requirement. Weekly manual snapshots (Option B) give a seven-day RPO and are error-prone. Lifecycle rules (Option D) change storage class, not geographic redundancy. A nightly copy job (Option E) yields a 24-hour RPO and adds a VM to operate. Object Versioning (Option F) protects against overwrites but the data remains in a single region. This is a reliability-pillar decision.
hint: Core Rule (Disaster recovery): Backup for GKE captures both Kubernetes configuration and persistent volume data on a schedule and can restore into a cluster in another region, meeting the RTO/RPO for the stateful service.

whyWrong.1: Option B) give a seven-day RPO and are error-prone.
whyWrong.3: Option D) change storage class, not geographic redundancy.
whyWrong.4: Option E) yields a 24-hour RPO and adds a VM to operate.
whyWrong.5: Option F) protects against overwrites but the data remains in a single region.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's personalized recommendations are generated by a nightly Cloud Run function that ranks content by overall popularity, so all users see similar suggestions and new episodes take a day to appear. Altostrat wants per-user recommendations that update as users watch, take a user's real-time session into account, and improve content virality, with minimal data-science staffing. What should you do?
options: Keep the nightly function but add a per-genre popularity ranking table in BigQuery.
Use Vertex AI Search for media (recommendations) by importing the catalog and streaming user events, then call the recommendation serving API from the platform.
Train a matrix-factorization model in BigQuery ML each week and export the top-10 list per user to Memorystore.
Have the mobile app call Gemini with the user's entire viewing history and ask it to suggest content.
explanation: Vertex AI Search for media provides managed, Google-quality recommendation models (recommended-for-you, others-you-may-like, more-like-this) that learn from streamed user events in near real time and require no data-science team, which satisfies the case study's personalized-recommendation and virality goals. Option A remains non-personalized and stale. Option C is personalized but weekly, cannot react to the current session, and needs ML maintenance. Option D sends large prompts on every request (cost), lacks real-time catalog awareness, and offers no evaluation or tuning loop, so it is not a reliable recommendation architecture.
hint: Core Rule (Recommendation systems): Vertex AI Search for media provides managed, Google-quality recommendation models (recommended-for-you, others-you-may-like, more-like-this) that learn from streamed user events in near real time and require no data-science team, which satisfies the case study's personalized-recommendation and virality goals.

whyWrong.0: Option A remains non-personalized and stale.
whyWrong.2: Option C is personalized but weekly, cannot react to the current session, and needs ML maintenance.
whyWrong.3: Option D sends large prompts on every request (cost), lacks real-time catalog awareness, and offers no evaluation or tuning loop, so it is not a reliable recommendation architecture.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. As part of the CI/CD modernization, Altostrat's security team wants to guarantee that only container images built by the official Cloud Build pipeline, stored in Artifact Registry, and free of critical vulnerabilities can run on the production GKE clusters. Images pushed manually by developers must be rejected at deployment time. What should you do?
options: Enable Binary Authorization on the production clusters with a policy that requires attestations created by the Cloud Build pipeline and by a vulnerability-scanning check, and deny all other images.
Restrict the artifactregistry.reader role so that only the GKE node service account can pull images.
Add a Cloud Build step that scans images with Trivy and posts the result to a Slack channel for manual review.
Configure an organization policy that restricts which Artifact Registry repositories can be created.
explanation: Binary Authorization is the deploy-time admission control that enforces policy on GKE: images must carry signed attestations (for example, 'built by Cloud Build' and 'vulnerability scan passed' from Artifact Analysis), and anything else is blocked. This is the Google-recommended way to secure the software supply chain. Option B restricts who can read images, but a developer with push access could still deploy an image the nodes can read. Option C produces a report but has no enforcement. Option D controls repository creation, not what images are deployed. This is a security pillar control.
hint: Core Rule (Software supply chain security): Binary Authorization is the deploy-time admission control that enforces policy on GKE: images must carry signed attestations (for example, 'built by Cloud Build' and 'vulnerability scan passed' from Artifact Analysis), and anything else is blocked.

whyWrong.1: Option B restricts who can read images, but a developer with push access could still deploy an image the nodes can read.
whyWrong.2: Option C produces a report but has no enforcement.
whyWrong.3: Option D controls repository creation, not what images are deployed.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. A security review found that all of Altostrat's Cloud Run functions (transcoding, metadata extraction, recommendations) run with the default Compute Engine service account, which holds the Editor role on the project. The metadata extraction function only needs to read from the media bucket and write rows into one BigQuery dataset. You want to remediate this following the principle of least privilege. What should you do?
options: Keep the default service account but downgrade its project role from Editor to Viewer.
Create a shared 'functions' service account with the Storage Admin and BigQuery Admin roles and assign it to every function.

Create a dedicated service account for the metadata extraction function, grant it Storage Object Viewer on the media bucket and BigQuery Data Editor on the target dataset only, and repeat the pattern for each function.
Generate a JSON key for the default service account and store it in Secret Manager for the functions to load at startup.
explanation: Least privilege means a dedicated identity per workload with the narrowest roles scoped to the specific resources it uses; a per-function service account with bucket-level and dataset-level grants achieves this and is the documented recommendation for Cloud Run. Option A would break the functions (Viewer cannot write to BigQuery) and still shares one identity across all workloads. Option B is still over-privileged (Admin roles at project scope) and shared. Option D introduces a long-lived key, which is a security anti-pattern, and does nothing to reduce the excessive permissions.
hint: Core Rule (IAM least privilege): Least privilege means a dedicated identity per workload with the narrowest roles scoped to the specific resources it uses; a per-function service account with bucket-level and dataset-level grants achieves this and is the documented recommendation for Cloud Run.

whyWrong.0: Option A would break the functions (Viewer cannot write to BigQuery) and still shares one identity across all workloads.
whyWrong.1: Option B is still over-privileged (Admin roles at project scope) and shared.
whyWrong.3: Option D introduces a long-lived key, which is a security anti-pattern, and does nothing to reduce the excessive permissions.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat is adding a feature that lets community contributors upload video clips. Every clip must be screened for sexually explicit visual content before it becomes visible, and flagged segments must be identified with timestamps so moderators can review them quickly. The team wants a pre-trained service and no model training. What should you do?
options: Extract one frame per second with FFmpeg and send each frame to the Vision API SafeSearch feature.
Call the Video Intelligence API explicit content detection feature on each uploaded clip and hold clips with flagged frames for moderator review.
Train a custom image classifier on Vertex AI with labeled examples of explicit content.
Run the Natural Language API on the clip's title and description to detect inappropriate words.
explanation: Video Intelligence API explicit content detection analyzes video natively and returns per-frame likelihood annotations with time offsets, giving moderators exactly the timestamps they need without any training, which fulfils the 'detect and filter inappropriate content' requirement. Option A works but requires custom frame extraction, generates many more API calls, and loses the managed video handling. Option C requires curating a sensitive training dataset and maintaining a model. Option D inspects text metadata only and cannot detect what is visually in the clip.
hint: Core Rule: Video Intelligence API explicit content detection analyzes video natively and returns per-frame likelihood annotations with time offsets, giving moderators exactly the timestamps they need without any training, which fulfils the 'detect and filter inappropriate content' requirement.

whyWrong.0: Option A works but requires custom frame extraction, generates many more API calls, and loses the managed video handling.
whyWrong.2: Option C requires curating a sensitive training dataset and maintaining a model.
whyWrong.3: Option D inspects text metadata only and cannot detect what is visually in the clip.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's BigQuery costs have grown sharply. Most analyst queries filter the multi-terabyte playback-events table by event date and by content category, yet the table is neither partitioned nor clustered, and dashboards run the same queries repeatedly on on-demand pricing. Which two changes should you make to reduce cost while keeping the analysts' SQL workflow? (Choose two.)
options: Partition the playback-events table by event date, cluster it by content category, and require a partition filter on queries.
Export the table to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL and point the dashboards there.
Instruct analysts to use SELECT * so BigQuery can cache complete results.
Move the analytics project to a BigQuery Editions reservation with autoscaling slots (or set custom per-project query quotas) to cap and predict spend.
Store the events as CSV files in Cloud Storage and query them with external tables.
Increase the table's expiration so historical data is never deleted.
explanation: Partitioning by date and clustering by category means each query scans only the relevant slices, drastically reducing bytes billed, and requiring a partition filter prevents accidental full scans. For repetitive, predictable workloads, Editions reservations (or custom quotas) turn unpredictable on-demand charges into a controlled budget. Option B moves terabytes into an OLTP database that is not designed for analytical scans. Option C increases bytes scanned; selecting only needed columns reduces cost. Option E loses BigQuery's columnar storage and makes scans slower and more expensive. Option F affects retention, not query cost, and may increase storage cost.
hint: Core Rule (BigQuery cost optimization): Partitioning by date and clustering by category means each query scans only the relevant slices, drastically reducing bytes billed, and requiring a partition filter prevents accidental full scans.

whyWrong.1: Option B moves terabytes into an OLTP database that is not designed for analytical scans.
whyWrong.2: Option C increases bytes scanned; selecting only needed columns reduces cost.
whyWrong.4: Option E loses BigQuery's columnar storage and makes scans slower and more expensive.
whyWrong.5: Option F affects retention, not query cost, and may increase storage cost.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's executives state that reliability is a top priority, yet the engineering and product teams argue about whether the content API is 'reliable enough' to keep shipping features. The API is fronted by an external Application Load Balancer and runs on GKE. You want an objective, data-driven mechanism that balances feature velocity against reliability with minimal custom tooling. What should you do?
options: Set a target of zero errors and freeze all deployments whenever any 5xx response is observed.
Create an uptime check against the API and email the product team when it fails.
Track mean time to recovery in a spreadsheet and review it at the quarterly business review.

Define the content API as a service in Cloud Monitoring, create availability and latency SLOs based on load-balancer request metrics, and configure error-budget burn-rate alerts that gate releases when the budget is being exhausted.
explanation: SRE practice, embedded in the Well-Architected Framework's reliability and operational-excellence pillars, uses SLOs and error budgets as the shared contract between product and engineering: while budget remains, teams ship; when burn rate is high, they prioritize reliability. Cloud Monitoring's service monitoring builds SLOs directly from load-balancer or Istio metrics and provides burn-rate alerting out of the box. Option A is an unrealistic 100% target that halts all delivery. Option B measures only binary availability from a few probes and provides no budget. Option C is manual, lagging, and not actionable during the release cycle.
hint: Core Rule: SRE practice, embedded in the Well-Architected Framework's reliability and operational-excellence pillars, uses SLOs and error budgets as the shared contract between product and engineering: while budget remains, teams ship; when burn rate is high, they prioritize reliability.

whyWrong.0: Option A is an unrealistic 100% target that halts all delivery.
whyWrong.1: Option B measures only binary availability from a few probes and provides no budget.
whyWrong.2: Option C is manual, lagging, and not actionable during the release cycle.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's metadata extraction Cloud Run function is triggered by a Pub/Sub subscription. Occasionally the function processes a file slowly, the message is redelivered, and the same asset is extracted twice, producing duplicate rows in BigQuery and double API charges. A few malformed files also fail permanently and are redelivered forever, consuming capacity. You need to fix both problems following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?
options: Set the subscription's acknowledgement deadline to the maximum and disable retries on the function.

Make the function idempotent by keying its BigQuery writes on the asset's object name and generation (or using an insertId/dedup key), extend the ack deadline appropriately, and configure a dead-letter topic on the subscription with a bounded maximum delivery attempts.
Switch the trigger from Pub/Sub to a Cloud Scheduler job that lists the bucket every minute and processes new objects.
Enable exactly-once delivery on the subscription and rely on it to prevent all duplicate processing without changing the function.
explanation: Pub/Sub guarantees at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent; keying writes on a stable identifier such as object name plus generation makes duplicate deliveries harmless, while a dead-letter topic with a maximum delivery attempt count stops poison messages from being redelivered forever and preserves them for inspection. Option A merely delays redelivery and disabling retries loses legitimately failed messages. Option C replaces an event-driven design with polling that adds latency and its own duplicate-handling problems. Option D helps reduce duplicates in some cases but exactly-once delivery only applies within an ack deadline for pull subscriptions and does not address poison messages, so it is not a complete solution. This is an operational-excellence and reliability decision.
hint: Core Rule (Event-driven reliability): Pub/Sub guarantees at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent; keying writes on a stable identifier such as object name plus generation makes duplicate deliveries harmless, while a dead-letter topic with a maximum delivery attempt count stops poison messages from being redelivered forever and preserves them for inspection.

whyWrong.0: Option A merely delays redelivery and disabling retries loses legitimately failed messages.
whyWrong.2: Option C replaces an event-driven design with polling that adds latency and its own duplicate-handling problems.
whyWrong.3: Option D helps reduce duplicates in some cases but exactly-once delivery only applies within an ack deadline for pull subscriptions and does not address poison messages, so it is not a complete solution.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. The engineer is not yet fluent in Cloud Logging query syntax or in interpreting GKE events, and the team wants faster root-cause analysis without hiring more SREs. Open a P1 support case with Google Cloud Support and wait for the analysis.

Attach a debugger to the running pods with kubectl port-forward and step through the code.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat wants to generate summaries and metadata for its entire back catalog of roughly two million archived episodes, in addition to the real-time summaries generated for new uploads. Latency for the back catalog does not matter, but the finance team has capped the project budget, and the current approach of calling a Gemini Pro model synchronously per file from Cloud Run functions is projected to exceed it by a wide margin. What should you do?
options: Use Vertex AI batch prediction with a Gemini Flash-class model, submitting the catalog as a BigQuery or Cloud Storage input and writing results back to BigQuery, and keep the online path only for new uploads.
Keep the synchronous per-file calls but increase the Cloud Run function concurrency so the job finishes faster.
Provision dedicated GPUs on GKE and self-host an open model from Model Garden to avoid per-token pricing.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for Gemini Pro sized to process the whole backlog in one week.
explanation: The deciding factor is a fixed budget with no latency requirement. Batch prediction on Vertex AI is priced at a discount compared with online requests, and choosing a Flash-class model for straightforward summarization is far cheaper per token than a Pro model, together producing the largest cost reduction with no infrastructure to manage. Option B changes throughput, not price. Option C incurs continuous GPU and operations cost and requires ML operations skills the team does not have; it rarely beats managed batch pricing for a one-off backfill. Option D is designed for guaranteed capacity on latency-sensitive online workloads and would be the most expensive way to run an offline backfill. This is a cost-optimization decision.
hint: Core Rule (Generative AI cost optimization): The deciding factor is a fixed budget with no latency requirement.

whyWrong.1: Option B changes throughput, not price.
whyWrong.2: Option C incurs continuous GPU and operations cost and requires ML operations skills the team does not have; it rarely beats managed batch pricing for a one-off backfill.
whyWrong.3: Option D is designed for guaranteed capacity on latency-sensitive online workloads and would be the most expensive way to run an offline backfill.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's BigQuery warehouse contains subscriber PII and viewing histories, and the media buckets contain unreleased premium content. Following an incident in which a compromised developer credential was used to copy a BigQuery table to a bucket in an external project, the CISO requires that even a valid credential cannot move this data outside Altostrat's approved projects, while the GKE platform and Cloud Run functions in those projects continue to work. What should you do?
options: Enable Data Access audit logs for BigQuery and Cloud Storage and create an alert on export operations.
Apply customer-managed encryption keys from Cloud KMS to the datasets and buckets.
Remove the BigQuery Data Viewer role from all developers and route every query through a review process.

Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter that includes the data and platform projects with the BigQuery and Cloud Storage APIs restricted, add ingress and egress rules only for approved identities and projects, and enable Private Google Access so in-perimeter workloads keep functioning.
explanation: VPC Service Controls is the control designed to mitigate data exfiltration by a stolen credential: within the perimeter, calls to restricted APIs that would move data to a resource outside the perimeter are denied regardless of IAM permissions, while workloads inside continue to operate. Option A detects exfiltration after the fact but does not prevent it. Option B protects data at rest; a credential authorized to read the data can still decrypt and copy it. Option C harms productivity and does not stop a compromised account that still needs legitimate access. This is a defense-in-depth security pillar decision.
hint: Core Rule: VPC Service Controls is the control designed to mitigate data exfiltration by a stolen credential: within the perimeter, calls to restricted APIs that would move data to a resource outside the perimeter are denied regardless of IAM permissions, while workloads inside continue to operate.

whyWrong.0: Option A detects exfiltration after the fact but does not prevent it.
whyWrong.1: Option B protects data at rest; a credential authorized to read the data can still decrypt and copy it.
whyWrong.2: Option C harms productivity and does not stop a compromised account that still needs legitimate access.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's editorial team wants to detect trending topics within minutes of them emerging so it can promote related content while interest is high. Playback, search, and share events are emitted by the GKE platform at up to 200,000 events per second. The events must also land in the BigQuery warehouse for the existing historical analyses. The team wants a managed, autoscaling design. What should you do?
options: Write events to Cloud SQL from the platform and run a stored procedure every hour to compute trends.

Publish events to Pub/Sub, process them with a streaming Dataflow pipeline that computes windowed trend aggregates, and write both raw events and aggregates to BigQuery (or use the BigQuery subscription for raw events).
Append events to files in Cloud Storage and load them into BigQuery with a nightly batch job.
Send events directly to a Bigtable table and have editors query Bigtable with SQL.
explanation: Pub/Sub plus Dataflow is Google's managed, autoscaling streaming-analytics pattern: Dataflow handles windowing and late data for near-real-time trend detection, and BigQuery receives the results and raw events through streaming inserts or the Storage Write API (a Pub/Sub BigQuery subscription can also land raw events without code). Option A cannot absorb 200,000 events per second and produces hourly, not minute-level, insight. Option C delivers insight a day late, missing the virality window. Option D offers low-latency key lookups but is not an analytics warehouse for ad hoc trend queries, and it bypasses the existing BigQuery investment.
hint: Core Rule (Streaming analytics): Pub/Sub plus Dataflow is Google's managed, autoscaling streaming-analytics pattern: Dataflow handles windowing and late data for near-real-time trend detection, and BigQuery receives the results and raw events through streaming inserts or the Storage Write API (a Pub/Sub BigQuery subscription can also land raw events without code).

whyWrong.0: Option A cannot absorb 200,000 events per second and produces hourly, not minute-level, insight.
whyWrong.2: Option C delivers insight a day late, missing the virality window.
whyWrong.3: Option D offers low-latency key lookups but is not an analytics warehouse for ad hoc trend queries, and it bypasses the existing BigQuery investment.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's CFO has approved the generative-AI support assistant on the condition that its business value is measured and reviewed quarterly. You are asked to propose the key performance indicators that best demonstrate the assistant's return on investment relative to the business requirement of 24/7 self-service support. Which two KPIs should you propose? (Choose two.)
options: Number of GPU hours consumed by the assistant each month.
Self-service containment rate: the percentage of conversations resolved without escalation to a human agent.
Total number of prompts sent to the model per day.
Lines of code committed by the assistant development team.
Cost per resolved conversation compared with the cost of a human-handled contact, alongside customer satisfaction (CSAT) for assisted sessions.
Number of Gemini model versions evaluated during development.
explanation: ROI must link the investment to a business outcome. Containment rate shows how much support demand the assistant absorbs (the 24/7 self-service goal), and cost per resolved conversation versus human handling combined with CSAT quantifies savings without hiding a drop in quality. GPU hours, prompt counts, and model versions (Options A, C, F) are activity or cost inputs, not outcomes; more prompts could even indicate the assistant is failing to resolve issues. Lines of code (Option D) is a discredited productivity proxy. This aligns with the exam objective of defining success measurements such as KPIs and ROI.
hint: Core Rule (KPIs and ROI): ROI must link the investment to a business outcome.
