question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. After migrating to GKE, EHR Healthcare exposes patient-facing web portals to the internet and also runs internal administration consoles that operations staff currently reach through a jump host in the colocation facility. You must protect both classes of application in line with HIPAA expectations and Google-recommended practices. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Attach Cloud Armor security policies with preconfigured OWASP WAF rules and rate limiting to the global external Application Load Balancer that fronts the patient-facing portals.
Publish the administration consoles on public IP addresses protected by HTTP basic authentication.
Open TCP port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 on the GKE nodes so operators can troubleshoot from anywhere.
Place the administration consoles behind Identity-Aware Proxy with Cloud Identity groups and context-aware access levels instead of a VPN or jump host.
Store the portals' session data in a Firestore database in test mode so that developers can debug quickly.
explanation: Cloud Armor provides DDoS protection, OWASP Top 10 WAF rules, and rate limiting at the edge for internet-facing applications, while Identity-Aware Proxy implements a zero-trust access model for internal tools by authenticating each request with corporate identity and device context, eliminating the jump host. Both are Google-recommended controls in the security pillar. Option B exposes privileged consoles with weak authentication. Option C opens SSH to the world, a classic misconfiguration that attackers scan for. Option E disables security rules on a datastore holding PHI-adjacent session data, which is unacceptable.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Armor and Identity-Aware Proxy): Cloud Armor provides DDoS protection, OWASP Top 10 WAF rules, and rate limiting at the edge for internet-facing applications, while Identity-Aware Proxy implements a zero-trust access model for internal tools by authenticating each request with corporate identity and device context, eliminating the jump host.

whyWrong.4: Option E disables security rules on a datastore holding PHI-adjacent session data, which is unacceptable.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. The executive statement says EHR Healthcare has invested heavily in training staff on distinctly different systems and in managing similar but separate environments, and a business requirement is to decrease infrastructure administration costs. Which two design choices best support this requirement? (Choose two.)
options: Lift and shift every server to Compute Engine VMs so that existing operating procedures remain unchanged.
Build an internal platform team to operate the open-source databases as containers on GKE.
Run the containerized applications on GKE Autopilot so that node provisioning, patching, and scaling are handled by Google.
Move the whole estate to Google Cloud VMware Engine so that no retraining is required and keep operating it exactly as today.
Replace self-managed MySQL, SQL Server, and Redis with Cloud SQL and Memorystore so that backups, patching, and failover are managed services.
explanation: Administration cost drops when undifferentiated work (node patching, database backups, failover, capacity) shifts to managed services; GKE Autopilot and managed databases such as Cloud SQL and Memorystore do exactly that while standardizing the team on one platform and one skill set (cost-optimization and operational-excellence pillars). Option A preserves every existing manual procedure and therefore the existing cost. Option B adds headcount to keep running databases the hard way. Option D keeps the current operating model, including the outages and inconsistent monitoring the executive complains about, and is typically more expensive than native services.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. Redis is used by the customer-facing applications for session state and short-lived caching. During the migration you need a Redis deployment in Google Cloud that supports the 99.9% availability requirement and requires no patching or failover handling by the operations team. What should you do?
options: Provision Memorystore for Redis in Basic Tier because caches do not need redundancy.
Run Redis on a single Compute Engine VM and schedule persistent disk snapshots every hour.
Provision Memorystore for Redis in Standard Tier with replicas across zones (or Memorystore for Redis Cluster), which provides automatic failover and a 99.9% SLA.
Replace Redis with tables in Cloud SQL so that sessions benefit from database high availability.
explanation: Memorystore Standard Tier (and Memorystore for Redis Cluster) replicates data to another zone, fails over automatically, and carries a 99.9% availability SLA, and Google handles patching, so it satisfies both the availability and reduced-administration goals. Option A has no replica and no SLA; a Basic Tier maintenance event or zone failure would drop sessions. Option B is a single point of failure that the team must operate. Option D changes application code and adds latency, and a relational database is the wrong tool for high-throughput session caching.

topic: Private services access routing over Interconnect
question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. The legacy on-premises insurance-provider integrations must read from and write to the migrated Cloud SQL databases across the Dedicated Interconnect. The security team insists that database traffic never traverse the public internet. What should you do?
options: Configure Cloud SQL with a private IP through private services access, and configure Cloud Router custom route advertisements to announce the allocated private services range to the on-premises routers over the Interconnect.
Assign a public IP address to each Cloud SQL instance and add the on-premises NAT addresses to the authorized networks list.
Run the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy on a Compute Engine VM and expose it through an external passthrough Network Load Balancer for the on-premises systems.
Enable Private Google Access on the VPC subnets so that on-premises systems can reach Cloud SQL through Google's private API endpoints.
explanation: Cloud SQL private IP lives in a producer network reached through private services access peering; peered ranges are not advertised to on-premises by default, so you must add the allocated range as a custom route advertisement on the Cloud Router (and export custom routes on the peering) for the on-premises systems to reach the databases privately over Interconnect. Option B sends PHI over the public internet, which the security team forbids. Option C also exposes an internet-facing endpoint and adds a VM the team must run. Option D misunderstands Private Google Access, which covers Google APIs, not private services access peering ranges used by Cloud SQL.
hint: Core Rule (Private services access routing over Interconnect): Cloud SQL private IP lives in a producer network reached through private services access peering; peered ranges are not advertised to on-premises by default, so you must add the allocated range as a custom route advertisement on the Cloud Router (and export custom routes on the peering) for the on-premises systems to reach the databases privately over Interconnect.

whyWrong.2: Option C also exposes an internet-facing endpoint and adds a VM the team must run.
whyWrong.3: Option D misunderstands Private Google Access, which covers Google APIs, not private services access peering ranges used by Cloud SQL.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. During a compliance review you discover that some application logs now centralized in Cloud Logging contain patient names and insurance IDs. Engineers still need the logs for troubleshooting, and the fix in the application code will take several release cycles. What should you do?
options: Reduce log retention to one day for all applications so that exposure is limited.
Grant the Logs Viewer role only to the compliance team so engineers cannot see the PHI.
Disable application logging for all services that process patient data until the code is fixed.

Prioritize removing PHI from log statements in the applications, and in the interim route those logs through a Pub/Sub sink to a Dataflow pipeline that uses Sensitive Data Protection to de-identify PHI before writing to the central log bucket, restricting the raw data with log views and exclusion filters.
explanation: The correct approach fixes the root cause (do not log PHI) while applying a compensating control now: a log sink to Pub/Sub and a Dataflow pipeline with Sensitive Data Protection de-identification templates can mask or tokenize identifiers before storage, and log views plus exclusion filters limit who can see any raw data. Option A weakens troubleshooting and audit evidence without stopping PHI from being written. Option B removes engineers' ability to troubleshoot and does not remove PHI from the log store. Option C blinds operations, undermining the requirement for centralized visibility and the 99.9% availability target.
hint: Core Rule (Sensitive Data Protection for logs): The correct approach fixes the root cause (do not log PHI) while applying a compensating control now: a log sink to Pub/Sub and a Dataflow pipeline with Sensitive Data Protection de-identification templates can mask or tokenize identifiers before storage, and log views plus exclusion filters limit who can see any raw data.

topic: SQL Server licensing on Compute Engine
question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. Two of EHR Healthcare's SQL Server databases depend on CLR assemblies and SQL Server Agent jobs that are not supported by Cloud SQL for SQL Server. EHR owns SQL Server Enterprise licenses with active Software Assurance and wants to minimize licensing cost while keeping automatic failover within a region. What should you do?
options: Migrate the databases to Cloud SQL for SQL Server Enterprise Plus edition and rewrite the CLR components as T-SQL stored procedures.

Deploy SQL Server on Compute Engine in an Always On availability group across two zones, bring the existing SQL Server licenses through License Mobility with Software Assurance, and use pay-as-you-go Windows Server images.
Deploy SQL Server on Compute Engine sole-tenant nodes and bring both the Windows Server and SQL Server licenses, because bring-your-own-license is never permitted on shared hardware.
Migrate the databases to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL with Database Migration Service to eliminate Microsoft licensing entirely.
explanation: When required features are unavailable in Cloud SQL, SQL Server on Compute Engine with an Always On availability group across zones provides automatic in-region failover. SQL Server is eligible for License Mobility through Software Assurance, so existing licenses can be used on regular (shared-tenancy) VMs, while Windows Server (not eligible for License Mobility) is simply consumed pay-as-you-go from Google images; this is the lowest-cost compliant option. Option A requires rewriting application code, which the scenario rules out. Option C is unnecessarily expensive because sole-tenant nodes are only required to BYOL Windows Server (or other licenses without mobility), not SQL Server. Option D is a heterogeneous migration that would break the CLR-dependent code and does not meet the timeline.
hint: Core Rule (SQL Server licensing on Compute Engine): When required features are unavailable in Cloud SQL, SQL Server on Compute Engine with an Always On availability group across zones provides automatic in-region failover.

whyWrong.0: Option A requires rewriting application code, which the scenario rules out.
whyWrong.2: Option C is unnecessarily expensive because sole-tenant nodes are only required to BYOL Windows Server (or other licenses without mobility), not SQL Server.
whyWrong.3: Option D is a heterogeneous migration that would break the CLR-dependent code and does not meet the timeline.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. EHR Healthcare currently monitors its Kubernetes clusters with separately installed open-source Prometheus and Grafana instances per cluster, which is a major cause of the inconsistent monitoring the executive statement describes. You want centralized visibility across the new GKE clusters and the on-premises clusters that stay behind, with the least operational overhead. What should you do?
options: Keep a Prometheus server in every cluster and federate them into one large central Prometheus server on a Compute Engine VM.

Enable Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus on the GKE clusters and on the attached on-premises fleet clusters so all metrics land in Cloud Monitoring, and build unified dashboards and alerting policies there, optionally keeping Grafana as a front end via the Prometheus-compatible data source.
Write a script that exports cluster metrics to BigQuery every five minutes and build Looker Studio reports on top.
Rely on Cloud Monitoring uptime checks against the public endpoints, because they measure what customers experience.
explanation: Managed Service for Prometheus is a Google-operated, globally scalable Prometheus backend that works on GKE and on fleet-registered on-premises clusters; it removes per-cluster Prometheus servers, keeps PromQL and existing Grafana dashboards working, and integrates natively with Cloud Monitoring alerting, giving the single, consistent view the case study requires. Option A remains self-managed, has a single point of failure, and needs constant capacity tuning. Option C loses real-time alerting and is not a monitoring system. Option D provides only black-box availability signals and no resource or application-level visibility.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. A technical requirement is to dynamically scale and provision new environments. Product teams frequently need a complete new environment (project, network, GKE cluster, Cloud SQL instance, baseline workloads) for a large hospital customer's acceptance testing, and today this takes weeks of manual work. What should you do?
options: Clone an existing production project manually in the console by following a documented checklist.
Keep a set of gcloud scripts on the platform administrator's workstation and run them when a new environment is requested.

Define the environment as reusable Terraform modules (project, VPC, GKE, Cloud SQL) executed by a Cloud Build pipeline with remote state in Cloud Storage, and bootstrap the baseline workloads with Config Sync from a Git repository.
Take disk snapshots of the production VMs and restore them into a new project for each request.
explanation: Infrastructure as code with Terraform modules makes environments repeatable and reviewable, Cloud Build provides an auditable, shared execution path with remote state in Cloud Storage, and Config Sync applies the baseline Kubernetes workloads automatically once the cluster is registered, turning weeks of manual work into a pipeline run. Option A and Option B are manual, unaudited, and tied to individuals, reproducing the misconfiguration risk the executive statement highlights. Option D copies VM disks, which does not create projects, networks, GKE clusters, or Cloud SQL instances and is not how container environments are reproduced.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. You are designing the Google Cloud resource hierarchy for EHR Healthcare. The organization needs isolated development, test, and production environments, centralized network administration, organization-wide compliance guardrails for PHI, and a single place for security logs. Which design should you recommend?
options: Create an organization with folders per environment (dev, test, prod), a Shared VPC host project per environment with service projects per application, organization policy constraints such as resource location restriction and disabling service account key creation inherited from the organization node, and a dedicated project for centralized logging and monitoring.
Use a single project for all environments, separate them with different VPC networks, and label every resource with its environment.
Create one project per developer with the Owner role for agility and consolidate the resources into a production project later.
Create separate Google Cloud organizations for development and production to guarantee complete isolation between them.
explanation: Google's enterprise foundations guidance recommends folders that mirror environments or business units so IAM and organization policies can be inherited, Shared VPC so a central network team manages connectivity and firewall rules while application teams own service projects, constraints such as resource locations and disabling service account key creation to enforce compliance everywhere, and a central logging project for aggregated sinks. Option B removes IAM and billing isolation and makes blast radius and quota management unmanageable. Option C creates uncontrolled sprawl with excessive privileges. Option D doubles administrative overhead and breaks centralized policy, logging, and billing without a compliance reason to do so.
hint: Core Rule (Resource hierarchy design): Google's enterprise foundations guidance recommends folders that mirror environments or business units so IAM and organization policies can be inherited, Shared VPC so a central network team manages connectivity and firewall rules while application teams own service projects, constraints such as resource locations and disabling service account key creation to enforce compliance everywhere, and a central logging project for aggregated sinks.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. To increase its ability to provide insights into healthcare trends, EHR Healthcare wants to let a team of analysts explore multi-provider clinical data in BigQuery. The data contains PHI, and compliance requires that analysts see only the minimum necessary information. What should you do?
options: Grant the analysts the BigQuery Data Viewer role on the raw datasets and rely on Data Access audit logs to detect misuse.
Copy the raw data into a separate project with fewer controls so that analysts can work freely.
Give analysts access to Cloud SQL read replicas with database views instead of BigQuery.

Create de-identified datasets using the Cloud Healthcare API de-identification operation (or Sensitive Data Protection), and protect any remaining sensitive columns with policy tags for column-level security and row-level access policies in BigQuery, granting analysts access only to those datasets.
explanation: The minimum-necessary principle is best met by de-identifying data before analysts touch it; the Cloud Healthcare API de-identify operation and Sensitive Data Protection can redact, mask, or pseudonymize PHI at scale, while BigQuery policy tags (column-level security) and row-level security enforce fine-grained access to whatever sensitive fields remain. Option A exposes full PHI and relies on detection rather than prevention. Option B weakens controls on a copy of PHI, which is a compliance violation. Option C puts analytic load on operational replicas and does not scale to trend analysis across providers.
hint: Core Rule (De-identification and BigQuery access controls): The minimum-necessary principle is best met by de-identifying data before analysts touch it; the Cloud Healthcare API de-identify operation and Sensitive Data Protection can redact, mask, or pseudonymize PHI at scale, while BigQuery policy tags (column-level security) and row-level security enforce fine-grained access to whatever sensitive fields remain.

topic: Private Google Access for on-premises hosts
question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. The on-premises legacy integration servers must upload provider files to Cloud Storage and publish events to Pub/Sub. The servers have no internet egress by policy, but the colocation facility is connected to the VPC network with Dedicated Interconnect. What should you do?
options: Provide the servers with internet access through an outbound proxy so they can call storage.googleapis.com.

Configure Private Google Access for on-premises hosts by advertising the private.googleapis.com (or restricted.googleapis.com) range over the Interconnect through Cloud Router and creating matching DNS records on-premises.
Deploy Cloud NAT in the colocation facility so the servers receive translated public addresses.
Create VPC Network Peering between the on-premises network and the VPC network.
explanation: Private Google Access for on-premises hosts lets systems without internet access reach Google APIs over Interconnect or VPN by routing to the private.googleapis.com (199.36.153.8/30) or restricted.googleapis.com (199.36.153.4/30) ranges, which you advertise via Cloud Router custom advertisements and resolve through on-premises DNS. Option A violates the no-internet-egress policy. Option C is not possible; Cloud NAT is a Google Cloud service for VPC resources, not for on-premises networks. Option D is not possible either, because VPC Network Peering only connects VPC networks, not on-premises networks.
hint: Core Rule: Private Google Access for on-premises hosts lets systems without internet access reach Google APIs over Interconnect or VPN by routing to the private.googleapis.com (199.36.153.8/30) or restricted.googleapis.com (199.36.153.4/30) ranges, which you advertise via Cloud Router custom advertisements and resolve through on-premises DNS.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. EHR Healthcare wants to ship software updates several times a day on GKE while continuing to meet the 99.9% availability commitment to hospitals. Which two practices should you implement? (Choose two.)
options: Run a single replica of each service to minimize the cost of frequent deployments.
Configure readiness and liveness probes, run multiple replicas spread across zones with pod anti-affinity, and define PodDisruptionBudgets so upgrades never take all replicas down at once.
Deploy each release to all clusters simultaneously with kubectl replace to keep environments identical.
Use Cloud Deploy canary rollouts with automated verification and rollback so that a faulty release reaches only a small slice of traffic.
Disable the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler during releases to keep the number of pods stable.
explanation: Frequent releases are safe when the platform tolerates pod churn and when releases are progressive: probes keep unready pods out of rotation, multiple zone-spread replicas with PodDisruptionBudgets protect capacity during node upgrades and rollouts, and Cloud Deploy canary strategies with verification and automatic rollback limit the blast radius of a bad build. Option A creates an outage on every deployment and every node upgrade. Option C maximizes blast radius and kubectl replace can briefly delete resources. Option E removes the elasticity needed during a release-triggered spike and offers no reliability benefit.
hint: Core Rule (Release reliability on GKE): Frequent releases are safe when the platform tolerates pod churn and when releases are progressive: probes keep unready pods out of rotation, multiple zone-spread replicas with PodDisruptionBudgets protect capacity during node upgrades and rollouts, and Cloud Deploy canary strategies with verification and automatic rollback limit the blast radius of a bad build.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. A few of EHR Healthcare's containerized applications keep state on persistent volumes in GKE. The updated disaster recovery plan requires application-consistent backups of these workloads, including their Kubernetes configuration, with the ability to restore into a cluster in another region. What should you do?
options: Schedule Persistent Disk snapshots with a cron job and document how to recreate the Kubernetes objects by hand.
Install and operate Velero on every cluster and store its backups in Cloud Storage.
Enable Backup for GKE, create backup plans that cover the relevant namespaces and persistent volumes on a schedule, and restore them into the secondary-region cluster during DR tests and events.
Move the application state to local SSDs for performance and export it to Cloud Storage nightly.
explanation: Backup for GKE is the managed service that captures both Kubernetes resources and persistent volume data in one backup plan, supports scheduled and application-consistent (hook-based) backups, and can restore to a different cluster or region, exactly what a DR plan for stateful GKE workloads needs. Option A protects only disks, not the deployments, services, secrets, and config maps needed to run the application, and relies on manual reconstruction. Option B works but is self-managed software the team must upgrade and secure, contradicting the goal of lower administration cost. Option D is unsafe because local SSD data is lost when a node is stopped or fails.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. After migrating to GKE, incidents in the customer-facing applications still take hours to diagnose because requests span many microservices and engineers cannot tell where latency or errors originate. You want to shorten root cause analysis time. What should you do?
options: Instrument the services with OpenTelemetry to send distributed traces to Cloud Trace, emit structured logs that carry the trace ID for correlation, surface exceptions in Error Reporting, and use Gemini Cloud Assist investigations to speed up analysis during incidents.
Set the log level of all production services to DEBUG permanently so that every detail is captured.
Have on-call engineers use SSH to reach the GKE nodes and inspect container logs directly during incidents.
Wait for customer support tickets to identify affected features, then reproduce the problem in the development environment.
explanation: Distributed tracing shows exactly which service and call in a request path is slow or failing, log-trace correlation lets engineers jump from a trace span to the relevant log lines, Error Reporting groups new exceptions automatically, and Gemini Cloud Assist can correlate signals to propose likely root causes, which together shorten mean time to resolution. Option B floods the logging pipeline with cost and noise and still does not connect events across services. Option C is slow, insecure, and impossible on Autopilot nodes. Option D is reactive and makes customers the monitoring system.
hint: Core Rule (Root cause analysis and observability): Distributed tracing shows exactly which service and call in a request path is slow or failing, log-trace correlation lets engineers jump from a trace span to the relevant log lines, Error Reporting groups new exceptions automatically, and Gemini Cloud Assist can correlate signals to propose likely root causes, which together shorten mean time to resolution.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. A security review of the migrated GKE workloads finds that pods authenticate to Cloud SQL, Pub/Sub, and Cloud Storage with service account JSON keys mounted from Kubernetes Secrets. You need to remediate this in line with Google-recommended practices. What should you do?
options: Rotate the JSON keys every 90 days with an automated script and keep mounting them as Secrets.
Keep the JSON keys but store them in Kubernetes Secrets encrypted with application-layer secrets encryption.
Remove the keys and instead grant the node pool's default Compute Engine service account the Editor role.

Enable Workload Identity Federation for GKE so Kubernetes service accounts obtain short-lived credentials for IAM service accounts without keys, and move any remaining third-party secrets to Secret Manager.
explanation: Workload Identity Federation for GKE is the recommended way for pods to call Google APIs: each Kubernetes service account is mapped to an IAM identity and receives short-lived tokens, eliminating long-lived exportable keys and enabling per-workload least privilege. Secret Manager handles credentials for non-Google systems with versioning and audit logging. Option A and Option B still leave exfiltratable long-lived keys in the cluster; encryption and rotation reduce but do not remove the risk. Option C replaces one anti-pattern with another by granting a broad basic role to every pod on the node.
hint: Core Rule: Workload Identity Federation for GKE is the recommended way for pods to call Google APIs: each Kubernetes service account is mapped to an IAM identity and receives short-lived tokens, eliminating long-lived exportable keys and enabling per-workload least privilege.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. EHR Healthcare's second colocation facility, which hosts a subset of legacy provider integrations, will remain in service for two more years. It needs about 2 Gbps of consistent, low-latency private connectivity to Google Cloud with an SLA, but the facility is not in a location where Google offers Dedicated Interconnect and EHR does not want to over-invest for a site that will close. What should you do?
options: Order a 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect circuit and extend it to the facility with a leased fiber line from a carrier.
Configure a single HA VPN gateway with one tunnel to keep the design simple.
Order Partner Interconnect through a supported service provider with two VLAN attachments in different edge availability domains, sized at 2 Gbps each, to obtain a 99.9% SLA.
Set up Direct Peering with Google at the nearest exchange point to carry the traffic.
explanation: Partner Interconnect is designed for sites that cannot reach a Google colocation facility or that need less than 10 Gbps; attachments are available in 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps increments and two attachments in separate edge availability domains provide the 99.9% SLA topology, which matches both the bandwidth and the short remaining lifetime of the site. Option A is over-provisioned and requires expensive last-mile fiber for a site that closes in two years. Option B uses a single tunnel, so it has no SLA, and VPN over the internet cannot guarantee consistent latency. Option D is wrong because Direct Peering provides access to Google public services only and is not a way to reach a VPC network.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. Several hospital groups in the European Union will sign with EHR Healthcare only if their patient data is stored and processed exclusively within the EU, while North American customers have no such constraint. How should you design the deployment to meet this requirement with strong technical enforcement?
options: Deploy everything in a single US region and encrypt the EU customers' data with Cloud KMS keys located in an EU region.

Deploy separate regional stacks (GKE, Cloud SQL, Cloud Storage) in EU regions for EU customers, place them under a dedicated folder with the resource locations organization policy constraint limited to EU locations, and evaluate Assured Workloads for the EU data-residency control package.
Store all customer data in a dual-region Cloud Storage bucket spanning the US and the EU so that both customer groups are served.
Migrate all databases to a Spanner multi-region configuration that includes both American and European regions.
explanation: Data residency is enforced by where resources are created: a dedicated folder for EU tenants with the constraints/gcp.resourceLocations organization policy prevents anyone from creating resources outside EU regions, and Assured Workloads adds guardrails such as data location and personnel access controls. Option A leaves the data physically in the US; key location does not satisfy residency. Option C and Option D deliberately replicate data to the US, which is exactly what the EU customers prohibit.
hint: Core Rule: Data residency is enforced by where resources are created: a dedicated folder for EU tenants with the constraints/gcp.resourceLocations organization policy prevents anyone from creating resources outside EU regions, and Assured Workloads adds guardrails such as data location and personnel access controls.

whyWrong.0: Option A leaves the data physically in the US; key location does not satisfy residency.
whyWrong.2: Option C and Option D deliberately replicate data to the US, which is exactly what the EU customers prohibit.
whyWrong.3: Option D deliberately replicate data to the US, which is exactly what the EU customers prohibit.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. About forty applications in the expiring colocation facility still run as traditional Linux and Windows VMs on KVM hosts and cannot be containerized before the lease ends. You need to move them to Google Cloud with minimal downtime and minimal manual effort. What should you do?
options: Use Migrate to Virtual Machines to replicate the VMs continuously to Compute Engine, test clones in an isolated network, and cut over with minutes of downtime, evaluating Migrate to Containers for suitable workloads afterward.
Export each VM as a disk image, upload it to Cloud Storage, create custom images by hand, and rebuild every VM manually.
Rewrite the applications as Cloud Run services before the lease expires.
Move the VMs to Google Cloud VMware Engine and keep them there permanently regardless of cost.
explanation: Migrate to Virtual Machines performs agentless, continuous replication from VMware, KVM-based, AWS, or Azure sources to Compute Engine, lets you test clones before cutover, and requires only a short final sync, which minimizes both downtime and manual effort; Migrate to Containers can later modernize eligible VMs into containers for the GKE platform. Option B is slow, error-prone, and manual for forty VMs. Option C is unrealistic before the deadline and contradicts the stated constraint. Option D targets vSphere estates, which these KVM hosts are not, and 'regardless of cost' conflicts with the goal of reducing infrastructure costs.
hint: Core Rule: Migrate to Virtual Machines performs agentless, continuous replication from VMware, KVM-based, AWS, or Azure sources to Compute Engine, lets you test clones before cutover, and requires only a short final sync, which minimizes both downtime and manual effort; Migrate to Containers can later modernize eligible VMs into containers for the GKE platform.

whyWrong.1: Option B is slow, error-prone, and manual for forty VMs.
whyWrong.2: Option C is unrealistic before the deadline and contradicts the stated constraint.
whyWrong.3: Option D targets vSphere estates, which these KVM hosts are not, and 'regardless of cost' conflicts with the goal of reducing infrastructure costs.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. The operations team has spent years learning distinctly different on-premises systems and is anxious about running GKE, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Observability. The CIO asks how to prepare the team so the migration succeeds without stalling the lease-driven timeline. What should you recommend?
options: Outsource all cloud operations to a managed service provider and reassign the existing team.
Require every engineer to earn all Google Cloud professional certifications before migration work starts.
Migrate first to meet the lease deadline and schedule training for the team after the cutover.

Perform a skills assessment, deliver targeted role-based training on GKE and Cloud Observability, establish a cloud center of excellence with Google or partner support, and pilot a low-risk containerized application to build hands-on experience before the main migration waves.
explanation: Successful change management assesses readiness, closes specific skill gaps, gives the team a safe early win, and creates a center of excellence that captures standards and reusable patterns; this keeps the timeline while reducing the risk of misconfiguration by an untrained team. Option A discards institutional knowledge and does not address the goal of a consistent, self-managed platform. Option B delays the project unnecessarily and is not a targeted approach. Option C is how outages happen: the team would be operating unfamiliar production systems with no preparation.
hint: Core Rule (Team readiness and change management): Successful change management assesses readiness, closes specific skill gaps, gives the team a safe early win, and creates a center of excellence that captures standards and reusable patterns; this keeps the timeline while reducing the risk of misconfiguration by an untrained team.

whyWrong.0: Option A discards institutional knowledge and does not address the goal of a consistent, self-managed platform.
whyWrong.1: Option B delays the project unnecessarily and is not a targeted approach.
whyWrong.2: Option C is how outages happen: the team would be operating unfamiliar production systems with no preparation.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. The steering committee asks you to define key performance indicators that will show whether the Google Cloud migration delivers on the stated business requirements. Which three KPIs should you propose? (Choose three.)
options: Number of virtual machines migrated per week.
Measured availability of customer-facing systems against the 99.9% SLO, including error-budget consumption.
95th-percentile response latency for customers, broken down by geographic region.
Total number of Kubernetes clusters in the fleet.
Elapsed time to on-board a new insurance provider, from contract to first production data exchange.
Number of lines of infrastructure code committed each sprint.
explanation: KPIs should trace directly to business requirements: 99.9% availability, reduced latency for all customers, and faster on-boarding of insurance providers are three explicit goals, so availability against the SLO, regional p95 latency, and provider on-boarding lead time are meaningful outcome measures. Option A and Option F are activity metrics that say nothing about business value. Option D is a size metric; more clusters is not better and may even indicate the inconsistent sprawl the company is trying to eliminate.
hint: Core Rule (Success metrics and KPIs): KPIs should trace directly to business requirements: 99.9% availability, reduced latency for all customers, and faster on-boarding of insurance providers are three explicit goals, so availability against the SLO, regional p95 latency, and provider on-boarding lead time are meaningful outcome measures.

whyWrong.0: Option A and Option F are activity metrics that say nothing about business value.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. Measurements after the first migration wave show that clinicians in Asia and Europe experience page loads two to three times slower than North American users, even though the GKE services themselves respond quickly. The business requirement is to reduce latency to all customers. Which three changes should you make? (Choose three.)
options: Serve the applications through a global external Application Load Balancer with anycast IP and add GKE backends in regions close to European and Asian users.
Enable Cloud CDN for static assets and cacheable API responses so they are served from Google edge locations.
Switch the load balancer to Standard Tier networking to reduce cost per gigabyte.
Provide regional read paths for frequently read data, for example Cloud SQL read replicas or Memorystore caches in each serving region.
Consolidate all workloads into one very large zonal GKE cluster with bigger machine types.
Route all customer traffic through the colocation facility over the Interconnect before it reaches Google Cloud.
explanation: Cross-continent round trips dominate perceived latency, so the fixes are to terminate connections at the nearest Google edge (global external Application Load Balancer, Premium Tier), cache what can be cached at the edge (Cloud CDN), and place compute and read-heavy data close to users (regional backends with read replicas or caches). Option C makes things worse because Standard Tier hands traffic to the public internet near the region rather than carrying it on Google's backbone, and it does not support global load balancing. Option E increases distance for most users and introduces a single-zone failure point. Option F adds a hairpin through the data center and extra hops.
hint: Core Rule (Latency reduction): Cross-continent round trips dominate perceived latency, so the fixes are to terminate connections at the nearest Google edge (global external Application Load Balancer, Premium Tier), cache what can be cached at the edge (Cloud CDN), and place compute and read-heavy data close to users (regional backends with read replicas or caches).

whyWrong.2: Option C makes things worse because Standard Tier hands traffic to the public internet near the region rather than carrying it on Google's backbone, and it does not support global load balancing.
whyWrong.4: Option E increases distance for most users and introduces a single-zone failure point.
whyWrong.5: Option F adds a hairpin through the data center and extra hops.

question: For this question, refer to the EHR Healthcare case study. EHR Healthcare's compliance policy requires that Admin Activity and Data Access audit logs be retained for six years in a tamper-evident manner, while engineers only need interactive access to the most recent year. You want to meet the policy at the lowest cost. What should you do?
options: Keep all audit logs in the _Default log bucket with its 30-day retention and rely on Google's internal backups for older data.

Create a sink that routes audit logs to a Cloud Storage bucket using the Archive storage class with a locked six-year retention policy, and set a one-year retention on a Cloud Logging bucket for interactive analysis.
Export the audit logs to a BigQuery dataset with no table expiration and give the compliance team the BigQuery Data Editor role.
Copy the audit logs nightly to a Filestore share mounted on a Compute Engine VM in a locked-down project.
explanation: Cloud Storage with a locked bucket retention policy (Bucket Lock) prevents deletion or modification until the retention period ends, satisfying tamper-evidence, and the Archive class is the cheapest option for data that is rarely read; a Cloud Logging bucket with one-year retention keeps recent logs searchable in Logs Explorer for engineers. Option A violates the six-year requirement and Google does not provide customer-accessible backups of expired logs. Option C is more expensive for cold data and Data Editor permissions would let people alter or delete audit evidence. Option D is costly, not tamper-evident, and depends on a VM and manual copying.
hint: Core Rule (Log retention for compliance): Cloud Storage with a locked bucket retention policy (Bucket Lock) prevents deletion or modification until the retention period ends, satisfying tamper-evidence, and the Archive class is the cheapest option for data that is rarely read; a Cloud Logging bucket with one-year retention keeps recent logs searchable in Logs Explorer for engineers.

whyWrong.0: Option A violates the six-year requirement and Google does not provide customer-accessible backups of expired logs.
whyWrong.2: Option C is more expensive for cold data and Data Editor permissions would let people alter or delete audit evidence.
whyWrong.3: Option D is costly, not tamper-evident, and depends on a VM and manual copying.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives' IT is largely on-premises, with several dealer-facing applications already running on another major cloud provider. As part of its hybrid cloud strategy, KnightMotives will build its new data platform on Google Cloud and needs private, high-bandwidth, low-latency connectivity from both the headquarters data center and the other cloud to Google Cloud, without routing traffic over the public internet or through the headquarters as a hub. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Use HA VPN from the data center and a site-to-site VPN from the other cloud provider, both terminating on one Cloud Router.

Provision Dedicated Interconnect (or Partner Interconnect) from the headquarters data center and Cross-Cloud Interconnect to the other cloud provider, and attach both to a Network Connectivity Center hub for transitive routing.
Provision Dedicated Interconnect from headquarters and route traffic from the other cloud to Google Cloud through the headquarters data center.
Expose the applications in the other cloud through public load balancers and call them from Google Cloud over TLS.
explanation: Cross-Cloud Interconnect provides dedicated physical connectivity between Google Cloud and other major cloud providers, and Dedicated or Partner Interconnect serves the data center; connecting both as spokes to a Network Connectivity Center hub gives private, transitive site-to-site connectivity without hair-pinning through headquarters. Option A uses the public internet with limited per-tunnel bandwidth and higher latency. Option C makes headquarters a bottleneck and single point of failure, which the constraint excludes. Option D exposes internal systems publicly, unacceptable given the case study's security concerns after past breaches. This is a reliability and performance decision for a multicloud topology.
hint: Core Rule (Hybrid and multicloud networking): Cross-Cloud Interconnect provides dedicated physical connectivity between Google Cloud and other major cloud providers, and Dedicated or Partner Interconnect serves the data center; connecting both as spokes to a Network Connectivity Center hub gives private, transitive site-to-site connectivity without hair-pinning through headquarters.

whyWrong.0: Option A uses the public internet with limited per-tunnel bandwidth and higher latency.
whyWrong.2: Option C makes headquarters a bottleneck and single point of failure, which the constraint excludes.
whyWrong.3: Option D exposes internal systems publicly, unacceptable given the case study's security concerns after past breaches.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives' supply chain runs on an outdated mainframe whose COBOL batch programs calculate parts allocation for every plant. The business cannot tolerate any discrepancy in allocation results during modernization, and the few remaining mainframe engineers are near retirement. KnightMotives wants to modernize the workload to Google Cloud gradually while proving functional equivalence before cutover. What should you do?
options: Rewrite the batch programs in Java on GKE during a single release and cut over on a weekend after unit tests pass.
Move the mainframe workloads to Google Cloud VMware Engine to retire the mainframe hardware first.
Freeze the mainframe and keep it running indefinitely while building new applications around it.

Use the Mainframe Assessment Tool to analyze the code base, modernize or refactor the programs with Google Cloud mainframe modernization tooling, and run Dual Run to execute the mainframe and the Google Cloud version in parallel, comparing outputs until parity is proven before cutover.
explanation: Google Cloud's mainframe modernization approach begins with assessment (Mainframe Assessment Tool, which uses Gemini to document COBOL) and uses Dual Run to execute the legacy and modernized systems side by side on real production inputs, comparing results to establish confidence before switching, which addresses both the zero-discrepancy requirement and the skills gap. Option A is a big-bang rewrite with no production-parity evidence and high risk. Option B is wrong because mainframe workloads do not run on VMware Engine. Option C is the status quo that the case study says makes promotions and dealer discounts difficult to implement. This is a phased, risk-managed migration aligned with the reliability pillar.
hint: Core Rule: Google Cloud's mainframe modernization approach begins with assessment (Mainframe Assessment Tool, which uses Gemini to document COBOL) and uses Dual Run to execute the legacy and modernized systems side by side on real production inputs, comparing results to establish confidence before switching, which addresses both the zero-discrepancy requirement and the skills gap.

whyWrong.0: Option A is a big-bang rewrite with no production-parity evidence and high risk.
whyWrong.1: Option B is wrong because mainframe workloads do not run on VMware Engine.
whyWrong.2: Option C is the status quo that the case study says makes promotions and dealer discounts difficult to implement.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives' outdated Enterprise Resource Planning system makes new promotions and dealer discounts slow to implement. The CIO asks you to recommend a disposition for the ERP as part of the five-year modernization roadmap. The ERP implements standard finance, procurement, and pricing processes that are not a competitive differentiator, and the in-house team that customized it has largely left the company. What should you recommend?
options: Buy: replace the custom ERP with a modern packaged ERP such as SAP running on Google Cloud (or a SaaS ERP), integrating it with the data platform and dealer systems through APIs.
Build: rewrite the ERP from scratch as microservices on GKE so that promotions can be released daily.
Modify: lift-and-shift the existing ERP to Compute Engine and gradually patch the pricing module.
Deprecate: retire the ERP and manage pricing and procurement in spreadsheets stored in Google Drive.
explanation: Workload disposition strategy (build, buy, modify, or deprecate) is an explicit exam objective. Non-differentiating, standardized business processes with a depleted internal team are the classic case for buying a packaged or SaaS ERP; SAP on Google Cloud is a common target and integrates with BigQuery for the data monetization goals. Option B spends years of scarce engineering effort recreating commodity functionality. Option C moves the problem to the cloud without solving the agility issue or the skills gap. Option D is not viable for a global manufacturer's finance and procurement processes. This reflects sound decision-making trade-offs in the business-process domain.
hint: Core Rule: Workload disposition strategy (build, buy, modify, or deprecate) is an explicit exam objective.

whyWrong.1: Option B spends years of scarce engineering effort recreating commodity functionality.
whyWrong.2: Option C moves the problem to the cloud without solving the agility issue or the skills gap.
whyWrong.3: Option D is not viable for a global manufacturer's finance and procurement processes.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives' online build-to-order system runs on a single on-premises application server backed by a single relational database, and its unreliability is straining dealer relationships. The rearchitected system must serve customers in North America, Europe, and Asia from one global endpoint, remain available through a regional outage, and guarantee strongly consistent order and configuration records so that a dealer and a customer never see conflicting order states. What should you do?
options: Deploy the application on Compute Engine in one region behind a regional external Application Load Balancer, with Cloud SQL for MySQL and a read replica in a second region.
Deploy the application on Cloud Run in each continent behind separate regional load balancers, each with its own Cloud SQL instance, and reconcile orders nightly.
Deploy the application on Cloud Run (or GKE) in multiple regions behind a global external Application Load Balancer, and store orders and configurations in a multi-region Spanner instance.
Deploy the application on GKE in one region and store orders in Firestore in Datastore mode with eventual consistency.
explanation: The requirements—single global endpoint, survive a regional outage, strong consistency across continents—map directly to a global external Application Load Balancer fronting multi-region serverless or GKE compute with a multi-region Spanner instance, which offers a 99.999% availability SLA and external consistency. Option A remains single-region for writes and a Cloud SQL read replica cannot take strongly consistent writes during failover without manual promotion. Option B creates three independent sources of truth and nightly reconciliation, which is exactly the conflicting-state problem dealers complain about. Option D is single-region and explicitly eventually consistent. This applies the reliability pillar to a business-critical transactional workload.
hint: Core Rule (Highly available transactional systems): The requirements—single global endpoint, survive a regional outage, strong consistency across continents—map directly to a global external Application Load Balancer fronting multi-region serverless or GKE compute with a multi-region Spanner instance, which offers a 99.999% availability SLA and external consistency.

whyWrong.0: Option A remains single-region for writes and a Cloud SQL read replica cannot take strongly consistent writes during failover without manual promotion.
whyWrong.1: Option B creates three independent sources of truth and nightly reconciliation, which is exactly the conflicting-state problem dealers complain about.
whyWrong.3: Option D is single-region and explicitly eventually consistent.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. Dealers complain that the build-to-order system does not give them the order data they need. KnightMotives wants to expose order status, configuration, and delivery-estimate data to hundreds of independent dealers and their third-party dealer-management-system vendors as secure, versioned APIs, with per-dealer quotas, usage analytics, and a self-service developer portal. What should you do?
options: Give each dealer a service account key with read access to the orders database.
Publish the APIs through Apigee with API keys or OAuth per dealer application, rate-limiting and quota policies, analytics, and a developer portal for onboarding.
Expose the backend service directly through an external passthrough Network Load Balancer with an allowlist of dealer IP addresses.
Email dealers a nightly CSV export of orders generated by a Cloud Run job.
explanation: Apigee is Google Cloud's full-lifecycle API management platform and directly provides the required capabilities: partner onboarding through a developer portal, credential issuance per application, quota and spike-arrest policies, versioning, and analytics. Option A gives external parties direct database access with long-lived keys, a severe security anti-pattern given past breaches. Option C provides no authentication, quotas, or analytics, and IP allowlists are brittle for hundreds of partners. Option D is not real time and cannot deliver the transparency the case study asks for. API management best practices with Apigee are an explicit exam objective.
hint: Core Rule (API management with Apigee): Apigee is Google Cloud's full-lifecycle API management platform and directly provides the required capabilities: partner onboarding through a developer portal, credential issuance per application, quota and spike-arrest policies, versioning, and analytics.

whyWrong.0: Option A gives external parties direct database access with long-lived keys, a severe security anti-pattern given past breaches.
whyWrong.2: Option C provides no authentication, quotas, or analytics, and IP allowlists are brittle for hundreds of partners.
whyWrong.3: Option D is not real time and cannot deliver the transparency the case study asks for.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives wants to give service technicians and sales staff modern tools for inventory checks, service scheduling, and guided upsell during customer visits. The case study notes that dealers have no budget for new equipment; technicians already carry personal or dealership smartphones and the showroom has ordinary web browsers. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Ship ruggedized tablets with a native application to every dealership and bill the cost to the dealers.

Build responsive web and mobile applications (for example with AppSheet for simple workflows and Cloud Run backends for richer ones) that run in the browsers and phones dealers already have, secured with Identity Platform or federated dealer identities.
Deploy a virtual desktop infrastructure farm so dealers can remote into a Windows application.
Install a small on-premises server in each dealership to host the tools locally.
explanation: The binding constraint is that dealers have no budget for new equipment, so the tools must run on the browsers and phones already in use. Browser-based and mobile applications, including no-code AppSheet apps for simple workflows, satisfy this with no hardware spend and are centrally updated. Option A imposes exactly the equipment cost dealers cannot afford. Option C still requires client devices and adds licensing and operational cost, while providing a poor mobile experience for technicians on the shop floor. Option D adds hardware and on-site maintenance to hundreds of locations. This is a cost-aware design decision that supports the business requirement of better dealer tooling.
hint: Core Rule (Dealer tooling): The binding constraint is that dealers have no budget for new equipment, so the tools must run on the browsers and phones already in use.

whyWrong.0: Option A imposes exactly the equipment cost dealers cannot afford.
whyWrong.2: Option C still requires client devices and adds licensing and operational cost, while providing a poor mobile experience for technicians on the shop floor.
whyWrong.3: Option D adds hardware and on-site maintenance to hundreds of locations.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives is implementing a comprehensive CRM to track customer interactions and personalize experiences. The sales organization has selected a SaaS CRM. Customer interactions must flow bidirectionally between the CRM, the new build-to-order system, and the BigQuery data platform (for personalization models), with minimal custom integration code and reliable event handling. What should you do?
options: Use Application Integration with the CRM's Integration Connector for event-driven, bidirectional flows to the order system, and the BigQuery Data Transfer Service (or connector) to land CRM data in BigQuery for analytics.
Write custom Python scripts on a Compute Engine VM that poll the CRM API every five minutes and upsert records into Cloud SQL.
Replace the SaaS CRM with a custom CRM built on Firestore so that all data is already in Google Cloud.
Export CRM data manually to CSV each week and load it into BigQuery with the bq command-line tool.
explanation: Application Integration and Integration Connectors provide managed, low-code connectivity to popular SaaS systems, including event triggers and bidirectional data flows, and BigQuery data transfer connectors land CRM data in the warehouse for personalization models without custom pipelines. Option B introduces polling latency, a single VM to maintain, and bespoke code, contradicting the minimal-code constraint. Option C throws away the sales organization's selected product and rebuilds commodity software. Option D is manual, weekly, and one-directional, which cannot support real-time personalization or the build-to-order integration.
hint: Core Rule (CRM integration): Application Integration and Integration Connectors provide managed, low-code connectivity to popular SaaS systems, including event triggers and bidirectional data flows, and BigQuery data transfer connectors land CRM data in the warehouse for personalization models without custom pipelines.

whyWrong.1: Option B introduces polling latency, a single VM to maintain, and bespoke code, contradicting the minimal-code constraint.
whyWrong.2: Option C throws away the sales organization's selected product and rebuilds commodity software.
whyWrong.3: Option D is manual, weekly, and one-directional, which cannot support real-time personalization or the build-to-order integration.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives wants to monetize corporate data, but that data is siloed across plant systems, vehicle telemetry stores, dealer applications, and the mainframe. Business units want to discover and share trusted datasets with each other and with external partners without copying data, and the security team requires centralized data classification, lineage, and access policies. Which architecture should you recommend?
options: Give every business unit its own Cloud SQL instance and replicate data between them with Datastream.
Consolidate all data into a single BigQuery dataset in one project and grant BigQuery Data Viewer to all employees.

Build a BigQuery-based data platform organized by domain, govern it with Dataplex Universal Catalog (discovery, classification, lineage, policy tags), and share curated datasets internally and with partners through Analytics Hub listings.
Export datasets to Cloud Storage buckets and share signed URLs with partners on request.
explanation: This is the recommended data-mesh style pattern on Google Cloud: BigQuery provides the scalable warehouse, Dataplex Universal Catalog provides centralized governance with metadata, classification, lineage, and policy tags, and Analytics Hub enables zero-copy sharing of curated datasets with internal consumers and external subscribers, which is the foundation for monetization. Option A perpetuates silos in OLTP databases unsuited to analytics. Option B removes silos but destroys governance by granting broad access, unacceptable after past breaches. Option D copies data, loses lineage and access control, and cannot be revoked cleanly. This aligns with the security and operational-excellence pillars.
hint: Core Rule (Data platform and governance): This is the recommended data-mesh style pattern on Google Cloud: BigQuery provides the scalable warehouse, Dataplex Universal Catalog provides centralized governance with metadata, classification, lineage, and policy tags, and Analytics Hub enables zero-copy sharing of curated datasets with internal consumers and external subscribers, which is the foundation for monetization.

whyWrong.0: Option A perpetuates silos in OLTP databases unsuited to analytics.
whyWrong.1: Option B removes silos but destroys governance by granting broad access, unacceptable after past breaches.
whyWrong.3: Option D copies data, loses lineage and access control, and cannot be revoked cleanly.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. An insurance company wants to buy insights from KnightMotives' driving-behavior data to price usage-based policies, and KnightMotives sees this as a first data-monetization deal. Both companies' legal teams require that neither party can see the other's row-level customer data, that only aggregated results above a minimum group size can be extracted, and that EU data protection rules are respected. What should you do?
options: Share a de-identified copy of the telemetry table with the insurer through a Cloud Storage bucket after removing names and vehicle identification numbers.

Create a BigQuery data clean room in Analytics Hub, publish the telemetry data with analysis rules (aggregation thresholds and join restrictions), and let the insurer subscribe and run only privacy-constrained queries within an EU region.
Grant the insurer's service account the BigQuery Data Viewer role on the telemetry dataset with a row-level security policy.
Run the insurer's queries manually on their behalf and email them the results as spreadsheets.
explanation: BigQuery data clean rooms (built on Analytics Hub) are designed for exactly this: data contributors share data without copying it, analysis rules enforce aggregation thresholds and restrict joins so subscribers can only obtain privacy-safe aggregates, and locating the clean room in an EU region supports data residency. Option A relies on naive de-identification; location and behavioral traces are highly re-identifiable, and once copied the data cannot be controlled. Option C still exposes row-level data to the insurer. Option D does not scale, introduces human error, and provides no technical enforcement of the privacy rules. This is a security and compliance pillar decision enabling the monetization goal.
hint: Core Rule: BigQuery data clean rooms (built on Analytics Hub) are designed for exactly this: data contributors share data without copying it, analysis rules enforce aggregation thresholds and restrict joins so subscribers can only obtain privacy-safe aggregates, and locating the clean room in an EU region supports data residency.

whyWrong.0: Option A relies on naive de-identification; location and behavioral traces are highly re-identifiable, and once copied the data cannot be controlled.
whyWrong.2: Option C still exposes row-level data to the insurer.
whyWrong.3: Option D does not scale, introduces human error, and provides no technical enforcement of the privacy rules.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives' AI infrastructure is obsolete. The autonomous-driving team needs to train large perception models on multiple petabytes of sensor recordings stored in Cloud Storage. Training runs last days, require hundreds of accelerators with high-bandwidth interconnect, and are currently delayed for weeks because on-premises GPUs are unavailable. The team wants to start training within days, minimize idle accelerator cost, and avoid building a cluster from scratch. What should you do?
options: Order additional on-premises GPU servers and expand the data-center cooling capacity.
Launch individual Compute Engine VMs with a single consumer-grade GPU each and split the dataset across them manually.
Train the models on Vertex AI Workbench notebooks with an attached GPU, uploading data through the notebook.

Use AI Hypercomputer capabilities: run distributed training on Vertex AI training (or GKE) with TPU or GPU slices obtained through Dynamic Workload Scheduler, read data directly from Cloud Storage via Cloud Storage FUSE or Parallelstore, and release capacity when each run completes.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives must build a robust simulation environment to validate autonomous-driving software. Each software release triggers tens of thousands of independent, containerized simulation scenarios that run for 10–60 minutes each, can be safely restarted, and must complete overnight. Between releases the environment is idle. You want to minimize cost and operational overhead. What should you do?
options: Submit the scenarios as jobs to Batch (or a GKE Autopilot cluster using Kueue) running on Spot VMs with automatic retries, and scale to zero when no release is being tested.
Provision a permanently running GKE Standard cluster sized for peak load with standard VMs.
Run the scenarios sequentially on a single large Compute Engine VM with a persistent disk of results.
Use Cloud Run functions to run each scenario, chaining invocations when the 60-minute limit is reached.
explanation: Embarrassingly parallel, restartable, deadline-based work is the ideal candidate for Spot capacity, and Batch (or GKE with Kueue) handles queueing, retries, and scale-to-zero so nothing is paid between releases. Option B pays for peak capacity around the clock. Option C cannot finish tens of thousands of scenarios overnight and is a single point of failure. Option D forces awkward chaining around request time limits and is not designed for long-running compute jobs. This is a cost-optimization decision that also aligns with the sustainability pillar by avoiding idle resources.
hint: Core Rule (Batch simulation workloads): Embarrassingly parallel, restartable, deadline-based work is the ideal candidate for Spot capacity, and Batch (or GKE with Kueue) handles queueing, retries, and scale-to-zero so nothing is paid between releases.

whyWrong.1: Option B pays for peak capacity around the clock.
whyWrong.2: Option C cannot finish tens of thousands of scenarios overnight and is a single point of failure.
whyWrong.3: Option D forces awkward chaining around request time limits and is not designed for long-running compute jobs.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. Deploy a third-party vulnerability scanner on a Compute Engine VM and export results to a spreadsheet.

Activate Security Command Center Enterprise at the organization level, connect the other cloud provider's accounts, and use its posture, threat detection, attack-path simulation, and SecOps case-management capabilities.
Rely on Cloud NGFW intrusion prevention on all VPC networks as the primary security control.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives' internal engineering portals and dealer-tool administration consoles are currently reachable only through a corporate VPN, and a past breach began with stolen VPN credentials. The CISO wants employees and dealer administrators to access these web applications from managed devices anywhere, with access decisions based on user identity, device posture, and location, and without exposing the applications to the internet or maintaining the VPN. What should you do?
options: Move the VPN concentrator to Compute Engine and enforce longer passwords.
Front the applications with Identity-Aware Proxy and enforce Chrome Enterprise Premium access levels (device trust, location, user identity) through Access Context Manager, removing the VPN path.
Place the applications behind an external passthrough Network Load Balancer restricted to the IP ranges of dealer locations.
Publish the applications on the public internet with basic authentication and Cloud Armor rate limiting.
explanation: This is the zero-trust model: Identity-Aware Proxy authenticates every request and Chrome Enterprise Premium (formerly BeyondCorp Enterprise) adds context-aware access based on device posture and location, so a stolen credential alone is insufficient and no VPN or public exposure is needed. Option A keeps the perimeter model that failed and only marginally raises password strength. Option C relies on network location, which cannot verify identity or device health and breaks for mobile staff. Option D exposes the applications directly with weak authentication. Secure remote access via IAP and Chrome Enterprise Premium is an explicit security objective on the exam.
hint: Core Rule (Zero trust access): This is the zero-trust model: Identity-Aware Proxy authenticates every request and Chrome Enterprise Premium (formerly BeyondCorp Enterprise) adds context-aware access based on device posture and location, so a stolen credential alone is insufficient and no VPN or public exposure is needed.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives will process personal data from EU drivers of its emerging autonomous platform in Google Cloud. EU legal counsel requires that this data and its encryption keys remain in the EU, that Google support personnel outside the EU cannot access it, and that engineers cannot accidentally create resources holding this data in non-EU regions, while the rest of KnightMotives' global workloads remain unaffected. What should you do?
options: Create the EU projects in the same folder as the global projects and ask engineers to select only EU regions when deploying.
Encrypt all data with a Cloud KMS key located in a US region and grant EU staff exclusive access to the key.

Create a dedicated folder and place all EU driver-data projects under it with an organization policy restricting resource locations to EU regions, but keep support and key management global for simplicity.

Create an Assured Workloads folder with the EU Sovereign Controls control package for the EU driver-data projects, which enforces EU resource-location and key-management organization policies and restricts support access to EU personnel, and keep other workloads in standard folders.
explanation: Assured Workloads with EU Sovereign Controls is the Google Cloud mechanism for data sovereignty: it applies resource-location restrictions, requires EU-located customer-managed keys (with Key Access Justifications), and limits Google support and access to EU personnel, all scoped to a folder so global workloads are not constrained. Option A depends on human discipline and provides no enforcement or support-access controls. Option B places keys outside the EU, violating the requirement. Option C enforces location but leaves support access and key residency unaddressed, failing two of the three legal requirements. Designing for data sovereignty legislation is an explicit compliance objective.
hint: Core Rule (Data sovereignty and Assured Workloads): Assured Workloads with EU Sovereign Controls is the Google Cloud mechanism for data sovereignty: it applies resource-location restrictions, requires EU-located customer-managed keys (with Key Access Justifications), and limits Google support and access to EU personnel, all scoped to a folder so global workloads are not constrained.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives must deliver real-time AI features such as driver-assistance alerts and voice interaction in vehicles that frequently drive through rural areas with intermittent or no cellular coverage, while still collecting driving and road-condition telemetry for the central data platform. Which two design decisions should you make? (Choose two.)
options: Run latency-critical inference on-device using optimized models (for example LiteRT or on-device Gemini Nano-class models) deployed to the vehicle, and use the cloud for model training and periodic over-the-air updates.
Route every inference request to a Vertex AI endpoint and display an error when the vehicle has no connectivity.
Increase the bandwidth of the Interconnect between headquarters and Google Cloud to reduce vehicle latency.

Buffer telemetry locally in the vehicle and use a store-and-forward pattern that publishes batches over MQTT to a broker or directly to Pub/Sub when connectivity returns, with idempotent ingestion downstream.
Serve vehicle telemetry through Cloud CDN to improve rural performance.
Require vehicles to maintain a persistent VPN tunnel to the VPC for all data transmission.
explanation: Reliable real-time features under intermittent connectivity require inference at the edge, with the cloud responsible for training, evaluation, and over-the-air model distribution; telemetry must tolerate disconnection through local buffering and store-and-forward publication into Pub/Sub, with idempotent consumers to handle retransmission. Option B makes safety-relevant features depend on coverage that the case study says is unreliable. Option C addresses the wrong link; headquarters bandwidth does not change cellular coverage in rural areas. Option E is for content delivery to consumers, not for ingesting telemetry. Option F is fragile over intermittent links and scales poorly to a vehicle fleet. This is a reliability and performance decision for an IoT-style architecture.
hint: Core Rule (Edge and connected-vehicle architecture): Reliable real-time features under intermittent connectivity require inference at the edge, with the cloud responsible for training, evaluation, and over-the-air model distribution; telemetry must tolerate disconnection through local buffering and store-and-forward publication into Pub/Sub, with idempotent consumers to handle retransmission.

whyWrong.1: Option B makes safety-relevant features depend on coverage that the case study says is unreliable.
whyWrong.2: Option C addresses the wrong link; headquarters bandwidth does not change cellular coverage in rural areas.
whyWrong.4: Option E is for content delivery to consumers, not for ingesting telemetry.
whyWrong.5: Option F is fragile over intermittent links and scales poorly to a vehicle fleet.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. Network connectivity between KnightMotives' manufacturing plants and headquarters is a known weakness, and data traffic from plant systems to the new Google Cloud data platform will grow substantially. The company has 14 plants worldwide, most of which are not near a Google colocation facility, and it already uses an SD-WAN vendor for branch connectivity. KnightMotives wants private connectivity from every plant to Google Cloud and plant-to-plant transit without building a full mesh. What should you do?
options: Order Dedicated Interconnect circuits from every plant to the nearest colocation facility and manage routing statically.
Configure HA VPN from each plant to a separate VPC per plant and peer all VPCs with each other.

Use Network Connectivity Center as the hub: attach headquarters over Dedicated Interconnect, connect plants over Partner Interconnect or HA VPN spokes as appropriate, and deploy the SD-WAN vendor's router appliances in Google Cloud as router appliance spokes so plant traffic transits the hub.
Connect every plant to the public internet and access Google Cloud APIs directly over TLS.
explanation: Network Connectivity Center provides a hub-and-spoke model that unifies Interconnect, HA VPN, and third-party SD-WAN router appliances, enabling site-to-site data transfer through Google's backbone without a full mesh, which is the right fit for many geographically dispersed plants with an existing SD-WAN. Option A is impractical because Dedicated Interconnect requires presence at a colocation facility and static routing does not scale. Option B creates 14 VPCs and a peering mesh that is hard to manage and VPC Network Peering is not transitive. Option D lacks privacy and performance guarantees and conflicts with the security emphasis. This addresses the case study's explicit plant-connectivity upgrade requirement.
hint: Core Rule (Plant connectivity): Network Connectivity Center provides a hub-and-spoke model that unifies Interconnect, HA VPN, and third-party SD-WAN router appliances, enabling site-to-site data transfer through Google's backbone without a full mesh, which is the right fit for many geographically dispersed plants with an existing SD-WAN.
