question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives lists employee upskilling and better communication between business and technical teams as critical objectives of its five-year modernization. Early cloud projects have stalled because each team chooses different tools, business stakeholders do not understand the technical roadmap, and there is no shared set of standards. What should you recommend?
options: Outsource all cloud work to a system integrator so that internal staff do not need to learn new skills.

Establish a Cloud Center of Excellence with representatives from business and technology that defines standards, reusable patterns, and a role-based learning program (for example Google Cloud Skills Boost and certifications), and sponsors cross-functional pilot teams.
Require every engineer to complete a certification before any further cloud projects are approved.
Let each business unit continue to select its own tools and reconcile differences at the end of the program.
explanation: A Cloud Center of Excellence is the recommended organizational construct for cloud adoption: it aligns business and technical stakeholders, establishes shared guardrails and patterns, and runs structured upskilling, which directly addresses the case study's talent and communication objectives. Option A contradicts the stated goal of upskilling and attracting talent and creates dependency. Option C blocks delivery and treats certification as a gate rather than part of a learning culture. Option D perpetuates fragmentation, which the case study identifies as an existing problem with code bases and tools. This falls under the exam's team assessment and change-management objectives.
hint: Core Rule (Skills readiness and change management): A Cloud Center of Excellence is the recommended organizational construct for cloud adoption: it aligns business and technical stakeholders, establishes shared guardrails and patterns, and runs structured upskilling, which directly addresses the case study's talent and communication objectives.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. Establish FinOps practices: export billing data to BigQuery, enforce a labeling and project-hierarchy standard so costs map to business units, and configure budgets with alerts per business unit.
Keep buying on-premises hardware in parallel so that cloud spending can be paused at any time.
After right-sizing migrated workloads, buy committed use discounts sized to the measured steady-state baseline, using Spot and autoscaling for variable demand.
Disable autoscaling on all workloads so monthly costs are constant.
Grant every business unit the Billing Account Administrator role so they can manage their own spend.
explanation: The cost-optimization pillar recommends visibility and accountability first (billing export, labels, budgets, showback to business units) and then commitments sized to observed baselines after right-sizing. Option A locks in capacity before usage is known, risking large over-commitment for a five-year phased migration. Option C doubles spending and defeats the CapEx-to-OpEx goal. Option E sacrifices elasticity and often increases cost while reducing reliability. Option F violates least privilege and separation of duties on a sensitive role; cost visibility should come from budgets and reports, not billing administration rights.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives has multiple fragmented code bases across its BEV, hybrid, and ICE vehicle lines and significant technical debt from backward compatibility. It wants a consistent in-vehicle and companion-app experience across all models within five years while continuing to support vehicles already on the road. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Rewrite every vehicle line's software simultaneously on a new code base and stop supporting older vehicles.
Keep the separate code bases and hire more engineers for each line to add matching features in parallel.
Freeze new feature development for two years while a single monolithic in-vehicle system is built.

Define a shared, versioned API contract for vehicle services and build common backend capabilities once (for example on Cloud Run and GKE, managed through Apigee), then migrate each vehicle line to the shared platform incrementally behind adapters, with feature flags and a deprecation policy for legacy interfaces.
explanation: Consolidating onto a shared, API-first platform with versioned contracts lets KnightMotives deliver one consistent experience while adapters and a published deprecation policy handle legacy vehicles, and incremental migration limits risk, which is the strangler-fig pattern for reducing technical debt. Option A is a high-risk big bang that abandons customers, damaging the already declining satisfaction. Option B triples effort and preserves the fragmentation that caused the problem. Option C halts delivery for two years in a market where the company is already losing ground, and a monolith recreates coupling. This is an operational-excellence and business-agility decision.
hint: Core Rule (Platform consolidation and API-first design): Consolidating onto a shared, API-first platform with versioned contracts lets KnightMotives deliver one consistent experience while adapters and a published deprecation policy handle legacy vehicles, and incremental migration limits risk, which is the strangler-fig pattern for reducing technical debt.

Store all logs in Cloud Storage buckets and search them with gsutil when an incident is suspected.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. The rearchitected build-to-order system is about to launch on Cloud Run and Spanner. Dealers were burned by the old system's unreliability, and leadership wants evidence before launch that the new system meets its availability and latency targets at three times the expected peak configurator traffic, and that the team will know within minutes if those targets are at risk in production. What should you do?
options: Launch to all dealers and rely on Cloud Run autoscaling to absorb whatever traffic arrives.
Ask a few dealers to try the system manually the week before launch and report any slowness.

Provision the maximum instance count on Cloud Run and the largest Spanner configuration so that performance testing is unnecessary.
explanation: Reliability must be verified, not assumed: explicit SLOs make the target measurable, load testing at a multiple of peak validates the design (including Spanner schema hotspots and downstream dependencies) before dealers are exposed, and burn-rate alerts provide the production early warning leadership asked for. Option A repeats the old system's approach of discovering problems in production. Option B is unscientific and cannot reproduce peak load. Option D wastes money and still does not prove behavior under load, because bottlenecks such as hot keys or third-party dependencies are not solved by capacity. Testing frameworks and reliability validation are explicit exam objectives.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. The new build-to-order platform is deployed across two Google Cloud regions with a global external Application Load Balancer and multi-region Spanner. The architecture document claims the system survives a regional outage, but the claim has never been exercised, and the dealer council wants proof. Which two practices should you adopt to validate and continuously maintain this resilience? (Choose two.)
options: Review the architecture diagram annually with the dealer council and sign an attestation.

Schedule regular game days in which a region's backends are deliberately drained or failed (for example by disabling the backend service in one region or injecting faults) while measuring recovery time against the RTO.
Turn off health checks so the load balancer never removes backends and traffic is always served.
Run automated chaos experiments in pre-production on every release that inject latency and failures into dependencies, with the pipeline failing if SLOs are violated.
Keep a manual runbook that instructs the on-call engineer to change DNS records during an outage.
Reduce the Spanner configuration to a single region to simplify failover testing.
explanation: The Well-Architected Framework reliability pillar recommends proving recovery through regular DR drills and chaos engineering: game days validate real failover behavior and measure RTO, and automated fault-injection tests in the pipeline keep the guarantee true as the system evolves. Chaos engineering and reliability testing appear explicitly in exam objective 6.6.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives wants to deploy a computer-vision quality-inspection model on assembly lines in its plants. Inspection results must be returned in under 50 milliseconds to stop the line on a defect, the plants have limited and sometimes unreliable connectivity to headquarters and the cloud, and the AI team wants to keep training models in Vertex AI and manage plant deployments centrally with the same Kubernetes tooling used in the cloud. What should you do?
options: Stream camera frames to a Vertex AI endpoint in the nearest Google Cloud region and return the inference result to the line controller.
Run inference on Cloud Run functions triggered by frames uploaded to Cloud Storage.
Install standalone GPU workstations on each line with manually copied model files.

explanation: A 50-millisecond, line-stopping decision with unreliable WAN links must be computed on-premises; Google Distributed Cloud connected brings GKE-managed hardware with GPUs into the plant, operates during disconnection, and is managed centrally as part of a fleet, so models trained in Vertex AI can be rolled out consistently across all plants. question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. The platform team wants a single inventory of clusters, uniform security policies, and one deployment workflow across all three locations. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Register the on-premises and other-cloud Kubernetes clusters into the GKE Enterprise fleet as attached clusters (or run GKE on AWS/Azure) so they appear alongside the GKE clusters.
Migrate every cluster to Google Cloud before attempting any standardization.
Use Config Sync and Policy Controller at fleet scope to apply the same namespaces, RBAC, and policy constraints to all member clusters from Git.
Maintain a separate CI/CD pipeline and policy repository per cloud to respect each provider's conventions.
Build custom dashboards per environment by exporting each cluster's metrics to a spreadsheet.
Connect the clusters with VPC Network Peering between the clouds.
explanation: GKE Enterprise fleets are the multicloud management plane: attached clusters (and GKE on other clouds) bring external clusters into the same inventory, and fleet-scoped Config Sync and Policy Controller enforce identical configuration and guardrails everywhere from a single Git source, giving one workflow across Google Cloud, the other cloud, and on-premises. question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives' connected fleet will send sensor telemetry (speed, battery state, lane events) at millions of writes per second. Vehicle services need single-digit-millisecond retrieval of the most recent readings for a given vehicle, while data scientists need to run large analytical queries over months of history for safety statistics. You want a design with managed services and minimal operational overhead. What should you do?
options: Write all telemetry to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with a table partitioned by day and run analytics on a read replica.
Ingest through Pub/Sub into Dataflow, write hot per-vehicle time series to Bigtable with a row key of vehicle ID and reversed timestamp, and stream the same events into BigQuery for analytics.
Store every reading as a JSON object in Cloud Storage and query it with BigQuery external tables.
Write all telemetry directly to Spanner and run both operational and analytical queries there.
explanation: Bigtable is designed for massive write throughput and low-latency key-based reads of time-series data, and a vehicle-ID-plus-reversed-timestamp row key makes 'latest readings for a vehicle' a fast scan; BigQuery serves the analytical workload, and Pub/Sub plus Dataflow feeds both without custom infrastructure. Option A cannot sustain millions of writes per second. Option C produces billions of small objects and slow external-table scans, and cannot provide millisecond lookups. Option D is far more expensive at this ingest volume and Spanner is optimized for relational transactions, not petabyte-scale analytics. This is a performance and cost-optimization decision.
hint: Core Rule (Time-series storage selection): Bigtable is designed for massive write throughput and low-latency key-based reads of time-series data, and a vehicle-ID-plus-reversed-timestamp row key makes 'latest readings for a vehicle' a fast scan; BigQuery serves the analytical workload, and Pub/Sub plus Dataflow feeds both without custom infrastructure.

whyWrong.2: Option C produces billions of small objects and slow external-table scans, and cannot provide millisecond lookups.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. To bring modern features to legacy hybrid and ICE vehicles, KnightMotives will deliver multi-gigabyte over-the-air software packages to millions of vehicles worldwide. Packages must be downloadable only by authenticated vehicles, rolled out in stages (1%, 10%, 100%) so a bad release can be halted, and delivered quickly to vehicles in every region without overloading the origin. What should you do?
options: Host the packages on a Compute Engine web server in one region and let vehicles download directly.
Email dealers a USB image and have vehicles updated during service visits.
Publish packages to a public Cloud Storage bucket and announce the URL to all vehicles simultaneously.

Store packages in Cloud Storage behind Cloud CDN, issue short-lived signed URLs (or signed cookies) to authenticated vehicles from an update service that assigns each vehicle to a rollout cohort, and expand cohorts only when telemetry shows the release is healthy.
explanation: Cloud Storage with Cloud CDN scales global distribution of large binaries with edge caching, signed URLs restrict downloads to authenticated vehicles for a limited time, and an update service controlling cohorts implements staged rollout with the ability to halt, which together meet security, scale, and safety requirements. Option A is a single-region, single-server bottleneck with poor latency for distant vehicles. Option B contradicts the goal of modern, over-the-air experiences and takes months. Option C is insecure and a simultaneous global release cannot be halted if defective. This blends performance optimization with release-management safety.
hint: Core Rule (Content distribution and signed URLs): Cloud Storage with Cloud CDN scales global distribution of large binaries with edge caching, signed URLs restrict downloads to authenticated vehicles for a limited time, and an update service controlling cohorts implements staged rollout with the ability to halt, which together meet security, scale, and safety requirements.

whyWrong.1: Option B contradicts the goal of modern, over-the-air experiences and takes months.
whyWrong.2: Option C is insecure and a simultaneous global release cannot be halted if defective.

topic: Key management and separation of duties
question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. Following past breaches, KnightMotives' security team requires that all driver PII stored in BigQuery and Cloud Storage be encrypted with keys that the security team, not the data-platform team, controls; that keys be rotated automatically; that any data-platform administrator be unable to disable or destroy the keys; and that for the EU autonomous-platform data specifically, Google cannot decrypt the data without a justified, logged request approved by KnightMotives. What should you do?
options: Create Cloud KMS key rings in a dedicated security project owned by the security team with automatic rotation, grant the data-platform service agents only the CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter role, apply CMEK to the datasets and buckets, and for the EU data use Cloud EKM keys held in an external key manager with Key Access Justifications.
Rely on Google default encryption at rest for all data and enable Data Access audit logs so key usage can be reviewed.
Create Cloud KMS keys inside the data-platform project so the platform team can manage encryption alongside the data, and rotate keys manually every quarter.
Encrypt the data client-side with a key stored in Secret Manager in the data-platform project before uploading.
explanation: Separation of duties is achieved by keeping keys in a security-owned project where data administrators only have permission to use, not manage, the keys; CMEK with automatic rotation covers BigQuery and Cloud Storage; and Cloud External Key Manager with Key Access Justifications gives KnightMotives an externally held key and the ability to approve or deny each Google access to it, which satisfies the EU sovereignty requirement. Option B provides no customer control over keys. Option C puts key control in the hands of the team it must be separated from and relies on manual rotation. Option D creates an operational burden, breaks native BigQuery querying, and stores the key where the data team controls it. Managing CMEK with Cloud KMS is an explicit exam objective.
hint: Core Rule (Key management and separation of duties): Separation of duties is achieved by keeping keys in a security-owned project where data administrators only have permission to use, not manage, the keys; CMEK with automatic rotation covers BigQuery and Cloud Storage; and Cloud External Key Manager with Key Access Justifications gives KnightMotives an externally held key and the ability to approve or deny each Google access to it, which satisfies the EU sovereignty requirement.

whyWrong.2: Option C puts key control in the hands of the team it must be separated from and relies on manual rotation.
whyWrong.3: Option D creates an operational burden, breaks native BigQuery querying, and stores the key where the data team controls it.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. Dozens of KnightMotives product teams will start building on Google Cloud during the modernization. Today each new project takes weeks of tickets and ends up configured differently, and the security team fears repeating the misconfigurations that contributed to past breaches. You need teams to get compliant, consistently configured projects within hours, with security baselines they cannot remove. What should you do?
options: Grant each team lead the Organization Administrator role so they can create projects themselves.
Create one shared project for all teams to avoid the overhead of provisioning many projects.

Implement a Terraform-based project factory (for example from the Cloud Foundation Fabric or Toolkit modules) run through Cloud Build or Infrastructure Manager that creates projects in the correct folder with baseline logging, IAM, networking, and enforce organization policy constraints at the folder level; optionally expose it through Service Catalog for self-service.
Document a 40-page manual checklist that each team must follow when creating a project.
explanation: A project factory automates repeatable, reviewed provisioning of projects with the security baseline built in, and organization policy constraints inherited from the folder cannot be removed by project-level administrators, giving both speed and enforced guardrails; Service Catalog adds governed self-service. Option A hands out a highly privileged role, violating least privilege and inviting the misconfigurations feared. Option B eliminates isolation between teams and blast-radius containment. Option D is slow, unenforced, and will drift exactly as before. Service catalog and provisioning is an explicit exam objective under technical processes.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. Migrate the VMs to Google Cloud VMware Engine using HCX, keeping the vSphere tooling and licensing model, and modernize individual applications later.
Rebuild each application on Cloud Run and migrate the databases to Spanner.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. Save every model file with the training date in its filename in a Cloud Storage bucket.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives wants a conversational in-vehicle assistant that behaves identically across BEV, hybrid, and ICE models. Drivers should be able to ask questions answered from the correct owner's manual for their exact model and year, and issue commands such as 'schedule a service appointment at my dealer' that call KnightMotives' backend APIs. Answers must not be fabricated, and the assistant must be updatable centrally without changing vehicle firmware. What should you do?
options: Build the assistant on Vertex AI using a Gemini model with grounding on a Vertex AI Search data store of owner's manuals filtered by model and year, use function calling (tools) to invoke the dealer-scheduling and vehicle APIs, and expose it through a versioned API that the vehicles call.
Embed a different fine-tuned model in each vehicle line's firmware, trained on that line's manual.
Use the Natural Language API to extract entities from the driver's speech and match them against a keyword table of manual sections.
Prompt a Gemini model with no external data and instruct it to answer from its general knowledge of cars.
explanation: Grounding Gemini in a Vertex AI Search data store restricts answers to the authoritative manual content (with metadata filters for model and year), which prevents fabrication; function calling lets the model invoke backend actions; and exposing it as a centrally managed API delivers the cohesive experience across all models while allowing updates without firmware changes. Option B multiplies models, drifts across lines, and cannot be updated centrally, recreating the fragmentation problem. Option C is not conversational and cannot execute actions. Option D will hallucinate model-specific details and has no access to KnightMotives' systems. This supports the case study's consistent-experience and AI-feature requirements.
hint: Core Rule (Generative AI in-vehicle assistant): Grounding Gemini in a Vertex AI Search data store restricts answers to the authoritative manual content (with metadata filters for model and year), which prevents fabrication; function calling lets the model invoke backend actions; and exposing it as a centrally managed API delivers the cohesive experience across all models while allowing updates without firmware changes.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives wants to give hundreds of dealers self-service dashboards on inventory, order pipeline, and service performance built from the BigQuery data platform. Each dealer must see only its own data, KnightMotives analysts must see all dealers, and the business wants to avoid creating and maintaining a separate dashboard or dataset per dealer. What should you do?
options: Create a BigQuery dataset and a Looker Studio report for each dealer and share each one individually.
Export each dealer's data nightly to a spreadsheet and email it to the dealer principal.

Build the dashboards in Looker on a shared semantic model, and enforce dealer scoping with Looker user attributes mapped to dealer IDs (or BigQuery row-level security policies on the underlying tables), so one dashboard serves every dealer with filtered data.
Give every dealer the BigQuery Data Viewer role on the shared dataset and ask them to filter by their dealer ID.
explanation: Looker's governed semantic layer with user attributes (or BigQuery row-level security enforced at the data layer) lets a single dashboard definition serve all dealers while each user sees only permitted rows; analysts get an unrestricted attribute. Option A multiplies maintenance by the number of dealers, the very outcome to avoid. Option B is not self-service and leaks data through email. Option D relies on dealers voluntarily filtering and exposes every dealer's data to every other dealer, a serious confidentiality failure for a company recovering from breaches. This is an operational-efficiency and security decision supporting the dealer-experience requirement.

Enable Sensitive Data Protection discovery (data profiling) at the organization level for BigQuery and Cloud Storage, and publish the resulting profiles and risk scores to Dataplex Universal Catalog and Security Command Center.
Write SQL queries with regular expressions against every table each month to look for PII patterns.
Run the Cloud Data Loss Prevention API once on a sample of tables during the initial project and document the results.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. While the mainframe supply-chain system is being modernized over several years, the data platform team needs daily copies of the mainframe's parts inventory and supplier datasets in BigQuery so that dealer tools and monetization products can use them. The mainframe team will not allow new online transactions or agents that add MIPS-heavy processing during business hours, and the data is stored in EBCDIC-encoded VSAM and sequential files. What should you do?
options: Install a Datastream agent on the mainframe to capture changes from the VSAM files in real time.
Have dealer tools query the mainframe directly through a REST gateway during the day.

Use the Google Cloud Mainframe Connector in the mainframe's nightly batch JCL to transcode the EBCDIC datasets to a BigQuery-compatible format, upload them to Cloud Storage, and load them into BigQuery, offloading the transcoding to Cloud Run where possible to reduce mainframe CPU usage.
Print the datasets to PDF reports and process them with Document AI.
explanation: The Mainframe Connector is designed for exactly this case: it runs inside existing batch JCL, converts EBCDIC/copybook data, moves it to Cloud Storage, and loads BigQuery, and it supports remote transcoding on Cloud Run to minimize mainframe MIPS, respecting the constraint against daytime online load. Option A is wrong because Datastream does not support mainframe VSAM sources. Option B adds online load to the mainframe during business hours and leaves the data siloed rather than in the platform. Option D is an absurdly lossy and fragile path for structured data. This is an integration-pattern decision that unblocks the data-monetization goal during a phased migration.
hint: Core Rule (Mainframe data integration): The Mainframe Connector is designed for exactly this case: it runs inside existing batch JCL, converts EBCDIC/copybook data, moves it to Cloud Storage, and loads BigQuery, and it supports remote transcoding on Cloud Run to minimize mainframe MIPS, respecting the constraint against daytime online load.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. What should you do?
options: Provide Cloud Workstations with preconfigured, security-hardened images inside a VPC, accessed through the browser or local IDE with Identity-Aware Proxy, so code and credentials stay in Google Cloud.
Ship each contractor a company laptop and require them to install the tooling from a wiki page.
Let contractors use their own laptops but require them to email the code to the security team weekly for review.
Create a shared Compute Engine VM with a single user account that all contractors SSH into with a shared key.
explanation: Cloud Workstations provide managed, ephemeral, centrally configured development environments running inside KnightMotives' VPC; source and credentials never leave Google Cloud, images are standardized and patched centrally, and access is governed by IAM and IAP, meeting both the security and day-one productivity goals. Option B is slow, costly, and still places code on endpoints. Option C exposes code on unmanaged devices with only after-the-fact review. Option D uses shared credentials with no isolation or auditability, a serious anti-pattern. Cloud Shell Editor, Cloud Code, and developer tooling fall under exam objective 5.2.
hint: Core Rule (Secure developer environments): Cloud Workstations provide managed, ephemeral, centrally configured development environments running inside KnightMotives' VPC; source and credentials never leave Google Cloud, images are standardized and patched centrally, and access is governed by IAM and IAP, meeting both the security and day-one productivity goals.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. You must guarantee, not merely recommend, that every resource in the autonomous-platform projects for each launch country is created only in the approved in-country region, without slowing development elsewhere in the company. Create one folder per launch country, place that country's autonomous-platform projects in it, and set the constraints/gcp.resourceLocations organization policy on each folder to allow only the approved in-country region(s), leaving the constraint unrestricted on other folders.
Set the resourceLocations constraint at the organization root to allow only the two launch countries' regions.
Use a Terraform variable for region and trust code review to catch mistakes.
explanation: The resource-locations organization policy constraint is enforced by the platform at creation time, so resources cannot be created outside allowed locations; scoping it per country folder gives each launch its own allow list while other folders stay unrestricted, satisfying the 'guarantee' and 'do not slow other teams' requirements. Option A and Option D are advisory controls that depend on humans and only detect violations after the fact. Option C applies the restriction to the entire company, blocking legitimate global workloads and mixing the two countries' data locations together. Resource hierarchy and organization policy are core exam security topics.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. The old build-to-order system often failed silently, and dealers were the first to notice. The new system spans Cloud Run services, Apigee, Spanner, and a SaaS CRM. The engineering lead wants to detect user-visible degradation before dealers do and quickly find which component causes a slow or failed order. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Configure a single email alert that fires on every logged error across all services.

Instrument the services with OpenTelemetry to emit distributed traces and structured logs with a correlation ID, exported to Cloud Trace and Cloud Logging so an order can be followed across Cloud Run, Apigee, and Spanner calls.
Set every service's logging level to DEBUG permanently to capture maximum detail.
Define SLOs on order-submission success rate and latency measured at the edge (load balancer or Apigee), and alert on error-budget burn rate routed to an on-call rotation.
Review dashboards in a weekly meeting and file tickets for anomalies observed.
Rely on Cloud Profiler alone to identify slow orders.
explanation: Detecting user-visible degradation requires SLOs measured where users experience the service, with burn-rate alerts that reach an on-call responder before dealers notice, and diagnosing multi-service failures requires distributed tracing with correlated structured logs so a single order can be followed end to end. Option A is noisy, drowns real signals, and repeats the email-only failure pattern. Option C explodes log volume and cost without improving detection. Option E is far too slow for production incidents. Option F profiles CPU and memory in a process; it does not trace requests across services. Alerting strategies and observability tooling are core to exam section 6.
hint: Core Rule (Observability strategy): Detecting user-visible degradation requires SLOs measured where users experience the service, with burn-rate alerts that reach an on-call responder before dealers notice, and diagnosing multi-service failures requires distributed tracing with correlated structured logs so a single order can be followed end to end.

whyWrong.2: Option C explodes log volume and cost without improving detection.
whyWrong.4: Option E is far too slow for production incidents.
whyWrong.5: Option F profiles CPU and memory in a process; it does not trace requests across services.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. The build-to-order platform on Cloud Run receives frequent releases for new promotions and dealer discounts. A recent release contained a pricing bug that affected every dealer for two hours before it was rolled back manually. KnightMotives wants future releases to reach a small fraction of traffic first, be promoted automatically only if error rate and latency stay healthy, and roll back without human intervention otherwise. What should you do?
options: Deploy new revisions directly to 100% of traffic but schedule releases at 3 a.m. when order volume is low.
Maintain two identical Cloud Run services and switch DNS between them after manual verification.
Add more manual QA sign-offs before each release to catch bugs earlier.

Use Cloud Deploy with a canary deployment strategy for the Cloud Run target, shifting traffic in steps (for example 5%, 25%, 100%) with automated verification against Cloud Monitoring metrics and automatic rollback when verification fails.
explanation: Cloud Deploy natively supports canary strategies for Cloud Run using revision traffic splitting, with verification phases that can evaluate metrics and automatically roll back or halt promotion, which limits the blast radius of a bad release to a small share of traffic and removes the human delay. Option A still exposes all dealers to a defect and ignores global time zones. Option B is a blue/green pattern that relies on manual checks and DNS propagation, offering no gradual exposure. Option C slows delivery and cannot catch every production-only issue. Deployment and release management is an explicit exam objective in section 6.
hint: Core Rule (Progressive delivery): Cloud Deploy natively supports canary strategies for Cloud Run using revision traffic splitting, with verification phases that can evaluate metrics and automatically roll back or halt promotion, which limits the blast radius of a bad release to a small share of traffic and removes the human delay.

whyWrong.1: Option B is a blue/green pattern that relies on manual checks and DNS propagation, offering no gradual exposure.
whyWrong.2: Option C slows delivery and cannot catch every production-only issue.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives' incident response plan must cover a ransomware scenario in which an attacker with stolen administrator credentials encrypts or deletes production data. The dealer back-office systems run on Compute Engine and Google Cloud VMware Engine, and the build-to-order orders live in Spanner. The recovery point objective is 1 hour and backups must survive even if the attacker has project Owner permissions. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Take persistent disk snapshots into the same project and grant the backup operator the Owner role for convenience.

Use Backup and DR Service with a backup vault in a separate, tightly controlled project, with enforced minimum retention (immutable and indelible backups), for the Compute Engine and VMware Engine workloads.
Rely on Spanner's multi-region replication as the backup, because data is already copied to another region.

Enable Spanner point-in-time recovery with a retention period of several days, and schedule Spanner backups (copied to a separate project or region) to recover from logical deletion or malicious writes.
Store backups on a Filestore share mounted read-write on the production VMs for fast restores.
Disable Cloud Audit Logs to reduce the amount of data an attacker could tamper with.
explanation: Ransomware resilience requires backups that a compromised production administrator cannot alter: Backup and DR Service backup vaults are isolated from the source project and enforce retention so backups cannot be deleted early even by an Owner, and Spanner point-in-time recovery plus scheduled backups protect against malicious writes and deletes, which replication alone faithfully propagates. Option A keeps backups within the attacker's reach and over-privileges the operator. Option C confuses high availability with backup; replication copies the encryption or deletion instantly. Option E exposes backups to the same compromised hosts. Option F destroys forensic evidence needed for incident response. Disaster recovery and business continuity are core exam topics under section 4.
hint: Core Rule (Ransomware resilience and backup): Ransomware resilience requires backups that a compromised production administrator cannot alter: Backup and DR Service backup vaults are isolated from the source project and enforce retention so backups cannot be deleted early even by an Owner, and Spanner point-in-time recovery plus scheduled backups protect against malicious writes and deletes, which replication alone faithfully propagates.

whyWrong.0: Option A keeps backups within the attacker's reach and over-privileges the operator.
whyWrong.2: Option C confuses high availability with backup; replication copies the encryption or deletion instantly.
whyWrong.4: Option E exposes backups to the same compromised hosts.
whyWrong.5: Option F destroys forensic evidence needed for incident response.

question: For this question, refer to the KnightMotives Automotive case study. KnightMotives' steering committee must choose the first workload for its five-year modernization program. The in-vehicle software platform, because it has the largest long-term revenue potential.
The ERP, because finance owns the budget for the program.

Option C involves safety-critical embedded systems, hardware constraints, and regulatory complexity that are unsuitable for a first project. Option D selects based on budget ownership rather than risk and value. This reflects the exam's decision-making and stakeholder-management objectives.

whyWrong.1: Option B chooses the highest-risk, most entangled system with scarce skills as the first move, which could derail the program.

The platform must keep answering from the complete document rather than partial excerpts. What should you do?
options: Reduce the document to a 10-page summary and use it as the context for all questions.
Create a Gemini context cache containing the case file at the start of the session and reference the cache in each follow-up request.
Switch every request to batch prediction to benefit from discounted token pricing.
Increase the maximum output tokens so the model can answer more questions per request.
explanation: Context caching stores a large, repeated prompt prefix such as the full case file on the Vertex AI side so that subsequent requests reference the cache instead of resending the tokens, which cuts input cost significantly and reduces latency while still giving the model the entire document. Option A violates the requirement to answer from the complete document. Option C is for asynchronous offline workloads and would not support interactive sessions. Option D affects output length only and does nothing about repeated input tokens.
hint: Core Rule: Context caching stores a large, repeated prompt prefix such as the full case file on the Vertex AI side so that subsequent requests reference the cache instead of resending the tokens, which cuts input cost significantly and reduces latency while still giving the model the entire document.

whyWrong.0: Option A violates the requirement to answer from the complete document.
whyWrong.2: Option C is for asynchronous offline workloads and would not support interactive sessions.
whyWrong.3: Option D affects output length only and does nothing about repeated input tokens.

question: A customer-review platform uses a large Gemini Pro model to extract structured attributes from reviews with 96% accuracy, but at 50 million reviews per month the cost is unsustainable. Experiments with a small Flash-Lite model using the same prompt achieve only 85% accuracy. The team is willing to invest engineering effort once to bring cost down while keeping accuracy above 94%. What should you do?
options: Reduce the number of attributes extracted per review so the large model uses fewer output tokens.

Use the large model to label a representative sample of reviews, then perform supervised fine-tuning of the small model on those labels (distillation) and validate it meets the 94% target before switching traffic.
Send only every third review to the large model and mark the rest as unprocessed.
Run the large model through batch prediction and accept the resulting cost.
explanation: Distilling knowledge from a large teacher model into a small student model by generating high-quality labels and supervised-tuning the smaller model typically recovers most of the accuracy gap at a fraction of the inference cost, and validation against a held-out set confirms the 94% requirement before cutover. Option A changes the product output rather than the cost structure and does not solve the volume problem. Option C drops functionality for two thirds of reviews. Option D lowers cost only modestly and does not address the fundamental per-token expense of the large model.
hint: Core Rule (Model distillation): Distilling knowledge from a large teacher model into a small student model by generating high-quality labels and supervised-tuning the smaller model typically recovers most of the accuracy gap at a fraction of the inference cost, and validation against a held-out set confirms the 94% requirement before cutover.

whyWrong.0: Option A changes the product output rather than the cost structure and does not solve the volume problem.
whyWrong.2: Option C drops functionality for two thirds of reviews.
whyWrong.3: Option D lowers cost only modestly and does not address the fundamental per-token expense of the large model.

question: An engineering firm built a RAG assistant on Vertex AI Search over 50,000 technical PDFs containing tables and diagrams. Users report that answers often cite the wrong section, tables are misread, and exact part numbers are sometimes missed by semantic retrieval. Which two changes should you make to improve answer quality? (Choose two.)
options: Enable the layout parser with document chunking in the data store so tables, headings and sections are parsed into structured, well-bounded chunks.
Switch retrieval to a hybrid mode that combines semantic search with keyword matching, and apply the ranking API to rerank retrieved chunks before generation.
Increase the model temperature so the model can guess missing part numbers more creatively.
Replace the PDFs with screenshots of each page so the model sees the diagrams as images.
Remove citations from the response so users are not confused by wrong references.
explanation: Retrieval quality is the root cause: the layout parser with chunking preserves document structure such as tables and section boundaries so the right passages are retrieved and cited, while hybrid search restores exact keyword matching for identifiers like part numbers and reranking improves the ordering of context passed to the model. Option C increases hallucination rather than accuracy. Option D discards extractable text, making retrieval worse. Option E hides the symptom and reduces trust and verifiability.
hint: Core Rule (RAG quality): Retrieval quality is the root cause: the layout parser with chunking preserves document structure such as tables and section boundaries so the right passages are retrieved and cited, while hybrid search restores exact keyword matching for identifiers like part numbers and reranking improves the ordering of context passed to the model.

whyWrong.2: Option C increases hallucination rather than accuracy.
whyWrong.3: Option D discards extractable text, making retrieval worse.
whyWrong.4: Option E hides the symptom and reduces trust and verifiability.

question: A pan-African fintech records support calls in Swahili, Amharic, Yoruba and heavily accented English, and the legacy speech model's transcription accuracy is poor for these languages. The company wants a managed API with broad language coverage and strong accuracy on accented speech, and it also needs automatic language identification because many calls switch languages. options: Use Cloud Translation to translate the audio directly into English text.
Train a custom acoustic model per language on Vertex AI using thousands of hours of labeled audio.
Use the Natural Language API, which supports over 100 languages.
Use Speech-to-Text v2 with the Chirp universal speech model family, enabling multi-language recognition and language identification.

question: A national railway operator wants to generate spoken platform announcements and app notifications in 15 languages from text, with natural-sounding voices and the ability to control pronunciation of station names and pauses. options: Speech-to-Text with the output played back through the station speakers.
Gemini with a prompt asking it to describe how the announcement should sound.
Cloud Text-to-Speech with high-definition neural voices, using SSML for pronunciation, pauses and emphasis.
Dialogflow CX with a telephony gateway connected to the station audio system.

question: A logistics company is building an internal analytics agent with the Agent Development Kit that must answer questions by querying data in AlloyDB and BigQuery. Security requires that the agent can only run pre-approved, parameterized queries, that database credentials never appear in prompts, and that the same tools be reusable by other agents without duplicating connection code. Which design should you recommend?
options: Have the agent generate arbitrary SQL from natural language and execute it with a service account that has read access to all tables.

Expose the approved queries as tools through the MCP Toolbox for Databases (a Model Context Protocol server) that holds the connections and parameters, and connect the ADK agent to it as an MCP tool source.
Embed the database connection string and password in the system instruction so the model can connect directly.
Export both databases to CSV files nightly and place them in the model context for each request.
explanation: MCP Toolbox for Databases is Google's open-source MCP server that centralizes database connections, authentication and a curated set of parameterized tools; agents built with the Agent Development Kit consume those tools over the Model Context Protocol, so credentials stay out of prompts, only approved queries can run, and multiple agents reuse the same tools. Option A allows unbounded SQL and broad access, a serious security and correctness risk. Option C leaks secrets into prompts and models cannot open database connections. Option D provides stale data and does not scale to database-sized content.
hint: Core Rule (Agent tooling for databases): MCP Toolbox for Databases is Google's open-source MCP server that centralizes database connections, authentication and a curated set of parameterized tools; agents built with the Agent Development Kit consume those tools over the Model Context Protocol, so credentials stay out of prompts, only approved queries can run, and multiple agents reuse the same tools.

Conversational Agents (Dialogflow CX) with a webchat integration.

question: An insurer deployed a custom claims-severity regression model on a Vertex AI endpoint six months ago. Business users report that predictions have become less accurate, but the ML team has no visibility into whether the input data distribution has changed since training. They want automated detection and alerting for such changes using managed features. What should you do?
options: Retrain the model every week regardless of performance to keep it fresh.
Export prediction logs to BigQuery and ask analysts to review histograms monthly.
Replace the regression model with a Gemini prompt that estimates severity.
Enable Vertex AI Model Monitoring on the endpoint to detect training-serving skew and prediction drift for input features, with alert thresholds and notifications.

Move the integration to the Gemini API on Vertex AI, which supports IAM, VPC Service Controls, CMEK, regional endpoints and enterprise data governance terms.

question: A telecom operator wants to use Gemini on Vertex AI to summarize customer chat transcripts for agent hand-off. Privacy rules state that names, phone numbers and account identifiers must not be sent to the model or stored in its logs, while summaries must remain useful for agents. Which two design decisions should you include? (Choose two.)
options: Run each transcript through Sensitive Data Protection de-identification (for example, tokenization or replacement of detected PII infoTypes) before sending it to the model, and re-identify only where necessary in the agent UI.
Send the transcript unmodified but instruct the model in the system prompt to omit personal data from the summary.
Disable request-response logging for the Gemini calls and confirm the Vertex AI data governance terms so prompts are not retained for training.
Store the raw transcripts in a public Cloud Storage bucket so the model can retrieve them by URL.
Use the consumer Gemini app to paste transcripts because it is free of charge.

options: Filestore Basic HDD mounted on every node.
A multi-region Cloud Storage bucket to increase available bandwidth.
A Standard Persistent Disk attached to each node containing a copy of the dataset.
Google Cloud Managed Lustre (or Parallelstore) as a parallel file system, hydrating the dataset from Cloud Storage and using it for checkpoints.

question: A regional grocery chain is documenting requirements for a new online ordering platform on Google Cloud. During a stakeholder workshop, the product owner lists several statements. You need to separate the non-functional requirements, which will drive your infrastructure design, from the functional ones. Which statement is a non-functional requirement?
options: Customers must be able to filter products by dietary preference and brand.
Store managers must receive a daily email summarizing unfulfilled orders.
The checkout API must respond within 300 ms at the 95th percentile during peak traffic.
Loyalty points must be applied automatically when a customer enters a membership number.
explanation: Non-functional requirements describe how a system must behave (performance, availability, security, scalability, cost), while functional requirements describe what it must do. A latency target at a percentile under peak load is a classic non-functional requirement that directly influences architecture choices such as load balancer type, caching with Cloud CDN or Memorystore, and regional placement. Options A, B and D each describe a feature or business behavior the application must implement (filtering, notifications, loyalty logic), so they are functional requirements. Correctly identifying NFRs early is the first step in applying the Well-Architected Framework performance and reliability pillars.
hint: Core Rule (Functional vs non-functional requirements): Non-functional requirements describe how a system must behave (performance, availability, security, scalability, cost), while functional requirements describe what it must do.

question: The CIO of a mid-sized insurance company has sponsored a migration of the claims-processing platform to Google Cloud. question: A manufacturing company is evaluating whether to migrate 300 on-premises VMs to Google Cloud. The finance team built a spreadsheet comparing the annual hardware depreciation of the existing servers against the list price of equivalent Compute Engine instances and concluded that staying on-premises is 40% cheaper. You have been asked to review the analysis before it is presented to the board. What should you do?
options: Accept the analysis because hardware depreciation is the only cost that changes when moving to the cloud.
Recommend delaying the decision until the next hardware refresh so the comparison can be repeated with newer servers.
Replace the spreadsheet with a simple comparison of monthly on-premises power bills against the Google Cloud pricing calculator estimate.

Rebuild the comparison as a full TCO model that adds facilities, power and cooling, staff time, software licensing, hardware refresh and support, and that applies rightsizing and committed use discounts to the cloud side using Migration Center data.
explanation: A credible TCO comparison must include all direct and indirect costs of running on-premises (data center space, power, cooling, network, hardware refresh cycles, support contracts, operations staff, licensing) and must model the cloud side realistically: rightsized machine types based on observed utilization, committed use discounts, and the ability to turn off idle environments. Migration Center collects utilization data and generates a TCO report that automates much of this. Option A ignores the majority of on-premises costs and inflates cloud costs by using list price for oversized instances. Option B just defers the decision and does not fix the flawed methodology. Option C swaps one incomplete comparison for another by ignoring staff, licensing and refresh costs. This aligns with the cost optimization pillar of the Well-Architected Framework.
hint: Core Rule (TCO analysis): A credible TCO comparison must include all direct and indirect costs of running on-premises (data center space, power, cooling, network, hardware refresh cycles, support contracts, operations staff, licensing) and must model the cloud side realistically: rightsized machine types based on observed utilization, committed use discounts, and the ability to turn off idle environments.

question: A logistics company has run its core routing application on Compute Engine for 18 months. Utilization data shows a stable baseline of 60 vCPUs and 240 GB of memory in us-central1 around the clock, with occasional spikes during holiday seasons. The CFO wants predictable monthly spending and the lowest possible cost without changing the application. What should you recommend?
options: Purchase reserved capacity by paying for the servers up front as a capital expense and depreciate them over three years.
Purchase a 3-year resource-based committed use discount covering the baseline vCPU and memory, and rely on on-demand instances for the seasonal spikes.
Convert all instances to Spot VMs to obtain the largest available discount and accept occasional preemption.
Move the application to sole-tenant nodes so that the company controls the physical hardware and can amortize it.
explanation: In the cloud, compute is an operating expense; the way to obtain predictable, discounted pricing for a steady-state workload is a committed use discount (CUD). A resource-based CUD for the observed baseline delivers up to 55% savings (3-year) while the seasonal spikes stay on flexible on-demand capacity, so you never over-commit. Option A describes an on-premises capital purchasing model that does not exist in Google Cloud. Option C is wrong because Spot VMs can be preempted at any time and are unsuitable for a core production application that must run continuously. Option D adds significant cost and is meant for licensing or compliance isolation requirements, not for cost reduction. This is a direct application of the cost optimization pillar.
hint: Core Rule (CapEx vs OpEx): In the cloud, compute is an operating expense; the way to obtain predictable, discounted pricing for a steady-state workload is a committed use discount (CUD).

whyWrong.0: Option A describes an on-premises capital purchasing model that does not exist in Google Cloud.
whyWrong.2: Option C is wrong because Spot VMs can be preempted at any time and are unsuitable for a core production application that must run continuously.
whyWrong.3: Option D adds significant cost and is meant for licensing or compliance isolation requirements, not for cost reduction.

question: A media company has inventoried 40 on-premises applications ahead of a Google Cloud migration. The portfolio includes a self-hosted email and calendar server, an internal reporting tool that access logs show has had no logins in 14 months, a heavily customized mainframe billing system with 3 years of remaining vendor support, and a commodity ticketing application whose vendor offers an equivalent SaaS edition. Leadership wants to minimize migration effort and long-term operational overhead. Which two disposition decisions are consistent with Google-recommended practice? (Choose two.)
options: Refactor the mainframe billing system into microservices in the first migration wave because it is the most business-critical workload.
Retire the internal reporting tool after confirming with its former owners and archiving any required data to Cloud Storage.
Rehost the self-hosted email server onto a Compute Engine VM so that the existing administrators can keep managing it.
Replace the commodity ticketing application with the vendor's SaaS edition instead of migrating the servers.
Rebuild the ticketing application in-house on Cloud Run to avoid paying subscription fees.
explanation: Disposition (the six or seven Rs) should be driven by business value and effort. An application with no users for over a year is a retire candidate; confirming with stakeholders and archiving data protects against surprises. A commodity application with a SaaS equivalent is a replace (buy) candidate because it removes migration work and ongoing operations entirely. Option A is wrong because tackling the most complex, business-critical system first with the riskiest strategy (refactor) contradicts the recommended approach of starting with simpler workloads to build experience; the mainframe is a retain or later-wave candidate. Option C keeps operational overhead for a commodity capability that should be replaced with a SaaS offering such as Google Workspace. Option E rebuilds a non-differentiating capability, which is the most expensive option and does not minimize effort.
hint: Core Rule (Workload disposition strategies): Disposition (the six or seven Rs) should be driven by business value and effort.

question: A 200-employee specialty insurer needs a customer relationship management (CRM) capability to replace spreadsheets. The company has four developers who are fully occupied maintaining the policy administration system, which is the company's competitive differentiator. The CEO wants the CRM live within three months and asks whether the team should build it on Google Cloud. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Build a custom CRM on GKE Autopilot so that the developers gain Kubernetes experience for future projects.
Build a lightweight CRM on Cloud Run with Firestore because serverless keeps costs near zero at this scale.
Buy a SaaS CRM from Google Cloud Marketplace or a vendor and integrate it with the policy system through APIs, keeping developer time focused on the differentiating workload.
Deploy an open-source CRM on Compute Engine and modify it to the insurer's needs.
explanation: The deciding factors are a non-differentiating capability, a tiny development team already committed to the strategic system, and a three-month deadline. Google-recommended practice is to buy commodity capabilities and build only where it creates competitive advantage; a SaaS CRM (often procurable through Cloud Marketplace, which consolidates billing) meets the timeline with minimal operational overhead and can be integrated using APIs or Application Integration. Options A and B both consume scarce developer capacity on undifferentiated work and are very unlikely to meet the deadline with a mature feature set. Option D still requires the team to operate, patch and customize the software, shifting effort away from the policy system. This is a workload disposition decision favoring 'buy' over 'build'.
hint: Core Rule (Build vs buy): The deciding factors are a non-differentiating capability, a tiny development team already committed to the strategic system, and a three-month deadline.

question: A national retailer's architecture team must present the return on investment (ROI) of moving its e-commerce platform from a colocation facility to Google Cloud. The initial draft counts only the reduction in server and colocation costs and shows a marginal ROI, which the CFO finds unconvincing. How should you strengthen the business case?
options: Quantify additional benefits such as revenue protected by higher availability during peak sales, revenue from faster feature releases, avoided hardware refresh capital, and reduced operations effort, and measure each against a documented baseline.
Increase the projected savings by assuming that all instances will run on Spot VMs at the maximum discount.
Exclude the one-time migration and dual-running costs from the calculation so that the ROI appears higher.
Present only qualitative benefits such as innovation and modernization, because business value from cloud cannot be quantified.
explanation: A robust ROI model captures both cost side and value side benefits: avoided CapEx for the next hardware refresh, lower operations toil, revenue protected through improved availability and scalability during peak events, and revenue enabled by faster release cycles. Each benefit must be tied to a measured baseline so it can be validated after migration. Option B fabricates savings with an unrealistic assumption; a customer-facing e-commerce tier cannot run entirely on preemptible capacity. Option C hides real costs and would destroy credibility with finance. Option D abandons the quantitative case that the CFO explicitly requires; cloud benefits such as availability and delivery lead time can and should be quantified.
hint: Core Rule (ROI and business case): A robust ROI model captures both cost side and value side benefits: avoided CapEx for the next hardware refresh, lower operations toil, revenue protected through improved availability and scalability during peak events, and revenue enabled by faster release cycles.

whyWrong.1: Option B fabricates savings with an unrealistic assumption; a customer-facing e-commerce tier cannot run entirely on preemptible capacity.
whyWrong.2: Option C hides real costs and would destroy credibility with finance.
whyWrong.3: Option D abandons the quantitative case that the CFO explicitly requires; cloud benefits such as availability and delivery lead time can and should be quantified.

question: An online ticketing company runs its order platform in a single Google Cloud region. The business continuity plan states that after a regional outage the company can tolerate losing at most 5 minutes of orders and must be selling tickets again within 1 hour. The CFO wants the lowest-cost architecture that meets these targets. Which disaster recovery pattern should you implement?
options: Backup and restore: take nightly database backups to a multi-region Cloud Storage bucket and rebuild the environment in a second region from Terraform when needed.
Pilot light: continuously replicate the database to a second region and keep application tier definitions ready so that compute is provisioned and scaled up only during a failover.
Hot standby: run a fully scaled, active-active deployment across two regions behind a global external Application Load Balancer.
Cold standby: copy disk snapshots to the second region weekly and store application images in Artifact Registry.
explanation: The requirements translate to an RPO of 5 minutes and an RTO of 1 hour. Only continuous data replication can satisfy a 5-minute RPO, and a 1-hour RTO leaves enough time to start and scale the application tier from prepared instance templates or GKE manifests, so a pilot light (data replicated, minimal compute) is the cheapest pattern that meets both targets. Option A fails the RPO because nightly backups can lose up to 24 hours of data. Option C meets the targets but is the most expensive pattern, doubling compute cost, which violates the cost constraint. Option D fails both RPO (weekly) and probably RTO. Matching the DR pattern to RPO/RTO and cost is a core reliability pillar decision.
hint: Core Rule (Business continuity and DR patterns): The requirements translate to an RPO of 5 minutes and an RTO of 1 hour.

whyWrong.0: Option A fails the RPO because nightly backups can lose up to 24 hours of data.
whyWrong.2: Option C meets the targets but is the most expensive pattern, doubling compute cost, which violates the cost constraint.
whyWrong.3: Option D fails both RPO (weekly) and probably RTO.

question: A fintech startup's product manager writes the following requirement for a new payments API on Google Cloud: 'The API should be fast and almost never go down.' As the architect, you need this requirement to be testable and to drive design decisions. What should you do?
options: Accept the requirement as written and choose the largest machine types available to guarantee speed.
Ask the development team to interpret the requirement during implementation.
Work with the product manager to rewrite it as measurable targets, for example 99% of requests complete in under 200 ms and 99.9% monthly availability, and define how each will be measured.
Replace the requirement with a statement that the API will use a global external Application Load Balancer.
explanation: Vague non-functional requirements cannot be verified, priced or designed against. Turning them into service level objectives with explicit indicators (latency percentile, availability over a time window) and a measurement method (for example, load balancer request logs in Cloud Monitoring) makes the requirement testable and allows you to compute what redundancy and capacity the design needs. Option A over-provisions without knowing the target and still does not address availability. Option B pushes an unresolved business decision onto developers, leading to inconsistent interpretations. Option D substitutes a technology choice for a requirement; the load balancer is a possible means, not the requirement itself.
hint: Core Rule (Measurable non-functional requirements): Vague non-functional requirements cannot be verified, priced or designed against.

whyWrong.0: Option A over-provisions without knowing the target and still does not address availability.
whyWrong.1: Option B pushes an unresolved business decision onto developers, leading to inconsistent interpretations.
whyWrong.3: Option D substitutes a technology choice for a requirement; the load balancer is a possible means, not the requirement itself.

question: A software company's Google Cloud bill shows that development and test environments on Compute Engine account for 45% of monthly spend, even though engineers only use them during business hours on weekdays. The CI system also runs stateless build agents on standard VMs 24 hours a day. The finance team asks you to reduce OpEx with the least operational overhead and without affecting production. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Attach an instance schedule resource policy that automatically stops the dev and test VMs outside business hours and starts them each weekday morning.
Purchase a 3-year committed use discount that covers all dev, test and CI instances at their current size.
Run the stateless CI build agents on Spot VMs, using a managed instance group so preempted agents are recreated automatically.
Migrate all dev and test environments to sole-tenant nodes to consolidate them on fewer hosts.
Increase the machine types of the dev VMs so that engineers finish work faster and the VMs can be shut down sooner.
explanation: The two highest-impact, lowest-effort levers are eliminating idle time and using cheaper capacity for interruptible work. Instance schedules are a native Compute Engine resource policy that stop and start VMs on a calendar with no custom automation, directly removing roughly two-thirds of dev/test running hours. Stateless CI agents tolerate interruption, so Spot VMs (60-91% cheaper) in a managed instance group are the recommended fit. Option B is wrong because a long-term commitment for environments that should be running only a third of the time locks in waste. Option D increases cost; sole-tenant nodes carry a premium and are meant for licensing or isolation needs. Option E is speculative and raises per-hour cost without a guaranteed reduction in hours.
hint: Core Rule (Cost optimization for non-production): The two highest-impact, lowest-effort levers are eliminating idle time and using cheaper capacity for interruptible work.

whyWrong.1: Option B is wrong because a long-term commitment for environments that should be running only a third of the time locks in waste.
whyWrong.3: Option D increases cost; sole-tenant nodes carry a premium and are meant for licensing or isolation needs.
whyWrong.4: Option E is speculative and raises per-hour cost without a guaranteed reduction in hours.

question: A global gaming publisher is designing a player inventory service that will be used by players in North America, Europe and Asia. Business requirements state that inventory updates must be strongly consistent worldwide (a player cannot trade the same item twice), the service must survive the loss of an entire region with no data loss, and the team wants to avoid building custom replication logic. The finance team notes the storage budget is limited, so the team should not over-provision. Which design should you recommend?
options: Deploy Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with high availability in one region and asynchronous cross-region read replicas in the other two regions.
Use Bigtable with multi-cluster replication across three regions and single-row transactions.
Run Firestore in Datastore mode in a single multi-region location and add application-level locking in Memorystore.
Use Spanner with a multi-region instance configuration that spans the required continents, sizing compute with autoscaling to the actual load.
explanation: The deciding requirements are global strong consistency, zero data loss on regional failure (RPO 0) and no custom replication logic. Spanner multi-region configurations provide synchronous replication across regions with external consistency and 99.999% availability, and autoscaling lets you pay only for the compute needed, addressing the budget concern. Option A fails because cross-region Cloud SQL replicas are asynchronous, so a regional failure can lose committed writes and reads on replicas are eventually consistent. Option B is wrong because Bigtable replication is eventually consistent between clusters, so a double-trade could occur. Option C introduces a custom locking layer (which the business wants to avoid) and a single-region cache becomes a point of failure. This is a classic trade-off where the consistency and reliability requirements justify a higher unit price for Spanner.
hint: Core Rule (Design trade-offs): The deciding requirements are global strong consistency, zero data loss on regional failure (RPO 0) and no custom replication logic.

whyWrong.0: Option A fails because cross-region Cloud SQL replicas are asynchronous, so a regional failure can lose committed writes and reads on replicas are eventually consistent.
whyWrong.1: Option B is wrong because Bigtable replication is eventually consistent between clusters, so a double-trade could occur.
whyWrong.2: Option C introduces a custom locking layer (which the business wants to avoid) and a single-region cache becomes a point of failure.

question: A hospital group runs a 12-year-old human resources application on-premises that has accumulated hundreds of customizations. The vendor now offers a multi-tenant SaaS edition and will end support for the on-premises version in 24 months. The HR director wants the SaaS version, but the IT team is worried that the customizations will be lost. You are asked to plan the disposition of this workload. What should you do first?
options: Rehost the application to Compute Engine using Migrate to Virtual Machines so that support can be extended.

Run a fit-gap analysis that maps each existing customization to a business process and determines which are still required, which the SaaS edition covers natively, and which need integration or a process change.
Refactor the application into containers on GKE so the customizations can be maintained by the internal team indefinitely.
Sign the SaaS contract immediately to lock in pricing and migrate the data with Database Migration Service.
explanation: Before deciding between replace, modify or rehost, you need to understand which customizations still deliver business value. A fit-gap analysis is the recommended first step: it usually reveals that many legacy customizations are obsolete or can be replaced by standard SaaS features, and it identifies the few gaps that need integration (for example, through Apigee or Application Integration) or a business process change. Option A extends the life of the legacy stack without addressing the end-of-support deadline and keeps operational overhead. Option C is the most expensive path and commits the hospital to owning code for a non-differentiating HR function. Option D commits to a decision before the gaps are understood, and Database Migration Service is a tool for migrating relational databases into Cloud SQL or AlloyDB, not for loading data into a vendor SaaS.
hint: Core Rule (Workload disposition: replace with SaaS): Before deciding between replace, modify or rehost, you need to understand which customizations still deliver business value.

whyWrong.0: Option A extends the life of the legacy stack without addressing the end-of-support deadline and keeps operational overhead.
whyWrong.2: Option C is the most expensive path and commits the hospital to owning code for a non-differentiating HR function.
whyWrong.3: Option D commits to a decision before the gaps are understood, and Database Migration Service is a tool for migrating relational databases into Cloud SQL or AlloyDB, not for loading data into a vendor SaaS.

question: A regional bank's data center lease expires in nine months and will not be renewed. The bank has about 500 VMware VMs running a mix of Java web applications, Windows file servers and internal tools. The CTO wants to avoid a large capital purchase of new hardware and does not want to delay the exit. Which migration approach should you recommend?
options: Refactor every application into microservices on GKE before the lease ends so that the bank arrives in the cloud with a modern architecture.
Purchase a small amount of new hardware for a temporary colocation facility, then migrate to Google Cloud over the next three years.
Rehost the majority of VMs with Migrate to Virtual Machines (or Google Cloud VMware Engine for VMs that cannot be modified), meet the deadline, and then modernize selected workloads in later waves.
Rebuild all applications as serverless services on Cloud Run because it has the lowest operating cost.
explanation: The binding constraints are a hard nine-month deadline, avoidance of CapEx, and 500 heterogeneous VMs. Rehosting (lift and shift) with Migrate to Virtual Machines is the fastest, lowest-risk path for a large VM estate, and Google Cloud VMware Engine offers an even more transparent landing zone for VMs that depend on vSphere features. Once the data center exit is achieved, the bank can pursue a 'move and improve' strategy, modernizing high-value workloads with better information. Option A is unrealistic for 500 VMs in nine months and concentrates risk. Option B incurs the capital spend the CTO wants to avoid and merely defers the problem. Option D, like A, requires rewriting everything and ignores workloads such as Windows file servers that are not suitable for Cloud Run.
hint: Core Rule (Migration strategy under time constraint): The binding constraints are a hard nine-month deadline, avoidance of CapEx, and 500 heterogeneous VMs.

whyWrong.0: Option A is unrealistic for 500 VMs in nine months and concentrates risk.
whyWrong.1: Option B incurs the capital spend the CTO wants to avoid and merely defers the problem.
whyWrong.3: Option D, like A, requires rewriting everything and ignores workloads such as Windows file servers that are not suitable for Cloud Run.

question: The board of a payments processor has asked the cloud architecture team to produce a business continuity plan (BCP) for the Google Cloud platform that hosts its transaction services. The team's draft consists solely of a diagram showing a second region with database replication. Which two elements should you add so the document qualifies as a business continuity plan rather than only a technical disaster recovery design? (Choose two.)
options: A business impact analysis that ranks each business process by criticality and assigns an RTO and RPO to it.
A list of the Compute Engine machine types used in the secondary region.
A detailed comparison of Cloud Storage class pricing for backup retention.
Defined roles, decision authority for invoking failover, a communication plan for customers and regulators, and a schedule for regular testing of the plan.
The Terraform module version numbers used to build the environment.
explanation: A business continuity plan goes beyond infrastructure: it starts with a business impact analysis that identifies critical processes and sets their recovery objectives, and it defines the people and process side of recovery, including who decides to fail over, how stakeholders and regulators are informed, and how often the plan is exercised to prove it works. These elements ensure the technical DR design is proportionate to business risk and can be executed under stress. Options B, C and E are implementation details that belong in runbooks or infrastructure documentation; they do not make the plan a BCP. Testing and clear ownership are core recommendations of the reliability pillar of the Well-Architected Framework.
hint: Core Rule (Business continuity planning): A business continuity plan goes beyond infrastructure: it starts with a business impact analysis that identifies critical processes and sets their recovery objectives, and it defines the people and process side of recovery, including who decides to fail over, how stakeholders and regulators are informed, and how often the plan is exercised to prove it works.
