question: A municipal government has adopted a cloud-first strategy. A department requests a new document-approval workflow system and its IT lead proposes purchasing two servers for the city's server room because 'that is how we have always done it'. As the enterprise architect, how should you apply the cloud-first strategy to this request?
options: Approve the servers because the workload is small and the server room has spare capacity.
Require the department to build a custom application on Compute Engine VMs in Google Cloud.
Reject the request and ask the department to wait until a city-wide cloud migration program is finished.

Evaluate options in order of preference: an existing SaaS or Google Cloud Marketplace workflow product first, then a managed or serverless Google Cloud build (for example, Cloud Run with Firestore and Workflows), and permit on-premises hardware only with a documented justification.
explanation: Cloud-first means the default answer for any new capability is a cloud-delivered service, evaluated from the highest abstraction downward (SaaS, then managed and serverless platforms, then infrastructure), with on-premises hardware requiring an explicit exception based on constraints such as data sovereignty or connectivity. This maximizes agility and minimizes operational overhead and capital spend. Option A perpetuates capital purchases and undifferentiated operations. Option B prescribes the lowest abstraction and custom build without considering buy options. Option C blocks the business need unnecessarily; cloud-first applies to new work regardless of legacy migration status.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud-first design principle): Cloud-first means the default answer for any new capability is a cloud-delivered service, evaluated from the highest abstraction downward (SaaS, then managed and serverless platforms, then infrastructure), with on-premises hardware requiring an explicit exception based on constraints such as data sovereignty or connectivity.

whyWrong.0: Option A perpetuates capital purchases and undifferentiated operations.
whyWrong.1: Option B prescribes the lowest abstraction and custom build without considering buy options.
whyWrong.2: Option C blocks the business need unnecessarily; cloud-first applies to new work regardless of legacy migration status.

question: A shipping company completed a lift-and-shift of 300 VMs to Compute Engine three months ago. The CFO notes that the monthly bill is higher than the migration business case predicted and asks the platform team where to start. The team has limited time and wants data-driven, low-risk actions first. What should you do first?
options: Refactor the largest applications into microservices to reduce their resource usage.

Review the Recommender and Active Assist insights (idle VM, rightsizing, idle disk and committed use discount recommendations) and billing reports, apply the low-risk rightsizing and cleanup actions, then purchase commitments for the stable baseline.
Move all VMs to Spot VMs to obtain the maximum discount.
Switch the billing account to invoiced billing to negotiate a better rate.
explanation: Google's migration framework ends with an optimize phase, and the fastest wins after a rehost come from Google's built-in recommendations: machine type rightsizing based on observed usage, idle VM and disk cleanup, and commitment purchase recommendations, all of which are low-risk and data-driven. Only after the baseline is efficient does it make sense to buy committed use discounts. Option A is a long, expensive program with uncertain cost impact. Option C would cause outages for stateful and long-running production workloads. Option D changes payment mechanics, not consumption, and does not by itself reduce cost.
hint: Core Rule (Post-migration optimization): Google's migration framework ends with an optimize phase, and the fastest wins after a rehost come from Google's built-in recommendations: machine type rightsizing based on observed usage, idle VM and disk cleanup, and commitment purchase recommendations, all of which are low-risk and data-driven.

whyWrong.0: Option A is a long, expensive program with uncertain cost impact.
whyWrong.2: Option C would cause outages for stateful and long-running production workloads.
whyWrong.3: Option D changes payment mechanics, not consumption, and does not by itself reduce cost.

question: An online marketplace rehosted its three-tier PHP application to Compute Engine a year ago: a managed instance group of web servers, a self-managed MySQL primary with manual failover, static assets served from the web servers, and deployments done by hand over SSH. Leadership now wants a 12-month improvement roadmap that reduces operational toil and outage risk and prepares the platform for expansion into new markets, without rewriting the application. Which three improvements should the roadmap prioritize? (Choose three.)
options: Replatform the self-managed MySQL to Cloud SQL for MySQL with high availability and automated backups using Database Migration Service.
Rewrite the application in Go as microservices before making any other change.
Serve static assets from Cloud Storage behind Cloud CDN and a global external Application Load Balancer, reducing web tier load and latency for new markets.
Increase the number of web servers in the managed instance group to reduce the impact of any failure.
Adopt infrastructure as code (Terraform) and a CI/CD pipeline (Cloud Build and Cloud Deploy) to replace manual SSH deployments with repeatable, auditable releases.
Move MySQL to a larger VM with local SSD to speed up manual failover.
explanation: The roadmap should target the sources of toil and risk while respecting the no-rewrite constraint. Moving the database to Cloud SQL HA eliminates manual failover and backup work (reliability and operational excellence), Cloud Storage plus Cloud CDN behind a global load balancer offloads static content and improves latency for users in new markets (performance), and IaC with CI/CD replaces error-prone manual deployments with repeatable releases. Option B violates the no-rewrite constraint and delays every other benefit. Option D adds cost without addressing the real single points of failure (database and manual processes). Option F keeps the fragile self-managed database and manual failover, merely on bigger hardware.
hint: Core Rule (Roadmap after lift-and-shift): The roadmap should target the sources of toil and risk while respecting the no-rewrite constraint.

whyWrong.1: Option B violates the no-rewrite constraint and delays every other benefit.
whyWrong.3: Option D adds cost without addressing the real single points of failure (database and manual processes).
whyWrong.5: Option F keeps the fragile self-managed database and manual failover, merely on bigger hardware.

question: A regional insurer's migration business case shows that 35% of the projected Google Cloud run-rate for its policy administration system is the pay-as-you-go SQL Server Enterprise license charge on 24 vCPU VMs. The application's database uses only standard relational features, and the company does not own SQL Server licenses. The CFO asks how to reduce the financial impact of licensing over the next two years. What should you recommend?
options: Include the license cost explicitly in the TCO, then evaluate in order: rightsizing the vCPU count, moving to SQL Server Standard edition if Enterprise features are unused, and planning a later migration to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL or AlloyDB with Database Migration Service to remove the license cost entirely.
Remove the license line from the TCO because it is a Microsoft cost, not a Google Cloud cost.
Keep SQL Server Enterprise but run it on Spot VMs to offset the license fee.
Purchase a 3-year committed use discount for the VMs, which also discounts the SQL Server license charge.
explanation: Determining software license implications and their financial impact is an explicit migration-planning task. The license premium is billed per vCPU, so rightsizing reduces it immediately; if the application uses only standard features, Standard edition costs a fraction of Enterprise; and a planned heterogeneous migration to a PostgreSQL-compatible managed service (a replatform supported by Database Migration Service) removes the license entirely over the two-year horizon. Option B hides a real cost from decision makers. Option C is unsuitable for a production database because Spot VMs can be preempted. Option D is incorrect; committed use discounts apply to compute resources and do not discount premium OS or SQL Server license charges.
hint: Core Rule (License costs in TCO): Determining software license implications and their financial impact is an explicit migration-planning task.

whyWrong.1: Option B hides a real cost from decision makers.
whyWrong.2: Option C is unsuitable for a production database because Spot VMs can be preempted.
whyWrong.3: Option D is incorrect; committed use discounts apply to compute resources and do not discount premium OS or SQL Server license charges.

topic: Choosing PAYG vs BYOL per workload
question: A media company is migrating two groups of Windows Server workloads: a customer-facing IIS web tier that autoscales from 4 to 60 instances during live events, and 25 legacy back-office servers that run steadily around the clock. The company owns Windows Server licenses eligible for BYOL and wants the lowest overall licensing and infrastructure cost with the least operational complexity. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Use BYOL on sole-tenant nodes for all Windows workloads, sizing the node groups for the 60-instance peak.
Use pay-as-you-go Windows images for all workloads to avoid managing licenses.

Use pay-as-you-go Windows images in a managed instance group for the autoscaling web tier, and BYOL on sole-tenant nodes for the steady back-office servers where the dedicated node cost is offset by continuous license savings.
Use BYOL on regular shared-tenant VMs for both groups to avoid sole-tenant costs.
explanation: Licensing choices should be made per workload profile. An elastic tier benefits from pay-as-you-go licensing, which is billed only while instances run and needs no license inventory management, whereas keeping dedicated sole-tenant capacity for a 60-instance peak would sit mostly idle. Steady, always-on servers are where BYOL on sole-tenant nodes pays off, because the fixed node cost is amortized continuously against saved per-vCPU license fees. Option A over-provisions expensive dedicated hosts for a bursty workload. Option B forgoes real savings on the 25 steady servers. Option D violates Microsoft's requirement for dedicated hardware for Windows Server BYOL.
hint: Core Rule (Choosing PAYG vs BYOL per workload): Licensing choices should be made per workload profile.

whyWrong.0: Option A over-provisions expensive dedicated hosts for a bursty workload.
whyWrong.1: Option B forgoes real savings on the 25 steady servers.
whyWrong.3: Option D violates Microsoft's requirement for dedicated hardware for Windows Server BYOL.

topic: Evolving from fixed capacity to elastic design
question: A sports streaming service rehosted its stateless video-manifest API onto 40 fixed-size Compute Engine VMs sized for the largest match of the year. Traffic outside marquee events is about 5% of peak, and the company plans to add several new leagues next season, making peak demand unpredictable. Leadership wants the architecture to evolve so that cost tracks actual demand and new leagues can be onboarded without capacity projects. What should you recommend?
options: Keep the 40 VMs and buy a 3-year committed use discount for all of them to lower the unit price.
Add 20 more VMs before next season to cover the new leagues.
Ask each league to provide an audience forecast and resize the fleet manually before every event.
Containerize the API and run it on Cloud Run or GKE Autopilot with request-based autoscaling and a minimum instance count for baseline, using load tests to validate scale-out speed before the season.
explanation: Cloud-first design exploits elasticity: a stateless API is a natural fit for Cloud Run or GKE Autopilot, where autoscaling makes cost proportional to demand and unpredictable peaks no longer require capacity planning projects, while a minimum instance count avoids cold starts for the baseline. Load testing before the season validates that scale-out keeps pace with traffic spikes. Option A locks in payment for capacity that is 95% idle most of the year. Option B increases fixed waste and still relies on guesswork. Option C keeps a manual, forecast-driven process that breaks whenever an event over-performs.
hint: Core Rule (Evolving from fixed capacity to elastic design): Cloud-first design exploits elasticity: a stateless API is a natural fit for Cloud Run or GKE Autopilot, where autoscaling makes cost proportional to demand and unpredictable peaks no longer require capacity planning projects, while a minimum instance count avoids cold starts for the baseline.

whyWrong.0: Option A locks in payment for capacity that is 95% idle most of the year.
whyWrong.1: Option B increases fixed waste and still relies on guesswork.
whyWrong.2: Option C keeps a manual, forecast-driven process that breaks whenever an event over-performs.

question: A logistics company that standardized on Google Cloud has acquired a competitor whose entire platform runs on AWS. For at least two years both platforms will operate side by side, exchanging shipment data continuously at several gigabits per second with consistent latency. The integration must be private and highly available. Which connectivity option should you propose as the foundation for this evolving multicloud architecture?
options: Public internet endpoints protected by API keys, since both clouds are already internet-connected.
Cross-Cloud Interconnect, providing dedicated, redundant physical connectivity between the Google Cloud VPC and the AWS environment.
Cloud VPN over the internet with a single tunnel to keep cost low.
Shipping Transfer Appliances between the two providers' data centers monthly.
explanation: Cross-Cloud Interconnect is Google Cloud's managed dedicated connectivity between a Google Cloud VPC and another cloud provider such as AWS, delivering high bandwidth (10 or 100 Gbps), predictable latency and, when deployed redundantly, a high availability SLA, which is what a multi-year, high-throughput multicloud integration requires. Option A exposes business data flows to the public internet with variable latency and weaker security. Option C is capped in bandwidth per tunnel, offers no SLA with a single tunnel, and has variable internet latency. Option D is for bulk offline transfers, not continuous data exchange.
hint: Core Rule (Multicloud integration after an acquisition): Cross-Cloud Interconnect is Google Cloud's managed dedicated connectivity between a Google Cloud VPC and another cloud provider such as AWS, delivering high bandwidth (10 or 100 Gbps), predictable latency and, when deployed redundantly, a high availability SLA, which is what a multi-year, high-throughput multicloud integration requires.

whyWrong.0: Option A exposes business data flows to the public internet with variable latency and weaker security.
whyWrong.2: Option C is capped in bandwidth per tunnel, offers no SLA with a single tunnel, and has variable internet latency.
whyWrong.3: Option D is for bulk offline transfers, not continuous data exchange.

question: A mid-sized manufacturer runs SAP ECC on-premises with a small basis team that struggles to keep up with patching and upgrades. SAP mainstream maintenance for ECC ends in 2027, so the company must move to S/4HANA. Leadership wants the move to Google Cloud to reduce the operational burden as much as possible, prefers a subscription over capital spend, and wants the option to use Google Cloud analytics and AI on SAP data. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Adopt RISE with SAP on Google Cloud, where SAP delivers S/4HANA as a subscription-based, SAP-managed service running on Google Cloud, and integrate SAP data with BigQuery through the Google Cloud Cortex Framework.
Rehost the existing ECC system to Compute Engine with Migrate to Virtual Machines and postpone the S/4HANA conversion indefinitely.
Have the basis team perform a self-managed greenfield S/4HANA implementation on Compute Engine and operate it themselves.
Replace SAP with a custom ERP built on Cloud Run and Spanner.
explanation: The requirements point to a 'buy' disposition with the lowest operational burden: RISE with SAP on Google Cloud is SAP's subscription offering in which SAP operates S/4HANA on Google Cloud infrastructure, removing patching and upgrade work from the small basis team while keeping the data inside Google Cloud, where Cortex Framework accelerates SAP data integration with BigQuery and Vertex AI. Option B merely relocates the problem and does not address the 2027 end of maintenance. Option C is the highest-effort path for a team that already struggles with operations. Option D is an enormous, high-risk bespoke build for a commodity capability that no manufacturer should treat as a differentiator.
hint: Core Rule (SAP migration options and disposition): The requirements point to a 'buy' disposition with the lowest operational burden: RISE with SAP on Google Cloud is SAP's subscription offering in which SAP operates S/4HANA on Google Cloud infrastructure, removing patching and upgrade work from the small basis team while keeping the data inside Google Cloud, where Cortex Framework accelerates SAP data integration with BigQuery and Vertex AI.

whyWrong.3: Option D is an enormous, high-risk bespoke build for a commodity capability that no manufacturer should treat as a differentiator.

question: A payment switch operator runs a latency-critical Oracle RAC 19c database on-premises with a specialized configuration that its own DBAs tune extensively. It is migrating the application tier to Compute Engine in a specific Google Cloud region. The company must keep its existing Oracle licenses, needs RAC, requires sub-millisecond latency from the application VMs to the database, and wants to keep full control of the database software and operating system. Which platform should you recommend for the database?
options: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, migrated with Database Migration Service to eliminate Oracle.
Oracle RAC installed on a pair of large Compute Engine VMs using shared persistent disks.
Oracle Autonomous Database through Oracle Database@Google Cloud, which is fully managed by Oracle.

Bare Metal Solution: certified bare-metal servers in a regional extension adjacent to the Google Cloud region, connected to the VPC over a low-latency Partner Interconnect, with the company's own Oracle RAC installation and BYOL.
explanation: Bare Metal Solution provides dedicated, Oracle-certified hardware in a facility adjacent to the Google Cloud region with a managed low-latency interconnect into the VPC, where customers install and fully control their own Oracle RAC software and operating system under their existing licenses, which matches every requirement here. Option A ignores the requirement to keep Oracle and would be a re-platforming project. Option B is not supported by Oracle for RAC and creates licensing and support ambiguity. Option C is attractive for teams that want Oracle to manage the database, but it removes the operating system and deep tuning control that this operator's DBAs require.
hint: Core Rule (Oracle on Bare Metal Solution): Bare Metal Solution provides dedicated, Oracle-certified hardware in a facility adjacent to the Google Cloud region with a managed low-latency interconnect into the VPC, where customers install and fully control their own Oracle RAC software and operating system under their existing licenses, which matches every requirement here.

whyWrong.0: Option A ignores the requirement to keep Oracle and would be a re-platforming project.
whyWrong.1: Option B is not supported by Oracle for RAC and creates licensing and support ambiguity.
whyWrong.2: Option C is attractive for teams that want Oracle to manage the database, but it removes the operating system and deep tuning control that this operator's DBAs require.

question: An architecture review board at a growing marketplace company wants to define objective signals that indicate when a workload's architecture should be re-evaluated rather than simply scaled up. The company runs a monolithic order service on Compute Engine backed by a Cloud SQL instance. Which two signals most strongly indicate that an architectural change, not just resizing, is needed? (Choose two.)
options: Average CPU utilization of the order service VMs is 40% during business hours.
The Cloud SQL primary is at the largest available machine size, write latency is rising, and adding read replicas no longer helps because the bottleneck is write throughput.
The monthly bill increased 8% while order volume increased 10%.
Release frequency has dropped to once a month because any change to the monolith requires full regression testing of every business function, and teams block each other.
A new engineer suggests that Kubernetes is more modern than managed instance groups.
explanation: Envisioning future improvements should be driven by evidence that the current design has hit structural limits. A vertically maxed-out relational primary with a write-throughput bottleneck cannot be fixed by more replicas; it is a trigger to evaluate horizontally scalable options such as Spanner or a different data partitioning strategy. Likewise, when delivery speed collapses because of coupling, decomposing the monolith into independently deployable services (or extracting the most volatile domains) addresses the business need for agility. Option A is healthy utilization. Option C shows cost growing slower than volume, which is improving unit economics. Option E is a technology preference without a business or technical driver.
hint: Core Rule (Triggers for architectural evolution): Envisioning future improvements should be driven by evidence that the current design has hit structural limits.

whyWrong.0: Option A is healthy utilization.
whyWrong.2: Option C shows cost growing slower than volume, which is improving unit economics.
whyWrong.4: Option E is a technology preference without a business or technical driver.

question: A retailer's on-premises enterprise data warehouse appliance reaches end of life in 12 months, and the vendor has quoted a multi-million-dollar hardware and license renewal. The company has a cloud-first policy, a team fluent in SQL, and 400 nightly ETL jobs written in the appliance's SQL dialect. Leadership wants to avoid the capital renewal and modernize analytics, but is worried about the cost of translating 400 jobs. What should you recommend?
options: Run an assessment with the BigQuery Migration Service (including its SQL translation and assessment tooling) to size the translation effort, then migrate the warehouse to BigQuery in phases using BigQuery Data Transfer Service for data movement, declining the appliance renewal.
Renew the appliance for five more years and revisit cloud after the next end-of-life.
Lift the appliance software onto Compute Engine VMs to preserve the SQL dialect exactly.
Rewrite all 400 ETL jobs as Dataflow pipelines in Java before moving any data.
explanation: The cloud-first policy and the imminent capital renewal make this the ideal moment to replace the appliance with BigQuery, and Google provides tooling to de-risk the translation concern: BigQuery Migration Service includes assessment reports and batch SQL translation for major warehouse dialects, and BigQuery Data Transfer Service moves the data. A phased migration lets the team validate results before the renewal deadline. Option B commits significant CapEx against the company's own policy. Option C is generally not licensed or supported by appliance vendors and keeps the license cost. Option D is an unnecessary rewrite in a new language when SQL translation preserves the team's existing skills.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud-first data platform decision): The cloud-first policy and the imminent capital renewal make this the ideal moment to replace the appliance with BigQuery, and Google provides tooling to de-risk the translation concern: BigQuery Migration Service includes assessment reports and batch SQL translation for major warehouse dialects, and BigQuery Data Transfer Service moves the data.

whyWrong.1: Option B commits significant CapEx against the company's own policy.
whyWrong.2: Option C is generally not licensed or supported by appliance vendors and keeps the license cost.
whyWrong.3: Option D is an unnecessary rewrite in a new language when SQL translation preserves the team's existing skills.

question: A geospatial company uses a commercial simulation engine licensed per physical CPU core, with an annual fee per core that exceeds the cost of the servers themselves. The vendor's terms require that licensed software run only on hosts whose physical cores can be identified and counted. The company plans to run 30 instances of the engine on Google Cloud and wants to minimize the total cost of licenses plus infrastructure. What should you recommend?
options: Run the instances on regular Compute Engine VMs and count vCPUs as cores in the license report.
Run the instances on Spot VMs so that infrastructure savings offset the license cost.

Run the instances on sole-tenant nodes, which expose dedicated physical hosts with a known core count, and use node affinity plus CPU overcommit to pack as many instances as practical onto the fewest licensed cores.
Run the instances on GKE Autopilot so that the platform abstracts away physical hardware.
explanation: Sole-tenant nodes give you a dedicated physical server with a documented socket and core count, satisfying vendor terms that tie licenses to identifiable physical cores; node affinity keeps the licensed workloads on the licensed hosts, and CPU overcommit lets you run more VMs per node when the workload tolerates it, minimizing the number of cores that must be licensed. Option A cannot satisfy terms requiring physical core identification and typically over-counts licenses because two vCPUs map to one physical core. Option B does not address the licensing requirement at all and risks preemption. Option D abstracts hardware, making physical core attribution impossible.
hint: Core Rule (Per-core ISV licensing): Sole-tenant nodes give you a dedicated physical server with a documented socket and core count, satisfying vendor terms that tie licenses to identifiable physical cores; node affinity keeps the licensed workloads on the licensed hosts, and CPU overcommit lets you run more VMs per node when the workload tolerates it, minimizing the number of cores that must be licensed.

whyWrong.0: Option A cannot satisfy terms requiring physical core identification and typically over-counts licenses because two vCPUs map to one physical core.
whyWrong.1: Option B does not address the licensing requirement at all and risks preemption.
whyWrong.3: Option D abstracts hardware, making physical core attribution impossible.

question: After rehosting, a utility company runs 120 nightly batch scripts (Python and shell) on a single always-on Compute Engine VM driven by cron. The VM is idle 20 hours a day, a failed job is noticed only when someone checks the logs, and the VM has become a single point of failure. The company wants the next evolution of this workload to reduce cost, improve reliability and observability, and keep code changes minimal. What should you recommend?
options: Move the scripts to a larger VM with a second VM as a manual standby.
Rewrite each script as a Dataflow pipeline to gain parallelism.

Package the scripts as container images and run them as Cloud Run jobs triggered by Cloud Scheduler (or orchestrated by Workflows for dependencies), with execution logs, retries and alerting in Cloud Observability.
Keep the VM but add a Cloud Monitoring uptime check so that the team is alerted if the VM goes down.
explanation: Cloud Run jobs are designed for containerized batch tasks that run to completion: the scripts are packaged mostly unchanged, compute is billed only while jobs run (eliminating 20 idle hours), each execution is logged and can be retried, failures raise alerts, and there is no single VM to fail. Cloud Scheduler replaces cron and Workflows can express job dependencies. Option A doubles cost and remains manual. Option B is a rewrite into a different programming model that most simple scripts do not need. Option D detects VM failure but does not address idle cost, job-level visibility or the single point of failure.
hint: Core Rule (Evolving batch workloads toward serverless): Cloud Run jobs are designed for containerized batch tasks that run to completion: the scripts are packaged mostly unchanged, compute is billed only while jobs run (eliminating 20 idle hours), each execution is logged and can be retried, failures raise alerts, and there is no single VM to fail.

whyWrong.0: Option A doubles cost and remains manual.
whyWrong.1: Option B is a rewrite into a different programming model that most simple scripts do not need.
whyWrong.3: Option D detects VM failure but does not address idle cost, job-level visibility or the single point of failure.

question: A European insurer runs its claims platform in Google Cloud regions in the EU. Regulators have announced that within two years, insurers will be required to demonstrate that regulated data is stored and processed only in the EU, that Google support personnel accessing the data are located in the EU, and that customers control the encryption keys. The insurer wants to prepare now with minimal re-architecture and a clear audit trail. What should you recommend?
options: Wait for the regulation to take effect and then move the workloads to an on-premises data center.

Create an Assured Workloads folder with the appropriate EU sovereign controls package, migrate the claims projects into it so that data residency, personnel access and Cloud KMS key controls are enforced and monitored, and use Access Transparency and Access Approval for auditability.
Enable VPC Service Controls around the projects, which guarantees data residency and restricts support personnel access.
Encrypt all data client-side in the application before writing it to any Google Cloud service.
explanation: Envisioning future improvements includes anticipating regulatory change. Assured Workloads applies a controls package at the folder level that enforces resource location restrictions, limits Google support personnel by location, requires customer-managed keys where applicable, and continuously monitors for violations, while Access Transparency and Access Approval provide the audit trail for any Google access; moving projects into the folder is far less disruptive than re-architecting. Option A abandons cloud benefits and is unnecessary. Option C is wrong because VPC Service Controls mitigates data exfiltration between services; it does not enforce data residency or personnel location. Option D requires intrusive application changes, breaks server-side processing and analytics, and still does not address personnel or residency requirements.
hint: Core Rule (Anticipating regulatory evolution): Envisioning future improvements includes anticipating regulatory change.

whyWrong.0: Option A abandons cloud benefits and is unnecessary.
whyWrong.2: Option C is wrong because VPC Service Controls mitigates data exfiltration between services; it does not enforce data residency or personnel location.
whyWrong.3: Option D requires intrusive application changes, breaks server-side processing and analytics, and still does not address personnel or residency requirements.

question: A software company has just rehosted its platform to Compute Engine and spends a predictable amount each month. Its 24-month roadmap will move most services to Cloud Run and GKE Autopilot as they are containerized. The finance team wants to lock in discounts on the stable spend now but is worried about being stuck paying for Compute Engine resources that will no longer exist in a year. Which commitment strategy should you recommend?
options: Buy 3-year resource-based committed use discounts for the current Compute Engine vCPU and memory footprint to maximize the discount percentage.
Avoid all commitments until the modernization is complete, paying on-demand prices for two years.

Purchase spend-based Compute flexible committed use discounts, which apply to eligible spend across Compute Engine, Cloud Run and GKE Autopilot, so the commitment continues to be consumed as workloads move between these services.
Buy 1-year resource-based commitments for Cloud Run instances now in anticipation of the migration.
explanation: Compute flexible CUDs are spend-based commitments that apply to eligible usage across Compute Engine VM families, Cloud Run and GKE Autopilot, so as workloads are containerized and move platforms the commitment is still consumed; this fits a company whose total compute spend is stable but whose service mix will change. Option A ties the commitment to specific resource types and regions, creating exactly the stranded-commitment risk finance fears. Option B forgoes substantial savings on spend that is predictable in aggregate. Option D is invalid because Cloud Run is covered by spend-based flexible commitments, not resource-based instance commitments purchased in advance.
hint: Core Rule (Commitments during modernization): Compute flexible CUDs are spend-based commitments that apply to eligible usage across Compute Engine VM families, Cloud Run and GKE Autopilot, so as workloads are containerized and move platforms the commitment is still consumed; this fits a company whose total compute spend is stable but whose service mix will change.

whyWrong.0: Option A ties the commitment to specific resource types and regions, creating exactly the stranded-commitment risk finance fears.
whyWrong.1: Option B forgoes substantial savings on spend that is predictable in aggregate.
whyWrong.3: Option D is invalid because Cloud Run is covered by spend-based flexible commitments, not resource-based instance commitments purchased in advance.

question: A national newspaper is writing a three-year cloud architecture roadmap for its digital platform on Google Cloud. The editor-in-chief notes that the business model changed twice in the last three years (from advertising to subscriptions, and now toward AI-generated personalization), so the architecture must be able to absorb changes the company cannot yet predict. Which two design principles should anchor the roadmap? (Choose two.)
options: Standardize on a single large relational database shared by all applications so that data is always in one place.

Build the platform as loosely coupled services with well-defined APIs and asynchronous events (for example, Pub/Sub), so individual capabilities can be replaced or extended without rewriting the whole platform.
Freeze the technology stack for three years to avoid the cost of change.

Prefer managed and serverless Google Cloud services and infrastructure as code, so the team's effort goes into new business capabilities rather than operating infrastructure, and environments can be recreated or evolved quickly.
Require every new feature to be approved by the board to reduce the rate of change.
explanation: Architectures that absorb unpredictable business change share two traits: loose coupling through APIs and events, which lets capabilities such as a personalization engine be added or swapped without a platform rewrite, and a bias toward managed services and infrastructure as code, which minimizes undifferentiated operations and makes environments reproducible and easy to evolve. Both are core Well-Architected Framework recommendations for operational excellence and cloud-first design. Option A creates a tightly coupled data monolith that makes every change risky. Option C guarantees the platform falls behind the business. Option E slows delivery without improving adaptability.

question: A startup has built a stateless REST API packaged as a Docker container. Traffic is highly variable: near zero overnight and thousands of requests per second during marketing campaigns. The two-person engineering team has no Kubernetes experience and wants to pay only for the resources consumed while requests are being served. Which compute platform should you recommend?
options: Deploy the container to a GKE Standard cluster with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and cluster autoscaler enabled.
Deploy the container on a Compute Engine managed instance group with autoscaling based on CPU utilization.
Deploy the container as a Cloud Run service with request-based autoscaling and the default minimum of zero instances.
Deploy the container to a GKE Autopilot cluster and configure the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.
explanation: The deciding factors are a stateless container, no Kubernetes skills, bursty traffic, and pay-per-use. Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless container platform that scales from zero to thousands of instances per request load and bills only while instances are handling requests, which is the cost-optimization and operational-excellence sweet spot here. Option A requires the team to operate Kubernetes and pay for nodes even when idle. Option B keeps VMs running (no scale to zero) and adds OS patching and image management. Option D removes node management but still requires Kubernetes knowledge (Deployments, HPA, Services) and Autopilot does not scale a Deployment to zero pods on its own.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Run): The deciding factors are a stateless container, no Kubernetes skills, bursty traffic, and pay-per-use.

whyWrong.0: Option A requires the team to operate Kubernetes and pay for nodes even when idle.
whyWrong.1: Option B keeps VMs running (no scale to zero) and adds OS patching and image management.
whyWrong.3: Option D removes node management but still requires Kubernetes knowledge (Deployments, HPA, Services) and Autopilot does not scale a Deployment to zero pods on its own.

question: A financial services company runs a nightly risk-calculation job that is split into roughly 5,000 independent tasks, each running for 10 to 20 minutes in a container. The tasks are idempotent and write results to Cloud Storage. The job must finish within an 8-hour window, and the company wants the lowest possible compute cost without managing a scheduler or a cluster. What should you do?
options: Submit the work as a Batch job that uses Spot VMs, with a retry policy so preempted tasks are automatically re-run.
Create a GKE Standard cluster with a Spot node pool and run the tasks as Kubernetes Jobs.
Run the tasks on a Compute Engine managed instance group of standard VMs that is scaled up by a Cloud Scheduler trigger each night.
Implement each task as a Cloud Run function invoked by Pub/Sub messages published by Cloud Scheduler.
explanation: Batch is Google's fully managed service for scheduling, queuing, and executing batch jobs on Compute Engine; it provisions the VMs, runs container tasks in parallel, supports Spot VMs, and retries failed or preempted tasks, so no cluster or custom scheduler is needed. Because the tasks are idempotent and there is an 8-hour window, Spot pricing (60-91% discount) is appropriate and preemptions are absorbed by retries. Option B works technically but requires operating a GKE cluster, which violates the no-cluster requirement. Option C uses full-price VMs and requires custom task-distribution logic. Option D fails because event-driven Cloud Run functions have a maximum execution time of 9 minutes (HTTP functions up to 60 minutes) and tasks run 10-20 minutes; it is also more expensive per vCPU-hour than Spot VMs.
hint: Core Rule: Batch is Google's fully managed service for scheduling, queuing, and executing batch jobs on Compute Engine; it provisions the VMs, runs container tasks in parallel, supports Spot VMs, and retries failed or preempted tasks, so no cluster or custom scheduler is needed.

whyWrong.2: Option C uses full-price VMs and requires custom task-distribution logic.
whyWrong.3: Option D fails because event-driven Cloud Run functions have a maximum execution time of 9 minutes (HTTP functions up to 60 minutes) and tasks run 10-20 minutes; it is also more expensive per vCPU-hour than Spot VMs.

question: A manufacturing company operates 400 VMs on VMware vSphere in a data center whose lease expires in six months. The applications depend on vSphere features such as vMotion, DRS, and NSX-based microsegmentation, and the operations team's runbooks are all built around vCenter. Leadership wants to exit the data center on time without refactoring applications. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Use Migrate to Virtual Machines to convert every VM to a Compute Engine instance and recreate the network segmentation with VPC firewall policies.
Containerize the applications with Migrate to Containers and deploy them to GKE Autopilot.
Replace the VMs with equivalent managed services such as Cloud SQL and Cloud Run over the six-month period.
Deploy a Google Cloud VMware Engine private cloud and migrate the VMs with VMware HCX, keeping vCenter and NSX as the management plane.
explanation: The constraints are a hard deadline, dependence on vSphere/NSX features, and an operations team skilled in vCenter. Google Cloud VMware Engine provides a fully managed VMware SDDC (vSphere, vSAN, NSX-T, HCX) running on dedicated Google hardware, so workloads move with HCX live or bulk migration and existing runbooks and tooling remain valid; this is the lowest-risk path to meet the deadline. Option A is a valid lift-and-shift path but forces re-implementation of NSX microsegmentation and retraining of the team on Compute Engine, which is risky in six months for 400 VMs. Option B requires containerization suitability assessment and re-platforming of every application. Option C is a full modernization that cannot realistically be completed for 400 VMs in six months and contradicts the no-refactoring requirement.
hint: Core Rule (VMware Engine): The constraints are a hard deadline, dependence on vSphere/NSX features, and an operations team skilled in vCenter.

question: A telecom company runs a mission-critical Oracle Real Application Clusters (RAC) database on-premises. The database license is tied to physical cores, the vendor does not certify the product on virtualized public cloud instances, and the application servers that use it are being migrated to Compute Engine in the same region. The company requires sub-millisecond latency between the application tier and the database. What should you do?
options: Migrate the database to a memory-optimized M3 Compute Engine instance with Hyperdisk Extreme and keep the RAC configuration.
Provision Bare Metal Solution servers in the regional extension connected to the VPC through a Partner Interconnect, and run Oracle RAC on them.
Migrate the database to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL using Database Migration Service with the Oracle-to-PostgreSQL conversion workspace.
Run Oracle RAC on sole-tenant nodes in Compute Engine so that the physical host is dedicated to the company.
explanation: Bare Metal Solution exists precisely for specialized workloads such as Oracle RAC that need certified, non-virtualized hardware and core-based licensing; the servers sit in a regional extension with low-latency (sub-millisecond) connectivity to the VPC in the same region via a Partner Interconnect that Google manages. Option A places RAC on a virtualized instance, which the vendor does not certify, and Compute Engine does not support the shared-storage clustering RAC expects. Option C is a database re-platforming project that changes the engine, which is not what was asked and carries high risk for a mission-critical system. Option D dedicates the host but is still a virtualized environment, so it does not satisfy the certification constraint.

question: A retail company's platform team wants to standardize on Kubernetes so developers can keep using their existing Helm charts and kubectl workflows. However, the team does not want to size node pools, patch node operating systems, or pay for idle node capacity, and its workloads have no requirement for privileged containers or custom node configuration. Which option best meets these requirements?
options: Create a GKE Standard cluster with node auto-provisioning and enable auto-upgrade on all node pools.
Create a GKE Autopilot cluster and deploy the workloads with the existing Helm charts.
Deploy the containers as Cloud Run services and convert the Helm charts to Cloud Run service YAML.
Create a GKE Standard cluster with a single large node pool and use Vertical Pod Autoscaler to tune requests.
explanation: GKE Autopilot is the Google-recommended mode when you want the Kubernetes API without managing nodes: Google provisions, scales, patches and secures the nodes, and you are billed per pod resource request rather than per node, so there is no idle-node cost. Because the workloads need no privileged access or custom node settings, Autopilot's restrictions are not a blocker. Option A reduces but does not remove node management (you still choose machine families, manage OS images, and pay for unused node capacity). Option C abandons the Kubernetes API and Helm ecosystem the team wants to keep. Option D pays for a large, mostly idle node pool and still requires node maintenance.
hint: Core Rule: GKE Autopilot is the Google-recommended mode when you want the Kubernetes API without managing nodes: Google provisions, scales, patches and secures the nodes, and you are billed per pod resource request rather than per node, so there is no idle-node cost.

question: A cybersecurity vendor is moving its network-inspection product to GKE. Each node must run a privileged DaemonSet that loads a custom kernel module, uses host networking, and requires specific sysctl settings on the node operating system. The vendor also wants some pods to use node-attached local SSDs formatted with a custom file system. Which cluster mode should you choose?
options: GKE Standard, because it allows privileged DaemonSets, host networking, custom node system configuration, and local SSD node pools.
GKE Autopilot, because it supports privileged workloads through the allowlisted partner workloads program.
GKE Autopilot with the Performance compute class, because it grants pods exclusive access to the whole node.
GKE Autopilot with a custom ComputeClass that specifies the node system configuration.
explanation: Autopilot deliberately restricts host-level access: arbitrary privileged containers, host networking, kernel module loading, and low-level node customization are blocked so that Google can guarantee the node security posture. GKE Standard gives you full control of node pools, node images (for example Ubuntu for out-of-tree kernel modules), node system configuration, and local SSD node pools, which is what a network-inspection agent needs. Option B is wrong because the partner allowlist covers only specific approved third-party agents, not a customer's own privileged product. Option C's Performance compute class gives dedicated node capacity but still enforces Autopilot's security restrictions. Option D is wrong because custom ComputeClasses control node attributes such as machine family and Spot priority, not kernel modules or host networking.
hint: Core Rule (GKE Standard): Autopilot deliberately restricts host-level access: arbitrary privileged containers, host networking, kernel module loading, and low-level node customization are blocked so that Google can guarantee the node security posture.

whyWrong.2: Option C's Performance compute class gives dedicated node capacity but still enforces Autopilot's security restrictions.
whyWrong.3: Option D is wrong because custom ComputeClasses control node attributes such as machine family and Spot priority, not kernel modules or host networking.

question: A global logistics company is migrating an SAP HANA scale-up production system to Google Cloud. The database requires about 6 TB of memory in a single instance, and SAP requires the instance to run on a machine type that is certified for HANA. Which machine family should you choose?
options: N2 with extended memory, because custom extended memory can reach the required capacity.
C3 high-memory, because it offers the newest Intel processors and the highest memory bandwidth.
M3 memory-optimized, because it provides multi-terabyte, SAP-certified shapes for in-memory databases.
A3 accelerator-optimized, because HANA benefits from GPU acceleration for analytics.
explanation: The memory-optimized family (M1/M2/M3) is designed for large in-memory databases such as SAP HANA; M3 shapes go up to about 4 TB (M2 up to 12 TB) and are SAP-certified, which is the hard requirement here. Option A fails because N2 custom machine types cap out well below 6 TB (N2 maximum is 864 GB) and are not certified for scale-up HANA at this size. Option B is a general-purpose high-performance family whose largest shapes still do not reach 6 TB and are not on SAP's certified list for HANA of this size. Option D is for GPU workloads; HANA does not use GPUs and A3 memory sizes are tied to GPU count, making it both unsuitable and far more expensive.
hint: Core Rule (Machine families): The memory-optimized family (M1/M2/M3) is designed for large in-memory databases such as SAP HANA; M3 shapes go up to about 4 TB (M2 up to 12 TB) and are SAP-certified, which is the hard requirement here.

question: A healthcare organization is migrating 60 Windows Server VMs that run Microsoft SQL Server. The organization holds existing per-core SQL Server licenses without Software Assurance, and its licensing rules require that these licenses be used only on dedicated physical hardware. The organization also wants to minimize licensing cost by controlling how many physical cores are consumed. What should you do?
options: Run the VMs on standard N2 instances with pay-as-you-go SQL Server images from Google Cloud.
Run the VMs on Confidential VMs so that the hypervisor cannot access the workload memory.
Run SQL Server on Cloud SQL for SQL Server and bring your own licenses.
Run the VMs on sole-tenant nodes with a node affinity policy, bring the existing licenses, and use CPU overcommit or in-place restart settings to limit physical core consumption.
explanation: Sole-tenant nodes give you physical servers dedicated to your project, which is what per-core, bring-your-own-license (BYOL) Windows and SQL Server scenarios without License Mobility require; node affinity labels pin the VMs to those hosts, and features such as CPU overcommit and restart-in-place maintenance let you pack VMs and keep them on the same licensed cores. Option A discards the existing licenses and pays again for license-included images on shared hosts, which violates the licensing rule. question: A startup wants to run a dozen development and test environments on Compute Engine. The workloads are small web servers and CI runners that are not sensitive to occasional CPU sharing, and the primary goal is the lowest cost per VM. Which machine family should you choose?

question: An aerospace engineering firm runs computational fluid dynamics simulations that use MPI across 64 nodes. Job runtime is dominated by inter-node communication, and engineers report that performance varies significantly between runs on their current cloud provider. The firm wants consistent, low-latency node-to-node communication and high per-core performance for the simulation cluster. What should you do?
options: Use C3 or H3 compute-optimized instances created with a compact placement policy so that nodes are physically close, and enable gVNIC.
Use E2 instances spread across three zones with a regional managed instance group to maximize availability.
Use N2 instances with a spread placement policy to avoid resource contention between nodes.

Option C uses a spread policy, which intentionally separates VMs onto different hosts and increases latency. Option D is wrong because a CFD solver running on CPUs does not use the GPU fabric; A3 is expensive and inappropriate unless the code is GPU-accelerated.
hint: Core Rule (HPC compute): Tightly coupled MPI workloads need two things: high per-core, consistent performance (compute-optimized C3/H3 with no CPU sharing) and minimal network latency between nodes, which a compact placement policy delivers by placing VMs on physically close hosts in the same zone; gVNIC and Tier_1 networking further reduce latency and increase bandwidth.

question: An AI research company plans to pre-train a large language model with hundreds of billions of parameters. A3 accelerator-optimized instances with eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs, provisioned through a reservation or Dynamic Workload Scheduler to guarantee capacity for the run.
Cloud TPU v5p slices, because TPUs are the only option for training models of this size.

question: A visual effects studio wants to move its render farm to Compute Engine. Render frames are independent, each frame takes about 5 minutes, and the studio is highly cost-sensitive but must meet a delivery deadline for each project. Which two design choices should you make to minimize cost while still meeting deadlines? (Choose two.)
options: Run the render workers on Spot VMs in a managed instance group and let the group recreate preempted instances.
Run the render workers on sole-tenant nodes to guarantee capacity.
Purchase a three-year committed use discount sized for peak rendering demand.
Design workers to pull frames from a queue and write completed frames to Cloud Storage so that a preempted worker only loses its in-progress frame.
Use a single very large M3 instance so that all frames render on one machine.
explanation: Rendering is the canonical Spot VM workload: frames are short, independent, and restartable, so the 60-91% Spot discount can be captured and a MIG will automatically recreate preempted instances. Option B is the most expensive option and unnecessary because rendering does not require dedicated hardware. Option C commits to peak, not baseline, so most of the commitment would be wasted between projects. question: A real estate website stores property photos in a Cloud Storage bucket. Each time a photo is uploaded, the company needs to generate three thumbnail sizes and store them in a second bucket. The team wants to write only the resizing logic and avoid managing servers, containers, or clusters. What should you do?
options: Create a Compute Engine VM that polls the bucket every minute and resizes new objects.
Deploy a GKE Autopilot cluster with a Deployment that subscribes to bucket notifications.

Option B forces the team to build a container and manage Kubernetes objects for a trivial task. Option D is a heavyweight streaming pipeline with always-on workers; Dataflow is designed for large-scale data transformation, not per-object image handling.

question: A company runs a large application on the App Engine standard environment consisting of eight services routed through dispatch.yaml and using Cloud Tasks queues. A new service needs a Rust runtime and a native library that the App Engine standard environment does not support. The team wants to keep the new service inside the same App Engine application so that existing routing rules and service-to-service calls continue to work unchanged. What should you do?
options: Deploy the new service to the App Engine flexible environment using a custom runtime defined by a Dockerfile.
Deploy the new service to Cloud Run and register it as an App Engine service in dispatch.yaml.

Create a separate App Engine application in a new project for the Rust service.
explanation: A single App Engine application can contain services in both the standard and flexible environments, and the flexible environment supports custom runtimes built from any Dockerfile, so a Rust service with native dependencies can live alongside the existing standard services and be addressed by dispatch.yaml and the usual service URLs. question: A multinational bank operates 40 GKE clusters across three Google Cloud regions plus Kubernetes clusters in two on-premises data centers. Security requires consistent policy enforcement across every cluster (for example, only signed images from an approved registry), centralized detection of configuration drift, and mutual TLS between services without changing application code. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Install open-source Istio and Open Policy Agent separately on each cluster and manage the configurations with a Git repository and Cloud Build.
Consolidate all workloads into a single large regional GKE Autopilot cluster to reduce the management surface.
Use VPC Service Controls and organization policy constraints to enforce cluster configuration.
Register all clusters to a GKE Enterprise fleet and use Config Sync, Policy Controller, Binary Authorization, and Cloud Service Mesh managed from the fleet.
explanation: GKE Enterprise is Google's multi-cluster, hybrid platform: fleets group clusters (in Google Cloud, on-premises, or other clouds) so that Config Sync applies a single Git source of truth with drift remediation, Policy Controller enforces guardrails, Binary Authorization enforces signed images, and Cloud Service Mesh provides mutual TLS transparently through sidecars or ambient mode. Option A is technically possible but leaves the bank to operate and upgrade 40 independent Istio and OPA installations, which is high operational overhead and error-prone. Option B is not feasible for on-premises workloads, ignores regional resilience, and creates a single blast radius. Option C addresses API-level data exfiltration and resource settings but cannot enforce in-cluster Kubernetes policies or provide mTLS.
hint: Core Rule: GKE Enterprise is Google's multi-cluster, hybrid platform: fleets group clusters (in Google Cloud, on-premises, or other clouds) so that Config Sync applies a single Git source of truth with drift remediation, Policy Controller enforces guardrails, Binary Authorization enforces signed images, and Cloud Service Mesh provides mutual TLS transparently through sidecars or ambient mode.

question: A logistics company has containerized a Python program that compiles monthly invoices. The program runs for about 45 minutes, does not expose an HTTP endpoint, and needs to run on the first day of each month. The company wants a serverless solution with minimal configuration. What should you do?
options: Deploy the container as a Cloud Run service and have Cloud Scheduler send an HTTP request to it on the first of each month.
Deploy the container as a Cloud Run job and trigger it with Cloud Scheduler on the first of each month.
Deploy the program as a Cloud Run function with a Pub/Sub trigger published by Cloud Scheduler.
Create a Compute Engine VM with a cron entry that runs the container monthly.
explanation: Cloud Run jobs are designed for run-to-completion containers that do not serve requests: a job can run for up to 24 hours per task, needs no HTTP listener, and can be executed on a schedule by Cloud Scheduler with a single trigger. Option A would require adding an HTTP server to the code and keeping the request open for 45 minutes, which is fragile and mis-uses the request/response model. Option C fails because event-driven Cloud Run functions are limited to 9 minutes of execution. Option D works but is not serverless and leaves a VM to patch and pay for all month for a 45-minute task.
hint: Core Rule: Cloud Run jobs are designed for run-to-completion containers that do not serve requests: a job can run for up to 24 hours per task, needs no HTTP listener, and can be executed on a schedule by Cloud Scheduler with a single trigger.

whyWrong.2: Option C fails because event-driven Cloud Run functions are limited to 9 minutes of execution.
whyWrong.3: Option D works but is not serverless and leaves a VM to patch and pay for all month for a 45-minute task.

question: A hospital network is migrating a commercial off-the-shelf laboratory information system to Google Cloud. The vendor supports installation only on Windows Server VMs, requires a fixed hostname and internal IP address, and stores data on a local NTFS volume. The application is not designed to scale horizontally. The hospital wants the simplest vendor-supported deployment. What should you do?
options: Containerize the application with Migrate to Containers and run it on GKE Windows Server node pools.
Deploy the application to Cloud Run using a Windows container image.
Deploy the application on a Compute Engine Windows Server VM with a reserved internal IP address and a Persistent Disk or Hyperdisk data volume, using scheduled snapshots for backup.
Deploy the application to the App Engine flexible environment with a custom Windows runtime.
explanation: When a vendor supports only a VM-based Windows installation with a stable identity and local block storage, Compute Engine is the correct mapping: a reserved internal IP and fixed hostname satisfy the vendor, a Persistent Disk or Hyperdisk volume provides NTFS block storage, and snapshot schedules give simple backups; this is the lowest-risk, vendor-supported choice. Option A changes the deployment model to containers, which the vendor does not support and which offers no benefit for a non-scalable app. Option B is impossible because Cloud Run runs only Linux containers. Option D is impossible because App Engine flexible custom runtimes are Linux-based Docker images.
hint: Core Rule: When a vendor supports only a VM-based Windows installation with a stable identity and local block storage, Compute Engine is the correct mapping: a reserved internal IP and fixed hostname satisfy the vendor, a Persistent Disk or Hyperdisk volume provides NTFS block storage, and snapshot schedules give simple backups; this is the lowest-risk, vendor-supported choice.

whyWrong.1: Option B is impossible because Cloud Run runs only Linux containers.
whyWrong.3: Option D is impossible because App Engine flexible custom runtimes are Linux-based Docker images.

question: A software company has 800 Compute Engine VMs that run 24x7. A cost review shows average CPU utilization of 12% across the fleet, and the company has never purchased any discounts. Which two actions should you take first to reduce compute cost without affecting availability? (Choose two.)
options: Migrate all 800 VMs to Spot VMs to obtain the maximum discount.
Apply the machine type rightsizing recommendations from Active Assist to reduce over-provisioned VMs.
Purchase committed use discounts covering the steady-state usage that remains after rightsizing.
Move all VMs to sole-tenant nodes to consolidate workloads on fewer hosts.
Manually enable sustained use discounts on each VM.
explanation: The Well-Architected cost-optimization pillar recommends first eliminating waste and then committing to what remains: Active Assist's machine type recommender identifies VMs that can be downsized based on observed utilization (12% average indicates heavy over-provisioning), and after rightsizing, committed use discounts of up to 57% (3-year) can be applied to the predictable 24x7 baseline. Committing before rightsizing would lock in over-provisioned spend. Option A is wrong because Spot VMs can be preempted at any time and are unsuitable for the general fleet where availability must be preserved. Option D increases cost; sole-tenant nodes carry a premium and are for licensing or isolation needs. Option E is invalid because sustained use discounts are applied automatically and cannot be manually enabled.
hint: Core Rule (Compute cost optimization): The Well-Architected cost-optimization pillar recommends first eliminating waste and then committing to what remains: Active Assist's machine type recommender identifies VMs that can be downsized based on observed utilization (12% average indicates heavy over-provisioning), and after rightsizing, committed use discounts of up to 57% (3-year) can be applied to the predictable 24x7 baseline.

whyWrong.3: Option D increases cost; sole-tenant nodes carry a premium and are for licensing or isolation needs.
whyWrong.4: Option E is invalid because sustained use discounts are applied automatically and cannot be manually enabled.

question: A pharmaceutical company must process a partner's genomic data under a contract that requires the data to be encrypted not only at rest and in transit but also while in use, so that neither the cloud provider's hypervisor nor its administrators can read memory contents. The processing runs on Linux VMs and uses no GPUs. Which compute configuration should you recommend?
options: Confidential VMs on N2D (AMD SEV) or C3 (Intel TDX) machine types, or Confidential GKE Nodes if the workload is containerized.
Shielded VMs with Secure Boot, vTPM, and integrity monitoring enabled on E2 machine types.
Standard VMs with customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) applied to the boot and data disks.
Sole-tenant nodes so that no other customer shares the physical host.
explanation: Encryption in use is provided by Confidential Computing: Confidential VMs use hardware-based memory encryption (AMD SEV/SEV-SNP on N2D/C2D/C3D, Intel TDX on C3) with keys that are generated and held by the CPU, so memory content is opaque to the hypervisor and to Google operators; Confidential GKE Nodes extend the same protection to containers. Option B protects boot integrity against rootkits and firmware tampering but does not encrypt memory. Option C protects data at rest only; memory is still in clear text to the host. Option D provides physical host isolation from other tenants but the hypervisor still has full access to guest memory, so it does not satisfy the in-use encryption requirement.
hint: Core Rule: Encryption in use is provided by Confidential Computing: Confidential VMs use hardware-based memory encryption (AMD SEV/SEV-SNP on N2D/C2D/C3D, Intel TDX on C3) with keys that are generated and held by the CPU, so memory content is opaque to the hypervisor and to Google operators; Confidential GKE Nodes extend the same protection to containers.

whyWrong.2: Option C protects data at rest only; memory is still in clear text to the host.
whyWrong.3: Option D provides physical host isolation from other tenants but the hypervisor still has full access to guest memory, so it does not satisfy the in-use encryption requirement.

question: A retailer serves a computer-vision model that classifies product photos uploaded by merchants. Request volume is unpredictable, with hours of no traffic followed by short bursts, and each inference needs an NVIDIA L4 GPU to meet a two-second latency target. The team already deploys stateless containers and wants to avoid paying for idle GPUs. What should you do?
options: Deploy the model on a Compute Engine G2 instance that runs continuously behind an internal load balancer.
Deploy the model on a GKE Standard cluster with a G2 node pool fixed at two nodes.
Deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint with dedicated GPU resources and a minimum of one replica.
Deploy the container as a Cloud Run service with an NVIDIA L4 GPU attached and allow it to scale to zero.
explanation: Cloud Run supports attaching NVIDIA L4 GPUs to service instances and, unlike the other options, scales to zero when there is no traffic, so no GPU is billed during the idle hours; fast GPU instance start-up handles the bursts, and the team keeps its existing container deployment workflow. Option A bills a GPU 24x7 regardless of traffic. Option B keeps two GPU nodes permanently allocated and adds Kubernetes operations. Option C is a good serving platform, but Vertex AI online prediction endpoints with dedicated resources require at least one replica to stay running, so idle GPU cost remains.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Run GPUs): Cloud Run supports attaching NVIDIA L4 GPUs to service instances and, unlike the other options, scales to zero when there is no traffic, so no GPU is billed during the idle hours; fast GPU instance start-up handles the bursts, and the team keeps its existing container deployment workflow.

whyWrong.1: Option B keeps two GPU nodes permanently allocated and adds Kubernetes operations.
whyWrong.2: Option C is a good serving platform, but Vertex AI online prediction endpoints with dedicated resources require at least one replica to stay running, so idle GPU cost remains.

question: A payments company needs its authorization service, which runs on Compute Engine, to remain fully available even if one zone in the region fails. The service needs 60 vCPUs of capacity at peak. During a recent zone outage at another provider, the company learned that surviving zones may not have spare capacity when many customers fail over simultaneously. Which design should you recommend?
options: Deploy a zonal managed instance group with 60 vCPUs and enable autohealing so instances are recreated quickly.
Deploy a regional managed instance group across three zones with 60 vCPUs total and rely on autoscaling to add capacity in the remaining zones after a failure.
Deploy a regional managed instance group across three zones with 90 vCPUs total so that any two zones can carry the peak load, and create zonal reservations so the capacity is guaranteed.
Deploy two zonal managed instance groups of 60 vCPUs each in two different regions behind a global load balancer.
explanation: The reliability pillar recommends over-provisioning for N+1 zone failure (with three zones, each zone holds one third, so 1.5x peak capacity lets any two zones serve 100% of load) and, critically, using reservations to guarantee that the required VMs can actually be created or are already running in the surviving zones, addressing the capacity-shortage risk the company identified. Option A has no zone redundancy at all. Option B is correct in shape but relies on autoscaling into zones that may be capacity-constrained during a mass failover, exactly the scenario the company wants to avoid. Option D doubles cost across regions, adds cross-region latency for a synchronous payments path, and still does not reserve capacity.
hint: Core Rule (Regional MIG capacity): The reliability pillar recommends over-provisioning for N+1 zone failure (with three zones, each zone holds one third, so 1.5x peak capacity lets any two zones serve 100% of load) and, critically, using reservations to guarantee that the required VMs can actually be created or are already running in the surviving zones, addressing the capacity-shortage risk the company identified.

whyWrong.0: Option A has no zone redundancy at all.
whyWrong.1: Option B is correct in shape but relies on autoscaling into zones that may be capacity-constrained during a mass failover, exactly the scenario the company wants to avoid.
whyWrong.3: Option D doubles cost across regions, adds cross-region latency for a synchronous payments path, and still does not reserve capacity.

question: A small nonprofit needs to run a Python script every hour that calls a partner's API and stores the results in Firestore. The script runs for about 90 seconds. The organization has no operations staff and wants to avoid paying for idle resources. What should you do?
options: Deploy the script as a Cloud Run function and invoke it hourly with a Cloud Scheduler job.
Run the script on an e2-micro Compute Engine instance using cron.
Deploy the script to a GKE Autopilot cluster as a Kubernetes CronJob.
Create a Cloud Composer environment with a DAG scheduled hourly.
explanation: A short, periodic piece of code with no infrastructure requirements maps directly to Cloud Run functions triggered by Cloud Scheduler: the function bills only for the 90 seconds it runs each hour and there is nothing to patch or scale. Option B leaves a VM running and needing maintenance 24x7 for 24 minutes of work per day. Option C introduces Kubernetes concepts and a cluster fee that is disproportionate to the task. Option D is the most expensive choice; Cloud Composer runs a managed Airflow environment with always-on components and is meant for complex multi-step data pipelines, not a single hourly script.
hint: Core Rule (Serverless scheduling): A short, periodic piece of code with no infrastructure requirements maps directly to Cloud Run functions triggered by Cloud Scheduler: the function bills only for the 90 seconds it runs each hour and there is nothing to patch or scale.

question: A media company runs two workload types on a GKE Standard cluster: a latency-sensitive video API that must never be evicted, and a fault-tolerant transcoding queue whose pods can be restarted at any time. Compute is 70% of the company's cloud bill. Which two changes should you make to reduce cost without affecting the API? (Choose two.)
options: Create a separate node pool of Spot VMs with a taint, and add a matching toleration and node affinity to the transcoding pods.
Run the video API on the Spot node pool with a PodDisruptionBudget of zero to prevent eviction.
Keep the video API on an on-demand node pool and purchase a committed use discount for that baseline capacity.
Enable cluster autoscaling with a maximum of one node so the cluster never over-provisions.
Move both workloads to a single node pool of the largest available M3 machines.
explanation: The recommended GKE cost pattern is to segregate workloads by tolerance for disruption: fault-tolerant transcoding goes on a tainted Spot node pool (60-91% cheaper) that only pods with the matching toleration and affinity land on, while the latency-sensitive API stays on on-demand nodes whose predictable baseline is covered by a committed use discount. Option B is dangerous: Spot nodes are preempted regardless of PodDisruptionBudgets, so the API would be evicted. Option D would starve both workloads and break the API under load. Option E puts the API and transcoding on the same expensive memory-optimized nodes, removing isolation and increasing cost.
hint: Core Rule (GKE cost optimization): The recommended GKE cost pattern is to segregate workloads by tolerance for disruption: fault-tolerant transcoding goes on a tainted Spot node pool (60-91% cheaper) that only pods with the matching toleration and affinity land on, while the latency-sensitive API stays on on-demand nodes whose predictable baseline is covered by a committed use discount.

whyWrong.4: Option E puts the API and transcoding on the same expensive memory-optimized nodes, removing isolation and increasing cost.

question: An insurance company must retain scanned policy documents for seven years to satisfy regulators. After the first month, documents are almost never read; a regulator request happens less than once a year and can tolerate a few seconds of retrieval time. The company wants the lowest storage cost. Which Cloud Storage class should you use for the long-term copy?
options: Standard storage, because it has no minimum storage duration.
Archive storage, because it has the lowest at-rest cost and data is still available within milliseconds when a request occurs.
Nearline storage, because it is intended for data accessed less than once a month.
Coldline storage, because it is the lowest-cost class that can be read without a restore operation.
explanation: Archive storage is designed for data accessed less than once a year and has the lowest per-GB storage price; unlike tape-style archives at other providers it still serves objects online with millisecond first-byte latency, so the occasional regulator request is fine. Its 365-day minimum storage duration and higher retrieval price are irrelevant for a seven-year, rarely read retention. Option A is the most expensive at rest and is meant for hot data. Option C (Nearline) and Option D (Coldline) target monthly and quarterly access respectively and cost more per GB than Archive; the claim that Archive requires a restore operation is false in Cloud Storage.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Storage classes): Archive storage is designed for data accessed less than once a year and has the lowest per-GB storage price; unlike tape-style archives at other providers it still serves objects online with millisecond first-byte latency, so the occasional regulator request is fine.

whyWrong.2: Option C (Nearline) and Option D (Coldline) target monthly and quarterly access respectively and cost more per GB than Archive; the claim that Archive requires a restore operation is false in Cloud Storage.
whyWrong.3: Option D (Coldline) target monthly and quarterly access respectively and cost more per GB than Archive; the claim that Archive requires a restore operation is false in Cloud Storage.

question: A media analytics company ingests several petabytes of user-generated content into Cloud Storage. Some objects are read heavily for weeks, others are never read again, and the data team cannot predict which is which at upload time. The company wants to minimize total storage cost with the least operational effort and without paying unexpected early-deletion or retrieval fees. What should you do?
options: Store all objects in Coldline and pay retrieval fees only for the objects that turn out to be popular.
Store all objects in Standard and write a monthly script that reads access logs and rewrites cold objects to Archive.
Configure Object Lifecycle Management rules that move every object to Nearline after 30 days and Archive after 90 days.
Enable Autoclass on the bucket so that each object transitions between classes automatically based on its own access pattern.
explanation: Autoclass is built for exactly this situation: unpredictable or mixed access patterns. It moves each object individually to colder classes when it is not accessed and back to Standard when it is read, and it waives early-deletion and retrieval charges, so cost optimizes itself with zero rules to maintain. Option A incurs retrieval fees and 90-day minimum-duration charges on popular objects. Option B is custom tooling that must be operated and still guesses at future access. Option C applies the same age-based schedule to every object regardless of actual access, so popular 60-day-old objects would incur Nearline retrieval charges, and objects moved to Archive then read again pay retrieval fees.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Storage Autoclass): Autoclass is built for exactly this situation: unpredictable or mixed access patterns.
