whyWrong.1: Option B addresses migration mechanics, while the delays are caused by governance decisions such as networking and identity design.
whyWrong.2: Option C changes the reporting format without giving anyone the authority to enforce priorities.

question: A public sector agency is moving its data center operations to Google Cloud. The infrastructure operations team of 40 people is openly resisting the program because they fear their roles will disappear once managed services replace manual server administration. Leadership wants to retain this team and reduce resistance. Which two actions should you recommend? (Choose two.)
options: Outsource all cloud operations to a managed service provider so that the existing team's resistance does not affect the migration timeline.
Involve operations team members in the pilot wave and in designing the target operating model so they shape the new roles rather than have them imposed.
Announce a fixed cutover date and remove administrative access to the legacy environment to force adoption.
Publish a role-based training plan with Google Cloud Skills Boost learning paths and certification targets that maps each existing role to a cloud role such as SRE or platform engineer.
Keep the existing runbooks unchanged and lift-and-shift every server so that day-to-day tasks remain identical.
explanation: Resistance rooted in fear of job loss is addressed by building Desire and Ability in ADKAR terms: giving the team ownership through participation in the pilot and operating-model design (option B) and providing a credible path to new roles through structured training and certification (option D). Option A confirms the team's fears and loses institutional knowledge. Option C is coercive, increases risk during cutover and typically drives attrition rather than adoption. Option E avoids the change instead of managing it and forfeits the operational and cost benefits of managed services that motivated the migration.
hint: Core Rule (Change management): Resistance rooted in fear of job loss is addressed by building Desire and Ability in ADKAR terms: giving the team ownership through participation in the pilot and operating-model design (option B) and providing a credible path to new roles through structured training and certification (option D).

whyWrong.0: Option A confirms the team's fears and loses institutional knowledge.
whyWrong.2: Option C is coercive, increases risk during cutover and typically drives attrition rather than adoption.
whyWrong.4: Option E avoids the change instead of managing it and forfeits the operational and cost benefits of managed services that motivated the migration.

question: A retail bank has a single digital team running several customer-facing apps on Google Cloud. Resources are created manually in the console, each project has its own ad hoc IAM setup, and there is no shared networking or central governance. The board has approved moving 60% of all workloads to Google Cloud over two years. Using the Google Cloud Adoption Framework, how should you characterize the current state and what should you prioritize?
options: The bank is in the Strategic phase; prioritize the Learn theme by sending all engineers to advanced certification programs before migrating further.

The bank is in the Tactical phase; prioritize the Lead and Scale themes by establishing a Cloud Center of Excellence, a landing zone, and Infrastructure as Code templates before onboarding more teams.
The bank is in the Transformational phase; prioritize the Secure theme by deploying VPC Service Controls around every existing project.
The bank is in the Tactical phase; prioritize the Learn theme by hiring a partner to migrate the remaining workloads as quickly as possible.
explanation: Manual provisioning, project-by-project IAM and no central governance are the hallmarks of the Tactical maturity phase in the Google Cloud Adoption Framework; moving to Strategic requires investment in the Lead theme (a cross-functional Cloud Center of Excellence with sponsorship) and the Scale theme (landing zone, templated Infrastructure as Code, reusable patterns) so additional teams can onboard consistently. Option A mislabels the maturity phase and treats training alone as the fix, when governance and automation are the gaps. Option C mislabels the phase and jumps to a single security control rather than building a foundation. Option D outsources speed without building the internal capability the framework's Learn and Lead themes require, and would reproduce the current sprawl at greater scale.
hint: Core Rule: Manual provisioning, project-by-project IAM and no central governance are the hallmarks of the Tactical maturity phase in the Google Cloud Adoption Framework; moving to Strategic requires investment in the Lead theme (a cross-functional Cloud Center of Excellence with sponsorship) and the Scale theme (landing zone, templated Infrastructure as Code, reusable patterns) so additional teams can onboard consistently.

whyWrong.0: Option A mislabels the maturity phase and treats training alone as the fix, when governance and automation are the gaps.
whyWrong.2: Option C mislabels the phase and jumps to a single security control rather than building a foundation.
whyWrong.3: Option D outsources speed without building the internal capability the framework's Learn and Lead themes require, and would reproduce the current sprawl at greater scale.

question: A logistics startup with six developers must launch a new containerized order-tracking API within three months. The team is strong in Python and REST APIs but has no Kubernetes or infrastructure operations experience, and there is no budget to hire. You want to minimize delivery risk given the team's skills. Which platform should you recommend?
options: GKE Standard, so that the team learns Kubernetes on production infrastructure from the start.
Compute Engine managed instance groups with a custom container runtime installed through startup scripts.
Cloud Run, so that the team deploys containers without managing clusters, nodes, or scaling configuration.
GKE Enterprise with Config Sync, so that governance is in place before the team learns Kubernetes.
explanation: When a team lacks infrastructure skills and time is short, the Google-recommended practice is to offset the skills gap with a fully managed service; Cloud Run runs containers with autoscaling, TLS and revisions handled by the platform, which matches the team's application-centric skills. Option A pushes a Kubernetes learning curve onto a production deadline. Option B recreates cluster orchestration by hand with even more operational burden. Option D adds fleet-level governance and licensing complexity that a six-person startup does not need for one API. Choosing services that match team skills is part of the operational excellence pillar.
hint: Core Rule (Skills readiness): When a team lacks infrastructure skills and time is short, the Google-recommended practice is to offset the skills gap with a fully managed service; Cloud Run runs containers with autoscaling, TLS and revisions handled by the platform, which matches the team's application-centric skills.

whyWrong.0: Option A pushes a Kubernetes learning curve onto a production deadline.
whyWrong.1: Option B recreates cluster orchestration by hand with even more operational burden.
whyWrong.3: Option D adds fleet-level governance and licensing complexity that a six-person startup does not need for one API.

question: A hospital network is migrating 80 clinical and administrative applications to Google Cloud in six waves. After the second wave, department heads complained that they learned about cutovers only when logins failed, and the help desk was overwhelmed with tickets. You are asked to prevent this in the remaining waves. What should you do?
options: Create a stakeholder-specific communication plan that publishes the wave schedule, sends targeted pre- and post-cutover messages to affected user groups, briefs the help desk in advance, and provides a feedback channel.
Schedule all remaining cutovers for weekends so that fewer users notice the change.
Send a single organization-wide email listing all 80 applications and their planned migration dates.
Ask the help desk to create a knowledge base article for each application after its cutover is complete.
explanation: Effective change management requires that each stakeholder group receives the right message at the right time through the right channel, and that support staff are prepared before, not after, a change; a formal communication plan tied to the wave schedule achieves this and adds a feedback loop. Option B reduces immediate visibility but clinical systems are used around the clock, and hiding change does not build adoption. Option C is a one-time broadcast that department heads will not retain and that is not targeted to who is affected when. Option D is reactive and leaves the help desk unprepared at the moment of cutover.
hint: Core Rule: Effective change management requires that each stakeholder group receives the right message at the right time through the right channel, and that support staff are prepared before, not after, a change; a formal communication plan tied to the wave schedule achieves this and adds a feedback loop.

whyWrong.1: Option B reduces immediate visibility but clinical systems are used around the clock, and hiding change does not build adoption.
whyWrong.2: Option C is a one-time broadcast that department heads will not retain and that is not targeted to who is affected when.
whyWrong.3: Option D is reactive and leaves the help desk unprepared at the moment of cutover.

question: The CISO of a payments company is blocking a proposal to move the fraud analytics platform to Google Cloud. Her stated concern is 'we lose control over who can access our data and we cannot prove compliance to auditors.' The CTO asks you to change her position without escalating over her head. What should you do?
options: Present the Google Cloud compliance certifications list and ask the CTO to approve the project on the basis that Google is already audited.
Propose a hybrid design that keeps all sensitive data on-premises indefinitely so that the CISO's objection no longer applies.
Escalate to the CEO with a business case showing the revenue impact of delaying the fraud platform.

Run a shared-responsibility workshop with the security team, then execute a scoped proof of concept that demonstrates the specific controls she cares about, such as Organization Policy constraints, VPC Service Controls, Cloud Audit Logs, Access Transparency, and Assured Workloads.
explanation: Influencing a skeptical stakeholder means addressing her actual concerns with evidence she can validate herself; a shared-responsibility workshop clarifies what Google controls versus what the customer controls, and a scoped proof of concept lets her team verify data access controls and audit evidence directly. Option A relies on Google's certifications, which cover Google's side of the shared responsibility model but do not answer how her organization controls and proves access. Option B avoids the conversation and forfeits the business value of the platform. Option C is exactly the escalation the CTO asked you to avoid and would damage the working relationship with the security organization.
hint: Core Rule (Influencing stakeholders): Influencing a skeptical stakeholder means addressing her actual concerns with evidence she can validate herself; a shared-responsibility workshop clarifies what Google controls versus what the customer controls, and a scoped proof of concept lets her team verify data access controls and audit evidence directly.

whyWrong.1: Option B avoids the conversation and forfeits the business value of the platform.
whyWrong.2: Option C is exactly the escalation the CTO asked you to avoid and would damage the working relationship with the security organization.

question: A global airline is beginning a multi-year migration to Google Cloud. The CIO wants an early, visible success to build momentum and win over skeptical business units. The candidate workloads for the first wave are: the booking engine (mission-critical, complex, owned by a cautious team), an internal crew-scheduling reporting tool (moderate complexity, owned by an enthusiastic team, used daily by operations staff), a static intranet site (trivial, little visibility), and the mainframe-based loyalty system (high complexity, no in-house expertise). Which workload should you recommend for the pilot wave?
options: The booking engine, because a successful migration of the most critical system will silence skeptics fastest.
The crew-scheduling reporting tool, because it is visible to the business, moderately complex enough to validate the landing zone and processes, and owned by a team willing to champion the change.
The static intranet site, because it carries the lowest risk of any production impact.
The loyalty system, because the mainframe is the largest cost driver and offers the biggest savings.
explanation: A good pilot balances low risk with meaningful learning and visibility: it should exercise the landing zone, migration tooling and operating processes, be visible enough to demonstrate value, and be owned by a team that will become internal champions. Option A concentrates the highest business risk in the phase where processes are least mature. Option C is so trivial that it validates nothing and generates no momentum. Option D combines the highest complexity with the lowest skills readiness, which is the profile most likely to fail publicly. Google's migration guidance recommends starting with workloads that are easy to migrate yet representative enough to prove the approach.
hint: Core Rule (Pilot selection): A good pilot balances low risk with meaningful learning and visibility: it should exercise the landing zone, migration tooling and operating processes, be visible enough to demonstrate value, and be owned by a team that will become internal champions.

whyWrong.0: Option A concentrates the highest business risk in the phase where processes are least mature.
whyWrong.2: Option C is so trivial that it validates nothing and generates no momentum.
whyWrong.3: Option D combines the highest complexity with the lowest skills readiness, which is the profile most likely to fail publicly.

question: A telecommunications company plans to move its data warehouse from an on-premises appliance to BigQuery and rebuild its ETL pipelines on Dataflow. The head of engineering wants an objective view of whether the 25-person data team is ready, rather than relying on managers' opinions. What should you recommend?
options: Ask each engineer to self-assess their cloud proficiency on a five-point scale and start the migration if the average is above three.
Require every engineer to pass the Professional Data Engineer certification before any migration work begins.

Define the target roles and required competencies for the new platform, assess the team against them using role-based skills assessments, and produce a gap analysis that drives a learning plan with Skills Boost paths and hands-on labs in sandbox projects.
Hire an external partner to run the migration and defer team assessment until the new platform is in production.
explanation: Skills readiness should be measured against the competencies the target architecture actually requires; a structured gap analysis per role produces an actionable learning plan and lets leadership decide where to upskill, hire or use partners. Option A is subjective and does not tie to required competencies. Option B makes a certification a blocking gate for all 25 people, delaying the program unnecessarily and ignoring that certifications are one signal of readiness, not a prerequisite for every role. Option D defers the assessment entirely, which leaves the company unable to operate the platform when the partner leaves. This aligns with the Learn theme of the Google Cloud Adoption Framework.
hint: Core Rule (Skills gap analysis): Skills readiness should be measured against the competencies the target architecture actually requires; a structured gap analysis per role produces an actionable learning plan and lets leadership decide where to upskill, hire or use partners.

question: A pharmaceutical company has created a Cloud Center of Excellence (CCoE) with eight engineers. Within three months, the CCoE has become a bottleneck because every product team submits tickets asking the CCoE to create projects, write Terraform, and deploy applications on their behalf. Product teams complain about delays, and the CCoE complains about burnout. How should the CCoE's role be redefined?
options: Reposition the CCoE as an enablement team that publishes guardrails, reusable Terraform modules, reference architectures and training, and provides self-service project provisioning so product teams deploy their own workloads.
Double the size of the CCoE so that it can keep up with deployment requests from all product teams.
Disband the CCoE and let each product team manage its own Google Cloud environment independently.
Restrict product teams to submitting one deployment request per sprint to protect the CCoE's capacity.
explanation: A CCoE scales by enabling others, not by doing the work for them: its charter should be standards, guardrails (Organization Policy, IAM patterns), reusable modules, a service catalog or self-service provisioning, and coaching. Option B scales the bottleneck rather than removing it. Option C throws away consistency and governance, which is what leads to sprawl and security gaps. Option D rations the bottleneck and slows the whole organization. This reflects the Lead and Scale themes of the Google Cloud Adoption Framework and the operational excellence pillar's emphasis on automation and self-service.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Center of Excellence): A CCoE scales by enabling others, not by doing the work for them: its charter should be standards, guardrails (Organization Policy, IAM patterns), reusable modules, a service catalog or self-service provisioning, and coaching.

whyWrong.1: Option B scales the bottleneck rather than removing it.
whyWrong.2: Option C throws away consistency and governance, which is what leads to sprawl and security gaps.
whyWrong.3: Option D rations the bottleneck and slows the whole organization.

question: A fast-growing gaming studio has invested heavily in cloud training: most engineers hold Google Cloud certifications and teams ship to Google Cloud daily. However, an assessment reveals that each team uses its own Google accounts and consumer Gmail identities, there is no organization resource, projects are created by anyone with a credit card, and no one is accountable for cloud strategy. Which two actions should you prioritize to raise maturity across the Adoption Framework themes? (Choose two.)
options: Establish an organization resource with Cloud Identity as the central identity provider, a folder hierarchy, and baseline Organization Policy constraints.
Fund an additional round of advanced certifications so that engineers deepen their expertise.
Create a cross-functional Cloud Center of Excellence with an executive sponsor that owns cloud strategy, standards and cost governance.
Purchase three-year committed use discounts across all existing projects to lock in savings.
Migrate all teams to a single project to simplify management.

Option B invests further in the theme that is already mature. Option D commits spend before the organization has governance or visibility, which risks purchasing commitments for the wrong resources. Option E is an anti-pattern: a single project removes the isolation, IAM boundaries and cost separation that the resource hierarchy provides.

question: A 30-person healthtech startup must migrate a HIPAA-regulated patient portal to Google Cloud within ten weeks to meet a contractual obligation with a hospital customer. The team has no prior Google Cloud experience and no security or compliance specialists. Which approach best balances timeline, compliance risk and long-term capability?
options: Have the founders complete the Cloud Architect learning path and lead the migration themselves.
Delay the migration by six months so that the team can be trained and certified first.
Hire two senior cloud engineers and start the migration once they are onboarded.

Engage a Google Cloud partner with a healthcare specialization to deliver the migration, with explicit knowledge-transfer sessions and shadowing so the internal team can operate the platform afterwards.

Option C is uncertain (senior hires can take months) and still lacks healthcare compliance expertise. hint: Core Rule (Partner engagement): When a hard deadline and regulatory obligations meet a skills gap, engaging a specialized partner is the Google-recommended way to de-risk delivery, and building knowledge transfer into the engagement avoids long-term dependency.

whyWrong.2: Option C is uncertain (senior hires can take months) and still lacks healthcare compliance expertise.

question: A financial services firm introduced a standardized Cloud Build and Cloud Deploy pipeline with Binary Authorization for all services. Three months later, most development teams still deploy manually with kubectl from laptops, citing that the pipeline is 'slow and confusing'. Awareness campaigns and emails have not changed behavior. Using an ADKAR-style approach, what should you do next?
options: Send another round of communications explaining the security benefits of the pipeline.

Address the Desire and Ability stages: embed champions from each team in a pilot, run hands-on enablement sessions, fix the friction points that make the pipeline slow, and make the golden path the easiest way to deploy before enforcing it.
Immediately revoke all developers' kubectl access to production so that the pipeline is the only option.
Replace Cloud Deploy with a third-party CD tool that developers say they prefer.

Option A repeats a stage that is already complete. Option C is pure enforcement without ability-building and will cause outages and shadow workarounds; enforcement is appropriate as reinforcement after the pipeline is usable. Option D changes tooling without evidence that the tool, rather than the onboarding and friction, is the problem.
hint: Core Rule (Handling resistance): Developers already have Awareness (they know the pipeline exists and why) but lack Desire and Ability; ADKAR says further awareness messaging is wasted, and the right levers are champions, hands-on enablement and removing friction so the compliant path is also the fastest path, followed by reinforcement.

question: You are presenting two options to the CTO of an e-commerce company for its checkout service: a multi-region active-active design on Spanner, or a single-region design with a warm standby in a second region using Cloud SQL cross-region replicas. The CTO has 15 minutes and must decide today. How should you frame the trade-off?
options: Explain the consistency models of Spanner and Cloud SQL and the replication lag behaviour of each.
Recommend the active-active design because it is the most reliable option available.

Quantify each option's RTO, RPO and monthly cost, and express them against the estimated revenue loss per hour of checkout downtime so the CTO can choose the level of resilience the business is willing to pay for.
Ask the CTO to defer the decision until a full proof of concept of both designs has been completed.

question: At an ad-tech company, the data platform team insists that a new reporting workload belongs in BigQuery, while the application team insists it should query their existing Spanner database directly. The debate has stalled the project for a month, and both teams escalate to you as the architect to 'pick a side'. What is the most effective way to facilitate a decision?
options: Run a facilitated workshop where both teams first agree on the decision criteria and their weights (for example latency, cost, operational load, data freshness, team skills), then score both options together and record the outcome in an architecture decision record.
Decide in favour of BigQuery because it is the Google-recommended analytics service and inform both teams by email.
Ask each team to build a prototype and let the executive sponsor choose the more impressive demo.
Split the workload so that half of the reports run on BigQuery and half on Spanner to satisfy both teams.
explanation: Good facilitation separates agreeing on criteria from evaluating options: when stakeholders co-own the criteria and weights, the scoring becomes objective, and recording the result in an architecture decision record prevents the debate from being reopened. Option B may be technically right but imposes a decision without buy-in, which typically resurfaces as passive resistance. Option C turns an architecture decision into a demo contest and wastes engineering time. Option D is a compromise that creates two systems to operate and doubles the cost and complexity without resolving the underlying disagreement.
hint: Core Rule: Good facilitation separates agreeing on criteria from evaluating options: when stakeholders co-own the criteria and weights, the scoring becomes objective, and recording the result in an architecture decision record prevents the debate from being reopened.

whyWrong.1: Option B may be technically right but imposes a decision without buy-in, which typically resurfaces as passive resistance.
whyWrong.2: Option C turns an architecture decision into a demo contest and wastes engineering time.
whyWrong.3: Option D is a compromise that creates two systems to operate and doubles the cost and complexity without resolving the underlying disagreement.

question: A university system has 400 applications across three data centers, with poorly documented dependencies between them. Leadership wants a migration plan with predictable waves and minimal disruption to term-time operations. Which approach should you recommend for defining the migration waves?
options: Order applications alphabetically within each department and migrate 20 per month so that progress is easy to track.
Migrate all applications in a single wave during the summer break to avoid any cross-data-center dependencies during term time.
Start with the applications that have the highest infrastructure cost, because they deliver the largest savings first.

Use Migration Center discovery to inventory the estate and map network dependencies, cluster tightly coupled applications into move groups, and schedule waves that start with low-complexity, low-risk groups and place term-critical systems in academic breaks.
explanation: Undocumented dependencies are the main risk in wave planning: automated discovery and dependency mapping let you form move groups that migrate together so that latency-sensitive or tightly coupled applications are not split across environments, and sequencing by complexity and business calendar controls risk. Option A ignores dependencies entirely and will break applications whose peers remain on-premises. Option B concentrates all risk in one window with no opportunity to learn from early waves and is unrealistic for 400 applications. Option C prioritizes savings over risk and typically front-loads the most complex systems before the team and processes are mature.
hint: Core Rule (Migration waves): Undocumented dependencies are the main risk in wave planning: automated discovery and dependency mapping let you form move groups that migrate together so that latency-sensitive or tightly coupled applications are not split across environments, and sequencing by complexity and business calendar controls risk.

whyWrong.0: Option A ignores dependencies entirely and will break applications whose peers remain on-premises.
whyWrong.1: Option B concentrates all risk in one window with no opportunity to learn from early waves and is unrealistic for 400 applications.
whyWrong.2: Option C prioritizes savings over risk and typically front-loads the most complex systems before the team and processes are mature.

question: An energy utility ran a two-week Google Cloud bootcamp for 120 engineers at the start of its migration program. Nine months later, the first production workloads are going live and the same engineers are struggling with basic tasks such as IAM bindings and Cloud Logging queries. The program director asks how to avoid this for the remaining waves. What should you recommend?
options: Repeat the same two-week bootcamp for all 120 engineers immediately.

Adopt a just-in-time training plan aligned to each migration wave, combining role-specific Skills Boost learning paths with hands-on labs in sandbox projects and pairing during the wave so skills are applied as soon as they are learned.
Require all engineers to obtain the Associate Cloud Engineer certification before their wave begins.
Give every engineer a Cloud Shell tutorial link and rely on self-study.
explanation: Skills decay when there is a long gap between training and application, so training should be delivered just in time, be role-specific, and be reinforced by hands-on practice and pairing during real work. Option A repeats the pattern that failed: a one-time event disconnected from use. Option C is a blunt gate that delays waves and does not guarantee practical ability in the specific tasks needed. Option D provides no structure, no reinforcement and no accountability. This is the Learn theme of the Google Cloud Adoption Framework applied with an ADKAR focus on Knowledge and Ability.
hint: Core Rule (Training plans): Skills decay when there is a long gap between training and application, so training should be delivered just in time, be role-specific, and be reinforced by hands-on practice and pairing during real work.

whyWrong.0: Option A repeats the pattern that failed: a one-time event disconnected from use.
whyWrong.2: Option C is a blunt gate that delays waves and does not guarantee practical ability in the specific tasks needed.
whyWrong.3: Option D provides no structure, no reinforcement and no accountability.

question: The CIO of a food-distribution company has agreed to be the executive sponsor of the Google Cloud adoption program and asks you what she should personally do in that role to make the program succeed. What should you tell her?
options: Review and approve every architecture decision record so that the technical direction stays consistent.
Attend the daily stand-ups of the migration team to monitor progress closely.

Communicate the vision and business rationale across the organization, secure and protect funding and staffing, remove organizational blockers, and hold business unit leaders accountable for their commitments.
Personally negotiate the committed use discount contract with Google to secure the best pricing.
explanation: An executive sponsor's value is organizational: setting and repeating the vision, guaranteeing resources, resolving cross-functional conflicts, and creating accountability among peers, which is what the Lead theme of the Adoption Framework describes. Option A makes the sponsor a technical approval bottleneck, which is the CCoE's or architecture board's role. Option B is micromanagement at the wrong altitude and does not use the sponsor's authority where it matters. Option D is a procurement task that the sponsor should delegate to finance and procurement.
hint: Core Rule (Executive sponsorship): An executive sponsor's value is organizational: setting and repeating the vision, guaranteeing resources, resolving cross-functional conflicts, and creating accountability among peers, which is what the Lead theme of the Adoption Framework describes.

whyWrong.0: Option A makes the sponsor a technical approval bottleneck, which is the CCoE's or architecture board's role.
whyWrong.1: Option B is micromanagement at the wrong altitude and does not use the sponsor's authority where it matters.
whyWrong.3: Option D is a procurement task that the sponsor should delegate to finance and procurement.

question: Six months after a successful migration, an insurance company notices that teams are drifting back to old habits: infrastructure changes are made directly in the Cloud console instead of through Terraform, and post-incident reviews are no longer held. The CCoE lead asks how to reinforce the new ways of working. Which three actions should you recommend? (Choose three.)
options: Enforce the Infrastructure as Code path technically by removing broad editor roles from humans, granting change rights to CI/CD service accounts, and using Organization Policy constraints as guardrails.
Run another migration to move workloads between regions so that teams have to use Terraform again.
Publish adoption metrics such as percentage of resources managed by IaC and post-incident review completion per team, and review them in a regular forum with leadership.
Reduce the CCoE budget because the migration is complete and no further change management is required.
Recognize and reward teams that follow the new practices, and gather feedback from teams on what makes the practices hard to follow so the friction can be removed.
explanation: Reinforcement, the final ADKAR stage, requires a combination of technical guardrails that make regression difficult (option A), visibility and accountability through measured adoption (option C), and positive reinforcement plus a feedback loop to remove friction (option E). Option B creates artificial work and disruption rather than sustainable habits. Option D removes the capacity needed for reinforcement at exactly the point where drift shows it is needed. Together the three correct actions align with the operational excellence pillar's focus on automation, measurement and continuous improvement.
hint: Core Rule (Change reinforcement): Reinforcement, the final ADKAR stage, requires a combination of technical guardrails that make regression difficult (option A), visibility and accountability through measured adoption (option C), and positive reinforcement plus a feedback loop to remove friction (option E).

whyWrong.1: Option B creates artificial work and disruption rather than sustainable habits.
whyWrong.3: Option D removes the capacity needed for reinforcement at exactly the point where drift shows it is needed.

question: A fintech company's platform team keeps re-debating decisions that were made months earlier, such as why Cloud SQL was chosen over AlloyDB and why a Shared VPC was adopted. New engineers cannot find the rationale, and senior engineers have left. The head of engineering wants decisions to stick and be understood. What should you recommend?
options: Record every decision in the minutes of the weekly architecture meeting and email them to the team.

Adopt architecture decision records (ADRs) stored alongside the code in the repository, each capturing context, options considered, the decision, and its consequences, and require an ADR for significant changes.
Create a wiki page listing the services the company uses and the date each was adopted.
Require the CTO to personally approve any proposal to revisit a past decision.
explanation: ADRs are a lightweight, Google-recommended practice for making the reasoning behind significant decisions durable and discoverable; because they record the alternatives considered and the trade-offs accepted, they let new engineers understand why, and allow decisions to be superseded deliberately rather than relitigated informally. Option A buries decisions in meeting minutes that are hard to find and lack structured context. Option C records what was chosen but not why, which is the missing information. Option D makes the CTO a gatekeeper rather than fixing the knowledge gap, and discourages legitimate re-evaluation when context changes.
hint: Core Rule (Architecture decision records): ADRs are a lightweight, Google-recommended practice for making the reasoning behind significant decisions durable and discoverable; because they record the alternatives considered and the trade-offs accepted, they let new engineers understand why, and allow decisions to be superseded deliberately rather than relitigated informally.

whyWrong.0: Option A buries decisions in meeting minutes that are hard to find and lack structured context.
whyWrong.2: Option C records what was chosen but not why, which is the missing information.
whyWrong.3: Option D makes the CTO a gatekeeper rather than fixing the knowledge gap, and discourages legitimate re-evaluation when context changes.

question: A mid-size HR services company needs an internal IT ticketing and asset management system. Its 12-person engineering team is fully occupied building the customer-facing payroll product, which is the company's differentiator. The COO asks whether the team should build the ticketing system on Google Cloud. What should you recommend?
options: Build a custom ticketing system on Cloud Run and Firestore because the team already knows those services.
Build the system on Compute Engine using an open-source ticketing package to retain full control.
Assign two engineers to build a minimal version and expand it over time.
Buy a SaaS ticketing solution, for example through Google Cloud Marketplace, and keep engineering capacity focused on the differentiating payroll product.
explanation: The deciding factor in build-versus-buy is whether the capability differentiates the business; ticketing is a commodity, so buying preserves scarce engineering capacity for the payroll product where custom development creates competitive value. Option A and option B both consume engineering time and create a system that must be maintained indefinitely. Option C still diverts scarce engineers and typically yields a system that is worse than commercial alternatives. Workload disposition (build, buy, modify, deprecate) is an explicit PCA consideration, and the cost optimization pillar stresses focusing spend on business value.
hint: Core Rule (Build vs buy): The deciding factor in build-versus-buy is whether the capability differentiates the business; ticketing is a commodity, so buying preserves scarce engineering capacity for the payroll product where custom development creates competitive value.

whyWrong.0: Option A and option B both consume engineering time and create a system that must be maintained indefinitely.
whyWrong.1: Option B ("Build the system on Compute Engine using an open-source ticketing package to retain full control.") is incorrect because it does not meet the scenario's core requirement; Option D (Buy a SaaS ticketing solution, for example through Google Cl) is the Google Cloud recommended pattern here.
whyWrong.2: Option C still diverts scarce engineers and typically yields a system that is worse than commercial alternatives.

question: A regional bank's finance team produced an analysis concluding that Google Cloud would be 40% more expensive than its current data center. On inspection, the analysis compares the three-year purchase price of the existing servers against a three-year estimate of on-demand Compute Engine list prices for identically sized VMs. The CIO asks you to review the model before it goes to the board. What should you do?
options: Rebuild the model as a full TCO comparison: include data center facilities, power and cooling, network, hardware refresh, software licenses, and staff costs on the on-premises side, and apply rightsizing from Migration Center assessment data and committed use discounts on the cloud side.
Accept the finance team's model but recommend Spot VMs for all workloads to close the 40% gap.
Reject the model and instead present the cloud option purely on agility benefits, since costs cannot be compared meaningfully.
Ask Google for a larger discount so that the on-demand estimate matches the server purchase price.
explanation: The finance model is flawed on both sides: it omits the majority of on-premises costs (facilities, power, networking, refresh cycles, licenses and staff) and inflates cloud costs by assuming like-for-like sizing at on-demand list price rather than rightsized capacity with committed use discounts; a credible TCO corrects both, ideally using Migration Center's utilization data and TCO reporting. Option B applies Spot VMs to workloads that cannot tolerate preemption, such as core banking systems, to paper over a modeling error. Option C dodges the financial question, which a board will not accept. Option D treats the symptom (a number) rather than the flawed method and is unlikely to succeed.
hint: Core Rule (TCO modeling): The finance model is flawed on both sides: it omits the majority of on-premises costs (facilities, power, networking, refresh cycles, licenses and staff) and inflates cloud costs by assuming like-for-like sizing at on-demand list price rather than rightsized capacity with committed use discounts; a credible TCO corrects both, ideally using Migration Center's utilization data and TCO reporting.

question: A ticketing marketplace must choose between Spanner and AlloyDB for a new order service that will experience extreme spikes when popular events go on sale. The team has read the documentation but cannot agree on which database will meet the p99 latency target under peak write load, and the vendor benchmarks do not match their access pattern. Which decision-making approach should you recommend?
options: Choose Spanner because it offers the higher availability SLA and revisit the decision after launch if latency is a problem.
Choose AlloyDB because the team already knows PostgreSQL, and rely on read pools to absorb spikes.

Run a time-boxed proof of concept for both databases with a representative schema and load profile, define measurable success criteria (p99 latency, cost at peak, operational effort) up front, and decide based on the results.
Escalate the decision to the CTO and ask for a ruling within the week.
explanation: When the decision depends on empirical behaviour under a specific access pattern, a time-boxed PoC with pre-agreed success criteria is the appropriate decision-making tool; defining the criteria before testing prevents the results from being interpreted to fit a preference. Option A and option B each pick on a single attribute (SLA or familiarity) without evidence on the critical requirement, peak write latency, and a post-launch database change is very costly. Option D transfers the decision to someone with less information rather than generating the missing information.

question: A government agency's cloud migration program has been surprised twice: once by a vendor license that did not permit cloud deployment, and once by a Dedicated Interconnect lead time of several months. The program board wants such issues anticipated and visible before they become emergencies. What should you introduce?
options: A weekly email from each workstream lead listing what went wrong in the previous week.

A program risk register in which each risk has a probability and impact rating, an owner, a mitigation plan and a trigger, reviewed at every steering committee meeting with the top risks escalated to the sponsor.
A change advisory board that must approve every technical change in the program.
A requirement that all vendors and carriers sign contracts before any migration planning starts.
explanation: A risk register is the standard decision-support artifact for surfacing uncertain future events, quantifying them, assigning ownership and tracking mitigation; reviewing it regularly with governance forums turns surprises into managed risks such as license restrictions and connectivity lead times. Option A is retrospective reporting of issues, not anticipation of risks. Option C controls changes but does not identify external risks such as procurement lead times. Option D is impractical and would delay the program without addressing the broader class of risks.
hint: Core Rule: A risk register is the standard decision-support artifact for surfacing uncertain future events, quantifying them, assigning ownership and tracking mitigation; reviewing it regularly with governance forums turns surprises into managed risks such as license restrictions and connectivity lead times.

question: A B2B SaaS company measures its API availability with an internal SLO of 99.9% per month. The head of sales proposes writing 99.9% availability into customer contracts with service credits for breaches, arguing 'we already hit that target'. As the architect, what should you advise?
options: Agree, because the SLO and SLA should always be identical to keep reporting simple.
Raise the internal SLO to 99.99% and offer 99.9% in contracts only after the new SLO has been met for a year.
Remove the internal SLO and manage reliability directly against the contractual SLA.

Set the contractual SLA looser than the internal SLO (for example 99.5%), so that the SLO acts as an early warning and the company is not paying credits every time it dips slightly below its internal target.
explanation: An SLA is a contractual commitment with financial consequences, whereas an SLO is an internal target used to drive engineering decisions; Google's SRE guidance is to keep the SLO stricter than the SLA so that breaching the internal target triggers action before customers are owed credits. Option A removes all safety margin and turns every minor SLO miss into a contractual breach. Option B sets an unnecessarily demanding internal target and delays the commercial offer for a year without need. Option C discards the engineering tool that provides the early warning.
hint: Core Rule (SLA vs SLO): An SLA is a contractual commitment with financial consequences, whereas an SLO is an internal target used to drive engineering decisions; Google's SRE guidance is to keep the SLO stricter than the SLA so that breaching the internal target triggers action before customers are owed credits.

whyWrong.0: Option A removes all safety margin and turns every minor SLO miss into a contractual breach.
whyWrong.1: Option B sets an unnecessarily demanding internal target and delays the commercial offer for a year without need.
whyWrong.2: Option C discards the engineering tool that provides the early warning.

question: At an online education company, the product organization pushes for weekly feature releases while the SRE team wants to slow releases after a series of outages. Each side escalates to the VP of Engineering, who asks you for a mechanism that lets the two groups make this trade-off objectively rather than through escalation. What should you propose?
options: Define SLOs for the learning platform and agree an error budget policy: while budget remains, product ships at will; when the budget is exhausted, releases are limited to reliability fixes until the budget recovers.
Require the SRE team to approve every release through a change advisory board.
Freeze all feature releases for one quarter so that the platform can stabilize.
Move release approval to the VP of Engineering so that a single person decides each case.
explanation: An error budget converts the reliability target into a quantified allowance for failure that both product and SRE agree on in advance, making the velocity-versus-reliability trade-off a data-driven business rule rather than a negotiation; this is the SRE practice endorsed in the Well-Architected Framework's reliability pillar. Option B adds a manual gate that slows every release regardless of actual reliability. Option C is a blanket freeze that ignores whether the platform is actually within its reliability target. Option D institutionalizes the escalation the VP wants to eliminate.
hint: Core Rule (Error budgets): An error budget converts the reliability target into a quantified allowance for failure that both product and SRE agree on in advance, making the velocity-versus-reliability trade-off a data-driven business rule rather than a negotiation; this is the SRE practice endorsed in the Well-Architected Framework's reliability pillar.

whyWrong.1: Option B adds a manual gate that slows every release regardless of actual reliability.

question: A 40-person startup runs its production e-commerce platform on Google Cloud. It currently has no paid support plan. After an incident at 2 a.m. where the team could not reach Google support, the founders want 24/7 access to technical support with a one-hour response time for critical-impact issues, at the lowest cost that meets this need. Which support offering should you recommend?
options: Basic Support, because it is free and includes access to documentation and community forums.
Standard Support, because it provides unlimited technical support cases.
Enhanced Support, because it provides 24/7 support for critical-impact cases with a one-hour target response time.
Premium Support, because it provides a 15-minute response time and a named Technical Account Manager.

Option A provides only billing support and community resources, with no technical case handling. Option B provides technical support during business hours only, with a four-hour P2 response target, so it would not have helped at 2 a.m. Option D meets the requirement but adds a Technical Account Manager and a 15-minute response the startup did not ask for, at a much higher price.

question: A global broadcaster is launching a streaming service on Google Cloud for a major sporting event with tens of millions of expected viewers. Premium Support, which includes a named Technical Account Manager, 15-minute P1 response, Event Management Service and third-party technology support.
Standard Support plus a consulting engagement with Google Cloud Consulting for the launch.
Basic Support combined with a Google Cloud partner's managed service contract.

question: A travel booking company wants to define SLOs for its search API as part of a customer success initiative. The operations team proposes using average node CPU utilization and the number of running pods as the service level indicators. You want the SLIs to reflect the customer's experience and be usable for an error budget. Which two SLIs should you recommend instead? (Choose two.)

Average CPU utilization across the GKE node pool, measured in Cloud Monitoring.
The number of pods in the Ready state for the search deployment.
The proportion of search requests served in under 500 ms, measured at the load balancer.
The total daily count of search requests, measured from application logs.

Option B and option C are internal resource metrics that can look healthy while users see errors, and they cannot be expressed as a good-events ratio. Option E measures traffic volume, which is a demand signal rather than a quality signal.

question: A large retailer's platform team launched an internal developer platform on Google Cloud with golden paths for deploying services. Three months later only four of thirty product teams use it, and the platform team does not understand why. The VP of Platform asks you to establish a customer success practice for the platform. What should you do first?

Mandate that all product teams migrate to the platform within one quarter.
Add more golden paths and features to make the platform more attractive.
Hire a marketing specialist to promote the platform internally.

Treating internal teams as customers with measured outcomes is consistent with the operational excellence pillar's continuous improvement principle.

question: An insurance company is defining disaster recovery requirements for 45 applications before migrating them to Google Cloud. Each application owner has stated that their system needs 'zero downtime and zero data loss'. Implementing that for every application would exceed the entire IT budget. How should you derive realistic RTO and RPO targets?
options: Assign every application a uniform RTO of 4 hours and RPO of 1 hour so that the design is consistent and affordable.
Let each application owner keep their stated targets but implement only what the budget allows, starting alphabetically.

Run a business impact analysis that quantifies the financial, regulatory and reputational impact of outage duration and data loss for each business process, classify applications into tiers by maximum tolerable downtime, derive RTO and RPO per tier, and map each tier to a DR pattern (cold, warm, hot) with its cost.
Select the ten applications with the highest infrastructure cost for hot multi-region DR and give the rest backups only.
explanation: RTO and RPO must be derived from business impact, not from owner preferences or technical convenience: a business impact analysis quantifies the cost of downtime and data loss per process, which lets the organization tier applications, agree targets per tier, and fund DR patterns proportionately, which is exactly what Google's DR planning guide recommends. Option A ignores real differences in impact and will overspend on some systems and under-protect others. Option B leaves unrealistic targets in place and allocates protection arbitrarily. Option D confuses infrastructure cost with business criticality; a cheap application can be the most critical.
hint: Core Rule: RTO and RPO must be derived from business impact, not from owner preferences or technical convenience: a business impact analysis quantifies the cost of downtime and data loss per process, which lets the organization tier applications, agree targets per tier, and fund DR patterns proportionately, which is exactly what Google's DR planning guide recommends.

whyWrong.0: Option A ignores real differences in impact and will overspend on some systems and under-protect others.

question: A regional bank has a thoroughly tested technical disaster recovery plan on Google Cloud: databases replicate to a second region and infrastructure can be recreated with Terraform within the RTO. During a regulatory review, the examiner notes that the bank has a DR plan but not a business continuity plan and asks what would happen if the head office were inaccessible while systems stayed up. Which two elements would a business continuity plan add that the DR plan does not cover? (Choose two.)
options: Automated failover of Cloud SQL instances to the secondary region.
Procedures for staff to continue critical business operations, including alternate work locations, secure remote access, and manual workarounds for processes whose systems are degraded.
A crisis management and communication structure defining who declares an incident, who communicates with customers, regulators and the press, and how decisions are made.
Cross-region replication of Cloud Storage buckets holding regulatory records.
A shorter RPO for the core banking database.
explanation: Disaster recovery addresses restoring technology; business continuity addresses keeping the business operating and is broader, covering people, facilities, processes, communications and governance during a crisis. The missing elements are therefore workforce and process continuity (option B) and a crisis management and communication structure (option C). Options A, D and E are technical DR controls that improve recovery of systems but do not address the examiner's scenario, in which the systems are fine and the organization is what is disrupted.
hint: Core Rule (BCP vs DR): Disaster recovery addresses restoring technology; business continuity addresses keeping the business operating and is broader, covering people, facilities, processes, communications and governance during a crisis.

question: A healthcare SaaS provider documented a disaster recovery plan for its Google Cloud environment two years ago. Since then the architecture has changed significantly, and the plan has never been executed. A prospective enterprise customer's security questionnaire asks for evidence of DR testing. What should you recommend to close this gap sustainably?
options: Update the DR document to reflect the current architecture and provide it as evidence.
Perform a one-time DR test before the customer's deadline and archive the results.
Ask the customer to accept Google Cloud's regional availability SLAs as a substitute for DR testing.

Establish a recurring DR testing schedule (at least annually and after major architectural changes), automate recovery with Infrastructure as Code so tests are repeatable, and record results and remediation actions as auditable evidence.
explanation: A DR plan that is not regularly exercised is unproven, and architectural drift over two years makes it likely to fail; the sustainable answer is a defined testing cadence, automation so tests are cheap and repeatable, and a record of outcomes and follow-ups, which is what auditors and enterprise customers expect. Option A produces a document, not evidence of capability. Option B satisfies one questionnaire but repeats the same decay problem. Option C confuses Google's responsibility for infrastructure availability with the customer's responsibility for recovering its own application and data, and does not answer the question asked.
hint: Core Rule (DR testing cadence): A DR plan that is not regularly exercised is unproven, and architectural drift over two years makes it likely to fail; the sustainable answer is a defined testing cadence, automation so tests are cheap and repeatable, and a record of outcomes and follow-ups, which is what auditors and enterprise customers expect.

question: During a four-hour outage of a payroll SaaS platform, customers received no updates, three different executives posted conflicting explanations on social media, and support agents gave inconsistent timelines. The technical recovery itself went to plan. The CEO asks you to make sure the communication side never fails like this again. What should you put in place?
options: Add more engineers to the on-call rotation so that outages are resolved before customers notice.

Define a crisis communication plan as part of the business continuity plan: a single incident commander and communications lead, pre-approved message templates, a public status page updated at fixed intervals, internal briefings for support staff, and clear rules on who may speak publicly.
Disable executives' social media access during incidents.
Publish a detailed post-incident report after each outage to explain what happened.
explanation: Business continuity includes managing communication during a crisis; assigning explicit communication roles, using pre-approved templates and a status page with a fixed update cadence, and briefing customer-facing staff keeps messaging consistent and timely regardless of how long the technical recovery takes. Option A addresses recovery time, which was not the problem. Option C is a control on one symptom and not a plan. Option D is valuable for learning but does nothing for customers and staff during the incident, when consistent communication matters most.
hint: Core Rule (Crisis communication): Business continuity includes managing communication during a crisis; assigning explicit communication roles, using pre-approved templates and a status page with a fixed update cadence, and briefing customer-facing staff keeps messaging consistent and timely regardless of how long the technical recovery takes.

question: A logistics company ran its first regional DR failover test on Google Cloud. The order management application and its database came up correctly in the secondary region within the RTO, but the application was unusable because it depended on an internal authentication service, a license server and a Pub/Sub topic that were only deployed in the primary region. The COO asks how to prevent this class of failure. What should you recommend?
options: Perform systematic dependency mapping for each tier-1 business service, including upstream and downstream services, third-party endpoints and shared platform components, bring every critical dependency into DR scope, and validate with end-to-end failover tests of the whole business process rather than individual applications.
Increase the RTO for the order management application so that the dependencies can be recreated manually after failover.
Deploy all applications in the company as multi-region active-active so that dependencies are always available.
Add the authentication service and license server to the DR runbook and consider the test passed.
explanation: The failure is a scoping error caused by missing dependency mapping; recovering a business service requires that its entire dependency graph, including shared platform services and messaging, is recoverable, and only end-to-end tests of the business process prove this. Option B degrades the business target to accommodate a plan gap rather than fixing the plan. Option C is a blanket, very expensive design decision that is disproportionate for most applications and still fails if dependencies are not identified. Option D fixes the three dependencies found in this test but not the process, so the next unknown dependency will cause the same failure.

question: An EU-based bank is moving its core payment processing to Google Cloud. Its regulator requires that critical ICT services have documented and tested continuity arrangements, that concentration risk on a single provider is managed, and that the bank can demonstrate a credible exit strategy. The CISO asks how the architecture and processes should reflect these obligations. What should you recommend?
options: Deploy in a single region with Assured Workloads and rely on Google's compliance certifications to satisfy the regulator.
Keep the payment system on-premises indefinitely because regulatory continuity requirements cannot be met in a public cloud.

Design multi-region resilience within the EU with tested failover, use portable building blocks (containers, open-source databases or open interfaces) where practical, document a tested exit and data-portability plan, and include continuity testing evidence and third-party risk assessments in the governance process.
Run the payment system active-active across Google Cloud and a second cloud provider from day one to eliminate concentration risk.
explanation: Regulations such as the EU's DORA require financial entities to manage ICT third-party risk, test continuity, and maintain exit strategies; the architecture should provide tested in-region resilience, and the governance process should produce evidence of testing, risk assessment and a realistic exit plan supported by portable technology choices. Option A addresses data residency and compliance attestations but not continuity testing, concentration risk or exit. Option B forfeits the migration on a false premise; regulators permit cloud use with appropriate controls. question: A media company is choosing between three options for its video transcoding platform: a managed Transcoder API, a GKE-based open-source pipeline, and keeping the existing on-premises farm with a burst to Compute Engine. The engineering lead's scoring matrix favours GKE, the finance lead's matrix favours the managed API, and the operations lead's favours the hybrid option; each built their matrix with different criteria. How should you resolve this?
options: Convene the three leads to agree on a single set of decision criteria and their relative weights first, then jointly score the three options against the agreed matrix and document the result.
Average the three matrices' scores and select the option with the highest mean.
Select the option preferred by the most senior of the three leads.
Ask Google Cloud to recommend the option that best fits the company's needs.
explanation: A trade-off matrix only produces a legitimate decision when the stakeholders first agree on what matters and how much; agreeing criteria and weights before scoring removes the bias of each party choosing criteria that favour their preferred option. Option B averages incompatible matrices and hides the disagreement instead of resolving it. Option C substitutes hierarchy for reasoning and forfeits buy-in from the other two leads. Option D delegates a decision that depends on the company's own priorities to an outside party.

question: A SaaS analytics vendor promises customers a contractual 99.95% monthly availability. Its platform is deployed in a single zone and relies on several Google Cloud services, each of which carries its own SLA of 99.9% or higher for that configuration. Customers have started claiming credits after two short outages. The CEO asks how the company should approach its availability commitment. Which two actions should you recommend? (Choose two.)
options: Calculate the composite availability implied by the serial dependencies in the current single-zone design, and redesign with zonal or regional redundancy so the engineered availability comfortably exceeds the contractual 99.95%.
Rely on the individual Google Cloud SLAs, since each is at least 99.9%, and reject customer credit claims on that basis.
Raise the contractual SLA to 99.99% to reassure customers that reliability is a priority.
Set an internal SLO tighter than the contractual SLA with an error budget policy so that engineering action is triggered before customer credits are owed.
Remove the availability commitment from contracts until the platform has been stable for a year.
explanation: The availability of a system with serial dependencies is the product of its components' availabilities, so several 99.9% services in a single zone cannot support a 99.95% promise; the engineering fix is redundancy that raises the designed availability above the commitment, and the process fix is an internal SLO stricter than the SLA with an error budget that forces action early. Option B misreads SLAs: Google's SLAs entitle the vendor to credits from Google, they do not guarantee the vendor's composite availability to its own customers. Option C increases the gap between promise and capability. Option E damages commercial trust and does not solve the underlying design problem.

question: A non-profit runs a donor management application on Compute Engine and Cloud SQL in one region. The business impact analysis set an RTO of 24 hours and an RPO of 4 hours for this application, and the finance director has asked for the lowest-cost DR approach that meets those targets. What should you recommend?
options: Deploy an active-active configuration across two regions behind a global external Application Load Balancer with a multi-region database.
Run a warm standby in a second region with a Cloud SQL cross-region read replica and a scaled-down managed instance group.
Enable a Cloud SQL high-availability instance with a standby in a second zone of the same region.

Take automated Cloud SQL backups and persistent disk snapshots at least every 4 hours to a multi-region Cloud Storage location, keep the infrastructure defined in Terraform, and rebuild in another region when needed.

Option A and option B are hot and warm patterns that provide much lower RTO and RPO than needed at continuous extra cost. Option C protects against a zonal failure but not a regional one, so it does not provide disaster recovery for the region. Matching DR investment to business impact reflects both the reliability and cost optimization pillars.

question: The CFO of a manufacturing company supports moving to Google Cloud but is uncomfortable that a variable monthly bill replaces the predictable, depreciated capital spend she is used to. She asks how the company can get cloud benefits while keeping a large share of spending predictable. What should you recommend?
options: Provision all resources at peak capacity from day one so that the bill never changes.
Purchase committed use discounts for the stable baseline of compute and database usage, keep elastic usage on demand, and set budgets with alerts so that variance is visible and controlled.
Prepay the estimated annual cloud spend to Google in January so that it can be capitalized like hardware.
Use only Spot VMs, whose lower price makes the monthly bill less significant.
explanation: The cloud model shifts spending from CapEx to OpEx, and predictability is achieved by committing to the baseline (committed use discounts provide a fixed, discounted charge for known steady-state usage) while paying on demand only for the elastic portion, with budgets and alerts giving finance visibility. Option A removes elasticity and overspends, defeating the purpose of the migration. Option C is not how Google Cloud billing works and prepayment does not by itself make the spending predictable or optimized. Option D uses preemptible capacity for workloads that may not tolerate it and does not make spending predictable.

question: A SaaS company runs a steady 24/7 Compute Engine footprint of roughly 2,000 vCPUs. Over the next year the platform team plans to move workloads from N2 to newer machine families and to shift some capacity from us-east1 to europe-west4 as its customer base changes. The CFO wants the largest discount that will not be stranded by these changes. Which discount should you recommend?
options: Three-year resource-based committed use discounts for N2 vCPUs and memory in us-east1.
Rely on sustained use discounts, which apply automatically regardless of machine family and region.
Spend-based flexible committed use discounts for Compute Engine, which apply to an hourly spend commitment across machine families and regions.
One-year resource-based committed use discounts split evenly between us-east1 and europe-west4.
explanation: Spend-based (flexible) committed use discounts commit to an hourly spend amount rather than a specific machine family in a specific region, so the commitment continues to apply as workloads move between machine families and regions; that flexibility is worth accepting a slightly lower discount rate than resource-based commitments. question: A bank has completed its migration and now runs a stable core of 600 N2 VMs in europe-west3 that has not changed size or machine type in nine months; a hardware refresh is not planned for at least three years. Finance wants the maximum possible discount on this fleet. Which option should you recommend?
options: Purchase three-year resource-based committed use discounts for the N2 vCPU and memory in europe-west3, sized to the fleet's baseline.
Purchase one-year spend-based flexible committed use discounts and renew annually.
Convert the fleet to Spot VMs, which offer a larger discount than any commitment.
Do nothing, because sustained use discounts already give the maximum discount for VMs that run all month.
explanation: For a fleet that is stable in size, machine family and region over a multi-year horizon, three-year resource-based committed use discounts provide the deepest discount, and the stability removes the stranding risk that would otherwise argue for flexibility. Option C is inappropriate for core banking VMs because Spot VMs can be preempted at any time with no availability guarantee. Option D is wrong because sustained use discounts are much smaller than a three-year commitment.

question: A visual effects studio renders frames overnight on Compute Engine. Each frame job takes about 10 minutes, is idempotent and can be restarted safely, and there is no hard deadline as long as the batch finishes by morning. Compute is 70% of the studio's cloud bill. How can the studio reduce compute cost the most without redesigning the workload?
options: Purchase three-year committed use discounts for the render fleet.
Move the render jobs to GKE Autopilot to benefit from per-pod billing.
Reduce the machine size of each render VM so jobs take longer but cost less per hour.
Run the render workers as Spot VMs in a managed instance group with a job queue that requeues work when an instance is preempted.
explanation: Fault-tolerant, restartable batch work with flexible timing is the ideal profile for Spot VMs, which offer the largest Compute Engine discount in exchange for the possibility of preemption; a managed instance group and a queue handle recreation and requeueing so preemptions do not lose work. Option A locks in spend for a nightly workload that is idle most of the day and delivers a smaller discount than Spot pricing. Option B changes the platform without a clear cost advantage for GPU-heavy or CPU-heavy render jobs. Option C reduces hourly cost but not total cost, because the same amount of compute work still has to be done.

question: A retailer lifted and shifted 250 VMs to Compute Engine using the same sizes they had on-premises. Cloud Monitoring shows most VMs average under 10% CPU and 30% memory utilization. The FinOps lead wants a low-effort, data-driven way to reduce this waste. What should you do?
options: Halve the machine type of every VM and increase it again if users complain.
Review the Active Assist machine type (rightsizing) recommendations for the VMs, which are based on observed utilization, and apply them in a controlled change window.
Migrate all VMs to Spot VMs so that oversizing is less expensive.
Set up a quarterly manual review of Cloud Monitoring dashboards for each VM.

question: A software company has 300 Google Cloud projects created by engineers over five years. Billing has grown steadily even though headcount is flat. You suspect a large amount of spend comes from forgotten resources: stopped VMs with attached disks, unattached persistent disks, reserved external IP addresses, and entire projects no one has touched in months. Which approach identifies this waste with the least manual effort?
options: Write a script that lists all resources in every project and email the output to team leads for review.
Delete every project that has no owner listed in its labels.
Use Active Assist recommenders, including the idle VM, idle persistent disk, idle IP address and unattended project recommenders, and review the recommendations centrally in the Recommendation Hub.
Enable Cloud Asset Inventory and manually inspect the asset export in BigQuery each month.

question: A media conglomerate wants each of its twelve product teams to see their own Google Cloud spend broken down by service, environment and application, with historical trends and the ability to add custom views, without giving teams access to the billing account. What should you do?

Grant every team member the Billing Account Viewer role so they can use the built-in Billing reports.
Download the monthly invoice PDF and email a spreadsheet summary to each team.

question: A university provides Google Cloud sandbox projects to students for coursework. The IT director wants spending in these sandbox projects to stop automatically at the budget limit, accepting that running workloads will be interrupted. What should you do?

Configure the budget to automatically block resource creation once the limit is reached.
Ask students to run gcloud billing projects unlink manually when they finish their work.

question: A market research firm uses BigQuery on-demand pricing. Last month a single analyst ran an unfiltered query across a multi-petabyte table repeatedly from a dashboard, generating a five-figure charge in one day. The data platform lead wants to prevent any single user or project from generating such charges again while keeping on-demand pricing for now. What should you do?
options: Set a Cloud Billing budget on the BigQuery service with an alert at 80% of the expected monthly cost.
Configure BigQuery custom quotas that cap the query bytes billed per user per day and per project per day, and enable partitioning and require partition filters on the largest tables.

Revoke the BigQuery Job User role from all analysts and route every query through a data engineer.

question: A conglomerate needs to allocate Google Cloud costs to business units, applications and environments for monthly chargeback. question: A financial data provider runs BigQuery workloads with a heavy, predictable baseline of scheduled transformations 24 hours a day, plus unpredictable end-of-quarter spikes when analysts run large ad hoc queries. On-demand costs have become both high and volatile, and the CFO wants lower, more predictable spend without throttling the quarter-end analysts. Which pricing approach should you recommend?
options: Use BigQuery Enterprise edition with a one- or three-year slot commitment sized for the baseline and autoscaling slots configured to absorb the quarter-end spikes.
Stay on on-demand pricing and set custom quotas that block analyst queries at quarter end.
Use BigQuery Standard edition with a three-year commitment for all slots needed at peak.
Move the scheduled transformations to Dataproc and keep only ad hoc queries in BigQuery on demand.
explanation: Slot-based editions pricing suits sustained heavy usage: a commitment covers the predictable baseline at a discounted, fixed price, and slot autoscaling handles peaks with pay-as-you-go slots, giving both predictability and elasticity. Option B keeps volatile on-demand pricing and explicitly throttles the analysts, violating the constraint. Option C is wrong because the Standard edition does not support commitments, and committing for peak capacity would overpay for capacity idle most of the year. Option D adds a second platform and operational overhead without addressing the pricing model for the analytical work.
hint: Core Rule (BigQuery pricing models): Slot-based editions pricing suits sustained heavy usage: a commitment covers the predictable baseline at a discounted, fixed price, and slot autoscaling handles peaks with pay-as-you-go slots, giving both predictability and elasticity.

whyWrong.3: Option D adds a second platform and operational overhead without addressing the pricing model for the analytical work.

question: A small marketing agency has three analysts who run a handful of exploratory BigQuery queries per week against a 2 TB dataset. Usage is sporadic and unpredictable, and the agency wants the simplest, lowest-cost pricing arrangement. What should you recommend?
options: Purchase a one-year commitment of 100 slots in BigQuery Enterprise edition.
Create a reservation with a baseline of 50 slots and autoscaling up to 200 slots.
Purchase a three-year commitment in BigQuery Enterprise Plus edition for the best per-slot rate.
Use on-demand pricing, in which the agency pays only for the bytes each query processes.
explanation: On-demand pricing charges per TiB of data processed with no fixed cost, so low and sporadic query volume is cheapest and simplest on demand; slot-based commitments and reservations only pay off when utilization is high and sustained. Option A and option C commit to capacity that would sit idle most of the time. Option B sets a baseline of always-paid slots for a workload that is idle most days. Choosing the pricing model that matches the usage pattern is a core cost optimization practice.
hint: Core Rule (BigQuery pricing models): On-demand pricing charges per TiB of data processed with no fixed cost, so low and sporadic query volume is cheapest and simplest on demand; slot-based commitments and reservations only pay off when utilization is high and sustained.

whyWrong.0: Option A and option C commit to capacity that would sit idle most of the time.
