question: A genomics company stores petabytes of sequencing output in Cloud Storage. Some datasets are read intensively for weeks after creation and then never touched; others are revisited unpredictably months later when a new study starts. The storage team cannot predict which datasets fall into which category and wants to minimize storage cost without incurring surprise retrieval charges or manual class management. What should you do?
options: Store all data in Archive storage, because it has the lowest per-GB price.
Enable Autoclass on the buckets so that objects transition automatically between storage classes based on access patterns, with no retrieval fees or minimum storage durations.
Store all data in Standard storage and ask researchers to manually move datasets to Coldline when they finish a study.
Create a lifecycle rule that moves all objects to Coldline 30 days after creation.
explanation: Autoclass is designed precisely for unknown or changing access patterns: it moves objects to colder classes when they are not accessed and back to Standard when they are read, and it eliminates early deletion and retrieval fees, so unpredictable re-reads do not cause surprise charges. Option A would trigger high retrieval costs and minimum-duration charges for datasets that are read heavily after creation. Option C relies on manual action that will not happen consistently at petabyte scale. Option D applies a fixed rule to heterogeneous data, so datasets revisited after 30 days incur Coldline retrieval fees.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Storage classes): Autoclass is designed precisely for unknown or changing access patterns: it moves objects to colder classes when they are not accessed and back to Standard when they are read, and it eliminates early deletion and retrieval fees, so unpredictable re-reads do not cause surprise charges.

whyWrong.0: Option A would trigger high retrieval costs and minimum-duration charges for datasets that are read heavily after creation.
whyWrong.2: Option C relies on manual action that will not happen consistently at petabyte scale.
whyWrong.3: Option D applies a fixed rule to heterogeneous data, so datasets revisited after 30 days incur Coldline retrieval fees.

question: A payments company must retain transaction audit logs for seven years. Logs are queried frequently during the first 30 days for support cases, rarely between one and twelve months for disputes, and essentially never after the first year except for regulatory requests. The company wants to minimize storage cost while keeping the logs retrievable. Which configuration should you recommend?
options: Store the logs in Archive storage from the start and accept the retrieval cost for support cases.
Store the logs in Standard storage for seven years so that retrieval is always immediate and free.

Store the logs in Standard storage, and configure an Object Lifecycle Management policy that transitions objects to Nearline after 30 days, to Archive after 365 days, and deletes them after 7 years, with a retention policy or Bucket Lock to prevent early deletion.
Store the logs in Coldline storage and manually delete objects older than seven years each quarter.
explanation: The access pattern is known and age-based, which is exactly what lifecycle rules handle: Standard while data is hot, Nearline for occasional access within the first year (its 30-day minimum matches the transition), Archive for the long tail, and automatic deletion at seven years; a retention policy ensures compliance with the retention obligation. Option A pays retrieval and minimum-duration charges for the heavy first-month access. Option B pays the highest per-GB price for seven years of mostly idle data. Option D uses a single class that is too expensive for the long tail and relies on manual deletion, which is both error-prone and a compliance risk.
hint: Core Rule (Storage lifecycle management): The access pattern is known and age-based, which is exactly what lifecycle rules handle: Standard while data is hot, Nearline for occasional access within the first year (its 30-day minimum matches the transition), Archive for the long tail, and automatic deletion at seven years; a retention policy ensures compliance with the retention obligation.

whyWrong.1: Option B pays the highest per-GB price for seven years of mostly idle data.
whyWrong.3: Option D uses a single class that is too expensive for the long tail and relies on manual deletion, which is both error-prone and a compliance risk.

question: A geospatial analytics firm processes imagery in Google Cloud and transfers roughly 400 TB of results per month back to its on-premises data center over the public internet through a Cloud VPN tunnel. Network egress has become one of the largest line items on the bill. Which change would most reduce this cost while keeping the transfer secure and reliable?
options: Provision Dedicated Interconnect (or Partner Interconnect) to the data center so that traffic to on-premises is billed at the lower Interconnect egress rates.
Compress the results before transfer and continue to use the Cloud VPN tunnel.
Switch the VPN to HA VPN to obtain a discounted egress rate.
Transfer the results through a Cloud Storage bucket with Requester Pays enabled.
explanation: Egress over Cloud Interconnect is billed at significantly lower per-GB rates than internet egress, so for hundreds of terabytes per month the Interconnect port cost is quickly outweighed by the egress savings, and the connection also improves throughput and reliability. Option B may reduce volume somewhat but does not change the expensive internet egress rate. Option C improves availability but HA VPN traffic is still internet egress at standard rates. Option D shifts who pays for bucket egress rather than reducing it, and the firm would be paying itself.
hint: Core Rule (Egress cost minimization): Egress over Cloud Interconnect is billed at significantly lower per-GB rates than internet egress, so for hundreds of terabytes per month the Interconnect port cost is quickly outweighed by the egress savings, and the connection also improves throughput and reliability.

whyWrong.2: Option C improves availability but HA VPN traffic is still internet egress at standard rates.
whyWrong.3: Option D shifts who pays for bucket egress rather than reducing it, and the firm would be paying itself.

question: A news publisher serves images and video clips to a global audience from a Cloud Storage bucket behind a global external Application Load Balancer. Internet egress from the bucket has become the dominant cost, and readers in distant regions report slow load times. What should you do to reduce cost and improve performance with minimal changes?
options: Replicate the bucket to every region and use DNS geolocation routing to send readers to the nearest copy.
Move the bucket to a multi-region location so that it is served from the closest region.
Reduce image quality across the site to shrink the bytes transferred.
Enable Cloud CDN on the load balancer backend bucket so that content is cached at Google's edge locations, reducing origin egress and latency.
explanation: Cloud CDN caches cacheable static content at edge locations, so repeated requests are served from cache rather than the origin; cache egress is priced lower than origin egress and users get lower latency, and enabling it on an existing backend bucket is a configuration change. Option A multiplies storage cost and management effort and still pays egress from each region. Option B changes where the data is stored for durability and availability, not where it is served from to the user, and does not reduce egress charges. Option C degrades the product to save money and does not address latency for distant readers.
hint: Core Rule: Cloud CDN caches cacheable static content at edge locations, so repeated requests are served from cache rather than the origin; cache egress is priced lower than origin egress and users get lower latency, and enabling it on an existing backend bucket is a configuration change.

whyWrong.2: Option C degrades the product to save money and does not address latency for distant readers.

topic: Sustained use and committed use discounts
question: A ticketing company runs a fleet of N2 VMs in a managed instance group. About 40 instances run continuously, and the group scales to as many as 200 instances for a few days each month around major on-sale events. The FinOps team wants to maximize discounts on this fleet with minimal ongoing effort. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Purchase resource-based committed use discounts covering the 40 always-on instances' vCPUs and memory.
Purchase resource-based committed use discounts covering the full 200-instance peak.
Take no action for the burst instances: sustained use discounts are applied automatically to eligible N2 VMs based on how long they run within the month.
Switch the burst instances to E2 machine types so that they qualify for sustained use discounts.
Enable sustained use discounts in the Cloud Billing console for the project.
explanation: The correct pattern is to commit only to the baseline and let automatic discounts handle the variable portion: committed use discounts on the 40 steady instances give the deepest discount without stranding, and sustained use discounts apply automatically to eligible machine families such as N2 in proportion to monthly runtime, with nothing to configure. Option B would leave most of the commitment unused and billed during the majority of the month. Option D is wrong because E2 machine types are not eligible for sustained use discounts. Option E is wrong because sustained use discounts cannot be enabled or disabled; they are applied automatically.
hint: Core Rule (Sustained use and committed use discounts): The correct pattern is to commit only to the baseline and let automatic discounts handle the variable portion: committed use discounts on the 40 steady instances give the deepest discount without stranding, and sustained use discounts apply automatically to eligible machine families such as N2 in proportion to monthly runtime, with nothing to configure.

whyWrong.3: Option D is wrong because E2 machine types are not eligible for sustained use discounts.
whyWrong.4: Option E is wrong because sustained use discounts cannot be enabled or disabled; they are applied automatically.

question: An ad-tech company stores clickstream data in a Cloud Storage bucket in us-central1 and runs its nightly Dataflow and Dataproc processing jobs in europe-west1 because that is where the team originally set up its projects. The jobs read tens of terabytes each night. Billing analysis shows large network charges attributed to these jobs. Which change most directly reduces this cost?
options: Compress the clickstream files so that less data is transferred between regions.
Run the processing jobs in us-central1, the same region as the bucket, so that reads are within-region and do not incur inter-region data transfer charges.
Enable Cloud CDN in front of the Cloud Storage bucket to cache the files for the jobs.
Move the bucket to a multi-region location so that reads from Europe are free.
explanation: Reading Cloud Storage data from compute in a different region incurs inter-region data transfer charges on every read, so colocating processing with data eliminates the charge entirely and also improves throughput. Option A reduces the volume but still pays cross-region rates on every byte and adds CPU cost. Option C is designed for cacheable public content delivered to users, not for bulk analytical reads. Option D is wrong because reading a multi-region bucket from a region incurs data transfer charges too and increases storage cost.
hint: Core Rule (Data locality and network cost): Reading Cloud Storage data from compute in a different region incurs inter-region data transfer charges on every read, so colocating processing with data eliminates the charge entirely and also improves throughput.

question: A machine learning startup wants to cut its Compute Engine bill by moving as much as possible to Spot VMs. The architect must decide which workloads are appropriate. Which two workloads are good candidates for Spot VMs? (Choose two.)
options: The self-managed PostgreSQL primary instance that backs the customer-facing API.
Stateless CI build agents that pick up jobs from a queue and can be retried on failure.
The stateful game-session servers that hold in-memory player state for the duration of a match.
Model training jobs that checkpoint to Cloud Storage every few minutes and can resume from the last checkpoint.
The single VM that hosts the company's on-call paging integration.
explanation: Spot VMs can be preempted at any time with short notice and have no availability guarantee, so they suit workloads that are fault tolerant and can resume or be retried: queue-driven CI agents and checkpointed training jobs lose little work on preemption and benefit from the deep discount. Option A is a stateful primary database whose preemption would cause an outage and possible data loss. Option C holds unreplicated in-memory state that would be lost mid-match. Option E is a critical single point of failure for incident response and must not run on preemptible capacity.
hint: Core Rule (Spot VM suitability): Spot VMs can be preempted at any time with short notice and have no availability guarantee, so they suit workloads that are fault tolerant and can resume or be retried: queue-driven CI agents and checkpointed training jobs lose little work on preemption and benefit from the deep discount.

question: A software vendor runs 120 development and test VMs on Compute Engine that are used only during business hours on weekdays, yet they run 24/7. The engineering manager wants to cut the cost of these environments with minimal effort and without changing how developers work during the day. What should you do?
options: Purchase one-year committed use discounts for the development VMs.
Ask developers to stop their VMs at the end of each day.
Attach an instance schedule (resource policy) to the development VMs that stops them every evening and on weekends and starts them each weekday morning.
Convert the development VMs to Spot VMs.
explanation: Compute Engine instance schedules automatically start and stop VMs on a defined calendar, eliminating roughly two thirds of the running hours for weekday-only environments with no manual effort and no change to the daytime developer experience. Option A commits to paying for 24/7 usage that is not needed. Option B depends on developers remembering, which is the reason the VMs run 24/7 today. Option D exposes developers to preemption during working hours and does not stop billing at night.

question: A subscription streaming company's Google Cloud bill has tripled in 18 months while subscribers grew by 40%. Engineers say cost is 'finance's problem', finance receives one consolidated invoice it cannot interpret, and nobody can say what it costs to serve one subscriber. The CFO and CTO jointly ask you to fix the situation. What should you recommend?
options: Establish a FinOps practice: give engineering teams visibility of their own spend through billing export dashboards, define unit economics such as cost per subscriber, make cost a non-functional requirement in design reviews, and hold regular joint engineering-finance reviews of optimization opportunities.
Have finance approve every new resource request before it is provisioned so that spend is controlled centrally.
Ask Google for a larger enterprise discount so that the bill returns to the previous level.
Freeze all new cloud projects until the bill decreases.
explanation: The problem is cultural and organizational: cost is invisible to the people who create it and not connected to business value; FinOps addresses this by combining visibility (showback), accountability, unit economics and continuous optimization, which the Well-Architected Framework's cost optimization pillar describes as fostering a culture of cost awareness and aligning spend with business value. Option B introduces a central approval bottleneck that slows engineering without building awareness. Option C addresses price, not the efficiency and accountability gaps that caused spend to outpace growth. Option D halts business value creation and does nothing about existing waste.
hint: Core Rule (FinOps culture): The problem is cultural and organizational: cost is invisible to the people who create it and not connected to business value; FinOps addresses this by combining visibility (showback), accountability, unit economics and continuous optimization, which the Well-Architected Framework's cost optimization pillar describes as fostering a culture of cost awareness and aligning spend with business value.

whyWrong.2: Option C addresses price, not the efficiency and accountability gaps that caused spend to outpace growth.
whyWrong.3: Option D halts business value creation and does nothing about existing waste.

question: A hospital group's IT department currently absorbs all Google Cloud costs centrally. The CIO wants clinical and administrative departments to become accountable for their consumption, but department heads are wary of surprise internal bills and the labeling of resources is not yet reliable. How should the CIO introduce cost accountability?
options: Implement full chargeback immediately by invoicing each department for its share of the bill from next month.
Keep absorbing costs centrally and rely on IT to optimize on behalf of departments.

Start with showback, providing each department with regular reports of its attributed spend and trends while the labeling standard matures, and move to chargeback once attribution is trusted and departments have had time to adjust budgets.
Split the organization into a separate billing account per department so that each receives a separate invoice from Google.
explanation: Showback creates cost awareness and accountability without financial transfers, which is the right first step when attribution data is still imperfect and stakeholders need time to adapt; chargeback should follow once labels and allocation rules are reliable enough to be defensible. Option A introduces internal billing based on unreliable data, which will generate disputes and resistance. Option B leaves the incentive problem unsolved. Option D is an organizational restructuring that fragments billing and discount sharing to solve what is a reporting and change-management problem.
hint: Core Rule (Showback vs chargeback): Showback creates cost awareness and accountability without financial transfers, which is the right first step when attribution data is still imperfect and stakeholders need time to adapt; chargeback should follow once labels and allocation rules are reliable enough to be defensible.

whyWrong.1: Option B leaves the incentive problem unsolved.
whyWrong.3: Option D is an organizational restructuring that fragments billing and discount sharing to solve what is a reporting and change-management problem.

question: A holding company owns four legally separate subsidiaries that all use Google Cloud under a single organization resource. Each subsidiary's finance department must receive its own invoice in its own currency and legal entity name, but the group CTO wants central visibility and governance across all subsidiaries. How should you structure billing?
options: Use a single billing account for the organization and allocate costs to subsidiaries with labels and BigQuery reports.
Create a separate organization resource for each subsidiary, each with its own billing account.
Use one billing account with a Cloud Billing subaccount per subsidiary.

Keep the single organization for central governance and create a separate (invoiced) Cloud Billing account per subsidiary linked to that subsidiary's projects, granting group finance the Billing Account Viewer role on all of them.
explanation: Invoices are generated per Cloud Billing account, and each billing account has its own legal entity, currency and payment terms, so legally separate invoicing requires separate billing accounts; because billing accounts are independent of the resource hierarchy, all four can be used under one organization, preserving central IAM, Organization Policy and visibility. Option A produces one invoice to one legal entity, which fails the requirement. Option B fragments governance and identity across four organizations unnecessarily. Option C is wrong because subaccounts are intended for resellers and roll up into the parent account's invoice, so they do not produce separate legal invoices.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Billing hierarchy): Invoices are generated per Cloud Billing account, and each billing account has its own legal entity, currency and payment terms, so legally separate invoicing requires separate billing accounts; because billing accounts are independent of the resource hierarchy, all four can be used under one organization, preserving central IAM, Organization Policy and visibility.

whyWrong.1: Option B fragments governance and identity across four organizations unnecessarily.
whyWrong.2: Option C is wrong because subaccounts are intended for resellers and roll up into the parent account's invoice, so they do not produce separate legal invoices.

question: A financial analyst at a retail company needs to review Google Cloud spend, cost trends and invoices across all projects linked to the company's billing account. Following the principle of least privilege, the analyst must not be able to change billing settings, link projects, or modify any cloud resources. Which role should you grant?
options: Billing Account Administrator on the billing account.
Billing Account Viewer on the billing account.
Project Owner on every project linked to the billing account.
Billing Account User on the billing account.
explanation: Billing Account Viewer grants read-only access to cost information, transactions and reports for the billing account, which is exactly what a finance analyst needs and nothing more. question: A regional bank's online banking application runs on GKE with Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in one region. Its business impact analysis set an RTO of 1 hour and an RPO of 5 minutes. The architecture team proposed a fully active-active deployment across two regions with a globally distributed database, and the CFO has rejected the cost. Which DR pattern meets the targets at the lowest ongoing cost?
options: A warm standby: a Cloud SQL cross-region read replica that can be promoted, a minimal GKE cluster in the secondary region kept at low capacity, infrastructure defined in Terraform, and a rehearsed failover runbook that scales up the cluster and switches traffic.
A cold pattern: nightly Cloud SQL backups exported to a multi-region Cloud Storage bucket and full infrastructure rebuild in the secondary region on demand.
The proposed active-active design, because only a multi-region database can achieve a 5-minute RPO.
A single-region high-availability design with a Cloud SQL standby in a second zone and a regional GKE cluster.
explanation: An RTO of one hour and RPO of five minutes rule out cold recovery but do not require continuous active-active operation; asynchronous cross-region replication keeps data loss within minutes, and a small pre-provisioned standby footprint that scales on failover fits within an hour, at a fraction of the cost of a second full production stack. Option B has an RPO of up to 24 hours and a rebuild time that typically exceeds one hour. Option C is wrong because a cross-region replica achieves a 5-minute RPO without a globally distributed database, so the extra cost is not justified by the targets. Option D protects against zonal failure only and provides no recovery from a regional outage.
hint: Core Rule (Cost of DR tiers): An RTO of one hour and RPO of five minutes rule out cold recovery but do not require continuous active-active operation; asynchronous cross-region replication keeps data loss within minutes, and a small pre-provisioned standby footprint that scales on failover fits within an hour, at a fraction of the cost of a second full production stack.

whyWrong.3: Option D protects against zonal failure only and provides no recovery from a regional outage.

question: A research institute gives each lab its own Google Cloud project. Last month one lab accidentally launched dozens of A3 GPU VMs and consumed most of the institute's quarterly cloud budget in a week. The institute wants to prevent any single lab from provisioning more than a small, agreed amount of GPU capacity unless it requests more, without relying on after-the-fact alerts. What should you do?
options: Configure a Cloud Billing budget per lab project with alerts at 50%, 90% and 100%.
Remove the Compute Admin role from all lab members and require the central IT team to create every VM.
Use Cloud Quotas to set lower consumer quota overrides for GPU quotas on each lab project, and document a request process for temporary increases.
Apply an Organization Policy constraint that restricts which regions lab projects can use.
explanation: Quotas are preventive limits enforced at provisioning time; lowering the GPU quota on each lab project through quota overrides makes it impossible to exceed the agreed capacity without an explicit increase request, which is the direct control for this failure mode. Option D limits regions but does not restrict how many GPUs can be created in the allowed regions.
hint: Core Rule (Quotas as governance): Quotas are preventive limits enforced at provisioning time; lowering the GPU quota on each lab project through quota overrides makes it impossible to exceed the agreed capacity without an explicit increase request, which is the direct control for this failure mode.

whyWrong.1: Option B eliminates self-service for all labs and creates a bottleneck in central IT.
whyWrong.3: Option D limits regions but does not restrict how many GPUs can be created in the allowed regions.

question: A multinational retailer has 900 Google Cloud projects. The central FinOps team knows that Active Assist generates cost recommendations, but reviewing them project by project in the console is impractical, and the team wants to prioritize the largest savings across the organization and track whether teams act on them. What should you do?
options: Ask each project owner to check the Recommendation Hub monthly and report savings in a shared document.

Enable organization-level export of recommendations and insights to BigQuery through the Recommender service, build a Looker Studio dashboard ranking recommendations by estimated savings and owner, and review it in the FinOps cadence.
Grant the FinOps team the Owner role on all 900 projects so they can apply recommendations directly.
Write a script that applies every cost recommendation automatically across all projects.

Option C grants excessive privilege and makes the central team responsible for changes in systems they do not operate. hint: Core Rule (Active Assist at scale): The Recommender service supports exporting recommendations and insights for the whole organization to BigQuery, which lets a central team aggregate, rank by estimated savings, attribute to owners and track status over time; this converts scattered per-project hints into a managed optimization backlog.

The FinOps Hub in the Cloud Billing console, which shows a FinOps score and aggregated optimization opportunities, together with Gemini Cloud Assist cost insights to explain cost changes in natural language.

question: Two years ago, one product team at a retailer bought three-year resource-based committed use discounts for N1 vCPUs and memory in us-west1 in its own project. The team has since modernized onto Cloud Run and the commitment is now largely unused, but the company still pays for it, while other teams in the same billing account run N1 VMs on demand in us-west1. The FinOps lead asks how to reduce the waste now and avoid repeating it. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Enable committed use discount sharing on the billing account so that the unused N1 commitment in us-west1 is applied to matching usage in the other teams' projects.
Cancel the remaining commitment through the console to stop the charges.
Move the other teams' workloads to E2 machine types so they benefit from the commitment.

For future purchases, use the committed use discount recommender and centralize commitment decisions in the FinOps process, preferring spend-based flexible commitments where the machine family or region may change.
Open a support case asking Google to refund the unused portion of the commitment.
explanation: Resource-based commitments cannot be cancelled or refunded, but enabling CUD sharing at the billing account level lets the commitment apply to matching resources (same machine family and region) in any project under the account, which immediately reduces the waste; preventing recurrence requires data-driven, centrally governed purchasing using the recommender and flexible commitments when future usage is uncertain. Option B and option E are not possible: commitments are binding for their term. Option C is wrong because a resource-based N1 commitment applies only to N1 resources, so moving workloads to E2 would not consume it.
hint: Core Rule (Committed use discount pitfalls): Resource-based commitments cannot be cancelled or refunded, but enabling CUD sharing at the billing account level lets the commitment apply to matching resources (same machine family and region) in any project under the account, which immediately reduces the waste; preventing recurrence requires data-driven, centrally governed purchasing using the recommender and flexible commitments when future usage is uncertain.

whyWrong.1: Option B and option E are not possible: commitments are binding for their term.
whyWrong.2: Option C is wrong because a resource-based N1 commitment applies only to N1 resources, so moving workloads to E2 would not consume it.
whyWrong.4: Option E ("Open a support case asking Google to refund the unused portion of the commitment.") is incorrect because it does not meet the scenario's core requirement; Option A (Enable committed use discount sharing on the billing account), Option D (For future purchases, use the committed use discount recomme) is the Google Cloud recommended pattern here.

question: A regional online marketplace serves customers only in one country from a single Google Cloud region. It uses a regional external load balancer, does not use Cloud CDN, and does not require Google's global network for ingress. Internet egress is a significant cost. Which option would reduce egress cost without changing the application architecture?
options: Migrate to a global external Application Load Balancer to benefit from global routing discounts.
Switch the project's network service tier from Premium Tier to Standard Tier so that egress is billed at Standard Tier rates.
Purchase committed use discounts for network egress.
Enable Private Google Access on the subnets to make traffic free.
explanation: Standard Tier delivers traffic over the public internet rather than Google's premium global backbone and is billed at lower egress rates; it is appropriate for regional workloads that use regional load balancing and do not need global anycast or Cloud CDN, which is exactly this marketplace's profile. Option A moves in the opposite direction, requiring Premium Tier. Option C describes a discount type that does not exist for internet egress. Option D affects how VMs without external IPs reach Google APIs and has nothing to do with serving customers on the internet.
hint: Core Rule (Network Service Tiers): Standard Tier delivers traffic over the public internet rather than Google's premium global backbone and is billed at lower egress rates; it is appropriate for regional workloads that use regional load balancing and do not need global anycast or Cloud CDN, which is exactly this marketplace's profile.

whyWrong.0: Option A moves in the opposite direction, requiring Premium Tier.
whyWrong.2: Option C describes a discount type that does not exist for internet egress.
whyWrong.3: Option D affects how VMs without external IPs reach Google APIs and has nothing to do with serving customers on the internet.

question: A regional retailer's data center lease expires in nine months, and the COO wants to migrate all 150 applications to Google Cloud in a single weekend cutover to 'get it over with' and avoid running two environments. The applications share databases and message queues, and the operations team has never run a large cutover. Which approach should you recommend to the COO?
options: Agree to the single weekend cutover but rehearse it once in a test environment beforehand.
Postpone the migration and renew the lease for another year so that the team has more time to prepare.
Migrate only the databases in the first weekend and all applications the following weekend.

Plan phased migration waves based on dependency groups with defined entry and exit criteria and rollback plans per wave, run a pilot wave early, and use temporary hybrid connectivity so that cross-environment dependencies work during the transition; align the final wave with the lease expiry date.
explanation: A big-bang cutover of 150 interdependent applications by an inexperienced team concentrates all risk in one window with no opportunity to learn or roll back selectively; phased waves grouped by dependencies, each with go/no-go criteria and rollback, reduce risk while still meeting the fixed deadline, and hybrid connectivity mitigates the dual-environment concern. Option A retains the concentrated risk; one rehearsal cannot surface the issues that a nine-month program of waves would. Option B incurs large cost and delays value without addressing the approach. Option C splits data from the applications that use it, introducing cross-environment latency for every application for a week and still leaving a massive single cutover.
hint: Core Rule (Migration cutover strategy): A big-bang cutover of 150 interdependent applications by an inexperienced team concentrates all risk in one window with no opportunity to learn or roll back selectively; phased waves grouped by dependencies, each with go/no-go criteria and rollback, reduce risk while still meeting the fixed deadline, and hybrid connectivity mitigates the dual-environment concern.

whyWrong.0: Option A retains the concentrated risk; one rehearsal cannot surface the issues that a nine-month program of waves would.
whyWrong.1: Option B incurs large cost and delays value without addressing the approach.
whyWrong.2: Option C splits data from the applications that use it, introducing cross-environment latency for every application for a week and still leaving a massive single cutover.

question: Two weeks before the production go-live of a new customer data platform on Google Cloud, the company's general counsel learns of the project and states that certain customer records may not leave the country, which the multi-region design does not guarantee. The go-live is now at risk. Beyond fixing the immediate design, what process change should you recommend so that this does not recur on future projects?
options: Introduce a stakeholder analysis at project initiation that identifies all parties with requirements or veto power (including legal, compliance, security, finance and business owners), and maintain a requirements traceability matrix with formal sign-off from each before design is finalized.
Require the architecture team to obtain legal approval for every individual resource before it is created.
Add the general counsel to the daily engineering stand-up for all future projects.
Default all future projects to single-region deployments so that residency issues cannot arise.
explanation: The failure is one of stakeholder management: a stakeholder with binding requirements was never identified or consulted, so the fix is a systematic stakeholder analysis at initiation and traceable, signed-off requirements before design decisions are locked in. Option B is disproportionate and unworkable at resource granularity. Option C consumes the counsel's time on operational detail rather than engaging them at the requirements stage where their input matters. Option D is an architectural constraint imposed to avoid a process problem and would harm availability for workloads that have no residency restriction.
hint: Core Rule (Stakeholder identification): The failure is one of stakeholder management: a stakeholder with binding requirements was never identified or consulted, so the fix is a systematic stakeholder analysis at initiation and traceable, signed-off requirements before design decisions are locked in.

whyWrong.1: Option B is disproportionate and unworkable at resource granularity.
whyWrong.2: Option C consumes the counsel's time on operational detail rather than engaging them at the requirements stage where their input matters.
whyWrong.3: Option D is an architectural constraint imposed to avoid a process problem and would harm availability for workloads that have no residency restriction.

question: A regional bank must stand up a secure Google Cloud landing zone (organization hierarchy, Shared VPC, hybrid connectivity, centralized logging and Organization Policy guardrails) within six weeks to meet a regulatory commitment. Its four infrastructure engineers are capable but have never built a landing zone and are also responsible for daily operations. Leadership is weighing upskilling, hiring, and partner engagement. What should you recommend?
options: Send the four engineers on a four-week training course and have them build the landing zone in the remaining two weeks.
Post job openings for two senior cloud engineers and start the build when they are hired.

Engage a Google Cloud partner to deliver the landing zone using Google's landing zone blueprints and Terraform modules within the deadline, with the four engineers embedded in the delivery for knowledge transfer so they can own and extend it afterwards.
Have the four engineers build the landing zone by following the documentation, deferring daily operations for six weeks.
explanation: With a hard six-week deadline, no prior experience and no spare capacity, upskilling alone or hiring cannot deliver in time; a specialized partner using proven blueprints de-risks the deadline, and embedding the internal team ensures the bank can operate the foundation afterwards rather than remaining dependent. Option A leaves two weeks for an unfamiliar, security-critical build. Option B is unpredictable in timing and senior hiring routinely takes longer than six weeks. Option D ignores that operations cannot be deferred and that first-time landing zone builds without guidance frequently need rework.
hint: Core Rule (Skills sourcing decisions): With a hard six-week deadline, no prior experience and no spare capacity, upskilling alone or hiring cannot deliver in time; a specialized partner using proven blueprints de-risks the deadline, and embedding the internal team ensures the bank can operate the foundation afterwards rather than remaining dependent.

question: A credit union's regulator requires evidence that its business continuity plan has been exercised annually, including the decision-making and communication procedures, not only the technical recovery. The operations manager is worried that a full failover of production would be too disruptive. What should you recommend?
options: Skip the exercise this year and provide the written plan as evidence.

Run a tabletop exercise in which the crisis team walks through a realistic scenario end to end, combined with technical recovery tests (game days) in a non-production or isolated environment, and document decisions, gaps and remediation actions.
Trigger an unannounced full production failover to prove the plan works under real conditions.
Ask Google Cloud support to certify that the plan is adequate.
explanation: Tabletop exercises validate the people and process elements of a BCP (roles, decisions, communication) without touching production, and technical recovery can be exercised safely in a non-production environment; documenting outcomes provides the audit evidence regulators expect. Option A does not satisfy the requirement to exercise the plan. Option C exposes members to unnecessary risk when the objective can be met more safely, and unannounced full failovers should only be considered once lower-risk tests are routine. Option D misunderstands the shared responsibility model: Google does not certify a customer's continuity plan.
hint: Core Rule (Business continuity testing): Tabletop exercises validate the people and process elements of a BCP (roles, decisions, communication) without touching production, and technical recovery can be exercised safely in a non-production environment; documenting outcomes provides the audit evidence regulators expect.

whyWrong.0: Option A does not satisfy the requirement to exercise the plan.
whyWrong.2: Option C exposes members to unnecessary risk when the objective can be met more safely, and unannounced full failovers should only be considered once lower-risk tests are routine.
whyWrong.3: Option D misunderstands the shared responsibility model: Google does not certify a customer's continuity plan.

question: A claims-processing company updated its business continuity plan after a storm closed its main office for a week. During the closure, its systems on Google Cloud were fully available, but employees could not work because access to internal applications was restricted to the office network via VPN appliances that were also in the office, and no one could reach the on-premises source-code repositories. Which change best addresses this continuity gap?
options: Deploy a second VPN appliance at a backup office so that employees can travel there during a disruption.
Move the on-premises source repositories to a second data center in another city.
Publish printed copies of the runbooks so that staff can work manually while the office is closed.

Adopt a zero-trust access model using Identity-Aware Proxy and Chrome Enterprise Premium so that employees can securely reach internal applications from any location and device that meets policy, and move developer environments to Cloud Workstations and cloud-hosted repositories.
explanation: The gap is workforce continuity, not system availability: access depended on a physical location. Context-aware, identity-based access removes the office as a single point of failure for people, and cloud-hosted developer environments and repositories remove the remaining on-premises dependency, so the company can operate from anywhere. Option A moves the single point of failure to another building and assumes staff can travel during a regional event. Option B addresses only the repositories and still requires network access. Option C does not enable claims processing, which depends on the applications.
hint: Core Rule: The gap is workforce continuity, not system availability: access depended on a physical location.

whyWrong.0: Option A moves the single point of failure to another building and assumes staff can travel during a regional event.
whyWrong.1: Option B addresses only the repositories and still requires network access.
whyWrong.2: Option C does not enable claims processing, which depends on the applications.

question: A software company's architecture review board meets every two weeks and must approve every technical decision, from choosing a database engine to changing an autoscaler setting. Teams complain that trivial changes wait weeks, while the board complains it has no time to examine genuinely important decisions. How should you redesign the decision-making process?
options: Introduce a tiered decision process: classify decisions by reversibility and blast radius, let teams make easily reversible, low-impact decisions themselves within published guardrails and record them in ADRs, and reserve the review board for hard-to-reverse, high-impact decisions such as data platform choices or cross-team contracts.
Increase the board's meeting frequency to twice a week so that the queue clears faster.
Abolish the architecture review board and let every team decide everything independently.
Delegate all decisions to the CTO to remove the committee bottleneck.
explanation: Effective decision-making processes match the weight of governance to the consequences of the decision: reversible, contained decisions should be made quickly by the people closest to the work, while irreversible or broad-impact decisions merit deliberate review; guardrails and ADRs keep the delegated decisions consistent and auditable. Option B scales the bottleneck instead of removing unnecessary work from it. Option C removes governance for the decisions that genuinely need it and invites divergence. Option D moves the bottleneck to one person.
hint: Core Rule (Decision governance): Effective decision-making processes match the weight of governance to the consequences of the decision: reversible, contained decisions should be made quickly by the people closest to the work, while irreversible or broad-impact decisions merit deliberate review; guardrails and ADRs keep the delegated decisions consistent and auditable.

whyWrong.1: Option B scales the bottleneck instead of removing unnecessary work from it.
whyWrong.2: Option C removes governance for the decisions that genuinely need it and invites divergence.
whyWrong.3: Option D moves the bottleneck to one person.

question: An enterprise runs a Shared VPC host project, a Dedicated Interconnect, a centralized logging project and a GKE Enterprise fleet management plane that serve all business units. These shared platform costs are 20% of the bill and currently sit in a 'platform' cost center that business units do not see, which undermines the chargeback model. Which two practices should you adopt to allocate shared costs fairly? (Choose two.)

Label shared platform projects and resources with a designated shared-services identifier so their costs are cleanly separated in the billing export.

Agree an allocation key with finance and business unit leaders (for example proportional to each unit's direct cloud spend or measured consumption such as log volume) and apply it in the BigQuery chargeback queries to distribute shared costs.
Split the Interconnect into one dedicated connection per business unit so that each pays its own.
Charge shared costs entirely to the business unit with the highest revenue.

question: A logistics company went live on Google Cloud three months ago with Premium Support. Subscribe the CIO to the Google Cloud release notes feed and the status dashboard.

Establish a recurring operational and business review cadence with the Technical Account Manager covering SLO attainment against business KPIs, open risks and incidents, cost trends, upcoming changes and roadmap items, with actions tracked to closure.
Downgrade to Standard Support because the platform is stable and the money is better spent elsewhere.

question: To cut costs, a media archive team moved 500 TB of video masters from Standard to Archive storage in Cloud Storage. The following month the bill went up, not down, because editors regularly pull older masters for reissues and several datasets were deleted and re-uploaded after re-encoding. The team asks you what went wrong and what to do instead. What should you recommend?
options: Move everything back to Standard storage; storage class optimization is not worthwhile for media workloads.
Keep Archive storage and instruct editors to request masters only once per quarter.
Move the data to Coldline storage instead, which has no retrieval fees.

Analyze actual access patterns using Cloud Storage usage logs or insights, keep frequently reissued masters in Standard or Nearline, place truly dormant content in Archive, and use Autoclass for buckets whose access is unpredictable, because Archive charges retrieval fees and a 365-day minimum storage duration that penalize reads and early deletion.
explanation: Colder storage classes trade a lower per-GB price for retrieval fees and minimum storage durations (30 days Nearline, 90 days Coldline, 365 days Archive), so data that is read regularly or deleted early can cost more in Archive than in Standard; the right approach is to classify data by measured access frequency and use Autoclass where the pattern is unknown. Option A overcorrects and forgoes real savings on dormant content. Option B changes the business process to fit a storage decision and still incurs retrieval and early deletion charges. Option C is wrong because Coldline also charges retrieval fees and has a 90-day minimum.
hint: Core Rule (Storage class pitfalls): Colder storage classes trade a lower per-GB price for retrieval fees and minimum storage durations (30 days Nearline, 90 days Coldline, 365 days Archive), so data that is read regularly or deleted early can cost more in Archive than in Standard; the right approach is to classify data by measured access frequency and use Autoclass where the pattern is unknown.

whyWrong.1: Option B changes the business process to fit a storage decision and still incurs retrieval and early deletion charges.

question: A regional accounting firm runs a business-hours-only document processing application on Google Cloud with no paid support plan. During a recent issue, staff could only post in community forums and the problem took three days to resolve. The firm wants to be able to open technical support cases with Google during business hours at the lowest cost, and does not need 24/7 coverage. Which support offering should you recommend?

Premium Support, which includes a named Technical Account Manager.

question: The CTO of a Series B fintech startup wants to baseline the software delivery performance of the platform team before investing in a new CI/CD platform on Google Cloud. She asks you to recommend a small set of industry-standard, outcome-oriented metrics that can be compared against published benchmarks and tracked quarterly. Which set of metrics should you recommend?
options: Lines of code per developer, number of commits per week, unit-test coverage percentage, and average build duration

This maps to the operational excellence pillar of the Well-Architected Framework, which recommends measuring and continuously improving delivery throughput and stability.

The four DORA metrics (deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service) are exactly that: they are published yearly in the DORA State of DevOps report with elite/high/medium/low bands, and Google recommends them as the primary way to measure software delivery performance.

question: A media company hosts its application source in GitHub. Its existing Cloud Build triggers rely on Cloud Source Repositories mirrors that were created years ago, but Cloud Source Repositories is no longer available to new projects and the company is standing up a fresh set of projects for a new product line. You need to trigger builds on pull requests and on pushes to the main branch in the new projects, following Google-recommended practices and with the least operational overhead. What should you do?
options: Create a Cloud Build repositories (2nd gen) host connection to GitHub, link the repositories, and create pull-request and push triggers against the linked repositories
Create new Cloud Source Repositories in the new projects, configure GitHub mirroring, and point the triggers at the mirrored repositories
Run a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner on a Compute Engine instance that executes gcloud builds submit on every push and pull request
Create a Cloud Scheduler job that polls the GitHub API every minute and starts a build through the Cloud Build API when a new commit is detected
explanation: Cloud Build's 2nd-generation repository connections let you connect directly to GitHub (or GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, Bitbucket) through a host connection stored in Secret Manager, and then create pull-request and branch/tag triggers without any intermediary. This is the Google-recommended replacement for the Cloud Source Repositories mirroring pattern and involves no infrastructure to maintain. Option B is not viable because Cloud Source Repositories cannot be enabled in new projects after its deprecation. Option C adds a VM and a second CI system to operate, and Cloud Build cannot report pull-request status back to GitHub in that model without extra scripting. Option D is a polling anti-pattern that adds latency, API quota consumption, and custom code, and it cannot natively distinguish pull-request events. This aligns with the operational excellence pillar (automate and simplify the toolchain).
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Build triggers): Cloud Build's 2nd-generation repository connections let you connect directly to GitHub (or GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, Bitbucket) through a host connection stored in Secret Manager, and then create pull-request and branch/tag triggers without any intermediary.

whyWrong.1: Option B is not viable because Cloud Source Repositories cannot be enabled in new projects after its deprecation.
whyWrong.2: Option C adds a VM and a second CI system to operate, and Cloud Build cannot report pull-request status back to GitHub in that model without extra scripting.
whyWrong.3: Option D is a polling anti-pattern that adds latency, API quota consumption, and custom code, and it cannot natively distinguish pull-request events.

question: A payments company runs its services on GKE across dev, staging, and production clusters. Auditors require that every production deployment be explicitly approved by a named release manager, that the approval be recorded, and that developers cannot bypass the gate. The engineering team wants to keep using its existing Skaffold configuration. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Add a manual step to the Cloud Build pipeline that waits for a Slack reaction from a release manager before running kubectl apply against the production cluster
Protect the production branch in the Git provider so only release managers can merge, and let a push trigger deploy directly to production
Give release managers the Kubernetes Engine Admin role on the production cluster and require them to run the deployment manually from Cloud Shell
Define a Cloud Deploy delivery pipeline with dev, staging, and prod targets, set requireApproval on the prod target, and grant release managers only the Cloud Deploy Approver role

Because Cloud Deploy consumes Skaffold configuration, the team keeps its existing manifests. Option A is custom, unaudited automation; a Slack reaction is not a verifiable identity and a long-running Cloud Build step is fragile and costs build minutes. Option B controls merge rights, not deployment rights, and a merge does not produce a deployment-specific approval record. Option C is manual, error-prone, and grants broad cluster admin rights, violating least privilege and separation of duties. Cloud Deploy approvals satisfy both the operational excellence and security pillars of the Well-Architected Framework.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Deploy approvals): Cloud Deploy natively models environment promotion with targets; setting requireApproval: true on the production target pauses every rollout until a principal with roles/clouddeploy.approver approves it, and the approval is written to Cloud Audit Logs with the approver's identity.

whyWrong.1: Option B controls merge rights, not deployment rights, and a merge does not produce a deployment-specific approval record.

question: An online travel agency runs its booking API on Cloud Run. Past releases have caused customer-visible incidents because a new revision received 100% of traffic immediately. The team wants every production release to first receive 10% of traffic, then 50%, then 100%, with an automated smoke test executed at each stage and the rollout halted automatically if the test fails. They want to implement this with managed tooling and minimal custom scripting. What should you do?
options: Write a Cloud Build pipeline that deploys the revision with --no-traffic, then uses gcloud run services update-traffic in three sequential steps with a sleep between them
Create a Cloud Deploy delivery pipeline with a Cloud Run target that uses a canary strategy with percentages [10, 50] and enables deploy verification so the smoke test runs after each phase
Deploy two separate Cloud Run services (blue and green) behind a global external Application Load Balancer and shift traffic by editing the URL map weights after each manual test
Enable Cloud Run gradual rollouts with a maximum of 10% traffic per new revision and rely on Cloud Monitoring uptime checks to alert if errors rise
explanation: Cloud Deploy supports a declarative canary strategy for Cloud Run targets: you list the phases as percentages, Cloud Deploy manages the traffic split between the previous and new revisions, and the verify option runs a Skaffold verify container (your smoke test) after each phase. If verification fails, the phase fails and the rollout stops, which is exactly the required behavior with no custom orchestration code. Option A reproduces the same flow with imperative scripting and fixed sleeps rather than test-driven gates; it is fragile and provides no rollout history or approval model. Option C introduces a load balancer and two services purely for traffic shifting and still relies on manual testing, adding cost and operational overhead. Option D describes a feature that does not exist in that form; Cloud Run traffic splitting itself is not stage-aware, and alerting after the fact is detection, not an automated gate.
hint: Core Rule (Canary deployments on Cloud Run): Cloud Deploy supports a declarative canary strategy for Cloud Run targets: you list the phases as percentages, Cloud Deploy manages the traffic split between the previous and new revisions, and the verify option runs a Skaffold verify container (your smoke test) after each phase.

whyWrong.0: Option A reproduces the same flow with imperative scripting and fixed sleeps rather than test-driven gates; it is fragile and provides no rollout history or approval model.
whyWrong.2: Option C introduces a load balancer and two services purely for traffic shifting and still relies on manual testing, adding cost and operational overhead.

question: A retailer serves its web tier from a regional managed instance group (MIG) behind a global external Application Load Balancer. During peak season the operations team wants each release to be switchable to the new version in seconds and, if a problem is found, reverted to the previous version just as quickly without waiting for instances to be recreated. Cost of temporarily running double capacity is acceptable. Which deployment approach should you recommend?
options: Perform a MIG rolling update with maxSurge set to 100% and maxUnavailable set to 0 so all new instances are created before the old ones are removed
Perform a MIG canary update by adding the new instance template with a targetSize of 10%, then increase it to 100% once validated
Create a second MIG from the new instance template, attach it to a separate backend service, and use weighted traffic splitting in the URL map to move traffic between the two backend services
Use the MIG replace update type with minimal action RESTART so instances pick up the new version without being recreated
explanation: The requirement is atomic cutover plus an equally fast rollback, which is the definition of a blue/green deployment. Running two MIGs (blue = current, green = new) as separate backend services and shifting weights in the URL map of the global external Application Load Balancer moves traffic in seconds in either direction, because both fleets remain fully provisioned. Option A finishes with all old instances deleted, so a rollback requires another rolling update that recreates instances, which takes minutes. Option B is a canary, not a blue/green; it also ends by removing the old template instances, so rollback again needs instance recreation. Option D is incorrect because changing the instance template always requires instances to be replaced; a RESTART minimal action does not apply a new image. This is a reliability-pillar trade-off: paying for double capacity briefly in exchange for near-zero recovery time.

question: A logistics company still pushes container images to gcr.io using Container Registry. Google has shut down Container Registry, and the team must move quickly without rewriting the many build scripts and Kubernetes manifests that reference gcr.io paths. They also want automatic vulnerability scanning of new images. What should you do?
options: Export all images to a Cloud Storage bucket and configure GKE nodes to pull images from the bucket using a custom credential helper
Create Artifact Registry repositories with gcr.io domain support to keep the existing paths working, enable Artifact Analysis vulnerability scanning, and migrate the images
Create standard Artifact Registry repositories in pkg.dev, update every script and manifest to the new paths in one change, and disable scanning to reduce cost
Move the images to Docker Hub under a private organization and configure imagePullSecrets on all GKE workloads
explanation: Artifact Registry is the successor to Container Registry and provides gcr.io-domain-supported repositories that preserve the existing gcr.io hostnames, so builds and manifests keep working while the underlying storage moves to Artifact Registry; Artifact Analysis can then be enabled for automatic scanning on push. Option A is unsupported; Kubernetes pulls from OCI registries, not buckets. Option C works technically but forces a risky big-bang rewrite that the team wanted to avoid and disables the required scanning. Option D moves the supply chain outside Google Cloud, adds egress cost and credential management, and loses integration with Binary Authorization and Artifact Analysis. Keeping artifacts in a managed, scanned registry supports the security pillar of the Well-Architected Framework.
hint: Core Rule: Artifact Registry is the successor to Container Registry and provides gcr.io-domain-supported repositories that preserve the existing gcr.io hostnames, so builds and manifests keep working while the underlying storage moves to Artifact Registry; Artifact Analysis can then be enabled for automatic scanning on push.

whyWrong.0: Option A is unsupported; Kubernetes pulls from OCI registries, not buckets.
whyWrong.2: Option C works technically but forces a risky big-bang rewrite that the team wanted to avoid and disables the required scanning.
whyWrong.3: Option D moves the supply chain outside Google Cloud, adds egress cost and credential management, and loses integration with Binary Authorization and Artifact Analysis.

question: A manufacturing company's Cloud Build pipeline must pull Maven dependencies from an on-premises Nexus server that is reachable only through the company's Cloud VPN, and must run integration tests against a Cloud SQL instance that has only a private IP. Corporate policy prohibits exposing either system to the internet. You need to make the builds work with the least operational overhead. What should you do? (Choose two.)
options: Create a Cloud Build private pool and connect it to the company VPC through a private services access (VPC peering) connection
Enable export of custom routes on the private services access peering so the private pool can reach on-premises addresses through the Cloud VPN tunnel
Keep using the default Cloud Build pool and set the option --no-external-ip on each build step
Reserve a static external IP for the default Cloud Build pool and allowlist that address on the on-premises firewall
Replace Cloud Build with a self-managed Jenkins controller on a Compute Engine VM inside the VPC
explanation: Private pools are the Google-recommended way to give Cloud Build workers access to resources in a VPC: the pool runs in a Google-managed producer network that is peered to your VPC through private services access, so it can reach the Cloud SQL private IP directly. Because VPC peering is not transitive, the pool cannot reach on-premises networks behind Cloud VPN unless you export custom routes on that peering connection; doing so advertises the VPN routes to the producer network. Option C is invalid; the default pool has no such option and is not connected to any customer VPC. Option D is impossible because default-pool workers use ephemeral Google IP ranges that you cannot reserve, and allowlisting would also violate the no-internet-exposure policy. Option E works but replaces a managed service with a VM the team has to patch, scale, and secure, contradicting the least-overhead requirement.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Build private pools): Private pools are the Google-recommended way to give Cloud Build workers access to resources in a VPC: the pool runs in a Google-managed producer network that is peered to your VPC through private services access, so it can reach the Cloud SQL private IP directly.

whyWrong.2: Option C is invalid; the default pool has no such option and is not connected to any customer VPC.
whyWrong.3: Option D is impossible because default-pool workers use ephemeral Google IP ranges that you cannot reserve, and allowlisting would also violate the no-internet-exposure policy.
whyWrong.4: Option E works but replaces a managed service with a VM the team has to patch, scale, and secure, contradicting the least-overhead requirement.

question: A healthcare SaaS provider runs workloads on GKE. A recent security review found that an engineer deployed a container image that had been built on a laptop and never scanned. The CISO requires that only images built by the company's Cloud Build pipeline and free of critical vulnerabilities can run in production clusters, enforced at deploy time rather than by policy documents. What should you do?
options: Enable Binary Authorization on the production clusters with a policy that requires attestations from an attestor, and have the Cloud Build pipeline create the attestation only after vulnerability scanning passes
Configure an Artifact Registry repository with a naming convention for production images and instruct engineers to deploy only from that repository
Enable Artifact Analysis vulnerability scanning on the registry and create a Cloud Monitoring alert that notifies the security team when a critical CVE is found in a deployed image
Restrict kubectl access to the production clusters to a small group of senior engineers who are trained to verify image provenance before deploying
explanation: Binary Authorization is the deploy-time admission control for GKE and Cloud Run: a cluster policy can require that every image carry a signed attestation, and the pipeline creates that attestation (for example with the built-by-cloud-build attestor or a custom attestor after a vulnerability check step) so that unsigned laptop builds are rejected at admission. Option B relies on convention and is trivially bypassed by pushing an unscanned image into the 'production' repository. Option C is detective, not preventive; the vulnerable image would already be running when the alert fires. Option D is a people control that does not scale and does not technically prevent an unverified deployment. This is a supply-chain control under the security pillar and is part of Google's Software Delivery Shield guidance.
hint: Core Rule: Binary Authorization is the deploy-time admission control for GKE and Cloud Run: a cluster policy can require that every image carry a signed attestation, and the pipeline creates that attestation (for example with the built-by-cloud-build attestor or a custom attestor after a vulnerability check step) so that unsigned laptop builds are rejected at admission.
