whyWrong.2: Option C is detective, not preventive; the vulnerable image would already be running when the alert fires.
whyWrong.3: Option D is a people control that does not scale and does not technically prevent an unverified deployment.

question: A global bank operates 40 GKE clusters across several regions. Platform engineers have found namespaces, RBAC bindings, and network policies that differ between clusters because changes were applied with kubectl during incidents and never recorded. The bank wants every cluster's baseline configuration to be defined in Git, applied consistently to all clusters, and automatically restored if someone changes it manually. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Create a Cloud Build trigger that runs kubectl apply against all 40 clusters whenever the configuration repository changes
Store the manifests in Terraform using the Kubernetes provider and run terraform apply nightly from Cloud Scheduler
Use Cloud Deploy with a multi-target that fans out to all clusters and require an approval before each rollout
Enable Config Sync on every cluster, point it at a root repository that holds the cluster baseline, and enable drift prevention and self-healing so manual changes are reverted
explanation: The key requirement is continuous reconciliation, not just delivery: Config Sync is a GitOps agent that runs inside each cluster, continuously compares live state with the Git source of truth, and reverts out-of-band changes (self-healing); drift prevention can additionally block conflicting manual writes. It scales naturally to a fleet because each cluster pulls its own configuration. Option A is a push model that applies changes only when the repository changes; a kubectl edit made afterwards persists until the next commit. Option B has the same gap, with at most nightly correction and added state-file management. Option C is designed for progressive delivery of application releases, not for enforcing persistent baseline configuration, and would require a human approval to fix every drift. Config Sync is Google's recommended GitOps mechanism for GKE Enterprise fleets and supports the operational excellence pillar.
hint: Core Rule (GitOps with Config Sync): The key requirement is continuous reconciliation, not just delivery: Config Sync is a GitOps agent that runs inside each cluster, continuously compares live state with the Git source of truth, and reverts out-of-band changes (self-healing); drift prevention can additionally block conflicting manual writes.

whyWrong.0: Option A is a push model that applies changes only when the repository changes; a kubectl edit made afterwards persists until the next commit.
whyWrong.1: Option B has the same gap, with at most nightly correction and added state-file management.
whyWrong.2: Option C is designed for progressive delivery of application releases, not for enforcing persistent baseline configuration, and would require a human approval to fix every drift.

question: A gaming studio has 60 engineers working on a single backend service. Each feature is developed on a branch that lives for four to eight weeks, and integration at the end of each cycle takes days of conflict resolution and produces a large risky release. Leadership wants to deploy to production daily while making sure that half-finished features are never visible to players. Which combination of practices should you recommend?
options: Keep the feature branches but require developers to rebase onto main every morning, and schedule a release train every two weeks with a code freeze
Adopt trunk-based development with branches living less than a day, merge incomplete work behind feature flags so it is dark in production, and decouple deployment from release by toggling flags
Create a long-lived release branch per environment (dev, staging, prod) and cherry-pick approved commits forward so production only contains finished features
Split the service into one repository per feature team and use Cloud Deploy to deploy each repository independently on its own schedule
explanation: DORA research identifies trunk-based development (short-lived branches, at least daily integration into main) as a key predictor of high delivery performance, and feature flags are the mechanism that allows incomplete code to be merged and deployed while remaining invisible until it is explicitly released; together they enable daily deployments with small, low-risk changes. Option A reduces but does not remove long-lived branches, and a biweekly release train with code freezes is the opposite of continuous deployment. Option C is the environment-branch anti-pattern that causes divergence and makes cherry-picks a manual, error-prone bottleneck. Option D reorganizes repositories but does not address branch lifetime or how unfinished features are hidden, and a monolithic service cannot be deployed per-repository without a real decomposition effort.
hint: Core Rule (Trunk-based development and feature flags): DORA research identifies trunk-based development (short-lived branches, at least daily integration into main) as a key predictor of high delivery performance, and feature flags are the mechanism that allows incomplete code to be merged and deployed while remaining invisible until it is explicitly released; together they enable daily deployments with small, low-risk changes.

whyWrong.0: Option A reduces but does not remove long-lived branches, and a biweekly release train with code freezes is the opposite of continuous deployment.
whyWrong.2: Option C is the environment-branch anti-pattern that causes divergence and makes cherry-picks a manual, error-prone bottleneck.
whyWrong.3: Option D reorganizes repositories but does not address branch lifetime or how unfinished features are hidden, and a monolithic service cannot be deployed per-repository without a real decomposition effort.

question: Developers at an insurance company complain that the way they build and run microservices on their local minikube clusters differs from how the CI/CD pipeline builds and deploys to GKE, which leads to 'works on my machine' defects. The company already uses Cloud Deploy for production rollouts. You want to remove this inconsistency with minimal additional tooling. What should you do?
options: Ask developers to run Cloud Build locally with cloud-build-local for every change so the same builder images are used
Give every developer a personal GKE Autopilot cluster and require them to deploy through Cloud Deploy instead of using minikube
Standardize on a single skaffold.yaml per service with profiles for local and CI, use Cloud Code for the local inner loop, and have Cloud Deploy render and deploy from the same skaffold.yaml
Replace minikube with Docker Compose files that developers maintain separately and add a CI check that both definitions reference the same image tags
explanation: Skaffold is the common denominator: Cloud Code (in VS Code, JetBrains, or Cloud Shell Editor) drives the developer inner loop from skaffold.yaml, and Cloud Deploy uses the same skaffold.yaml to render manifests and deploy, so build and deploy logic is defined once and parameterized with profiles rather than duplicated. Option A is not a maintained approach and only covers building, not deployment. Option B is expensive, slows the inner loop by forcing every change through a release pipeline, and still does not unify the build definition. Option D creates a second, parallel definition that must be kept in sync, which is precisely the source of drift you are trying to eliminate. Reducing toolchain divergence is an operational excellence practice.
hint: Core Rule (Skaffold and Cloud Code): Skaffold is the common denominator: Cloud Code (in VS Code, JetBrains, or Cloud Shell Editor) drives the developer inner loop from skaffold.yaml, and Cloud Deploy uses the same skaffold.yaml to render manifests and deploy, so build and deploy logic is defined once and parameterized with profiles rather than duplicated.

whyWrong.0: Option A is not a maintained approach and only covers building, not deployment.
whyWrong.1: Option B is expensive, slows the inner loop by forcing every change through a release pipeline, and still does not unify the build definition.
whyWrong.3: Option D creates a second, parallel definition that must be kept in sync, which is precisely the source of drift you are trying to eliminate.

question: A subscription video service uses Cloud Deploy to promote releases from staging to a production GKE target. Ten minutes after the latest production rollout succeeded, the on-call engineer sees a spike in checkout errors clearly linked to the new release. The engineer needs to restore the previous working version as quickly as possible with a recorded, repeatable action. What should you do?
options: Run gcloud deploy targets rollback for the production target so Cloud Deploy creates a new rollout of the previously deployed release
Run kubectl rollout undo on each affected Deployment in the production cluster
Revert the offending commit in Git, wait for CI to build a new image, and promote the new release through staging to production
Delete the failed release in Cloud Deploy so the target automatically reverts to the prior release
explanation: Cloud Deploy provides a first-class rollback: gcloud deploy targets rollback (or the console button) creates a new rollout of the last successfully deployed release to that target, using the already-rendered manifests, so recovery takes only as long as the deploy itself and is fully recorded in Cloud Deploy history and audit logs. Option B may work for a single Deployment but bypasses the delivery pipeline, leaves Cloud Deploy's view of the target out of sync, and does not cover ConfigMaps, Services, or other rendered resources. Option C is the correct long-term fix but is far slower and violates the 'as quickly as possible' constraint; it should follow the rollback, not replace it. Option D is wrong because deleting a release does not change what is running in the cluster. Fast, tested rollback capability is a core reliability-pillar recommendation.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Deploy rollback): Cloud Deploy provides a first-class rollback: gcloud deploy targets rollback (or the console button) creates a new rollout of the last successfully deployed release to that target, using the already-rendered manifests, so recovery takes only as long as the deploy itself and is fully recorded in Cloud Deploy history and audit logs.

whyWrong.1: Option B may work for a single Deployment but bypasses the delivery pipeline, leaves Cloud Deploy's view of the target out of sync, and does not cover ConfigMaps, Services, or other rendered resources.
whyWrong.2: Option C is the correct long-term fix but is far slower and violates the 'as quickly as possible' constraint; it should follow the rollback, not replace it.
whyWrong.3: Option D is wrong because deleting a release does not change what is running in the cluster.

question: A pharmaceutical company must prove to regulators that the exact binary validated in its QA environment is the binary that runs in production. Today each environment's pipeline rebuilds the container image from the same Git branch, and QA and production images occasionally differ because of upstream base-image and dependency updates. Which changes should you make to the delivery process? (Choose two.)
options: Build the image once in CI, tag it with the Git commit SHA, and promote the same image digest through QA and production without rebuilding
Keep rebuilding per environment but pin the base image tag so the rebuilt images are more likely to be identical
Use Cloud Deploy releases, which render manifests once at release creation and pin image references by digest, so promotion between targets reuses the identical artifact
Tag every build as latest and configure each environment to pull the latest tag at deploy time
Maintain separate Artifact Registry repositories per environment and rebuild the image when copying it between them
explanation: The regulatory requirement is artifact identity, which can only be guaranteed by building once and promoting an immutable artifact identified by its digest. Tagging with the commit SHA and promoting the digest ensures QA and production run byte-identical images; Cloud Deploy reinforces this because a release renders manifests once and resolves image tags to digests, so every target in the pipeline receives the same artifact. Option B still rebuilds, so transitive dependency resolution, timestamps, and base-image digests under a mutable tag can differ; 'more likely' is not evidence for an auditor. Option D uses a mutable tag that can point to different images at different times, destroying traceability. Option E deliberately reintroduces rebuilding; if images need to live in separate repositories, they should be copied (gcrane/Artifact Registry copy) by digest, never rebuilt. Immutable, promotable artifacts are central to the security pillar's supply-chain guidance.
hint: Core Rule (Artifact promotion): The regulatory requirement is artifact identity, which can only be guaranteed by building once and promoting an immutable artifact identified by its digest.

whyWrong.1: Option B still rebuilds, so transitive dependency resolution, timestamps, and base-image digests under a mutable tag can differ; 'more likely' is not evidence for an auditor.
whyWrong.3: Option D uses a mutable tag that can point to different images at different times, destroying traceability.
whyWrong.4: Option E deliberately reintroduces rebuilding; if images need to live in separate repositories, they should be copied (gcrane/Artifact Registry copy) by digest, never rebuilt.

question: A regional telecom deploys its customer portal to Cloud Run every two weeks in a single large release, and roughly one in three releases requires a hotfix or rollback. Management believes deploying less often would reduce risk. As the cloud architect, you are asked to recommend how to reduce the change failure rate in line with DORA research and Google-recommended practices. What should you recommend?
options: Move to a monthly release cadence with a longer manual regression test phase before each release
Keep the biweekly cadence but add a mandatory change advisory board meeting to review every release
Require 100% unit-test coverage before any code can be merged and add a second code reviewer for every pull request
Deploy smaller changes more frequently, gate each deployment with automated tests in CI, and use progressive delivery so faults affect a fraction of users and are rolled back automatically
explanation: DORA data consistently shows that throughput and stability are not a trade-off: elite performers deploy many times per day with a lower change failure rate because small batches are easier to test, review, and diagnose, and progressive delivery (canary or traffic splitting on Cloud Run) limits blast radius and makes rollback quick. Option A increases batch size, which increases risk per release and lengthens time to restore. Option B adds an external approval step that DORA research links to lower performance without improving stability. Option C improves code quality signals but does not address batch size or blast radius; a 100% coverage mandate is a proxy metric that is easily gamed. Reducing batch size and automating quality gates are explicit operational excellence recommendations.
hint: Core Rule: DORA data consistently shows that throughput and stability are not a trade-off: elite performers deploy many times per day with a lower change failure rate because small batches are easier to test, review, and diagnose, and progressive delivery (canary or traffic splitting on Cloud Run) limits blast radius and makes rollback quick.

whyWrong.0: Option A increases batch size, which increases risk per release and lengthens time to restore.
whyWrong.1: Option B adds an external approval step that DORA research links to lower performance without improving stability.
whyWrong.2: Option C improves code quality signals but does not address batch size or blast radius; a 100% coverage mandate is a proxy metric that is easily gamed.

question: A SaaS vendor wants Cloud Build to run a release pipeline only when an engineer creates a semantic-version Git tag such as v2.14.0 on the main repository. Commits and other tags such as nightly-2025-06-01 must not start the release pipeline. The pipeline must push the image to Artifact Registry and create a Cloud Deploy release. How should you configure the trigger?
options: Create a push trigger on the main branch and add a build step that exits early if the commit message does not contain a version number
Create a tag trigger with the regular expression ^v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ and a cloudbuild.yaml that builds, pushes, and runs gcloud deploy releases create
Create a manual trigger that release engineers run from the console, passing the version as a substitution variable
Create a pull-request trigger that fires when a pull request titled with a version number is merged
explanation: Cloud Build triggers can match on branch or tag names using RE2 regular expressions; a tag trigger anchored to the semantic-version pattern fires only for tags like v2.14.0 and ignores branch pushes and nightly tags, and the same cloudbuild.yaml can push to Artifact Registry and call gcloud deploy releases create so the release enters the Cloud Deploy pipeline. Option A wastes build minutes on every push, relies on commit-message conventions, and still creates builds that show up as executed. Option C removes automation and introduces human error in typing versions, which is inconsistent with continuous delivery. Option D is not possible because pull-request triggers fire on PR events, not on tag creation, and PR titles are not a reliable release signal.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Build tag triggers): Cloud Build triggers can match on branch or tag names using RE2 regular expressions; a tag trigger anchored to the semantic-version pattern fires only for tags like v2.14.0 and ignores branch pushes and nightly tags, and the same cloudbuild.yaml can push to Artifact Registry and call gcloud deploy releases create so the release enters the Cloud Deploy pipeline.

whyWrong.0: Option A wastes build minutes on every push, relies on commit-message conventions, and still creates builds that show up as executed.
whyWrong.2: Option C removes automation and introduces human error in typing versions, which is inconsistent with continuous delivery.
whyWrong.3: Option D is not possible because pull-request triggers fire on PR events, not on tag creation, and PR titles are not a reliable release signal.

question: A ticketing platform runs a stateless API as a Kubernetes Deployment on GKE with 20 replicas. During recent releases, latency-sensitive customers noticed brief error bursts because pods began receiving traffic before their JVM had finished warming up, and capacity dipped while pods were replaced. You need to eliminate both problems during routine releases without adding new infrastructure. What should you do?
options: Change the Deployment strategy to Recreate so old and new pods never overlap, and increase replicas to 30 to compensate
Keep RollingUpdate but set maxSurge to 0 and maxUnavailable to 50% so the update completes faster
Keep RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable set to 0 and maxSurge set to 25%, and add readiness (and startup) probes so pods receive traffic only after warm-up
Convert the Deployment to a StatefulSet so pods are updated one at a time in ordinal order
explanation: Two settings solve the two symptoms: maxUnavailable: 0 with a positive maxSurge guarantees that the Deployment never drops below the desired replica count during a rollout (new pods are added before old ones are removed), and readiness/startup probes ensure the Service only routes to pods that have finished warming up, which removes the error bursts. Option A introduces a full outage window between the old pods terminating and new pods becoming ready. Option B does the opposite of what is needed: removing half the replicas at once causes a large capacity dip. Option D is a misuse of StatefulSets, which exist for stable identity and storage; ordinal updates would make the rollout slower and would still not fix premature traffic without readiness probes. Graceful rollouts with health checks are a reliability-pillar best practice.
hint: Core Rule (GKE rolling updates): Two settings solve the two symptoms: maxUnavailable: 0 with a positive maxSurge guarantees that the Deployment never drops below the desired replica count during a rollout (new pods are added before old ones are removed), and readiness/startup probes ensure the Service only routes to pods that have finished warming up, which removes the error bursts.

whyWrong.0: Option A introduces a full outage window between the old pods terminating and new pods becoming ready.
whyWrong.1: Option B does the opposite of what is needed: removing half the replicas at once causes a large capacity dip.
whyWrong.3: Option D is a misuse of StatefulSets, which exist for stable identity and storage; ordinal updates would make the rollout slower and would still not fix premature traffic without readiness probes.

question: A financial data provider runs the same service in three regional GKE clusters (us-east4, europe-west3, asia-northeast1) for latency and residency reasons. Releases must go to a staging cluster first and then to all three production clusters, and the release manager wants a single production rollout that can be approved once, observed as one unit, and rolled back as one unit. Which Cloud Deploy design should you recommend?
options: Define one staging target and one production multi-target whose child targets are the three regional clusters, set requireApproval on the multi-target, and use a delivery pipeline with two stages
Define one staging target and three production targets in a four-stage pipeline so each region is promoted separately with its own approval
Define three separate delivery pipelines, one per region, each with staging and production targets, and create three releases from the same image
Define a single production target that points to a GKE fleet and rely on Multi Cluster Ingress to distribute the deployment to all member clusters
explanation: Cloud Deploy multi-targets exist precisely for this case: a multi-target groups several child targets so that a single rollout deploys to all of them in parallel, is approved once, shows aggregate status, and can be rolled back as one unit. Option B works but creates three sequential approvals and three independent rollouts, contradicting the 'approve once, observe and roll back as one unit' requirement. Option C triples the operational surface and again breaks the single-rollout requirement. Option D is technically incorrect: a Cloud Deploy target references a specific cluster or Cloud Run service, not a fleet, and Multi Cluster Ingress handles traffic distribution, not workload deployment. Parallel multi-target rollouts help both operational excellence (one pipeline) and reliability (consistent versions across regions).
hint: Core Rule: Cloud Deploy multi-targets exist precisely for this case: a multi-target groups several child targets so that a single rollout deploys to all of them in parallel, is approved once, shows aggregate status, and can be rolled back as one unit.

whyWrong.2: Option C triples the operational surface and again breaks the single-rollout requirement.
whyWrong.3: Option D is technically incorrect: a Cloud Deploy target references a specific cluster or Cloud Run service, not a fleet, and Multi Cluster Ingress handles traffic distribution, not workload deployment.

question: A data analytics startup's Cloud Build pipeline for a Python service takes 35 minutes, most of it spent reinstalling unchanged dependencies and rebuilding identical container layers on every commit. Developers wait for CI feedback before merging, which is hurting lead time. You want to cut build time substantially while keeping the pipeline in Cloud Build. What should you do?
options: Split the pipeline into parallel builds triggered by Pub/Sub, each rebuilding a subset of the image layers
Move dependency installation into a Cloud Run job that runs before the build and writes the virtual environment to a Cloud Storage bucket
Increase the build timeout to 60 minutes and switch to a private pool so builds do not queue
Use Kaniko (or BuildKit) layer caching with the cache stored in Artifact Registry, order the Dockerfile so dependency layers precede source code, and select a higher-vCPU machine type for the build
explanation: The waste is repeated work, so caching is the fix: Kaniko or Docker BuildKit can push intermediate layers to an Artifact Registry cache repository and reuse them across builds when layer inputs are unchanged, and ordering the Dockerfile so that the requirements install happens before copying application source keeps the expensive layer cache-hit on most commits. A larger machineType option further reduces wall-clock time for CPU-bound steps. Option A adds orchestration complexity and does not remove the redundant work. Option B builds a bespoke caching system around a Cloud Run job that must be kept in sync with Python versions and does not integrate with Docker layer caching. Option C addresses queueing and timeouts, not the duration of the build itself. Faster feedback loops directly improve lead time for changes, an operational excellence outcome.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Build performance): The waste is repeated work, so caching is the fix: Kaniko or Docker BuildKit can push intermediate layers to an Artifact Registry cache repository and reuse them across builds when layer inputs are unchanged, and ordering the Dockerfile so that the requirements install happens before copying application source keeps the expensive layer cache-hit on most commits.

whyWrong.0: Option A adds orchestration complexity and does not remove the redundant work.
whyWrong.1: Option B builds a bespoke caching system around a Cloud Run job that must be kept in sync with Python versions and does not integrate with Docker layer caching.
whyWrong.2: Option C addresses queueing and timeouts, not the duration of the build itself.

question: A startup's single Cloud Build trigger uses one service account with the Project Editor role to build images, run tests, and deploy to both staging and production Cloud Run services. A new security lead wants to reduce the blast radius of a compromised pipeline while keeping deployments automated. What should you do first?
options: Export the service account key, store it in Secret Manager, and rotate it every 30 days

Create separate build and deploy triggers, each with its own user-specified service account granted only the roles needed (for example Artifact Registry Writer for build, Cloud Run Developer scoped to the target service for deploy)
Replace the Editor role with the Owner role so the pipeline has consistent permissions across all environments
Move production deployments to a manual gcloud run deploy executed by the CTO from a laptop
explanation: Google recommends per-trigger user-specified service accounts with least-privilege roles, so a compromised build step can at most push an image, and only the deploy trigger's identity can change the production service. Splitting build and deploy stages also enables separation of duties and clearer audit trails. Option A introduces a long-lived key that Cloud Build does not need (it uses the attached service account directly), which increases risk rather than reducing it. Option C widens permissions. Option D removes automation and creates a single-person bottleneck without addressing the pipeline's excessive permissions. This is a security-pillar recommendation (least privilege, no service-account keys).
hint: Core Rule (CI/CD least privilege): Google recommends per-trigger user-specified service accounts with least-privilege roles, so a compromised build step can at most push an image, and only the deploy trigger's identity can change the production service.

topic: Artifact Registry remote and virtual repositories
question: An e-commerce company's builds pull base images from Docker Hub and packages from the public npm registry. Builds occasionally fail because of Docker Hub rate limits, and the security team wants a single, controllable entry point for third-party dependencies where internal packages take precedence over public ones with the same name. What should you do?
options: Configure Cloud NAT with a larger IP pool so builds are less likely to hit Docker Hub rate limits, and add npm audit to every build
Mirror Docker Hub and npm nightly into a Cloud Storage bucket with a scheduled Dataflow job and configure builds to use the bucket

Create Artifact Registry remote repositories for Docker Hub and npmjs.org, a standard repository for internal packages, and a virtual repository that prioritizes the internal repository over the remotes; point builds at the virtual repository
Vendor all third-party dependencies into the application Git repositories so builds never contact external registries
explanation: Artifact Registry remote repositories cache upstream public registries (Docker Hub, npm, PyPI, Maven Central, and others) so repeated pulls are served from Google Cloud and do not consume upstream rate limits, and a virtual repository aggregates multiple upstreams behind one endpoint with explicit priorities, which lets internal packages shadow public ones and protects against dependency-confusion attacks. Option A treats the symptom and does not create a controlled entry point. Option B is a custom mirror that does not speak the Docker or npm protocols and is heavy to maintain. question: A food-delivery company deploys its order service to GKE with Cloud Deploy. It wants every production rollout to start as a 5% canary using the Gateway API, hold for ten minutes while the new pods' HTTP 5xx ratio is compared with the baseline, and be automatically rolled back if the ratio exceeds 1%; otherwise it should advance without a human. Which approach should you recommend?

Automated canary analysis with automatic rollback is a reliability-pillar practice for progressive delivery.

question: A B2B software company is redesigning the continuous integration pipeline for its container-based services on Google Cloud. The goals are to stop defects and vulnerable images from reaching the deployment stage and to produce verifiable evidence for downstream policy enforcement, while keeping developers' feedback loop fast. Which practices should you include in the Cloud Build pipeline? (Choose three.)
options: Use a pull-request trigger that runs unit and integration tests and reports status back to the Git provider so merges are blocked on failure
Scan the built image with the On-Demand Scanning API in the build and fail the build when vulnerabilities at or above a defined severity are found
Tag every successful image as latest so deployment manifests never need to change
Sign the image and create a Binary Authorization attestation as the final build step when all previous steps succeed
Grant the build service account the Owner role so no step fails because of missing permissions
Run the full test suite only in a nightly build to keep pull-request builds under one minute
explanation: The three correct practices form Google's recommended secure CI flow: test on pull requests with status checks so broken code never merges; use Artifact Analysis On-Demand Scanning inside the build to block images with critical vulnerabilities before they are pushed or deployed; and, once all gates pass, sign the image and create an attestation that Binary Authorization on GKE or Cloud Run can require at deploy time, giving verifiable provenance. Option C uses a mutable tag that destroys traceability and makes rollbacks ambiguous. Option E grossly violates least privilege and expands the blast radius of any compromised build. Option F delays defect detection until after merge, increasing change failure rate; the right way to keep feedback fast is caching and parallel steps, not skipping tests. These practices sit at the intersection of the security and operational excellence pillars.
hint: Core Rule (Secure CI pipeline design): The three correct practices form Google's recommended secure CI flow: test on pull requests with status checks so broken code never merges; use Artifact Analysis On-Demand Scanning inside the build to block images with critical vulnerabilities before they are pushed or deployed; and, once all gates pass, sign the image and create an attestation that Binary Authorization on GKE or Cloud Run can require at deploy time, giving verifiable provenance.

question: A regional bank suffered a four-hour outage of its mobile banking API after an engineer applied a firewall rule change directly in production. The COO wants to discipline the engineer and add a mandatory sign-off from a director for all future changes. As the architect advising the operations organization, you want to follow Google SRE practices to prevent recurrence. What should you recommend?
options: Support the disciplinary action so that engineers understand the seriousness of production changes, and add the director sign-off

Run a blameless postmortem that documents the timeline, contributing factors, and detection gaps, and produces tracked action items such as moving firewall changes into a reviewed infrastructure-as-code pipeline
Restrict production IAM permissions to a single senior administrator who executes all changes requested by the team
Close the incident once service is restored and schedule a general training session on firewall configuration for all engineers
explanation: Google SRE practice holds that incidents are caused by systems that allow a mistake to become an outage, not by individuals; a blameless postmortem surfaces the real contributing factors (no peer review, no automated validation, no canary, slow detection) and converts them into owned, tracked action items such as putting network changes through Terraform with plan review and policy checks. Option A creates a culture in which people hide mistakes, so future incidents are learned from less, and a director sign-off is a low-value manual gate that DORA research associates with slower delivery and no stability gain. Option C creates a single point of failure and a bottleneck without removing the possibility of error. Option D skips the analysis entirely, so the systemic causes remain. Blameless postmortems are a cornerstone of the operational excellence pillar.

question: A marketplace runs 30 microservices on GKE. Users report that about 2% of checkout requests take more than five seconds, but no single service shows elevated latency in its dashboard. Engineers spend hours copying request IDs between service logs to reconstruct a slow request. You want the team to see, for any slow request, which service and which operation consumed the time, and to jump from a trace directly to the related log lines. What should you do?
options: Increase the log level of every service to DEBUG and create a log-based metric for entries containing the word 'slow'
Install Cloud Profiler agents in every service and compare CPU flame graphs during the slow periods
Create an uptime check for the checkout endpoint with a five-second timeout and alert when it fails

Option B measures CPU usage within a process; it cannot show waiting on downstream calls, which is the usual source of distributed latency. question: A media company's image-processing service on Cloud Run has seen its per-request CPU cost triple over the last two releases with no change in traffic volume or image sizes. Add the Cloud Profiler agent to the service, deploy, and compare CPU-time flame graphs for the current version against the version from two releases ago using Profiler's version comparison

question: During a recent multi-hour outage at an online education provider, twelve engineers joined the incident call, several made conflicting configuration changes, executives interrupted for status, and customer support gave inconsistent messages. question: A fintech company has designed its trading platform on GKE and Spanner to survive a zonal failure, but the design has never been exercised. The head of SRE wants to introduce chaos engineering. Several engineers propose starting by deleting a production node pool during trading hours to 'see what happens.' Which approach should you recommend?
options: Start in a pre-production environment with a documented steady-state hypothesis and a limited blast radius, run controlled experiments such as draining a single zone, observe SLIs, fix weaknesses, and only then run scheduled experiments in production with an abort plan
Proceed with the proposed production experiment because only production reflects real behavior, and announce it in advance so all teams are watching
Replace chaos experiments with a tabletop discussion of failure scenarios, since real experiments are too risky for a trading platform
Run chaos experiments only in production, but do so at 3 a.m. on weekends when trading volume is lowest

Option C leaves the zonal-failover design unverified; tabletop exercises complement but do not replace actual experiments. Verified resilience through controlled failure injection is a reliability-pillar recommendation.

question: A developer team building an order-processing service that uses Pub/Sub and Firestore wants to run unit and integration tests on laptops and in pull-request builds without creating cloud resources for each developer, without incurring cost, and with tests that still exercise the real client libraries. question: A logistics company's staging environment was built by hand two years ago: it uses a single-zone Cloud SQL instance without a read replica, a zonal GKE cluster, and different firewall rules from production, which is regional and highly available. Several recent incidents were caused by behavior (failover, connection handling, network policy) that appeared only in production. Leadership wants staging to catch these issues while keeping cost reasonable. What should you recommend?
options: Rebuild staging from the same Terraform modules used for production, keeping topology (regional HA, replicas, network policies) identical and varying only sizes through variables
Make staging an exact full-size clone of production, including instance sizes and node counts, so that every behavior is reproduced
Keep staging as is and add a rule that all changes touching failover or networking are tested directly in production during a maintenance window
Replace staging with the developers' local minikube clusters and the Cloud SQL Proxy pointed at production databases in read-only mode
explanation: Environment parity is about matching configuration and topology, not raw capacity: provisioning staging from the same Terraform modules guarantees identical failover behavior, replica configuration, and network policy, while machine sizes and node counts can be reduced through variables to control cost. This is the Google-recommended way to make pre-production a faithful test of production behavior. Option B achieves parity but at unnecessary cost that leadership rejected. Option C uses production as the test environment, which is the failure mode they are trying to eliminate. Option D removes the shared integration environment entirely and points developers at production data, which is a security and reliability anti-pattern. Consistent, code-defined environments are an operational excellence recommendation.
hint: Core Rule (Pre-production parity): Environment parity is about matching configuration and topology, not raw capacity: provisioning staging from the same Terraform modules guarantees identical failover behavior, replica configuration, and network policy, while machine sizes and node counts can be reduced through variables to control cost.

whyWrong.1: Option B achieves parity but at unnecessary cost that leadership rejected.
whyWrong.2: Option C uses production as the test environment, which is the failure mode they are trying to eliminate.
whyWrong.3: Option D removes the shared integration environment entirely and points developers at production data, which is a security and reliability anti-pattern.

question: A platform team publishes internal Terraform modules (VPC, GKE, Cloud SQL) that 40 application teams consume. A recent module change passed terraform validate but broke every consumer because a renamed output was not detected. The team wants a testing strategy that catches syntax, style, policy, and real behavioral regressions before a module version is published, while keeping cost under control. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Require consumers to pin module versions and test new versions in their own pipelines; publish modules without additional checks
Run terraform fmt -check and terraform validate in the module pipeline and consider the module tested if both pass
Deploy each module change to the production project of one volunteer application team as a canary before tagging the release

Build a module pipeline that runs terraform fmt, validate, and tflint, then gcloud beta terraform vet against a plan, and finally an automated integration test (for example Terratest or the Terraform test framework) that applies the module into an ephemeral test project, asserts outputs and resource behavior, and destroys everything afterward
explanation: Static checks (fmt, validate, tflint) catch syntax and style, policy validation catches compliance issues, but only an apply-based integration test in a disposable project detects behavioral regressions such as renamed outputs, wrong dependencies, or provider-version breakage; the ephemeral project is created and destroyed by the pipeline, so cost is bounded to the test duration. Option A pushes the testing burden to 40 teams and discovers regressions after publication. Option B is exactly the insufficient approach that missed the recent failure. Option C uses a production environment as a test bed and puts one team at risk. Automated testing of infrastructure code is part of the exam objective 'testing and validation of software and infrastructure' and the operational excellence pillar.
hint: Core Rule (Testing Terraform modules): Static checks (fmt, validate, tflint) catch syntax and style, policy validation catches compliance issues, but only an apply-based integration test in a disposable project detects behavioral regressions such as renamed outputs, wrong dependencies, or provider-version breakage; the ephemeral project is created and destroyed by the pipeline, so cost is bounded to the test duration.

whyWrong.0: Option A pushes the testing burden to 40 teams and discovers regressions after publication.
whyWrong.1: Option B is exactly the insufficient approach that missed the recent failure.
whyWrong.2: Option C uses a production environment as a test bed and puts one team at risk.

question: An online retailer runs its catalog API on Cloud Run with traffic split 20% to a new revision and 80% to the previous one. Ten minutes after the split, overall 5xx errors rise from 0.1% to 0.6%. The on-call engineer must decide within minutes whether the new revision is responsible before deciding to shift traffic back. What is the fastest reliable way to make that determination?
options: Open Error Reporting and look at the total count of errors in the last hour
In Cloud Monitoring, chart the Cloud Run request count metric filtered by response_code_class 5xx and grouped by revision_name, and compare the error ratio of each revision
Run a load test against the new revision's tag URL from Cloud Shell and observe whether errors occur
Query Cloud Audit Logs to confirm the time the revision was deployed and correlate it with the start of the error increase
explanation: Cloud Run's built-in request metrics carry the revision_name label, so grouping the 5xx request count (or ratio) by revision immediately shows whether the 20% revision is generating a disproportionate share of errors, which is the direct evidence needed to justify a traffic rollback. Option A shows aggregate error groups without attribution to a revision. Option C takes time, adds synthetic load during an incident, and may not reproduce the real traffic mix that triggers the errors. Option D establishes temporal correlation only; the errors could equally come from an upstream dependency that changed at the same time, so it does not prove causation. Rapid attribution using labeled metrics is a core troubleshooting practice within the operational excellence pillar.
hint: Core Rule (Release correlation during troubleshooting): Cloud Run's built-in request metrics carry the revision_name label, so grouping the 5xx request count (or ratio) by revision immediately shows whether the 20% revision is generating a disproportionate share of errors, which is the direct evidence needed to justify a traffic rollback.

whyWrong.0: Option A shows aggregate error groups without attribution to a revision.
whyWrong.2: Option C takes time, adds synthetic load during an incident, and may not reproduce the real traffic mix that triggers the errors.
whyWrong.3: Option D establishes temporal correlation only; the errors could equally come from an upstream dependency that changed at the same time, so it does not prove causation.

question: Users of a travel booking site intermittently receive HTTP 502 responses from the global external Application Load Balancer, while the backend GKE service's own application logs show no corresponding errors. The team has been guessing at causes for two days. What should you do first to find the root cause?
options: Increase the number of backend pods by 50% and wait to see if the 502 errors stop
Enable Cloud Trace on the backend service and look for traces longer than the backend timeout

Enable logging on the load balancer's backend service and inspect the statusDetails field of the 502 entries in Cloud Logging to see whether the cause is backend connection closed, backend timeout, failed health check, or a similar documented condition
Replace the Application Load Balancer with a passthrough Network Load Balancer so requests reach the backend without proxying
explanation: Application Load Balancer logs include a statusDetails field that names the precise reason the proxy generated a response, such as backend_connection_closed_before_data_sent_to_client, backend_timeout, or failed_to_pick_backend; because the 502 is generated by the proxy, the backend never sees the request as an error, which is why application logs are silent. Reading this field turns guesswork into a specific fix (for example, raising the backend keepalive timeout above the load balancer's 600-second idle timeout). Option A is a blind change that does not diagnose anything. Option B cannot capture requests that never reached the application or that the proxy aborted. Option D changes the architecture without understanding the problem and would lose TLS termination, Cloud Armor, and CDN capabilities. Data-driven root cause analysis before making changes is a fundamental troubleshooting best practice.
hint: Core Rule (Load balancer troubleshooting): Application Load Balancer logs include a statusDetails field that names the precise reason the proxy generated a response, such as backend_connection_closed_before_data_sent_to_client, backend_timeout, or failed_to_pick_backend; because the 502 is generated by the proxy, the backend never sees the request as an error, which is why application logs are silent.

whyWrong.0: Option A is a blind change that does not diagnose anything.
whyWrong.1: Option B cannot capture requests that never reached the application or that the proxy aborted.
whyWrong.3: Option D changes the architecture without understanding the problem and would lose TLS termination, Cloud Armor, and CDN capabilities.

question: A retail company's CI pipeline for a set of microservices takes 90 minutes because almost all automated testing consists of browser-based end-to-end tests against a fully deployed environment. About 10% of runs fail for reasons unrelated to the change and are simply re-run. Developers have started merging without waiting for results. How should you restructure the test strategy?
options: Follow the test pyramid: shift most coverage to fast, isolated unit tests and service-level integration or contract tests that run on every pull request, keep a small set of critical end-to-end journeys, and quarantine and fix flaky tests rather than re-running them
Run the end-to-end suite on more powerful Cloud Build machine types so that it finishes in 45 minutes
Remove automated end-to-end tests and rely on a manual QA pass before each production release
Move the end-to-end suite to a nightly schedule and allow merges to main without any automated tests
explanation: The test pyramid places many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration and contract tests in the middle, and very few end-to-end tests at the top; this gives developers feedback in minutes, reduces the flakiness inherent in full-stack tests, and preserves confidence with a handful of critical user journeys. Treating flaky tests as defects to quarantine and fix restores trust in the signal, which is what makes developers wait for results again. Option B halves the time but leaves the flakiness and slow feedback structure intact. Option C replaces automation with slow, expensive manual work and reduces deployment frequency. Option D removes the quality gate from the merge decision entirely, which increases change failure rate. Fast, reliable automated testing is a DORA capability tied to the operational excellence pillar.
hint: Core Rule (Test strategy): The test pyramid places many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration and contract tests in the middle, and very few end-to-end tests at the top; this gives developers feedback in minutes, reduces the flakiness inherent in full-stack tests, and preserves confidence with a handful of critical user journeys.

whyWrong.2: Option C replaces automation with slow, expensive manual work and reduces deployment frequency.
whyWrong.3: Option D removes the quality gate from the merge decision entirely, which increases change failure rate.

question: A payments processor runs its production workloads on several GKE Standard clusters. Twice in the past year an automatic control-plane or node upgrade introduced a Kubernetes API deprecation or a node image change that broke a workload before the team noticed. The company wants to keep receiving timely security patches but validate upgrades before they reach production and control when they happen. Which actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Disable auto-upgrade on all production clusters and upgrade manually once a year

Enroll pre-production clusters in a faster release channel (for example Rapid or Regular) than production (Regular or Stable) so the same versions are exercised by the test suite before production receives them
Move all production clusters to GKE Autopilot, which never applies upgrades automatically
Configure maintenance windows and exclusions on production clusters, use rollout sequencing across fleet clusters, and act on deprecation insights from Recommender before upgrading
Set the production node pools to a fixed node image and never change it
explanation: Release channels provide a natural validation pipeline: because each channel receives the same versions in sequence, running pre-production on a faster channel means workloads and tests see a new Kubernetes minor version and node image weeks before production, so deprecations surface early. Maintenance windows and exclusions give control over when upgrades occur, rollout sequencing lets fleets upgrade clusters in a defined order (test before prod), and GKE deprecation insights identify workloads calling removed APIs before the upgrade. Option A falls out of support (GKE supports a limited number of minor versions) and leaves clusters unpatched, contradicting the security requirement. Option C is false; Autopilot clusters are also auto-upgraded within their channel. Option E is impossible long-term since node versions must remain compatible with the control plane and would leave nodes unpatched. Controlled, tested change is an operational excellence and reliability practice.
hint: Core Rule (Validating GKE upgrades): Release channels provide a natural validation pipeline: because each channel receives the same versions in sequence, running pre-production on a faster channel means workloads and tests see a new Kubernetes minor version and node image weeks before production, so deprecations surface early.

whyWrong.0: Option A falls out of support (GKE supports a limited number of minor versions) and leaves clusters unpatched, contradicting the security requirement.
whyWrong.2: Option C is false; Autopilot clusters are also auto-upgraded within their channel.
whyWrong.4: Option E is impossible long-term since node versions must remain compatible with the control plane and would leave nodes unpatched.

topic: Log retention for root cause analysis
question: While investigating a data-corruption issue that began roughly six weeks ago, the SRE team at a SaaS company discovered that the relevant application logs in Cloud Logging had already been deleted because the default retention period had passed. They want to make sure application logs are kept for at least one year for future investigations, at the lowest cost and without building a custom pipeline. What should you do?
options: Create a log sink that exports all application logs to BigQuery and rely on BigQuery's default table expiration
Ask developers to also write logs to local files on each instance and back the files up to Cloud Storage weekly
Increase the retention of the _Required log bucket to 365 days
Create a dedicated Cloud Logging log bucket with a 365-day retention period and route application logs to it with a log sink; optionally lock the bucket
explanation: Cloud Logging log buckets support configurable retention from 1 to 3650 days; creating a user-defined bucket with 365-day retention and routing the application logs to it with a sink keeps the logs searchable in Logs Explorer and Log Analytics with no extra pipeline, and locking the bucket prevents anyone from shortening retention. Option A works technically but BigQuery table expiration defaults to none for sink-created tables (so cost grows unbounded) and forces the team to use SQL rather than the logging tools; it also does not answer 'without building a custom pipeline' as neatly. Option B is a fragile manual process that misses ephemeral instances. Option C is not possible: the _Required bucket has a fixed 400-day retention and only holds Admin Activity audit logs and similar mandatory logs, not application logs. Retaining evidence for RCA is an operational excellence practice.
hint: Core Rule (Log retention for root cause analysis): Cloud Logging log buckets support configurable retention from 1 to 3650 days; creating a user-defined bucket with 365-day retention and routing the application logs to it with a sink keeps the logs searchable in Logs Explorer and Log Analytics with no extra pipeline, and locking the bucket prevents anyone from shortening retention.

whyWrong.2: Option C is not possible: the _Required bucket has a fixed 400-day retention and only holds Admin Activity audit logs and similar mandatory logs, not application logs.

question: A manufacturing company's inventory service on GKE has degraded once a week for the past month. Each time, different engineers restart pods, scale the node pool, and flush a Memorystore cache simultaneously; the problem goes away for a few days and nobody knows which action helped or what the cause was. The engineering director asks you to define how the team should troubleshoot the next occurrence. What should you recommend?
options: Automate the three remediation actions in a Cloud Run job triggered by the alert so degradation is fixed without human intervention
Increase resource requests for all pods and the size of the Memorystore instance to remove any capacity-related cause

Adopt a hypothesis-driven method: first capture the state (logs, metrics, traces, recent changes) while the problem is active, form a specific hypothesis, change one variable at a time, and observe whether the SLI recovers, recording each step for the postmortem
Open a support case with Google Cloud at the next occurrence and take no action until support responds
explanation: Effective troubleshooting is scientific: preserve evidence first, then triage, examine, diagnose with a specific hypothesis, and test with a single change so that the outcome is attributable; recording the steps feeds a postmortem that leads to a permanent fix. Making three changes at once destroys causal information, which is exactly why the team is still in the dark after a month. Option A automates the guesswork and hides the underlying defect, which will eventually manifest in a way the script cannot fix. Option B is an expensive shotgun change without evidence that capacity is the issue. Option D abdicates responsibility; support can help, but the team must still collect data and mitigate customer impact. The operational excellence pillar and the SRE book both stress systematic, evidence-based troubleshooting.
hint: Core Rule (Root cause analysis methodology): Effective troubleshooting is scientific: preserve evidence first, then triage, examine, diagnose with a specific hypothesis, and test with a single change so that the outcome is attributable; recording the steps feeds a postmortem that leads to a permanent fix.

whyWrong.0: Option A automates the guesswork and hides the underlying defect, which will eventually manifest in a way the script cannot fix.
whyWrong.1: Option B is an expensive shotgun change without evidence that capacity is the issue.
whyWrong.3: Option D abdicates responsibility; support can help, but the team must still collect data and mitigate customer impact.

question: A marketing technology company runs a web frontend on Cloud Run. Product managers want to review every pull request in a live environment before it is merged, and QA wants to run end-to-end tests against the same environment. Maintaining a fixed set of shared review environments has caused conflicts and stale deployments. You want a cost-efficient solution with minimal management. What should you do?
options: Create ten permanent Cloud Run services named review-1 through review-10 and have a spreadsheet track which pull request owns which service

Configure the pull-request Cloud Build trigger to deploy the built image as a new Cloud Run revision with --no-traffic and a revision tag derived from the PR number, post the tag URL to the pull request, and remove the tag when the PR closes
Deploy each pull request to a dedicated GKE Autopilot cluster created by Terraform and deleted after merge
Deploy each pull request to the staging service and ask reviewers to coordinate on a shared calendar
explanation: Cloud Run revision tags create a stable, unique URL for a specific revision that receives no production traffic, so each pull request gets an isolated preview that scales to zero when idle (near-zero cost), is created and torn down entirely by the pipeline, and is exactly what QA and product managers can test. Option A is a manual pool with limited capacity and coordination overhead. Option C provides isolation but a cluster per PR is slow to create and far more expensive and complex than needed for a Cloud Run workload. Option D reintroduces the shared-environment conflicts the team is trying to remove. Ephemeral, on-demand environments are an operational excellence and cost-optimization practice.
hint: Core Rule (Ephemeral test environments): Cloud Run revision tags create a stable, unique URL for a specific revision that receives no production traffic, so each pull request gets an isolated preview that scales to zero when idle (near-zero cost), is created and torn down entirely by the pipeline, and is exactly what QA and product managers can test.

whyWrong.2: Option C provides isolation but a cluster per PR is slow to create and far more expensive and complex than needed for a Cloud Run workload.
whyWrong.3: Option D reintroduces the shared-environment conflicts the team is trying to remove.

question: A bank's internet banking portal is deployed with Cloud Deploy to GKE. After each production rollout an SRE manually logs in, performs a transfer between test accounts, and checks that statements render, which takes 20 minutes and is often skipped at night. The bank wants this multi-step user journey verified continuously from outside Google Cloud's network path, with alerts if it fails, and also executed as a gate right after each deployment. What should you do?
options: Add readiness and liveness probes to the portal pods that call the transfer and statement endpoints
Create an uptime check on the login page URL and alert when it returns a non-200 status
Schedule a Cloud Run job that runs the manual test script every hour and writes pass/fail to a spreadsheet

Implement the journey as a Cloud Monitoring synthetic monitor (Puppeteer script running in Cloud Run functions) with an alerting policy, and run the same script as a Cloud Deploy verification step so the rollout fails if the journey breaks

Option A misuses health probes, which are meant to be cheap and local; multi-step business transactions in probes would cause pod restarts during transient issues. Option B validates only that the login page loads, not the transfer or statement functionality. Option C is bespoke, has no alerting integration, and is not connected to the deployment pipeline. Automated validation after deployment is a reliability and operational excellence recommendation.
hint: Core Rule (Post-deployment validation): Cloud Monitoring synthetic monitors execute a scripted browser or API journey on a schedule from Google-managed infrastructure and integrate with alerting, which covers the continuous external validation; reusing the same script as a Cloud Deploy verify step makes the journey a deployment gate, so a broken transfer flow fails the rollout instead of being discovered later.

question: A government tax portal must handle a filing-deadline peak that is about 12 times normal traffic. Last year the site failed at peak even though a load test had 'passed'; the postmortem found that the test hit a single cached endpoint with a constant request rate from a single region, while real users perform multi-step authenticated sessions from many locations with ramping arrival rates. You are asked to redesign the load test so its result is trustworthy. What should you do?
options: Model realistic user journeys (login, form steps, submission) with think times, ramp the number of simulated users to 12x over a realistic window, generate load from multiple regions against a production-like environment, and define pass/fail on the same SLIs used in production (p99 latency, error rate, saturation of downstream dependencies)
Run the previous test again but at 20x the request rate to add a safety margin
Use production traffic mirroring to send a copy of live requests to staging for a week before the deadline
Skip load testing and instead set very high autoscaling limits on all services so capacity is never the constraint
explanation: A load test is only as valid as its model of production: realistic journeys exercise authentication, session state, database writes, and downstream calls that a single cached GET never touches; ramping reproduces autoscaler and connection-pool behavior; multi-region generation reflects load balancer and CDN behavior; and pass/fail based on production SLIs plus dependency saturation catches the bottleneck (often a database or third-party API) before the deadline. Option B repeats an unrepresentative test at higher volume and would still miss the write path. Option C mirrors current traffic, which is 1x, not 12x, and mirroring authenticated multi-step sessions with side effects is impractical. Option D ignores non-scalable dependencies such as databases and quotas, which are usually what fails at peak. Realistic load testing is a reliability-pillar recommendation for capacity planning.
hint: Core Rule (Load test design): A load test is only as valid as its model of production: realistic journeys exercise authentication, session state, database writes, and downstream calls that a single cached GET never touches; ramping reproduces autoscaler and connection-pool behavior; multi-region generation reflects load balancer and CDN behavior; and pass/fail based on production SLIs plus dependency saturation catches the bottleneck (often a database or third-party API) before the deadline.

whyWrong.2: Option C mirrors current traffic, which is 1x, not 12x, and mirroring authenticated multi-step sessions with side effects is impractical.
whyWrong.3: Option D ignores non-scalable dependencies such as databases and quotas, which are usually what fails at peak.

question: A ride-hailing startup runs its API gateway on Cloud Run, its pricing service on GKE, and a legacy driver-matching service on Compute Engine. Traces in Cloud Trace currently appear as disconnected fragments per service, which makes root cause analysis of latency incidents slow. You want end-to-end traces with the least vendor lock-in. Which actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Enable 100% trace sampling on the Cloud Run gateway so every fragment is captured
Instrument all three services with the OpenTelemetry SDK and export spans to Cloud Trace through the Google Cloud exporter or an OpenTelemetry Collector
Ensure every service propagates the W3C traceparent (or X-Cloud-Trace-Context) header on outbound HTTP and gRPC calls, including the legacy service's HTTP client
Replace the legacy Compute Engine service with a Cloud Run service so that tracing is automatic
Create a log-based metric that counts requests per service and correlate the counts over time
explanation: Fragmented traces are a context-propagation problem, not a sampling problem: spans from different services are stitched into one trace only when each service reads the incoming trace context header and forwards it on its outbound calls, so every service (including the legacy one) must propagate traceparent or X-Cloud-Trace-Context. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard Google recommends; its SDKs handle propagation and span creation, and the Google Cloud exporter or a Collector sends data to Cloud Trace while leaving the option to send elsewhere later. Option A increases cost and volume but still produces fragments if headers are not propagated. Option D is a rewrite that is unnecessary for tracing; Cloud Run adds request-level spans but application code must still propagate context downstream. Option E is a coarse correlation technique that cannot reconstruct individual request paths. Standardized instrumentation supports the operational excellence pillar.
hint: Core Rule (Distributed tracing instrumentation): Fragmented traces are a context-propagation problem, not a sampling problem: spans from different services are stitched into one trace only when each service reads the incoming trace context header and forwards it on its outbound calls, so every service (including the legacy one) must propagate traceparent or X-Cloud-Trace-Context.

whyWrong.0: Option A increases cost and volume but still produces fragments if headers are not propagated.
whyWrong.3: Option D is a rewrite that is unnecessary for tracing; Cloud Run adds request-level spans but application code must still propagate context downstream.
whyWrong.4: Option E is a coarse correlation technique that cannot reconstruct individual request paths.

question: A multinational insurer has 25 business units that repeatedly ask the central cloud team to create the same kinds of environments: a hardened GKE cluster, a Cloud SQL instance with private IP, and a data-science workstation. The cloud team writes and reviews each request by hand, which takes two weeks. Leadership wants business units to deploy these approved patterns themselves, but only the approved, security-reviewed versions. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Grant business-unit leads the Project Editor role and publish the approved Terraform code in a shared Git repository for them to run
Create a shared Cloud Build trigger that business units invoke with substitutions for the pattern name and parameters

Package the approved Terraform configurations as Service Catalog solutions, share the catalog with the business units' folders, and let users launch the solutions from the Google Cloud console with parameters they are permitted to change
Record a video walkthrough of the console steps for each pattern and ask business units to follow it
explanation: Service Catalog is Google Cloud's mechanism for curated self-service: the central team publishes Terraform-based (or link-based) solutions, controls their versions and exposed parameters, and shares the catalog at the organization, folder, or project level, so business units deploy only vetted patterns while the platform team retains governance and can see who launched what. Option A gives broad permissions and relies on users running raw Terraform correctly, with no version control over which revision they apply. Option B is possible but requires each unit to hold Cloud Build permissions and know substitution details, and it lacks a discoverable catalog and per-solution access control. Option D is manual and inherently non-compliant with the 'approved version' requirement. Curated self-service provisioning is an operational excellence recommendation.

whyWrong.1: Option B is possible but requires each unit to hold Cloud Build permissions and know substitution details, and it lacks a discoverable catalog and per-solution access control.

question: A retail group creates about 15 new Google Cloud projects per month. Each project must be attached to the correct billing account and folder, have a standard set of APIs enabled, be attached as a service project to the appropriate Shared VPC, carry cost-center labels, and have baseline IAM groups bound. Today an administrator performs these steps in the console and often forgets one, causing compliance findings. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Implement a Terraform-based project factory that takes a small set of inputs (name, folder, cost center, Shared VPC host) and creates the project with all standard settings, executed through a reviewed pull-request workflow in CI
Create a detailed checklist in the ticketing system and require a second administrator to verify each new project

Option B still depends on humans following steps, which is the root cause of the findings. Option C harms isolation, IAM boundaries, and quota management, contrary to the resource hierarchy guidance. Option D automates part of the work but still leaves a manual console step, does not enforce ordering, and has no review or state tracking. Consistent, automated provisioning is an operational excellence and security recommendation.

whyWrong.3: Option D automates part of the work but still leaves a manual console step, does not enforce ordering, and has no review or state tracking.

question: A hospital network runs several hundred Compute Engine VMs. Security requires every VM to start from a CIS-hardened image with the monitoring agent, endpoint protection, and corporate certificates pre-installed. Teams currently install these components with startup scripts, which frequently fail and leave VMs non-compliant for hours. What should you do?
options: Keep the startup scripts but add retries and a Cloud Monitoring alert if a script has not finished within 30 minutes
Use OS Config guest policies to install the agents after each VM boots
Ask each team to manually build a base VM, install the components, and create an image from it

Build golden images in an automated pipeline (for example Packer in Cloud Build) that applies hardening and installs the agents, publish them to an image family, and require teams to use the family through an organization policy for trusted images
