options: Maintain a long-lived release branch per feature and deploy the branch only when the product team gives approval
Deploy each new feature as a separate Cloud Run service and use Cloud Armor to allow only employee IP ranges initially
Use GKE namespaces per feature and switch the Ingress between namespaces when the product team approves

Decouple deployment from release by wrapping new features in feature flags that are evaluated at runtime and controlled through a configuration service, targeting employees first, then a percentage of users, with a kill switch
explanation: Feature flags separate deploying code from releasing functionality: code can ship continuously in a dark state, then be enabled for specific cohorts or percentages and disabled instantly through configuration, without any redeployment, which is exactly what the two teams need. Long-lived branches (option A) recreate integration risk and block continuous deployment. A service per feature behind IP allow-lists (option B) does not scale, cannot do percentage rollouts, and identifies employees poorly. Namespace switching (option C) is a coarse environment swap, not a per-feature, per-cohort control.
hint: Core Rule: Feature flags separate deploying code from releasing functionality: code can ship continuously in a dark state, then be enabled for specific cohorts or percentages and disabled instantly through configuration, without any redeployment, which is exactly what the two teams need.

question: A logistics company needs to rename the column customer_ref to customer_id in a heavily used Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL table. The service that uses the table runs on GKE with rolling deployments, so old and new pods coexist for several minutes, and the business requires zero downtime. Which two practices should you follow? (Choose two.)
options: Use the expand/contract pattern: add the new column, deploy code that writes to both columns and reads from the old one, backfill, switch reads to the new column, and only then drop the old column in a later release
Run a single ALTER TABLE RENAME COLUMN statement immediately before starting the rolling deployment so that the schema and code change at the same time
Stop the GKE Deployment, apply the rename, and start the Deployment again to guarantee consistency
Ensure every schema migration is backward compatible with the currently running application version and is applied as its own step, separate from and ahead of the application rollout
Put the table in read-only mode during the rolling deployment so that no writes can conflict with the rename
explanation: Zero-downtime schema changes require that at every moment the schema is compatible with both the old and the new code, because both run concurrently during a rolling deployment; expand/contract achieves this by adding, dual-writing, backfilling, switching, and only then removing, and treating each migration as a separately applied, backward-compatible step ensures the database is never ahead of or behind what the running code expects. An immediate rename (option B) breaks the old pods that still reference the old column. Stopping the Deployment (option C) is downtime. Read-only mode (option E) is also an outage for write traffic and still does not solve the compatibility problem.
hint: Core Rule (Database schema migrations): Zero-downtime schema changes require that at every moment the schema is compatible with both the old and the new code, because both run concurrently during a rolling deployment; expand/contract achieves this by adding, dual-writing, backfilling, switching, and only then removing, and treating each migration as a separately applied, backward-compatible step ensures the database is never ahead of or behind what the running code expects.

question: A government agency's QA team must test every new revision of a Cloud Run service against the production configuration and data sources before any citizen traffic reaches it. Developers want to keep a single Cloud Run service and avoid creating separate environments for this purpose. What should you do?
options: Deploy the new revision with 100% traffic during a low-traffic period and ask QA to test quickly
Create a copy of the service named qa in the same project and deploy new revisions there first
Deploy the new revision with --no-traffic and a revision tag such as qa, give the QA team the tag-specific URL to test the revision directly, and migrate traffic to it only after QA approval
Deploy the new revision to a Cloud Run service in a different region and use a global load balancer to route the QA team's requests there
explanation: Cloud Run revision tags create a dedicated URL for a specific revision that receives no share of the main traffic split, so QA can exercise the exact production revision, configuration, and dependencies before any public traffic is routed to it, all within the same service. Deploying with 100% traffic (option A) exposes citizens to untested code. A separate qa service (option B) diverges in configuration and is the extra environment the developers want to avoid. A second region with a global load balancer (option D) is heavy infrastructure for a testing need that tags already solve.
hint: Core Rule: Cloud Run revision tags create a dedicated URL for a specific revision that receives no share of the main traffic split, so QA can exercise the exact production revision, configuration, and dependencies before any public traffic is routed to it, all within the same service.

question: An online retailer uses Cloud Deploy to promote releases to production. After an incident caused by a Saturday-evening deployment, management requires that no production rollouts start on weekends or during the annual peak sales week, while still permitting an authorized release manager to override the restriction for emergency fixes. How should you implement this with the least custom code?
options: Create a Cloud Deploy deploy policy with rollout restrictions defining the weekend and peak-week time windows for the production target, and grant only release managers the permission to override the policy
Write a Cloud Build trigger that checks the current date and fails the build if it falls on a weekend or in the peak week
Remove the production target from the delivery pipeline on Fridays and add it back on Mondays using a scheduled script
Ask developers not to click Promote on weekends and record the rule in the team wiki
explanation: Cloud Deploy deploy policies let you define time-window restrictions on rollouts and other actions for specific targets or pipelines, and an override capability can be granted to a limited set of principals through IAM, which satisfies both the freeze and the emergency exception declaratively. A date check in Cloud Build (option B) is custom logic outside the deployment tool and is easily bypassed by promoting directly in Cloud Deploy. Scripting target removal (option C) is fragile and destroys pipeline history. A wiki rule (option D) is not a control at all.

question: A food-delivery company runs its order database on a Cloud SQL for MySQL high-availability instance. Twice in the past year, a Cloud SQL maintenance event caused a brief connection interruption during the Friday dinner peak. The company accepts short maintenance interruptions but wants them to occur only early on Tuesday mornings and never during the two weeks around the year-end holidays. What should you do?
options: Disable maintenance on the instance permanently to avoid any future interruptions
Configure the instance's maintenance window for early Tuesday mornings, set the maintenance timing preference, and configure a deny maintenance period covering the holiday weeks
Migrate the database to a self-managed MySQL on Compute Engine so that the team controls all patching

question: A ride-sharing company's trip-pricing service on GKE Autopilot returns a burst of HTTP 502 and connection-reset errors for a few seconds every time a new version is rolled out or a node is upgraded, even though readiness probes are configured. Investigation shows that pods are terminated while the load balancer is still sending them requests. What should you do to make rollouts and upgrades invisible to users?
options: Increase the number of replicas so that the proportion of failed requests during each rollout is smaller
Switch from a rolling update to a Recreate strategy so that all pods are replaced at once during a short window
Remove the readiness probe so that pods are added to the load balancer more quickly after they start

Add a preStop hook that delays shutdown for a few seconds so that endpoint removal propagates before the process stops, handle SIGTERM in the application to drain in-flight requests, and set terminationGracePeriodSeconds long enough for the drain to complete
explanation: The errors come from a race between pod termination and endpoint deregistration: the load balancer briefly continues to route to a pod that has already started shutting down. A preStop sleep gives the endpoint controller and load balancer time to remove the pod, proper SIGTERM handling lets in-flight requests finish, and a sufficient termination grace period ensures Kubernetes does not kill the process prematurely; together they make rollouts and node upgrades zero-error events. More replicas (option A) only dilutes the errors. Recreate (option B) causes a full outage on every deploy. Removing readiness probes (option C) addresses startup, not shutdown, and would route traffic to pods that are not yet ready.
hint: Core Rule (Graceful pod termination): The errors come from a race between pod termination and endpoint deregistration: the load balancer briefly continues to route to a pod that has already started shutting down.

question: A global gaming company serves players from Cloud Run services deployed in six regions behind a global external Application Load Balancer. Every release currently goes to all six regions simultaneously through a script, and a recent bad release caused a worldwide outage for twelve minutes. The company wants to limit the blast radius of releases while keeping the process automated. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Continue deploying to all regions at once but shorten the deployment script so that a rollback can be executed faster
Deploy new releases to a single region only and route all global traffic there during the release to simplify observation

Model the six regions as sequential targets in a Cloud Deploy pipeline, starting with the lowest-traffic region, with a bake period and automated SLI verification between stages, so that a bad release is detected and stopped before it reaches the remaining regions
Deploy only on weekends when player counts are lowest so that an outage affects fewer users
explanation: Rolling a release out region by region, beginning with the smallest population and waiting for verified health before proceeding, is the standard way to bound blast radius in multi-region systems; Cloud Deploy supports sequential targets with verification and automated promotion, keeping the process fully automated. Faster rollback of a global deployment (option A) still exposes all users to the initial failure. Concentrating all global traffic in one region (option B) creates a massive capacity and latency risk. Weekend-only releases (option D) reduce exposure only marginally and slow delivery without addressing blast radius.
hint: Core Rule (Regional progressive rollout): Rolling a release out region by region, beginning with the smallest population and waiting for verified health before proceeding, is the standard way to bound blast radius in multi-region systems; Cloud Deploy supports sequential targets with verification and automated promotion, keeping the process fully automated.

question: A healthcare SaaS provider has a policy that any production release must be revertible within five minutes. A recent attempt to roll back a GKE service failed because the previous container image had been deleted from the registry and the new release had already altered the database schema in an incompatible way. Which two practices should you adopt to make the five-minute rollback objective achievable? (Choose two.)
options: Retain previously deployed images in Artifact Registry, reference images by immutable digest in manifests, and configure cleanup policies so that images currently or recently in production are never purged
Store container images only on developer laptops so that they can be pushed quickly during a rollback
Apply schema changes in the same transaction as the application deployment so that both can be reverted together
Grant every developer cluster-admin on the production cluster so that anyone can execute a rollback
Make every database schema change backward compatible with the previous application version, so that rolling back the application never requires a schema rollback
explanation: Fast rollback depends on two things: the previous artifact must still exist and be exactly identifiable (immutable digests and retention-aware cleanup policies in Artifact Registry), and the database must still work with the previous code, which is guaranteed by making schema changes backward compatible rather than coupling them to the release. Images on laptops (option B) are unreliable and unauditable. Coupling schema and application changes (option C) makes rollbacks slower and riskier, not faster, because schema changes are often irreversible. Broad cluster-admin grants (option D) violate least privilege and do not address the technical causes of the failed rollback.
hint: Core Rule (Rollback readiness): Fast rollback depends on two things: the previous artifact must still exist and be exactly identifiable (immutable digests and retention-aware cleanup policies in Artifact Registry), and the database must still work with the previous code, which is guaranteed by making schema changes backward compatible rather than coupling them to the release.

question: An auditor has told a payments company that developers must not be able to deploy directly to production and that every production deployment must be approved by a designated release manager, with an audit trail. topic: Fault injection in a service mesh
question: A bank's microservices on GKE use Cloud Service Mesh. Developers have configured timeouts and retries in their services, but nobody knows whether they actually behave correctly when a downstream service is slow or returns errors, and testing this requires the downstream team to deliberately break their service. The reliability team wants a repeatable, low-risk way to verify this behavior. What should you recommend?
options: Ask each downstream team to add an environment variable that makes their service return errors on demand, and coordinate manual test sessions

Use Cloud Service Mesh fault injection in the VirtualService or route configuration to inject delays and HTTP errors for a controlled percentage of requests to the downstream service in a staging mesh, and observe the callers' timeout, retry, and circuit-breaking behavior through mesh telemetry
Block the downstream service's IP address with a firewall rule during business hours and watch what happens to callers
Run a CPU stress tool on the downstream service's nodes to make it slow, then observe the callers
explanation: Service mesh fault injection lets you introduce artificial latency or error responses at the proxy layer for a chosen fraction of traffic without modifying or breaking the downstream service, which makes resilience tests repeatable, targeted, and safe, and the mesh's built-in telemetry shows exactly how callers respond. Requiring downstream teams to add failure switches (option A) spreads test code through production services and depends on manual coordination. A firewall block (option C) is a crude, all-or-nothing failure that also affects other callers. CPU stress on nodes (option D) affects unrelated workloads on those nodes and produces unpredictable behavior.

question: A SaaS company's API runs on a managed instance group behind an external Application Load Balancer. The load balancer health check calls /healthz, which verifies connectivity to Cloud SQL and to a downstream inventory service. When the inventory service became slow last week, every instance failed its health check simultaneously, the load balancer had no healthy backends, and the entire API went down, although most endpoints did not use the inventory service. What should you change?
options: Increase the health check's unhealthy threshold to ten consecutive failures so that brief dependency slowdowns are tolerated
Remove the health check entirely so that the load balancer always sends traffic to all instances
Move the inventory dependency check to a separate endpoint that pages the on-call engineer but keep it in the load balancer health check as well

explanation: A load balancer health check should answer 'can this instance serve traffic', not 'are all dependencies healthy'; when a shared dependency is included, every instance fails together and a partial degradation becomes a total outage, which is a well-known cascading failure pattern. Shallow health checks keep instances in rotation, and per-request handling plus alerting on dependency status provide the needed visibility. Raising the unhealthy threshold (option A) only delays the same collapse. Removing the health check (option B) means truly dead instances keep receiving traffic. Keeping the dependency in the load balancer check (option C) preserves the failure mode.

question: A logistics company processes shipment events from a Pub/Sub subscription with a Cloud Run service. A single malformed event caused the service to throw an exception on every delivery attempt; Pub/Sub kept redelivering the same message, the subscription backlog grew for hours, and all subsequent shipments were delayed. question: A healthcare scheduling application runs on a zonal GKE Standard cluster with a three-replica stateless Deployment and a single-replica PostgreSQL StatefulSet on a zonal persistent disk. question: A 6-person startup is containerizing its web application and wants to run it on Kubernetes. question: A computer-vision company runs both a web frontend and GPU-based inference services in one GKE Standard cluster. The GPU node pool uses expensive A100 machines, and the team has noticed ordinary frontend pods being scheduled onto GPU nodes, consuming their CPU and memory and leaving GPU nodes running when no inference is needed. How should you ensure only inference pods land on the GPU nodes?

question: A ticketing website on GKE Standard experiences sudden 20x traffic spikes when popular events go on sale. Configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler on the frontend deployment targeting CPU utilization or requests per second.
Increase the node pool to its maximum expected size and disable autoscaling to avoid scheduling delays.
Enable the cluster autoscaler on the node pool with appropriate minimum and maximum node counts.
Set pod resource requests to zero so more pods fit on each node.

question: An online bank runs a stateful payment-authorization service with three replicas on a GKE Standard cluster in the Regular release channel. question: A SaaS company serves customers in Europe and North America from GKE clusters in europe-west1 and us-central1. It wants a single anycast IP address and hostname, requests routed to the nearest healthy cluster, automatic failover to the other region if a cluster becomes unhealthy, and the ability to shift a percentage of traffic between clusters during blue/green rollouts. Which design should you implement?

Expose each cluster's service through a regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer and use Traffic Director to balance between them.
Peer the two clusters' VPCs and have the us-central1 Ingress forward requests to europe-west1 pods when needed.
Register both clusters in a fleet, enable multi-cluster Gateway with the gke-l7-global-external-managed-mc class, and use Multi Cluster Services with HTTPRoute weights for traffic splitting.

Option A relies on DNS TTLs for failover, which is slow and inconsistent, and cannot do weighted cross-cluster splitting in one hostname. topic: GKE Enterprise Config Sync and Policy Controller
question: A retailer operates 30 GKE clusters across three regions and two on-premises sites. Security has mandated that every cluster carry the same namespaces, RBAC bindings, and network policies, and that no container may run as root or pull from an unapproved registry. Configuration drift on individual clusters has caused repeated audit findings. What should you do?
options: Write a Cloud Build pipeline that runs kubectl apply against each cluster every night and emails a diff report.
Register the clusters in a GKE Enterprise fleet, use Config Sync to apply a Git-based configuration to all clusters, and enforce the security rules with Policy Controller constraints.
Enable Binary Authorization on each cluster and rely on its attestations to prevent configuration drift.
Consolidate all workloads into a single large regional GKE cluster so only one configuration exists.
explanation: Config Sync continuously reconciles clusters with a Git source of truth (GitOps), automatically reverting drift, and Policy Controller (based on Open Policy Agent Gatekeeper) enforces admission constraints such as disallowing root containers or unapproved registries; fleets make both work uniformly across cloud and on-premises clusters. Option A is a home-grown, point-in-time push that does not prevent or revert drift between runs. Option C validates image provenance but has no notion of namespaces, RBAC, or network policies. Option D is not feasible for on-premises sites and multi-region resilience.
hint: Core Rule (GKE Enterprise Config Sync and Policy Controller): Config Sync continuously reconciles clusters with a Git source of truth (GitOps), automatically reverting drift, and Policy Controller (based on Open Policy Agent Gatekeeper) enforces admission constraints such as disallowing root containers or unapproved registries; fleets make both work uniformly across cloud and on-premises clusters.

question: A healthcare provider runs 80 microservices on GKE. Compliance now requires that all service-to-service traffic be encrypted and mutually authenticated, and the SRE team wants canary releases that shift 5% of traffic to a new version and per-service latency dashboards. The development teams have no capacity to modify application code. What should you recommend?
options: Add a TLS library to every service and implement traffic splitting in application configuration.
Use Kubernetes NetworkPolicies to restrict traffic and rely on VPC encryption in transit for compliance.
Enable managed Cloud Service Mesh on the cluster, enforce STRICT mTLS with a PeerAuthentication policy, and use VirtualService weights for canaries.
Place an internal Application Load Balancer in front of each service and configure weighted backend services.
explanation: Cloud Service Mesh injects sidecar (or ambient) proxies that provide mTLS, identity-based authentication, fine-grained traffic splitting, and telemetry for every service without changing application code, which meets the compliance and SRE goals simultaneously. Option A requires code changes in 80 services. Option B controls which pods may talk but does not provide mutual authentication at the application layer or traffic splitting. Option D would require 80 load balancers and still does not provide workload identity or mTLS between services.
hint: Core Rule: Cloud Service Mesh injects sidecar (or ambient) proxies that provide mTLS, identity-based authentication, fine-grained traffic splitting, and telemetry for every service without changing application code, which meets the compliance and SRE goals simultaneously.

question: A photo-sharing startup runs a CPU-intensive image-resizing service on Cloud Run with the default concurrency of 80 requests per instance and 1 vCPU. Under load, p95 latency rises to 6 seconds even though instance count stays low, and CPU utilization per instance is pinned at 100%. You want to reduce latency without rewriting the service. What should you do?
options: Lower the maximum concurrency per instance to a small value such as 1 to 4 and allow more instances to be created.
Increase the request timeout to 15 minutes so requests are not cut off.
Enable CPU always allocated so the instance keeps processing between requests.
Raise the maximum concurrency to 250 so fewer instances are needed.
explanation: Cloud Run scales instances based on concurrency; with a CPU-bound workload and 80 concurrent requests sharing one vCPU, each request is starved. Lowering concurrency makes Cloud Run spin up more instances sooner so each request gets dedicated CPU, which is the recommended tuning for CPU-heavy services. Option B only allows slow requests to run longer. Option C affects CPU allocation outside request handling, not contention during requests. Option D worsens the contention.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Run concurrency): Cloud Run scales instances based on concurrency; with a CPU-bound workload and 80 concurrent requests sharing one vCPU, each request is starved.

whyWrong.1: Option B only allows slow requests to run longer.
whyWrong.2: Option C affects CPU allocation outside request handling, not contention during requests.
whyWrong.3: Option D worsens the contention.

question: A bank exposes a customer-facing API on Cloud Run built with a Java framework that takes about 8 seconds to initialize. Traffic is low overnight, so instances scale to zero and the first morning requests time out. The API must respond within 500 ms at all times. Which configuration change should you make?
options: Increase the maximum number of instances to 1,000.
Set the concurrency to 1 so each request gets its own instance.
Move the service to a second region and load-balance across both.
Configure a minimum number of instances greater than zero and enable startup CPU boost.
explanation: Minimum instances keep warm instances ready so requests never hit a cold start, and startup CPU boost gives extra CPU during container initialization so any additional instances start faster. This is the documented remedy for cold-start latency in Cloud Run. Option A controls the upper bound, not warm capacity. Option B increases the number of cold starts. Option C adds redundancy but each region would still scale to zero and cold-start.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Run cold starts): Minimum instances keep warm instances ready so requests never hit a cold start, and startup CPU boost gives extra CPU during container initialization so any additional instances start faster.

question: A marketing platform's Cloud Run service returns an HTTP 202 to callers immediately and then continues to send emails in a background thread for another 20 seconds. Engineers notice that many background sends silently stall and complete only when the next request arrives. What is the most appropriate fix with minimal code change?
options: Increase the request timeout so the background thread has more time.
Set the service's CPU allocation to 'CPU always allocated' so instances keep CPU between requests.
Increase the instance memory limit to prevent the thread from being throttled.
Set the maximum concurrency to 1 so background work is not interrupted.
explanation: By default, Cloud Run throttles CPU to near zero once a request completes, so any background work started during a request stalls until the next request wakes the instance. Setting CPU to always allocated keeps CPU available between requests, allowing asynchronous background processing to finish; the more robust long-term pattern is to hand off work to Cloud Tasks or Pub/Sub, but the stated constraint is minimal code change. Option A does not matter because the request has already returned. Option C addresses memory, not CPU throttling. Option D limits concurrency but the CPU is still throttled after the response.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Run CPU allocation): By default, Cloud Run throttles CPU to near zero once a request completes, so any background work started during a request stalls until the next request wakes the instance.

whyWrong.0: Option A does not matter because the request has already returned.
whyWrong.2: Option C addresses memory, not CPU throttling.
whyWrong.3: Option D limits concurrency but the CPU is still throttled after the response.

question: An accounting firm needs to run a containerized reconciliation process every night at 02:00. The process reads from Cloud SQL, runs for about 90 minutes, does not serve HTTP requests, and must exit with a non-zero code on failure so the on-call team is alerted. The firm wants a serverless solution with no idle cost. What should you use?
options: A Cloud Run service with minimum instances set to 1 and an internal HTTP endpoint triggered by Cloud Scheduler.
A Compute Engine VM with a cron entry that starts the container.
A Cloud Run job executed on a schedule by Cloud Scheduler.
A Cloud Run function with a 90-minute timeout invoked by Pub/Sub.

Option A forces a batch process into a request/response model with request timeout limits and an always-on instance that costs money. Option B is not serverless and incurs 24x7 VM cost. Option D is limited by function timeouts (60 minutes for event-driven functions) and is not the right abstraction for a long batch process.

question: A payments gateway on Cloud Run must call a card-network partner's API. The partner allowlists a single static source IP, and the same service must also read from a Memorystore for Redis instance with a private IP. The team wants the lowest-latency, most cost-efficient networking configuration available. What should you do?
options: Configure Direct VPC egress with 'route all traffic to the VPC' and set up Cloud NAT on the subnet with a reserved static IP address.
Configure a Serverless VPC Access connector with 'route only private ranges to the VPC' and reserve a static IP on the connector instances.
Deploy an HTTP proxy VM with a static external IP and route the partner calls through it, while using Direct VPC egress for Redis.
Assign a static external IP directly to the Cloud Run service through a global external Application Load Balancer.
explanation: Direct VPC egress attaches the Cloud Run service to the VPC without connector VMs, giving lower latency and cost than Serverless VPC Access; routing all traffic through the VPC sends internet-bound requests via Cloud NAT, whose manually reserved static IP becomes the stable source IP the partner can allowlist, while private Redis traffic flows directly. Option B routes only private ranges, so partner traffic exits with a dynamic IP, and connectors add cost and hops. Option C adds a VM to manage and a single point of failure. Option D provides a static inbound IP for the service, not a static egress IP for outbound calls.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Run VPC egress): Direct VPC egress attaches the Cloud Run service to the VPC without connector VMs, giving lower latency and cost than Serverless VPC Access; routing all traffic through the VPC sends internet-bound requests via Cloud NAT, whose manually reserved static IP becomes the stable source IP the partner can allowlist, while private Redis traffic flows directly.

whyWrong.2: Option C adds a VM to manage and a single point of failure.
whyWrong.3: Option D provides a static inbound IP for the service, not a static egress IP for outbound calls.

question: An e-commerce company runs an internal pricing service on Cloud Run that should only be callable by its checkout service, which also runs on Cloud Run in the same project. The pricing service must never be reachable from the public internet, and calls must be authenticated with short-lived credentials rather than a shared API key. Which two configurations should you apply? (Choose two.)
options: Deploy the pricing service with 'Require authentication' and grant the checkout service's service account the Cloud Run Invoker role on it.
Allow unauthenticated invocations and validate a static API key header in the pricing service code.
Set the pricing service's ingress setting to 'internal' so only traffic from the VPC or internal Google Cloud sources is accepted.
Front the pricing service with a global external Application Load Balancer and a Cloud Armor allowlist of Google IP ranges.
Give the checkout service the Owner role on the project so it can call any service.

Option D exposes the service publicly and Google IP ranges are far too broad to be a meaningful allowlist. Option E grossly violates least privilege.

Eventarc triggers for the Cloud Storage object-finalized event and the Firestore document-created event, targeting the Cloud Run service.

question: A video platform transcodes uploaded files using worker VMs in a managed instance group. Workers pull tasks from a Pub/Sub subscription. Configure the autoscaler to use the Pub/Sub subscription's num_undelivered_messages Cloud Monitoring metric with a per-instance target.
Add a load-balancing serving capacity signal to the autoscaling policy.
Schedule the group to run at maximum size during business hours.

question: A manufacturer is migrating a Windows Server-based ERP system to Compute Engine. Which Compute Engine configuration should you choose?

Sole-tenant nodes with bring-your-own-license images, CPU overcommit disabled, and a node affinity that restarts VMs in place.

question: A visual-effects studio renders animation frames on Compute Engine. Each frame takes 5 to 10 minutes, jobs are pulled from a queue, and a failed frame can simply be re-rendered. The studio wants to cut compute cost by 60% or more and can tolerate delays of a few hours. What should you do?

Purchase a 3-year committed use discount for the current number of on-demand VMs.
Move the rendering to sole-tenant nodes to benefit from bulk pricing.
Run the renderers on the largest available machine type to finish faster and reduce billed hours.

Option D changes machine size but not the price per unit of compute.
hint: Core Rule: Spot VMs offer 60% to 91% discounts compared to on-demand pricing and are ideal for fault-tolerant, interruptible batch work like frame rendering where a preempted task can be re-queued.

question: A SaaS company's Compute Engine spend shows a steady baseline of 400 vCPUs and 1.6 TB of memory running continuously in us-central1, plus daytime peaks that add up to 300 more vCPUs for about 8 hours. The company expects to move some workloads to Cloud Run over the next year and wants to maximize discounts without risking payment for unused commitments. Which purchasing strategy should you recommend?

Rely on sustained use discounts only, since they apply automatically.
Buy a 1-year resource-based commitment for 700 vCPUs and use Spot VMs for the baseline.
Buy a 1-year commitment covering roughly the 400-vCPU baseline (using a compute flexible commitment if workloads may move to Cloud Run), and let the daytime peak run on-demand with autoscaling.

question: A government contractor must ensure that every Compute Engine VM starts from a hardened base image that includes agents for monitoring and security scanning. Use startup scripts on every VM to install the agents and apply patches at boot time.

question: A bank is connecting its primary data center to Google Cloud for a core banking workload that needs a sustained 10 Gbps of private connectivity with a 99.99% availability SLA. The data center is in a metro that has two Google colocation facilities. Which two design choices are required to achieve the 99.99% SLA? (Choose two.)
options: Provision at least four Dedicated Interconnect connections, two in each of two metros or edge availability domains, with a VLAN attachment on each.
Provision a single 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect connection and a backup HA VPN tunnel.
Use Cloud Router with static routes so failover does not depend on BGP convergence.
Deploy Cloud Routers in at least two Google Cloud regions with global dynamic routing enabled on the VPC.
Terminate all VLAN attachments on one Cloud Router to simplify BGP configuration.

question: A pharmaceutical company's on-premises analytics servers must load data into BigQuery and read from Cloud Storage over an existing Dedicated Interconnect. question: Developers at a fintech need to run Terraform locally against a staging project using the same permissions as the CI pipeline's deployment service account, so that plan output matches what CI will apply. The security team prohibits creating or downloading service account keys. What should you do?
options: Create a key for the deployment service account, store it in Secret Manager, and let developers fetch it when needed.
Grant developers the Service Account Token Creator role on the deployment service account and have them use gcloud and Terraform with service account impersonation.
Grant developers the same project roles as the deployment service account directly on their user accounts.
Add the developers as Service Account Users so they can attach the account to their laptops.

Option A still creates a long-lived key, which is what the policy prohibits. Option C duplicates permissions on human identities, drifts over time, and does not guarantee parity with the pipeline. Option D is for attaching a service account to resources such as VMs, not for obtaining credentials on a laptop.
hint: Core Rule: Service account impersonation lets an authenticated user request short-lived credentials for a service account they hold roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator on; gcloud's --impersonate-service-account flag and Terraform's impersonate_service_account provider setting then act exactly as the pipeline identity, with every action attributed to both the user and the service account in audit logs.

question: A software company uses GitHub Actions to build container images and deploy them to Cloud Run. The pipeline currently authenticates with a service account key stored as a GitHub secret, and a recent audit demanded removal of all long-lived cloud credentials from external systems. Deployments must continue only from the company's own GitHub organization and the main branch. What should you do?

Move the key into GitHub's encrypted environment secrets with required reviewers.
Run a self-hosted GitHub runner on a Compute Engine VM and use its attached service account.

Configure Workload Identity Federation with GitHub's OIDC provider, add an attribute condition restricting the repository owner and branch, and let the workflow exchange its OIDC token for short-lived Google credentials.

Add a VPC Service Controls perimeter around the folder's projects that denies access from non-EU IP addresses.

question: A hospital group stores de-identified research data in BigQuery and Cloud Storage. Its main concern is data exfiltration: if an analyst's credentials are phished, the attacker must not be able to copy data to a project or bucket outside the organization or query it from an unmanaged device. IAM roles are already tightly scoped. What additional control should you implement?
options: Enable CMEK on the datasets and buckets so exported data is unreadable outside the organization.
Require two-factor authentication for all analysts and shorten session lengths.

Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter around the research projects, include BigQuery and Cloud Storage as restricted services, and use access levels to allow access only from corporate networks and managed devices.
Turn on Data Access audit logs for BigQuery and Cloud Storage and review them daily.

question: A logistics company hosts an internal HR web application on a managed instance group behind an HTTPS load balancer. Remote employees currently connect through a legacy VPN to reach it. The company wants to retire the VPN, allow access only to employees signed in with corporate Google Workspace accounts from company-managed devices, and avoid modifying the application. What should you do?
options: Expose the application publicly and add a login page to the application that validates corporate credentials.
Enable Identity-Aware Proxy on the load balancer backend service, grant employees the IAP-secured Web App User role, and add an access level requiring managed devices.
Restrict the load balancer with a Cloud Armor policy allowing only the corporate office IP ranges.
Deploy a Cloud VPN gateway and issue certificates to each remote employee.
explanation: Identity-Aware Proxy enforces identity and context at the load balancer, so users authenticate with Google Workspace before any request reaches the backend, IAM roles decide who is allowed, and Access Context Manager access levels can require a company-managed device; the application needs no changes. question: A national bank's regulator requires that encryption keys protecting customer data in Cloud Storage and BigQuery be generated and stored in a key manager physically outside the cloud provider, that the bank be able to cut off Google's ability to decrypt the data at any moment, and that every key access be justified and logged. Which encryption approach should you use?
options: Google-managed encryption keys with Access Transparency logs enabled.
Customer-managed encryption keys in Cloud KMS using software keys with automatic rotation.
Customer-supplied encryption keys passed with every API request from the bank's applications.
Cloud External Key Manager (Cloud EKM) with keys held in the bank's external key manager and Key Access Justifications enabled.
explanation: Cloud EKM lets Google Cloud services such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery use keys that live in an external key manager outside Google; the bank retains sole custody, can deny key access instantly to render data unreadable, and Key Access Justifications provides a reason code for every access that can be approved or denied by policy. Option A leaves key custody entirely with Google. Option B stores keys inside Google Cloud, which does not meet the 'physically outside the provider' rule, although it provides control and logging. Option C is not supported by BigQuery for this pattern, requires the application to ship keys with each call, and provides no centralized justification or logging.

question: A code review at a retail company discovered database passwords and third-party API tokens hard-coded in Cloud Run environment variables defined in a Git repository. You need to remove secrets from source control, restrict which services can read each secret, keep a version history, and be able to rotate secrets without redeploying code. What should you do?
options: Move the values to a .env file excluded from Git and copy it manually to each environment.
Encrypt the values with Cloud KMS and commit the ciphertext to the repository.
Store each secret in Secret Manager, grant only the specific service's service account the Secret Accessor role, and mount or reference the latest secret version from Cloud Run.
Store secrets in a private Cloud Storage bucket and download them at container startup.

Option A relies on manual copies and offers no access control or audit trail. Option B keeps ciphertext in Git and still requires a custom decryption path and versioning discipline. Option D reinvents a secret store with weaker controls and no versioning semantics.

question: An insurer is launching a customer-facing chatbot built on Gemini through Vertex AI. question: A law firm must retain closed-case document archives for 10 years. Files are almost never accessed after closing, but when a regulator requests one it must be available within a few seconds, and no employee, including administrators, may delete a file before the retention period ends. Nearline storage class with a lifecycle rule that deletes objects after 10 years.
Coldline storage class with Object Holds applied by a nightly script.

question: A game studio distributes 2 GB game patches to millions of players worldwide from a Cloud Storage bucket in us-central1 behind a global external Application Load Balancer. Network egress is now the studio's largest cloud cost and players in Asia report slow downloads. What should you do to reduce cost and improve download speed?

Compress the patch files with gzip before uploading them to the bucket.

question: A university's research computing group runs 300 Compute Engine VMs across 40 projects. Monthly spend has doubled, a review found many VMs at 2% average CPU, and several projects were only discovered to be over budget when the invoice arrived. You need to reduce waste and prevent surprise overspend with the least manual effort. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

Review and apply the VM rightsizing and idle-resource recommendations from Recommender (Active Assist) across the projects.

Disable billing on projects that exceed their budget by hand at month end.

question: A global payments company is designing a new API platform that must keep serving reads and writes even if an entire Google Cloud region fails, with no manual failover steps and a single public endpoint for clients on three continents. Which three design elements should be part of your architecture? (Choose three.)
options: Spanner in a multi-region instance configuration as the transactional database.
Cloud SQL with a cross-region read replica that the on-call engineer promotes during an outage.
A global external Application Load Balancer with backend services containing healthy stateless backends in multiple regions.
A regional external Application Load Balancer in each region with clients choosing a region-specific hostname.
Stateless application tiers deployed in at least two regions, such as Cloud Run services or regional GKE clusters.
A single GKE cluster in the primary region with Persistent Disk snapshots copied to a second region.

Option B requires a human promotion step and interrupts writes. Option D gives clients region-specific endpoints and no automatic cross-region failover. Option F is a single-region design with a cold recovery path, which is exactly what the requirement rules out.

Which two components should you add? (Choose two.)

A Cloud SQL cross-region read replica in us-central1 that can be promoted to primary.
A second full-size managed instance group in us-central1 receiving 50% of production traffic.
A minimally sized managed instance group in us-central1 built from the same instance template, scaled up during failover, behind a global external Application Load Balancer with health checks.
A Spanner multi-region instance replacing Cloud SQL.

question: A travel booking site is served from a global external Application Load Balancer. Increase the load balancer health check frequency to every 5 seconds.
Enable Cloud CDN so requests are served from the edge even when the origin is unreachable.
Create a log-based metric on 5xx responses in the load balancer logs and alert when it rises.
explanation: Uptime checks probe the public endpoint from Google checker locations around the world, so they detect availability issues in the path between users and the load balancer that internal backend health checks cannot see, and alerting policies notify on-call through channels such as PagerDuty or SMS. Option B only verifies backend health from the load balancer, which is already reported as healthy. Option C may mask some failures but does not detect or alert on them. Option D catches server errors but not reachability failures where requests never arrive.
hint: Core Rule: Uptime checks probe the public endpoint from Google checker locations around the world, so they detect availability issues in the path between users and the load balancer that internal backend health checks cannot see, and alerting policies notify on-call through channels such as PagerDuty or SMS.

question: A media company runs 15 GKE clusters, each with its own self-managed Prometheus server. The servers frequently run out of memory, retention is limited to a few days, and there is no single place to query metrics across clusters. Developers have hundreds of PromQL dashboards in Grafana that they do not want to rewrite. What should you recommend?
options: Replace Prometheus with the Cloud Monitoring agent and rebuild dashboards in Cloud Monitoring.
Enable Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus on the clusters and point Grafana at its PromQL-compatible endpoint for global querying.
Federate the 15 Prometheus servers into one large central Prometheus VM with a bigger disk.
Export metrics from each Prometheus server to BigQuery and build Looker Studio dashboards.
explanation: Managed Service for Prometheus keeps the Prometheus collection model and full PromQL compatibility while storing metrics in Monarch, Google's globally scalable time-series store, with 24 months of retention and a single query surface across all clusters; existing Grafana dashboards work unchanged via the PromQL API. Option A discards the PromQL investment. Option C moves the scaling problem to a single larger bottleneck that still needs care and feeding. Option D turns a real-time monitoring system into batch analytics and breaks PromQL dashboards.
hint: Core Rule: Managed Service for Prometheus keeps the Prometheus collection model and full PromQL compatibility while storing metrics in Monarch, Google's globally scalable time-series store, with 24 months of retention and a single query surface across all clusters; existing Grafana dashboards work unchanged via the PromQL API.

whyWrong.0: Option A discards the PromQL investment.
whyWrong.2: Option C moves the scaling problem to a single larger bottleneck that still needs care and feeding.
whyWrong.3: Option D turns a real-time monitoring system into batch analytics and breaks PromQL dashboards.

question: An insurer is migrating 800 VMware virtual machines to Compute Engine within nine months. Applications are grouped into interdependent tiers, downtime per application must be limited to a single short cutover, and each application must be validated in Google Cloud before the production switch without affecting the source VMs. Which migration approach should you recommend?
options: Export each VM to an OVA file, upload it to Cloud Storage, and import it with the virtual disk import tool.
Rebuild every application from scratch on GKE to avoid moving legacy VMs.
Take VMware snapshots and copy them to Persistent Disk with a custom rsync script during a weekend outage.
Use Migrate to Virtual Machines to replicate VMs continuously, organize them into migration groups (waves) by application dependency, run test clones for validation, and perform cut-overs per wave.
explanation: Migrate to Virtual Machines is designed for large-scale VM migrations: it replicates source VMs continuously in the background, lets you group them into waves aligned to application dependencies, supports test clones that run in Google Cloud without disrupting the source, and performs a final short cut-over per group. Option A is a manual, one-VM-at-a-time process with long outages and no test capability, unsuitable for 800 VMs. Option B is a re-architecture project that cannot fit nine months for 800 VMs. Option C is an unsupported, error-prone approach requiring an extended outage.
hint: Core Rule: Migrate to Virtual Machines is designed for large-scale VM migrations: it replicates source VMs continuously in the background, lets you group them into waves aligned to application dependencies, supports test clones that run in Google Cloud without disrupting the source, and performs a final short cut-over per group.

whyWrong.0: Option A is a manual, one-VM-at-a-time process with long outages and no test capability, unsuitable for 800 VMs.
whyWrong.1: Option B is a re-architecture project that cannot fit nine months for 800 VMs.
whyWrong.2: Option C is an unsupported, error-prone approach requiring an extended outage.

question: A manufacturing company has decided to move its two on-premises data centers to Google Cloud but has incomplete documentation of its roughly 1,200 servers, their utilization, and their dependencies. The CFO wants a defensible total cost of ownership comparison before any migration work begins. What should you do first?
options: Order Transfer Appliances for both data centers so data movement can begin in parallel with planning.
Create a landing zone with Shared VPC and Interconnect so migrated workloads have a destination.
Deploy the Migration Center discovery client to collect server inventory, performance data, and dependencies, then generate TCO and rightsizing reports.
Start migrating the least critical applications with Migrate to Virtual Machines to learn by doing.
explanation: Assessment precedes planning and execution in Google's migration methodology. Migration Center's discovery client (or imported data from other tools) builds an inventory with utilization and dependency data and produces TCO estimates and Google Cloud sizing recommendations, giving the CFO the defensible comparison required. Option A commits to data transfer before knowing what data exists. Option B builds infrastructure before requirements are known. Option D skips assessment and risks migrating servers with unknown dependencies.
hint: Core Rule (Migration Center): Assessment precedes planning and execution in Google's migration methodology.

whyWrong.0: Option A commits to data transfer before knowing what data exists.
whyWrong.1: Option B builds infrastructure before requirements are known.
whyWrong.3: Option D skips assessment and risks migrating servers with unknown dependencies.

question: A telecom wants a chatbot that answers support agents' questions using 40,000 internal PDF and HTML documents that change weekly. Answers must cite the source document, must not invent policies, and the two-person team has no machine learning expertise. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Fine-tune a Gemini model on the documents monthly and deploy it to a Vertex AI endpoint.
Create a Vertex AI Search data store over the documents and build the chatbot with Vertex AI Agent Builder so Gemini responses are grounded in retrieved documents with citations.
Concatenate all documents into the system prompt of each Gemini request.
Train a custom sequence-to-sequence model on Vertex AI with the documents as training data.
explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation is the recommended pattern for question answering over frequently changing enterprise content: Vertex AI Search indexes the documents (with connectors and scheduled refresh), and grounding Gemini in retrieved passages produces answers with citations and greatly reduces hallucination, all through managed Agent Builder tooling that requires no ML expertise. Option A bakes knowledge into weights, becomes stale between tunings, and does not provide citations. Option C exceeds context limits for 40,000 documents and would be prohibitively expensive per request. Option D is a large ML project with worse results than a foundation model plus retrieval.
hint: Core Rule (RAG with Vertex AI Search): Retrieval-augmented generation is the recommended pattern for question answering over frequently changing enterprise content: Vertex AI Search indexes the documents (with connectors and scheduled refresh), and grounding Gemini in retrieved passages produces answers with citations and greatly reduces hallucination, all through managed Agent Builder tooling that requires no ML expertise.

whyWrong.0: Option A bakes knowledge into weights, becomes stale between tunings, and does not provide citations.
whyWrong.2: Option C exceeds context limits for 40,000 documents and would be prohibitively expensive per request.
whyWrong.3: Option D is a large ML project with worse results than a foundation model plus retrieval.

question: A medical coding company uses Gemini on Vertex AI to classify clinical notes into thousands of specialized billing codes. With careful prompt engineering and a dozen few-shot examples, accuracy plateaued at 78%, still below the required 92%. The company has 60,000 historically labeled notes. Latency and per-request cost must not increase. What should you do next?
options: Run supervised fine-tuning of the Gemini model on the labeled notes in Vertex AI and evaluate the tuned model against a held-out set before deployment.
Increase the number of few-shot examples in the prompt to several hundred to cover more codes.
Switch to the largest available model in Model Garden and raise the temperature to explore more codes.
Add retrieval of similar historical notes to each prompt so the model sees more context.
explanation: The decision rule is prompt first, tune when prompting plateaus and you have a sizeable labeled dataset for a narrow, specialized task. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model the domain-specific mapping directly, typically lifts accuracy well beyond few-shot prompting, and keeps prompts short so latency and token cost do not rise. Option B increases prompt length and cost substantially and still cannot cover thousands of codes. Option C increases cost and latency, and higher temperature reduces classification consistency. Option D lengthens each prompt (raising cost and latency) and is better suited to knowledge retrieval than to learning a precise classification scheme.
hint: Core Rule (Tuning vs prompting): The decision rule is prompt first, tune when prompting plateaus and you have a sizeable labeled dataset for a narrow, specialized task.

whyWrong.1: Option B increases prompt length and cost substantially and still cannot cover thousands of codes.
whyWrong.2: Option C increases cost and latency, and higher temperature reduces classification consistency.
whyWrong.3: Option D lengthens each prompt (raising cost and latency) and is better suited to knowledge retrieval than to learning a precise classification scheme.

question: A retailer's product-description generator built on Gemini is about to move from pilot to production. Leadership wants objective evidence that a new prompt template or model version is better than the current one before release, and ongoing detection of quality regressions or unsafe outputs after release. Which two practices should you implement? (Choose two.)
options: Use the Vertex AI Gen AI evaluation service to score candidate prompts and model versions against a curated evaluation dataset with metrics such as groundedness, fluency, and pairwise preference before promotion.
Rely on the model's default safety settings and promote new versions after a manual spot check of five outputs.
Log production prompts and responses to BigQuery, sample them regularly for automated and human review, and alert on drops in evaluation scores or increases in safety-filter triggers.
Retrain the model every week so quality never regresses.
Pin the application to the oldest model version indefinitely to avoid change.
explanation: Pre-release evaluation with the Gen AI evaluation service gives repeatable, metric-based comparisons (including model-based and pairwise judgments) so decisions are objective rather than anecdotal. Post-release, logging prompts and responses, sampling them for automated scoring and human review, and alerting on score or safety-trigger trends implements continuous quality monitoring, which is the operational-excellence approach for generative AI systems. Option B is not objective evidence. Option D confuses retraining with evaluation and would itself introduce unassessed changes. Option E avoids improvement and eventually collides with model deprecation.
hint: Core Rule (Evaluating and monitoring LLM outputs): Pre-release evaluation with the Gen AI evaluation service gives repeatable, metric-based comparisons (including model-based and pairwise judgments) so decisions are objective rather than anecdotal.

whyWrong.1: Option B is not objective evidence.
whyWrong.3: Option D confuses retraining with evaluation and would itself introduce unassessed changes.
whyWrong.4: Option E avoids improvement and eventually collides with model deprecation.

question: A mid-size company's platform team is stretched thin. Engineers spend hours correlating logs, metrics, and recent configuration changes when a GKE service degrades, and they also struggle to spot cost and reliability improvements across dozens of projects. The CTO wants to accelerate troubleshooting and optimization without hiring additional SREs. Which capability should you introduce?
options: Export all logs to BigQuery and train a custom anomaly-detection model on Vertex AI.
Purchase a third-party AIOps platform and integrate it with Cloud Logging.
Create more dashboards in Cloud Monitoring so engineers can see all signals on one screen.

Enable Gemini Cloud Assist so engineers can run AI-driven investigations that correlate logs, metrics, and changes, and use its recommendations and natural-language queries to find cost and reliability optimizations.
explanation: Gemini Cloud Assist is built into the Google Cloud console to help design, operate, troubleshoot, and optimize; its investigations feature analyzes logs, metrics, and configuration changes to propose root causes and remediations, and it surfaces cost and reliability recommendations across projects through natural-language interaction, directly addressing the team's capacity problem. Option A is a substantial ML project the stretched team cannot support. Option B adds cost and integration work when a native capability exists. Option C adds more data to look at but does not reduce the correlation effort.
hint: Core Rule: Gemini Cloud Assist is built into the Google Cloud console to help design, operate, troubleshoot, and optimize; its investigations feature analyzes logs, metrics, and configuration changes to propose root causes and remediations, and it surfaces cost and reliability recommendations across projects through natural-language interaction, directly addressing the team's capacity problem.

question: A logistics company runs its order-management system on Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. The database is 4 TB and growing, and the operations team now runs heavy aggregation reports against the primary instance during business hours, causing transactional latency to spike. The company wants to keep PostgreSQL wire compatibility, avoid changing application code, and eliminate the analytical impact on transactional workloads with the least operational overhead. What should you do?
options: Add two Cloud SQL read replicas and route all reports to the replicas through a connection pooler.
Migrate the database to Spanner using the PostgreSQL interface and run reports against Spanner Data Boost.
Migrate the database to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, enable the columnar engine, and direct reporting queries to a read pool instance.
Export nightly snapshots to BigQuery with Datastream and rewrite the reports as BigQuery SQL.
explanation: AlloyDB is fully PostgreSQL-compatible, so no application changes are required, and its columnar engine accelerates analytical queries by up to 100x while read pool instances isolate reporting traffic from the primary. This directly satisfies the compatibility, minimal-change, and performance constraints (performance-optimization pillar). Option A keeps the same row-oriented engine, so heavy aggregations remain slow and replicas add replication lag to manage. Option B requires schema and application changes because Spanner's PostgreSQL interface is not a drop-in replacement for an existing PostgreSQL database. Option D forces the team to rewrite reports and introduces data freshness gaps rather than solving the problem in place.
hint: Core Rule (AlloyDB vs Cloud SQL): AlloyDB is fully PostgreSQL-compatible, so no application changes are required, and its columnar engine accelerates analytical queries by up to 100x while read pool instances isolate reporting traffic from the primary.

whyWrong.0: Option A keeps the same row-oriented engine, so heavy aggregations remain slow and replicas add replication lag to manage.
whyWrong.1: Option B requires schema and application changes because Spanner's PostgreSQL interface is not a drop-in replacement for an existing PostgreSQL database.
whyWrong.3: Option D forces the team to rewrite reports and introduces data freshness gaps rather than solving the problem in place.

question: A global ticketing platform sells seats for events in North America, Europe, and Asia. Overselling a seat is unacceptable, so every purchase must be a strongly consistent transaction, and customers on every continent must be served with low read latency. The platform must remain available at 99.999% during a regional outage. Which database should you recommend?
options: Spanner in a multi-region instance configuration
Cloud SQL for MySQL with cross-region read replicas
Bigtable with multi-cluster replication across three regions
Firestore in Native mode in a multi-region location
explanation: Spanner multi-region configurations provide externally consistent (strongly consistent) transactions with a 99.999% availability SLA and place read-only or read-write replicas close to users on multiple continents, which is exactly what a global seat-inventory system needs. Option B offers eventually consistent replicas and a regional write endpoint with a 99.95%/99.99% SLA, so it cannot guarantee both consistency and 99.999% availability. Option C is a NoSQL wide-column store whose cross-cluster replication is eventually consistent, which risks overselling. Option D is strongly consistent but is a document database with per-transaction limits and write throughput characteristics unsuited to a high-contention, relational inventory model.
hint: Core Rule: Spanner multi-region configurations provide externally consistent (strongly consistent) transactions with a 99.999% availability SLA and place read-only or read-write replicas close to users on multiple continents, which is exactly what a global seat-inventory system needs.

whyWrong.1: Option B offers eventually consistent replicas and a regional write endpoint with a 99.
whyWrong.2: Option C is a NoSQL wide-column store whose cross-cluster replication is eventually consistent, which risks overselling.
whyWrong.3: Option D is strongly consistent but is a document database with per-transaction limits and write throughput characteristics unsuited to a high-contention, relational inventory model.

question: A startup uses Spanner for its production database. It also needs isolated development and QA environments that hold roughly 20 GB of data each and receive light, bursty traffic. Finance has asked you to minimize the monthly Spanner spend for these non-production environments without switching to a different database engine. What should you do?
options: Create each non-production environment as a 1-node Spanner instance in a single-region configuration.
Consolidate development and QA into one 3-node instance and use separate databases for isolation.
Use the Spanner emulator for both development and QA and skip cloud instances entirely.
Create each non-production instance with 100 processing units in a single-region configuration.
explanation: Spanner instances can be sized in processing units, and 1,000 processing units equal one node. A 100-PU instance costs one tenth of a node and supports up to 409.6 GB of storage (as of recent limits), so it easily hosts a 20 GB, low-traffic environment while keeping the same engine and features as production (cost-optimization pillar). Option A pays for ten times more capacity than needed. Option B over-provisions even more and removes environment isolation. Option C is useful for local unit tests, but the emulator does not support all production features, has no persistence guarantees, and cannot serve a shared QA environment reliably.
hint: Core Rule (Spanner processing units): Spanner instances can be sized in processing units, and 1,000 processing units equal one node.

whyWrong.0: Option A pays for ten times more capacity than needed.
whyWrong.1: Option B over-provisions even more and removes environment isolation.
whyWrong.2: Option C is useful for local unit tests, but the emulator does not support all production features, has no persistence guarantees, and cannot serve a shared QA environment reliably.

question: A smart-meter company ingests readings from 5 million meters into Bigtable every 15 minutes. The row key is currently the reading timestamp followed by the meter ID. Monitoring shows that writes concentrate on a single node and throughput is far below expectations despite adding nodes. The most common query retrieves all readings for one meter over a time range. How should you redesign the row key?
options: Keep the timestamp first but add more Bigtable nodes and enable autoscaling.
Use the meter ID followed by the reading timestamp so writes spread across the keyspace and per-meter scans stay contiguous.
Use a random UUID as the row key and store the meter ID and timestamp as column qualifiers.
Hash the timestamp and prepend the hash to the existing key to randomize placement.
explanation: A row key that begins with a monotonically increasing timestamp sends all new writes to the same tablet, creating a hotspot that adding nodes cannot fix. Putting a high-cardinality, well-distributed identifier (meter ID) first spreads writes across nodes, and keeping the timestamp as the suffix keeps each meter's readings lexicographically adjacent so range scans for one meter remain efficient. Option A does not remove the hotspot because the key design, not capacity, is the bottleneck. Option C removes hotspotting but destroys locality, forcing a full-table scan for the primary query. Option D randomizes placement but similarly breaks the ability to scan a meter's readings by time range.
hint: Core Rule (Bigtable row-key design): A row key that begins with a monotonically increasing timestamp sends all new writes to the same tablet, creating a hotspot that adding nodes cannot fix.

whyWrong.0: Option A does not remove the hotspot because the key design, not capacity, is the bottleneck.
whyWrong.2: Option C removes hotspotting but destroys locality, forcing a full-table scan for the primary query.
whyWrong.3: Option D randomizes placement but similarly breaks the ability to scan a meter's readings by time range.

question: An ad-tech company needs to store user-profile features that are looked up by a bidding service on every ad request. The service must read a single row by key in under 10 milliseconds at a sustained rate of 500,000 requests per second, and the data set is about 30 TB. Which storage service should you choose?
options: BigQuery with BI Engine acceleration enabled
Firestore in Datastore mode
Bigtable with SSD storage
Cloud Storage with a Cloud CDN cache in front
explanation: Bigtable is designed for single-digit-millisecond point reads at very high throughput on petabyte-scale key-value or wide-column data, so an SSD-backed Bigtable instance is the right fit for a low-latency feature store. Option A is an analytical warehouse; even with BI Engine, BigQuery is not a serving database and cannot sustain 500,000 point lookups per second with millisecond latency. Option B scales well but has higher per-operation latency and cost at this throughput and is not optimized for 30 TB of hot key-value data. Option D is an object store; per-object latency and request costs make it unsuitable as a real-time key-value lookup layer.
hint: Core Rule (Bigtable vs BigQuery): Bigtable is designed for single-digit-millisecond point reads at very high throughput on petabyte-scale key-value or wide-column data, so an SSD-backed Bigtable instance is the right fit for a low-latency feature store.

whyWrong.0: Option A is an analytical warehouse; even with BI Engine, BigQuery is not a serving database and cannot sustain 500,000 point lookups per second with millisecond latency.
whyWrong.1: Option B scales well but has higher per-operation latency and cost at this throughput and is not optimized for 30 TB of hot key-value data.
whyWrong.3: Option D is an object store; per-object latency and request costs make it unsuitable as a real-time key-value lookup layer.

question: A retailer stores 200 TB of point-of-sale transactions in a single BigQuery table. Analysts almost always filter by transaction_date and store_id, but every query scans the full table and monthly on-demand costs have tripled. You need to reduce query cost with the least change to the analysts' SQL. What should you do?
options: Recreate the table partitioned by transaction_date and clustered by store_id, then set require_partition_filter to true.
Split the table into one table per store and instruct analysts to query the appropriate table.
Create a materialized view for each store that filters on store_id and refresh it hourly.
Move the table to a flat-rate Enterprise edition reservation so scanned bytes no longer affect cost.
explanation: Partitioning by transaction_date prunes entire partitions when queries filter on date, and clustering by store_id sorts data within each partition so BigQuery skips irrelevant blocks; together they dramatically reduce bytes scanned with no change to query text beyond requiring a date filter. Option B creates an operational burden (hundreds of tables) and requires analysts to change how they query. Option C creates many refresh jobs and does not help queries that span stores. Option D changes the pricing model but does not reduce the work performed; slots would still be consumed by full scans, and it does not follow the cost-optimization principle of eliminating waste first.
hint: Core Rule (BigQuery partitioning and clustering): Partitioning by transaction_date prunes entire partitions when queries filter on date, and clustering by store_id sorts data within each partition so BigQuery skips irrelevant blocks; together they dramatically reduce bytes scanned with no change to query text beyond requiring a date filter.

whyWrong.1: Option B creates an operational burden (hundreds of tables) and requires analysts to change how they query.
whyWrong.2: Option C creates many refresh jobs and does not help queries that span stores.
whyWrong.3: Option D changes the pricing model but does not reduce the work performed; slots would still be consumed by full scans, and it does not follow the cost-optimization principle of eliminating waste first.

question: A financial analytics firm runs a steady 24x7 BigQuery workload that averages 800 slots but bursts to 2,500 slots for end-of-day batch jobs. On-demand pricing has become unpredictable, and the CFO wants a predictable monthly bill while keeping the batch jobs from slowing down. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Stay on on-demand pricing and set a project-level custom daily query quota to cap spend.
Purchase a 2,500-slot one-year commitment so the batch peak is always covered.
Purchase a 3-year commitment for 2,500 slots and disable autoscaling to avoid surprise charges.
Purchase an Enterprise edition commitment for about 800 baseline slots and configure a reservation with autoscaling up to 2,500 slots.
explanation: BigQuery editions let you commit to a baseline of slots at a discounted rate for steady-state usage and configure autoscaling that adds slots only during peaks, billed per second. Committing to the 800-slot baseline gives predictable core spend, while autoscaling to 2,500 slots preserves batch performance without paying for idle capacity 20+ hours a day (cost-optimization pillar). Option A caps spend but will fail jobs when the quota is hit and does nothing to make cost predictable at the peak. Options B and C pay for 2,500 slots continuously, which is roughly three times the average need and wastes money; option C additionally locks in the waste for three years.
hint: Core Rule (BigQuery slots and editions): BigQuery editions let you commit to a baseline of slots at a discounted rate for steady-state usage and configure autoscaling that adds slots only during peaks, billed per second.

whyWrong.0: Option A caps spend but will fail jobs when the quota is hit and does nothing to make cost predictable at the peak.
whyWrong.1: Option B ("Purchase a 2,500-slot one-year commitment so the batch peak is always covered.") is incorrect because it does not meet the scenario's core requirement; Option D (Purchase an Enterprise edition commitment for about 800 base) is the Google Cloud recommended pattern here.
whyWrong.2: Option C ("Purchase a 3-year commitment for 2,500 slots and disable autoscaling to avoid surprise charges.") is incorrect because it does not meet the scenario's core requirement; Option D (Purchase an Enterprise edition commitment for about 800 base) is the Google Cloud recommended pattern here.

question: A marketing team uses Looker Studio dashboards that query a 50 GB BigQuery table with dozens of interactive filters. Users complain that each filter change takes 5 to 8 seconds to render. The team wants sub-second dashboard interactions without changing the dashboards or moving the data. What should you do?
options: Export the table to Cloud SQL and repoint the dashboards.
Create a BI Engine reservation in the project and region that hosts the table.
Convert the dashboards to scheduled PDF reports delivered by email.
Enable BigQuery query result caching and increase the cache TTL.
explanation: BI Engine is an in-memory analysis service that transparently accelerates BigQuery queries from Looker Studio and other BI tools, so a reservation sized to hold the working set delivers sub-second responses without changing dashboards or data location. Option A moves data to a transactional database that is slower for analytical scans and adds ETL work. Option C removes interactivity, which the team wants to keep. Option D is already on by default; cached results only help identical repeated queries, not new filter combinations, and the TTL is not configurable in the way described.
hint: Core Rule (BigQuery BI Engine): BI Engine is an in-memory analysis service that transparently accelerates BigQuery queries from Looker Studio and other BI tools, so a reservation sized to hold the working set delivers sub-second responses without changing dashboards or data location.
