stem: According to the Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework (AI and ML perspective), which two architectural practices are essential for operating reliable and trustworthy production Generative AI systems on Vertex AI? Choose two.
options: Implementing automated evaluation pipelines (using Vertex AI Gen AI Evaluation Service) to continuously benchmark groundedness, safety, and instruction following before deploying prompt or model updates.
Enabling Vertex AI Model Monitoring and logging request/response telemetry to BigQuery to detect distribution drift, latency regressions, and safety filter triggers.
Deploying unversioned prompt changes directly into production without automated regression evaluation.
Sharing a single static service account JSON key across all developer laptops and production pods.
Disabling all safety filters and content moderation thresholds to reduce token latency.
hint: Production GenAI operational excellence requires pre-deployment automated evaluation (Vertex AI Gen AI Evaluation Service) paired with continuous production observability and drift monitoring.
explanation: The Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework AI/ML perspective emphasizes rigorous pre-deployment evaluation (using Vertex AI Gen AI Evaluation Service to score groundedness, coherence, and safety against golden datasets) alongside continuous production telemetry logging and drift monitoring in BigQuery and Cloud Monitoring.

whyWrong.2: Deploying unversioned prompts without evaluation risks silent quality regressions and hallucinations in production.
whyWrong.3: Static service account JSON keys violate Google Cloud zero-trust security best practices.
whyWrong.4: Disabling safety guardrails exposes the enterprise to brand, legal, and compliance risks.

topic: Hybrid Connectivity SLA Comparison: 99.9% vs 99.99% Dedicated Interconnect
question: A cloud architect is reviewing two Dedicated Interconnect designs for a healthcare enterprise. Design A deploys two redundant 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect connections in two different Edge Availability Domains within a single metropolitan area. Design B deploys four redundant 10 Gbps connections across two distinct metropolitan areas (two connections per metro) with Global Dynamic Routing enabled. What availability SLAs do Google Cloud provide for Design A and Design B respectively?
stem: A cloud architect is reviewing two Dedicated Interconnect designs for a healthcare enterprise. Design A deploys two redundant 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect connections in two different Edge Availability Domains within a single metropolitan area. Design B deploys four redundant 10 Gbps connections across two distinct metropolitan areas (two connections per metro) with Global Dynamic Routing enabled. What availability SLAs do Google Cloud provide for Design A and Design B respectively?
options: Design A provides a 99.9% SLA; Design B provides a 99.99% SLA.
Design A provides a 99.99% SLA; Design B provides a 99.999% SLA.
Both Design A and Design B provide only a 99.0% SLA.
Design A provides no SLA; Design B provides a 99.5% SLA.
hint: Dedicated Interconnect provides a 99.9% SLA for dual redundant links in a single metro (2 Edge Availability Domains) and a 99.99% SLA for four links across two separate metros with Global Dynamic Routing.
explanation: In Google Cloud networking, two redundant Dedicated Interconnect connections across separate Edge Availability Domains within a single metropolitan area qualify for a 99.9% SLA. Achieving the 99.99% SLA requires four redundant connections split across two distinct metropolitan areas (two per metro) combined with Global Dynamic Routing in the VPC.

whyWrong.1: Google Cloud Dedicated Interconnect offers 99.9% (single metro redundant) and 99.99% (dual metro redundant) SLAs, not 99.999%.
whyWrong.2: Redundant Dedicated Interconnect topologies provide 99.9% and 99.99% SLAs rather than 99.0%.
whyWrong.3: Properly configured redundant Dedicated Interconnect topologies carry formal 99.9% and 99.99% SLAs.

topic: Distinguishing Network Perimeter Security Controls on Google Cloud
question: An enterprise security architect needs to combine Google Cloud security controls to address three distinct threats: (1) Layer 7 DDoS and OWASP Top 10 web attacks targeting public HTTPS load balancers, (2) data exfiltration of sensitive BigQuery tables to unauthorized external projects by insiders with valid IAM credentials, and (3) exposing an internal GKE microservice to a partner's VPC without VPC Network Peering. Which mapping of Google Cloud services is correct?
stem: An enterprise security architect needs to combine Google Cloud security controls to address three distinct threats: (1) Layer 7 DDoS and OWASP Top 10 web attacks targeting public HTTPS load balancers, (2) data exfiltration of sensitive BigQuery tables to unauthorized external projects by insiders with valid IAM credentials, and (3) exposing an internal GKE microservice to a partner's VPC without VPC Network Peering. Which mapping of Google Cloud services is correct?
options: (1) Cloud Armor, (2) VPC Service Controls, (3) Private Service Connect
(1) VPC Service Controls, (2) Cloud Armor, (3) Cloud NAT
(1) Identity-Aware Proxy, (2) VPC Network Peering, (3) Direct Peering
(1) Binary Authorization, (2) Secret Manager, (3) Cloud Router
hint: Cloud Armor protects public L7 load balancers from web/DDoS attacks; VPC Service Controls prevents managed API data exfiltration; Private Service Connect exposes private services across VPCs without peering.
explanation: Cloud Armor provides Layer 7 WAF and DDoS protection at the global load balancer edge. VPC Service Controls creates a context-aware API perimeter around managed services like BigQuery to prevent data exfiltration across project boundaries. Private Service Connect publishes internal services privately to consumer VPCs without merging routing tables.

whyWrong.1: VPC Service Controls does not mitigate L7 web DDoS attacks, and Cloud NAT is for outbound internet access.
whyWrong.2: VPC Network Peering merges VPC networks rather than isolating partner service consumption.
whyWrong.3: Binary Authorization verifies container signatures and Secret Manager stores credentials; neither addresses network perimeter routing.

topic: Edge AI vs. Cloud Streaming Trade-Offs in Connected Fleet Architectures
question: When architecting connected vehicle and industrial IoT systems on Google Cloud, which workload characteristic mandates deploying quantized models to the edge device (using LiteRT / TensorFlow Lite) rather than streaming raw sensor/video data to Vertex AI online prediction endpoints?
stem: When architecting connected vehicle and industrial IoT systems on Google Cloud, which workload characteristic mandates deploying quantized models to the edge device (using LiteRT / TensorFlow Lite) rather than streaming raw sensor/video data to Vertex AI online prediction endpoints?
options: Sub-10ms safety-critical actuation requirements in environments with intermittent or zero cellular connectivity.
Monthly executive batch reporting over multi-year historical fleet fuel consumption.
Training a multi-terabyte 3D LiDAR perception model across hundreds of GPUs.
Cross-fleet global SQL analytics joining warranty claims with supplier part batches.
hint: Run inference at the Edge (LiteRT) whenever safety-critical latency (<10ms) or offline operation is required; run training and fleet-wide aggregation in Google Cloud (Vertex AI + BigQuery).
explanation: Edge AI inference (LiteRT / TensorFlow Lite running on embedded vehicle or factory silicon) is mandatory whenever workloads require deterministic millisecond response times for physical safety actuation (e.g., collision/drowsiness alerts) or must operate continuously in tunnels and cellular dead zones.

whyWrong.1: Monthly historical batch reporting has relaxed latency requirements ideally suited for BigQuery.
whyWrong.2: Multi-terabyte distributed deep learning training requires elastic cloud GPU/TPU clusters on Vertex AI Training.
whyWrong.3: Cross-fleet SQL joins across enterprise datasets belong in a centralized cloud data warehouse like BigQuery.

topic: End-to-End Generative Media Pipeline Architecture on Google Cloud
question: A media enterprise is modernizing its digital asset pipeline on Google Cloud. When a raw 4K video lands in Cloud Storage, the architecture must automatically: (1) screen the video for explicit content, (2) extract timestamped brand logos and scene changes, (3) generate a concise 3-sentence promotional summary, and (4) archive raw masters older than 365 days at the lowest storage cost. Which architecture satisfies all four requirements with minimal operational overhead?
stem: A media enterprise is modernizing its digital asset pipeline on Google Cloud. When a raw 4K video lands in Cloud Storage, the architecture must automatically: (1) screen the video for explicit content, (2) extract timestamped brand logos and scene changes, (3) generate a concise 3-sentence promotional summary, and (4) archive raw masters older than 365 days at the lowest storage cost. Which architecture satisfies all four requirements with minimal operational overhead?
options: Eventarc/Cloud Functions triggered on upload invoking Video Intelligence API (for explicit content, logos, and shot detection) and Gemini on Vertex AI (for multimodal summary generation), with a Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle policy transitioning objects >365 days to Archive storage.
Self-managed Kubernetes CronJobs polling buckets hourly to run custom OpenCV scripts on CPU nodes while keeping all files in Standard storage forever.
Using Cloud DLP to moderate video frames and Cloud SQL to store raw 4K video blobs.
Shipping hard drives via Transfer Appliance for daily promotional summary generation.
hint: Combine event-driven Cloud Storage triggers with Video Intelligence API (frame-level moderation/logos), Gemini on Vertex AI (multimodal abstractive summaries), and Object Lifecycle Management (Archive tiering).
explanation: Combining Eventarc / Cloud Functions triggers with Video Intelligence API (for frame-accurate explicit content moderation, logo tracking, and shot detection), Gemini on Vertex AI (for multimodal abstractive summary generation), and Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management (transitioning masters >365 days to Archive storage) delivers a fully serverless, cost-optimized media pipeline.

whyWrong.1: Hourly polling CronJobs with custom OpenCV scripts add high maintenance toil and waste money keeping archival masters in Standard storage.
whyWrong.2: Cloud DLP inspects text/structured PII rather than visual video scenes, and Cloud SQL is unsuitable for storing 4K video files.
whyWrong.3: Transfer Appliance is an offline bulk migration appliance unsuitable for real-time daily media processing.
